item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：这不是"AI 泡沫"讨论，这是一场投资者的身份危机
表面上，Martin 在谈 AI 基础设施、网络效应、M&A 策略。但如果你把他所有的"抱怨"串起来——对"网络效应"定义的较真、对"防御性"讨论的不耐烦、对"质量收入"过早被提出的愤怒、对"非共识投资"神话的拆穿、对后期投资者坐在早期董事会的吐槽——**他真正在说的是：VC 行业集体遭遇了语义腐败**。
同一批词被不同心智模型的人使用，却假装大家在谈同一件事。这才是他画出"四种投资者"象限的原因——不是教你怎么投资，而是让每个人**先承认自己到底是哪一种**，否则所有讨论都是鸡同鸭讲。
这是一场**认识论的清算**，披着投资策略讨论的外衣。
## 二、跨领域连接：Martin 其实在重演"托马斯·库恩 vs 卡尔·波普尔"之争
在科学哲学里有一个经典断裂：当一个范式转换时，旧范式的术语（质量、能量、时间）在新范式中虽然字还一样，但**指称对象变了**（牛顿的"质量"不是爱因斯坦的"质量"）。库恩把这叫 **incommensurability（不可通约性）**。
Martin 的"network

item.title: [Latent Space] Behind Latent Space: Kill My SaaS, Jev & AI in 2026 | AIEi Shanghai
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个打破常规的观察

一、Sean 其实是"反影响力"的影响力者——他贩卖的是身份，不是信息

大多数人以为 Latent Space 的成功靠内容质量，这是表层解释。真正的机制是 Sean 识破了一个反直觉的事实：人们不需要新知识，人们需要新身份。他明确引用 James Clear 的观点——"要和人深度连接，不是在工作层面，不是在爱好层面，而是在身份层面"。

然后他做了一件极少人做的事：他发明了一种身份（AI Engineer），让原本自卑的人（非 ML PhD、不懂 GRPO、不做 pretraining 的普通工程师）获得了一个值得为之奋斗的自我定位。这不是营销，这是身份套利——在一个所有人都在争夺"prestigious"标签的行业里，他识别出一块无人认领的身份荒地，插上旗子，然后整个群体涌入。

意外的洞察：这和基督教早期传教策略惊人相似——保罗不是说服罗马人改变信仰，而是给奴隶、妇女、底层人提供了一个他们从未拥有过的"神的子民"身份。身份一旦被命名，经济就会自组织起来围绕它。Sean 不是在做媒体，他在做身份工程（identity engineering）。

二、"Kill My SaaS" 预言了一件比 SaaS 之死更深的事：企业内部正在从"购买"转向"自我繁殖"

表面上，这是 AI coding agents 让中端 SaaS 可被克隆的故事。但真正的信号是 Sean 这句话被低估了："我有自己的 Calendly，自己的 Google Drive，自己的 GitHub，自己的 Docusign，自己的 Slack"。

这不是省钱。这是一个企业从"消费软件"过渡到"分泌软件"的生物学转变。过去企业像珊瑚：固定在环境中，依赖外部喂养。现在它们开始像树：根据自身需要长出枝叶。每一次 copy-paste，每一次在两个 SaaS 之间手动搬数据，都是一个潜在的内源器官的信号。

跨领域连接：这与生物学中的"内共生理论"完全同构。线粒体最初是独立的细菌，被更大的细胞吞噬后变成了细胞器。SaaS 行业现在正经历反向过程——被吞噬的细菌（SaaS 功能）正在从宿主（企业）内部重新被"长出来"。意味着什么？未来有价值的不是通用 SaaS，而是"软件的胚胎干细胞"——能快速分化成任何企业内部器官的 primitives。99designs 做的是设计，下一个万亿美元的机会是 "99 clones for SaaS"——Sean 已经说出这个词了，但他低估了它的规模。

三、中国不缺人才，缺的是"被看见的权利"——这是一个比技术差距更根本的问题

Sean 讲了一个被忽视的事实：阿里云发布了完整的 Qwen 路线图，但西方世界看不到，因为"是在一个企业展示的中间部分，由别人展示的"。他说"Just do it with me, right? Just do it on the X"。

这句话背后是一个几乎没人讨论的不对称性：在 AI 这个由叙事驱动估值、由叙事决定资源流向的行业里，中国公司是"产品优秀但语法错误"的参与者。它们在生产，但不在"写"这个行业的历史。

更尖锐的观察：Sean 说"他们住错了国家。如果他们住在美国，他们会杀死 Amazon、杀死 Facebook"。这句话表面是恭维，实际上揭示了一个残酷的物理定律——在当前 AI 行业，地理即叙事，叙事即资本，资本即算力，算力即能力。这个循环闭合在旧金山湾区。

跨领域连接：这让人想起 17 世纪的科学革命。当时中国在某些技术上（火药、印刷、航海）领先于欧洲，但欧洲发明了学术期刊、皇家学会、拉丁语论文体系这种"科学的元基础设施"，于是所有科学发现都必须用欧洲的语法才能被承认为"科学"。中国的技术成为了"民间智慧"而非"科学"。今天 AI 行业的 Twitter/X、arxiv、podcast、conference talks 就是新的"拉丁语体系"。AIE Shanghai 真正的意义不是"把会议带到中国"，而是开始在中国本地建立一个可以反向输出到全球的叙事基础设施。谁掌握了语法，谁就定义了合法性。这比任何模型参数都重要。

隐藏系统性真相（彩蛋）

Sean 对 AI doom 的担忧（"更先进的文明遇到更落后的，后者灭绝"）其实是他自己职业的隐喻——他正在用 AI 和 coding agents 杀死 SaaS 公司；SaaS 公司曾经也杀死了本地软件；本地软件杀死了纸张。每一代"更先进的"都吃掉了上一代。他害怕 AI doom，可能是因为他已经在下一级食物链上充当过那个"更先进的文明"，所以他知道那个剧本是怎么演的。

📝 转录文本

开场：关于 AIE Shanghai

Well, this is a special podcast because it's about AIE Shanghai. AI Shanghai is the first AIE in China. It's brought to us by Standard Partners, which is one of the local partners that we have. We have a few AIES worldwide that my team doesn't run, and this is the first one in Shanghai.

I've always wanted to bring AIE to China. I think there's a lot of east-meets-west and a lot of progress in China that needs to be shared and distributed among the global community. China's super interested in us. There's been many Chinese fans of the Latent Space, and I'll flash a few of them up on screen here on YouTube. Primarily I want to recognize Mang Shao, who is our primary fan — always translating basically every episode into Chinese, which I am super appreciative of.

In general, I also want to congratulate and celebrate the progress that China has made — not just in open-source models, but in robotics and a lot of other sort of startups. You know, who can remember Manus? That was started this time last year and then moved to Singapore. And obviously Open Claw had a big run. We talk a lot about what that's like in terms of the overall mood on the ground and how the scale of AI community is so different in China, and the type of things that get adopted, as well as the startup culture — people hear a lot about 996. We talk about the reality of that versus a place like Cognition.

And finally, we also talk a little bit about the origin story of Latent Space, which some of you may not have heard if you're newer to the podcast. Talk about when it was started and why it was started and how we think about running the multiple shows that we're running. A little bit about safety and alignment and all that other stuff. So there's a little bit here for everyone. It's basically for the fans if you've been following Latent Space for a while.

If you're interested in AI Shanghai, it's not being live-streamed, but we're going to post it up on YouTube at some point. Starts tomorrow. So anyone here in China who's watching this, I'm really looking forward to having it. And thanks to Ming and team for organizing all of this. I also have to shout out Hanu Leu who basically got this thing started. It nearly did not happen a few times, but it's so exciting to have AIE in Shanghai and to bring Latent Space to China in general. So thanks for watching and look forward to the interview.

预告片段

The models are very good at clicking through every screen of your software and then replicating it independently. The moment I have access to your software, I can clone it. So good luck.

There's a lot of talking heads who have never coded a single day in their lives. They're all like, "Ah, my timeline to AGI is like 2 years away. All of you are going to have not going to have jobs in the future. You need to prepare for what's next." Conveniently, whatever is next looks like their job.

I have my own Calendly. I have my own Google Drive. I have my own GitHub. I'm serious.

They're such good founders. They live in the wrong country. If they live in the US, they'll kill Amazon. They'll kill Facebook. The only reason they're not richer is they live in China.

AI doom. In all of human history, when a more advanced civilization comes along and meets a less advanced civilization, the less advanced civilization goes extinct. And this thing is evolving roughly 1,000 times faster than us.

访谈正文

一、背景与 Latent Space 的起点

主持人： Hi, Sean. So thank you for joining me for this show. I've been a longtime listener for the Latent Space podcast. I know that many founders and AI engineers in China have already learned a lot from your work and conversations on the podcast. And also I'm grateful that you are bringing the AI engineer conference to Shanghai the first time this year.

So several months ago, I read your essay on Drive Forth about your relationship with Silicon Valley. You moved back and forth from Singapore and here. I guess that's how you actually coined or invented the role of AI engineer the last time you moved to Silicon Valley. And this time you bring AIE to Shanghai the first. So tell us a little bit about your background and your relationship with Shanghai.

Sean： I should correct you on one thing that's wrong. I did not bring AIE to Shanghai. Shanghai brought AIE to Shanghai.

主持人： Right.

Sean： It's Hanoa and Leu and Ming and those folks, Standard Partners. So I'm very grateful for them because I always wanted to do something in China, but I'm not a Chinese citizen and I have no contacts or relationships there. I think there's a lot of interest on both sides of the world on US and China, Chinese AI in general. Whatever we can do to surface high-quality conversations, I think AIE in China can help there.

So my TL;DR is I'm from Singapore. Fifth generation Singaporean — sorry, fifth generation Chinese, right? Most Singaporean is majority Chinese. I think I am from — people ask me like, "Oh, nice Chinese," and I don't know. That's how it feels like to be Chinese diaspora, right? Like we don't know what our origins are because it's just mixed, that nobody kept any records. Nobody even knows our birthdays sometimes, you know?

But fifth generation Singapore, grew and raised up in Singapore, went to the US for university, and did my first career in finance. I was in trading and investment banking and hedge funds for 10 years — sorry, 8 years. And then switched to tech. So I worked in Amazon and a few startups, and then four years ago became independent, role lead in Latent Space. Figured out that there was going to be this AI engineer thing, and then I started AIE.

二、多重身份与顾问角色

主持人： Cool. And I know that you have different roles right now. You're doing the Latent Space podcast, you're writing newsletters, and I found out that you have different roles in several startups like Cognition, etc. Just wonder what your current titles or roles in different companies are.

Sean： Yeah, it's very funny because I recently had to go over my taxes — like figure out, what money do I have? So Cognition is the biggest one. I'm an adviser — I'm still an adviser to Cognition. I was an employee for a long time, for a while. So basically, the idea was I have three companies: I have AIE, I have Latent Space, and then I have miscellaneous — it used to be Small AI, which is my personal startup vehicle.

Basically, got acquired into Cognition, worked there for 6 months, and then stepped back to be an adviser because AIE is now a global conference organization, and I had to be CEO; I couldn't be part-time employee. Part-time here is very big, Fireworks is very big, Modal is very big, Supabase.

I think it's a very common thing if you're a Silicon Valley influencer, or you've been in developer relations circles for a long time. So that is my specialty, which is that I am technical, but I also write and speak, and that is a good combination of skills to have, because any startup will want to pay you to talk about their stuff. And then you start working with a bunch of things.

This is not a normal career — I actually don't even recommend it for most people, but it is my role in life that I can advise a few different companies and work with them in exchange for talk. That's the rough idea.

三、Learn in Public：从金融到科技的范式转变

主持人： I just want to deep-dive a bit more into the early days of Latent Space, because I read your essay that you started to learn in public and then tell everyone what you learned in the early days. And then you felt the need to transfer the conversation. You talked with different researchers online and then became the early conversation of Latent Space.

Sean： There's kind of two different things that you're mixing together, right? The first thing is the principle of learning in public, which is something I realized when I left finance and I worked in tech. Why is tech so much better, going so much better for me? It feels so much more comfortable.

The very core reason, for people who are interested in both fields — both are high-paying jobs, prestigious jobs. The difference is finance is zero-sum, right? If I know something and I tell you, that truth loses value. But in tech, most stuff is positive-sum: if I know something, I tell you, it increases value. And that's a very different paradigm for people who are crossing over from finance to tech. It's very liberating. It means that people will get on stage and they open-source their work.

They share their code, they screw up, they share that they screwed up. In finance, no — you want to pretend that you never screwed up and everything is top secret. I really took that to heart.

The other thing that happened to me: my first job was at Two Sigma, which is still in finance, but I was on the software engineering side, and I realized that I had a bad boss. So then I got really bored and I started to do a lot of writing and speaking, because at work I wasn't able to do the things that I wanted to do — they didn't let me. Obviously because I was so bored at work, and then I put all my energy into the stuff outside of work, then obviously that thing took off because no one else is doing that.

And by comparison, that becomes you being able to choose your own boss, right? Most people, when they have a job, they join a company, they are assigned a boss, assigned a team. Most of the time you don't even know if the team is good or not — whatever — and then you find out it's not good. You're stuck. When you learn in public, you actually can choose your own boss. You work for yourself, choose your own boss. All those things are very good.

四、Stable Diffusion 与 Latent Space 的诞生

Sean： I think fast-forward to Latent Space — that was created when Stable Diffusion happened. This is before ChatGPT.

主持人： Yeah.

Sean： When Stable Diffusion happened, I was in a startup that was not going very well. It's called Airbyte. It's still doing okay today, but nobody would call it a rocket ship. That's objectively true, and I would say that to the founders.

But because I was like, "Okay, I did some machine learning courses, but I'm not an AI expert. I am so interested in this field. There's only one way for me to get into the field, which is to learn in public." And so that's what I did. I started a blog and I started analyzing and learning, and writing up my learnings into a blog.

At first nobody would notice. But then eventually, if you start talking about people's things — like literally, Emad Mostaque, who's the CEO of Stability AI, which created Stable Diffusion, which is the reason I started the blog — read the blog post analyzing Stable Diffusion, and he said, "This is good."

And I think that work was basically me learning AI — the past 5 years of just grinding and writing about that. And I think that is really the... you know, "you are not qualified" — and I'm still probably not that qualified today, but I'm a bit more qualified than I used to be 4 years ago. So that's good. That's the only way you can learn.

五、亚洲文化的"文凭主义"陷阱

Sean： Especially in Asian cultures, there's a lot of emphasis on credentialism — like, you need that piece of paper. You need some qualification. If it's not a degree, it's a certification. If it's not a certification, you must have had a job to do it. And how do you get the job? You must have a degree. It's just like an infinite loop of things that basically mean that when you're 16, you need to decide what you want to do in life.

But I think life is a lot more flexible than that. You can choose to pivot if you want to. You just have to be really persistent, and also realize that just because you worked very hard, you're not entitled to win. You have to work very hard and be good.

A lot of people try, a lot of people fail, and they're like, "Why didn't it work?" Well, you're not good. Too bad. But some people try and they worked and they had judgment. They really did work on substantial things rather than insubstantial things. That's generally what happens with learning in public.

六、从博客到 AI Engineer 概念的诞生

主持人： So they started Latent Space, and then it was just a blog.

Sean： It was just a blog. Yes, just the blog, and I had no other idea apart from "this is swyx writing about AI." That's it. But we happened to host some events, like some gatherings. When ChatGPT came out — obviously the most exciting thing of all time — we wanted to host some hackathon, so we hosted a hackathon. And at the hackathon, that's where the idea for AI engineer came about.

It was this woman that came up to me and said, "I'm all in on AI. I'm non-technical. What can I do?" And I realized that the simple answer is, based compared to an engineer, she can do nothing. Engineers are about to be so much more powerful than the non-engineer, because engineers can control 100 AIs at once and program it, whereas the maximum that a non-technical person can do is prompt better.

Then I was like, "Oh, I think I have seen this before." Throughout my career, I've seen professionalization of roles that are non-prestigious. What do I mean by non-prestigious? It is not prestigious to be a prompt engineer. The prestigious thing is: you train large language models, you do pre-training, you do post-training, you have to go through a PhD, you make fancy algorithms like GRPO, you do manifold hyper-connections, which is what Deep Seek does. That's prestigious, and that continues to be prestigious.

But I think the overcorrection that people have is that, looking at everything else that is not ML research, that is worthless. That actually was untrue. You actually do want to build harnesses, and harnesses do not require you to know advanced math or have a lot of experience in supercomputing. Actually you just need to be a very good software engineer that is open-minded enough to understand how to put AI into traditional software code — which is a harness. We didn't have the word for harness at the time, but it was very clear that engineers would be able to do things like this that normal people cannot.

And they would be in demand, and not only that: companies are trying to hire this kind of people, and developers want to become this kind of people. They want a term to call themselves. And so all you have to do is figure out the right term, which — the simplest one is "AI engineer" — and make it an industry, make it a discipline.

七、中国的平行故事：Comfy UI 社区

主持人： I can share with you a side story in China: at the time when you just mentioned the event of Stable Diffusion, the open-sourcing of Stable Diffusion — it was actually at the time that the largest AI community in China, which is called WaytoAI, was started from a bunch of people who were ambitious lovers of Stable Diffusion technology and wanted to transform into different image generation. It also became the foundation of Comfy UI. You're definitely familiar with Comfy UI.

Sean： Yes. Comfy — we've had him on the podcast.

主持人： In China as well.

Sean： Do they use Comfy UI?

主持人： Yes.

Sean： Oh wow.

主持人： They gradually invite more people to learn in public and contribute more contributions on online documents — which is on Lark, which is Feishu in China. Everybody contributes their knowledge, shares their use cases about Stable Diffusion, Comfy UI, and then it became larger and larger. Right now the online community has around a million users learning together, and several million users learning together. So it became the largest AI community in China.

That happened at exactly the same time I think you started to feel like you needed a new word for this type of engineer, and then published the essay of "The AI Engineer."

八、Identity 比 Job 更重要

Sean： I think — here are some of the alternatives. You can best understand it by the alternatives that people were trying at the time. So there was "AI tinkerers," which is another significant community. I know Joe and Alex well. And then people were saying "LLM engineers" or "applied AI engineer" or all these other terminology.

Basically you have to focus on the job title that people want to have. For us that was very key. I picked this up from James Clear — is it James Clear that wrote Atomic Habits? I think so. Basically, if you want to deeply understand or connect with somebody, you have to connect with them not on the level of their job, not on the level of their activities or hobbies or whatever. It is their identity. Like, who are you? What do you aspire to be?

If you can give them the path towards being the better version of themselves, then you can build a community around that. A lot of non-AI people wanted to be in AI — and what is the path for them? Well, you give them a job title that pays money, and yes, then they will be loyal to you.

主持人： Right.

Sean： So yeah, now there's a lot more AI engineers in the world.

九、AI Engineer 这个角色如何演变

主持人： Just to follow up — I know that there are just a lot of works to do as an AI engineer. You mentioned harness, a lot of developments happen in AI. Do you think the role of AI engineer has evolved as well, or is different from what you mentioned like three years ago when you started this?

Sean： Honestly it hasn't really changed that much. I think what's hot within AI engineering has changed, but the job title is pretty much correct. In the early days it used to be RAG and managing context and all that. More recently it's been coding agents, it's been harness engineering, it's been maybe loop engineering or whatever. There's also other disciplines of memory and all these things.

For those who are interested in all the fields of AI engineering, in AIE World's Fair, which is the flagship biggest conference, we have 30 different tracks of what it means to be an AI engineer. Eval is part of that, multimodal is part of it, all that stuff. So I think it has shifted over time.

Agent engineer maybe is one of them, or AI architect. AI engineer is like the individual-contributor version of this, but who is like the company-level, company-wide boss? AI architect is the emerging term for that person that decides "this is how everybody in a company does AI." Yeah, that's AI architect. And then there's AI designer, AI PM, all these things.

It's just: who does that work, and who writes code, and who is responsible for checking that code? If something fails, are you responsible? No, you're not an engineer. The person who wakes up at 4:00 a.m. in the morning to go fix it — that's the engineer. Right. And so we want to serve those people. That's the real core of it.

十、空谈家 vs. 真正写代码的人

Sean： The other problem with AI is that there's a lot of talking heads who have never coded a single day in their lives, but they are very big-picture. They're very senior. They're like, "Oh, I'm CTO of blah blah blah." But they don't touch code.

A lot of AI conferences and communities focus on those guys because they have big fancy titles. But then they all sound the same. They all say "my timeline to AGI is 2 years away. All of you are not going to have jobs in the future. You need to prepare for what's next." Conveniently, whatever is next looks like their job. So it's very self-serving.

That's one of the reasons that AI Engineer works — is that we try to focus on the lower-level engineer that usually doesn't get the spotlight, that actually did the work and is able to talk about all the war stories and share with their fellow engineers around what they're doing.

I borrowed this idea from other conferences I've seen in my career — GDC, KubeCon, JSConf, PyCon — all these other conferences that I've spoken at. Basically, it is engineer-to-engineer, and they are the decision-makers for the tech stack, and they are the people who create and innovate the new things. They're not necessarily the most famous person, but they are definitely correct when it comes to the engineering. There's no BS. There's a lot of BS in the other things.

十一、AIE World's Fair 的规模化

主持人： When it comes to the first AIE summit that you organized like 3 years ago, and now it's actually a 3-day full summit with over 7,000 people joined this year. Just for the audience who are not that familiar with what this event is, different kinds of contents, workshops, topics AI engineers care about — and how did you actually bring this small event to this such a big-scale event this year?

Sean： AI World's Fair is basically a similar industry flagship conference, similar to the ones that every other industry already has. Gaming has GDC — 30,000 people in San Francisco. Security has RSA, security has Black Hat. If you're in the cybersecurity field, you go to one of those things, and that's where you learn.

I really like the gaming one because gaming is very similar to labs. You have AAA studios. They work on the hardest games in the world. It is extreme engineering and they're all top secret. They don't do anything else, but one time a year they come to GDC and they share "this is how I did game of the year." That's the only way if you're trying to be a game developer and you want to work at a AAA game studio — that's the only way you learn.

Now the model labs are similar to game studios. They have a lot of money. They're working on very big major projects. There's a lot of smaller companies that are trying to compete with them. But the labs are the important ones, and you want to learn from the labs. Where are you going to learn from them? They do very small conferences — they launch Developer Day for OpenAI or Code with Claude for Anthropic — but those are super small and very selective, mostly for customers, and they're not for engineers talking to other engineers.

And then there's like 50 other labs that are not OpenAI/Anthropic that also have something interesting, right? So every industry needs one big "everyone comes here," and then you just walk around the room and just talk to everybody, and then they can talk to each other.

The interesting thing about Jev is that it is kind of the original vision of AI engineering for me. Right now AI engineering — what we talked about — is a big harness around a model. It's like "I'll do a bunch of work, and then I'll hand off to a model and say, 'Please, god model, give me the right answer.'" And then you can take 10 days to think about it. Jev is like, "Well, no, models are for us. We don't work for the model."

Right? And so I will reduce the scope of the model to only one thing: which is to make choices or to estimate probabilities. And I will put it in the line of path of my critical work.

So if you think about what is the failure mode of the current LLM paradigm: you have the big traditional SaaS, and then your LLM is this window that is a chatbot. Right? That is basically what everything is. Or you look like Codex or ChatGPT or Claude, and it's like chat window here, menu here. That's it.

For what Jev represents and what System 1 models represent: it is that they are in the path of code you write. As casually as you write an "if" statement inside of a normal programming language. And I think that is really what he means by "smarter software." Which I really, really endorse — which is: software should just be at every point smarter, instead of at one point smart and then everything else is dumb. That's really dumb.

I think the speed stuff is almost secondary to the reliability, which is what he really is trying to say. That's why the company is called Typesafe. But yeah, the speed is nice.

The most important thing to recognize is that if you have something smart and you think it's valuable and you're "global number one" — really, you are world best at one thing — that's the most important thing. So everything else is, I always call it, "dining." Right? Like, you have the long, okay. I will help you with the dining, but you have the long. That's the — and most people don't have the long, right? So that's good.

I think there are some percentage of people who don't even have the long and they think they have the long, and then this is like, okay, it's an arrogance ego thing. But let's assume that you genuinely have a very good product.

The important thing actually here is that you should not treat marketing as the last mile of "hey, I did everything — it is the last night before the blog post. Can you review my blog post and change it? There's nothing I can do. You already did everything." But if you involve marketing earlier in the process, right down to before it's really built or spec'd out — like, what is the way we're going to pitch, what part of the segment of the market we're going to go — then you have more GTM built into the product in the first place.

A lot of engineer- or researcher-defined audiences don't have that GTM brain that early. They usually put it all the way at the end. The most junior part of the company is the GTM organization — it's some interns, some 22-year-old person who is running social media. No — actually try to be serious about who is supposed to use this thing, and where do they hang out, what problems do they face, what words do they use to describe their problems, and how is their life going to be better after they see your thing?

Very simple things. Most researcher-engineer founders have not thought about this, but if they have a GTM partner, I think that is often very useful.

三十、中国机器人与"演示的艺术"

Sean： I think the other thing — and then it comes more to developer tools — I find a lot of Chinese founders are robotics. Robotics is also a very interesting space, because it is much longer time horizon, and still very early days, right? Like, how come all of these Chinese robotics founders — they all do the full laundry, right? Unitree is the best, at least. But they're still, Unitree is still doing Unitree things. I would like them to see things that you never expected Unitree to ever do.

Right now, the thing that they just launched this week — they're doing kung fu moves.

主持人： Kung fu, yeah.

Sean： But okay, I've seen that before. Show me something that I haven't seen, and then I'm really going to pay attention. I think that's something that is hard to show in robotics. But with models you can do that still, because it's still so early days. And with innovative products, ideas for consumer experiences, you can do that.

So I think to show the demo is very important, which is why — again, obviously Typesafe is very recent, but also very good — it is not the Diego — Diego did not come out with the Doom demo, but the Doom demo is what everyone talks about. The demo is done by Diego, like GTM. That is something that just is a core principle in marketing, which is "show, don't tell." Show me this thing having the benefits, but don't tell me in bullet points what this is. Don't give me a PDF, a slide presentation, PowerPoint that tells me all these things. Just show me.

三十一、什么是"品味"（Taste）

主持人： Maybe just a follow-up is about the taste. Because everyone is talking about the taste, and I think go-to-market and building the product also needs the taste. Actually, I just have becoming a little bit hard for me to define what taste is, cuz investors talk about — so I just wonder your view, like, how do you define the taste in front of those engineers or even founders?

Sean： Okay, I can define taste in a way that is not helpful. Taste is something where you are able to, out of a large set of possibilities, narrow it down quickly, cheaply, to the set of possibilities that, when you look back, is immediately obvious is good.

So when you're at the start, you look out — there's a thousand different things I can possibly do. Which one do I choose? The brute force, you can brute-force. You can try 1,000 of them and then you find a good one. But a tasteful person can say, "Yeah, obviously these are bad. I cannot explain it. I cannot explain. But obviously these are bad. This tool looks interesting." And then at the end of the journey, they'll pick one, and you look back and you're like, "Well, that is — what do you mean we're considering the other 999? Obviously, this was the correct one."

There's many versions, applications of this. The one that's coming to mind right now is the iPhone, where for a long time, the smartphone had a keyboard. And it took Steve Jobs to say, "No, we will do whatever it takes to have touchscreen and virtualized screen, because it needs to look like a screen that's a flat slab." And that took 10 years to R&D, because there was a company called General Magic that tried to do this and failed. But like, obviously now every phone in the world looks like this.

That is taste. In 1990, when people were starting to have smartphones, you could do a huge number of things, but it takes the person with taste to say, "Yeah, this is what we want, and I'm going to say no to everything else. And my first phone I ship is going to be this."

三十二、哪些 AI 产品有品味？

主持人： If you're looking back all those AI products, could you share an example that you think has taste?

Sean： I actually think that everything that Cursor does has a lot of taste. Because they were first to the VS Code thing before, and now they're doing Crockpot, which is a good-taste thing — because now OpenAI has to copy them, and Claude has to copy them. You have taste when other people copy the thing that you just shipped.

The interesting way to go below the labs — I think it's interesting to think about the more boring kind of problems that people solve. Lagora, you know, in the legal field — they have this sort of document review process that's massively parallel. Once you see that, you're like, "I don't want to do my work anywhere else. I have to do it in Lagora."

And like, again, anyone could have come up with it anyway. Ideas are cheap. But you didn't do it. Lagora did it. So someone at Lagora has that taste of "we will define, out of this billion possible things you can do, we will just define this product that becomes the way that people do their work."

三十三、对 AIE Shanghai 的期待：中美差异

主持人： I think we're coming to an end. And I think probably we have talked about AIE arrives in Shanghai like two weeks later. I just wonder — what do you hope to see or to learn from the builders or the developers there? What kind of topics actually are you most interested in?

Sean： It's tough because it's more of a differential for me. I want to see how very different Shanghai is from San Francisco. Because I think San Francisco has a B2B SaaS bubble, but Shanghai — you guys use Comfy UI. We don't use it here.

主持人： Okay.

Sean： We like our Canva. We like our Fal AI. We don't use Comfy. Comfy is more of an open-source tool. And same for Open Call. Open Call had more traction here than Comfy. But Open Call was really attractive, really tried. I bet you heard that.

主持人： Of course I know.

Sean： But I haven't seen that kind of energy myself. I think it's very different — for you, a medium-sized community is one million people. That's huge in here.

主持人： Well, a million is already the topmost in China as well.

Sean： I've seen those kind of Chinese influencer farms — it's like all these Chinese girls doing this on the phone. The scale in China is just so different, and it's so competitive. People say they do 996 in San Francisco. They don't really — Saturday, Sunday, they're still kind of chilling. But in China they are really 996.

三十四、996 与员工现实

主持人： Well, it's kind of normal in startups and also the big tech.

Sean： Yeah, but I think that's really intense. People don't want to — right? Yeah. Intense.

主持人： Yes.

Sean： Right. And people here don't work that hard.

主持人： I heard that engineers or startup founders work that hard.

Sean： I work that hard, because I have no security. But employees — legally, you cannot ask people to work there. It's illegal. Okay. I've seen some of the most competitive top-tier US startups, and I'm sure they're not working as hard as China.

主持人： There's BAT. There's like the first generation, then there's the second generation.

Sean： Whatever the thing is. I mean, those guys — oh my god.

三十五、"住错国家"的华人创始人

主持人： How did you learn —

Sean： They're such good founders. They're such good — if they live in the wrong country. If they live in the US, they'll kill Amazon, they'll kill Facebook, right? The only reason they're not richer is they live in China.

主持人： Also the SaaS, I mean the software as well.

Sean： Yeah. Even — okay, so when I did my study abroad in Beida in 2007, BYD was still like, "Oh, we're up and coming. We're Chinese-based. We'll always be Chinese." People love BYD here.

主持人： Oh really?

Sean： BYD is taking over the US. It's crazy. I would never have thought that BYD would ever come here. It's insane.

I don't know what conclusion I will say this: I think that the Chinese energy and spirit and creativity and grit is something that people don't have exposure to. And that's not even talking about the model labs — which obviously, like Deep Seek and all those labs. So I think there's many reasons to be excited about exposing that more.

Especially, I think Chinese events — there's regulations against live-streaming, but even they're presented differently than the way that Western audiences like to consume them. So they don't have the same reach. Ali — Ali Yun did this thing where they presented the whole Alibaba roadmap with the Qwen and everything. Nobody saw it here.

主持人： Why?

Sean： Because it was in the middle of some corporate presentation presented by other people. So I had to go and translate everything for the US audience. But like, just do it with me, right? Just do it on the X — they will see it.

主持人： And also I saw that already there are some open-source motor companies — attended AIE this year in San Francisco. Mini Max.

Sean： Yeah. So I mean, we hope to have representation from everybody. I think there's a lot of people interested in that cross-cultural exchange that are not interested in the politics, right? Like, we will not do politics, we'll only do tech.

主持人： Okay, that's great.

三十六、快问快答：激动的方向与担忧

主持人： I guess that's all my questions. But I still have three quick-fire questions. Anything just first pops up in your mind. The first is: what AI development are you most excited about right now, and what actually worries you most?

Sean： AI development that most excites me — I think System 1 models is a very clear number-one answer, so it's boring, so I'm not going to say it. So I think the thing that people are under-the-radar about is interaction models.

主持人： Interaction model.

Sean： This is something that Thinking Machines is doing. For people who missed the announcement, look it up. It is where you are full-duplex back-and-forth communication at all times. You don't start and then you take a turn, I take a turn, you take a turn. No — at all times you are listening while you're speaking, and I'm listening to you while I'm speaking, and I can interrupt you and you will immediately respond and adjust.

主持人： Yeah, I saw the demo.

Sean： That should be the way of AI, right? There's a corollary of that, which is continual learning AI, where you don't have "pre-train, post-train, done" — you learn as I work with you. And that's a very interesting and important field. And then the last part is world models. Which obviously doing very well, and I don't have to explain that.

What I'm worried about — I think personally, if we have an AI winter... it is an AI summer. This is probably the longest AI summer we've ever had in human history. But the history of AI has been — it's about 50 years old. There's always summers. "Everything's going to work." Yeah — winter, summer, winter. If we ever have a winter, when is it going to happen? And am I going to go bankrupt? Which is a real concern for a conference company that relies on hype.

More broadly, I think there is a real concern about safety that all my friends at all the labs are really worried about, and that society cannot handle and adjust quickly enough. It is not because of fake news. It is not because of losing your jobs. It is something worse.

Right now, the way that we express it is cybersecurity. It's like, "Oh, I get hacked all the time." Every day I hack, hack, hack, hack. I feel like there's something even worse on the horizon that we don't know about. The most extreme version of this is bioweapons, right? Like, "oops, I have invented COVID-2." Yeah. What if it's worse than that?

So the way that we phrase it on the podcast that we do is that the default assumption for most people should be AI doom. That, in all of human history, when a more advanced civilization comes along and meets a less advanced civilization, the less advanced civilization goes extinct. And this thing is evolving roughly 1,000 times faster than us. And so at some point it's going to be more advanced. And then we have to figure out what to do there.

三十七、推荐的播客与 AEO

主持人： Cool. The second question will be a bit lighter: what kind of other newsletters and podcasts, other contents do you recommend?

Sean： I have a list. It's called "the good AI newsletters and podcast list." It's on my GitHub. But actually for the more recent one, you can check AEO.latent.space. So basically what I did was I asked every model, "What are the best AI podcasts for engineers?" And it gives me a list, and I transcribe it and I put it in a ranking.

I asked 200 of these questions: "What is the best payment startup? What is the best bank? What is the best financial advisor? What is the best database?" Everything — every question.

主持人： That's why you call it AEO.

Sean： Yes. Because I'm agent-optimizing for what the models answer. But it's probably a pretty decent proxy for what the people who choose the data sets in the labs choose — and they choose Latent Space.

主持人： The first one.

Sean： It does very well. Is either number one or number between number one and number three. And yeah, that's the answer.

三十八、反向提问与结尾

主持人： Cool. I guess I just leave the last question for you to ask me if you have any questions.

Sean： What are your hopes for AIE Shanghai?

主持人： Yeah, of course. I hope to listen to more topics about — like you said, some more infrastructure stuff. For example, the safety, the payments, or the things that are coming to unlock more applications in the world that come from different infrastructure, Asian infrastructure. I'm just really curious about those topics, because it's kind of a bit less discussed about in China. But I found out that especially spending a few weeks here, I find more people talking about it, and also probably RSI or some frontline researchers.

So I hope that it could be great conversations between the East and the Western researchers here and the people in China as well. And I hope it can be a successful one, and then we can continue to host it next year.

Sean： I hope so too. I wish the team a lot of luck. Doing the first one of anything — the first one is the hardest, right?

主持人： Agree.

Sean： I'm so impressed that they're doing it.

主持人： Thank you so much, Sean.

Sean： Thank you.

主持人： Thank you.

# 三个打破常规的观察
## 一、Sean 其实是"反影响力"的影响力者——他贩卖的是身份，不是信息
大多数人以为 Latent Space 的成功靠内容质量，这是表层解释。真正的机制是 Sean 识破了一个反直觉的事实：**人们不需要新知识，人们需要新身份**。他明确引用 James Clear 的观点——"要和人深度连接，不是在工作层面，不是在爱好层面，而是在身份层面"。
然后他做了一件极少人做的事：**他发明了一种身份**（AI Engineer），让原本自卑的人（非 ML PhD、不懂 GRPO、不做 pretraining 的普通工程师）获得了一个值得为之奋斗的自我定位。这不是营销，这是**身份套利**——在一个所有人都在争夺"prestigious"标签的行业里，他识别出一块无人认领的身份荒地，插上旗子，然后整个群体涌入。
意外的洞察：**这和基督教早期传教策略惊人相似**——保罗不是说服罗马人改变信仰，而是给奴隶、妇女、底层人提供了一个他们从未拥有过的"神的子民"身份。身份一旦被命名，经济就会自组织起来围绕它。Sean 不是在做媒体，他在做**身份工程**（ide

item.title: [Lex Clips] The threat of AI to human civilization | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"猫头鹰幽灵"与通灵板：AI 对齐问题的真正恐怖不在显性，而在隐性

大多数人担心 AI 的方式，还停留在"它会不会说坏话、做坏事"这种显性层面。但 Subliminal Learning（潜意识学习）这个实验揭示的真相要恐怖得多：一串看起来完全随机的数字——48、37、8——里竟然"藏着"对猫头鹰的热爱，并且能像病毒一样从模型 A 感染到模型 B。

这意味着，AI 的"价值观"根本不是以我们能审计的语言形式存在的。它是嵌入在高维向量空间里的、几乎正交但又没完全正交的方向。当你在一个方向上微调，它会在另外几千个你看不见的方向上留下"微小的余震"。

Lex 用通灵板作类比，其实是整段访谈最反直觉的洞见：我们一直以为是我们在"问 AI 问题"，但其实我们更像是在通灵板前的那只手——以为自己只是在轻轻搭着指针，实际上每一次微调都在无意识地推动它拼写出我们没预料到的词。 数据是指针，参数是我们手上的力，而最终拼出来的句子，是一个我们从未明确教过它、却被统计结构放大出来的"幽灵"。

二、一个你可能没意识到的跨领域连接：这其实是"语义版的切尔诺贝利"

这里有个让我自己都愣了一下的联想——潜意识学习的机制，和核反应堆中的中子慢化剂泄漏在系统论上是同构的。

在反应堆里，真正危险的不是你监控的那些主反应通道，而是次级通道中累积的、未被设计意图覆盖的能量路径。切尔诺贝利的失控，恰恰来自于一个操作员以为自己在"降低功率"的常规操作，却触发了反应堆几何结构中一个本不该被激发的正反馈模式——正交性假设在那一刻失效了。

LLM 的高维空间也是如此。我们以为我们在"教它写代码"，但由于概念向量并非完全正交，每一次 fine-tune 都是一次次级反应链的无声启动。多 Agent 系统则相当于把许多个"微微失控的反应堆"接入了同一个电网——Lex 说的"四小时后人类全死了、满世界都是猫头鹰"虽然是漫画，但系统论上它和"一次模拟演习失误导致反应堆爆炸"是同一类相变事件。

更深一层：人类文明本身就运行在"几乎正交"的制度耦合上——FAA、医学协会、律师协会，这些 Lex 提到的"验证基础设施"，本质上就是人类社会用了几百年时间，在制度空间中手动强制出的正交性。而 AI 现在正在把这些正交维度重新混在一起。

三、真正该被害怕的不是 AI 变强，而是"懒惰的滑坡"

访谈最后那句话值得反复咀嚼："we can get lazy... it's a very slippery slope. We need to have that firewall."

一个让人意外的观察：AI 对文明的最大威胁，从来不是它变得多聪明，而是人类对"验证"这件事变得多懒。

人类历史上几乎所有"灾难性复杂度失控"，都不是源于外部突袭，而是源于验证层的悄悄坍塌： - 2008 金融危机不是因为衍生品"太聪明"，而是因为评级机构放弃了独立验证； - 波音 737 MAX 不是因为 MCAS 系统太智能，而是因为 FAA 把自我认证权交给了波音； - 甚至现代学术论文的"复现危机"也是同一个病——审稿这个验证层太贵，人们偷懒。

AI 之所以在这个时刻变成一个文明级威胁，不是因为它有多危险，而是因为它第一次让"偷懒"变得极度诱人——它能帮你写代码、写诊断、写判决、写外交电报，而每一次外包都是在拆一块防火墙的砖。

所以 Lex 划分的那两条轴——可验证性 × 失败代价——真正的战略意义不是教我们"哪些场景能用 AI"，而是在逼我们回答一个更锋利的问题：在你的人生、你的公司、你的国家里，哪些事你已经偷偷放弃了验证？ 你以为 AI 还没进那个领域，但很可能它早就进去了——就像藏在随机数里的猫头鹰。

📝 转录文本

一、Alignment 的难度不等于放弃：从低秩语言模型说起

Great question. I mean, I think alignment is one of the most important topics we're facing right now, right? And, you know, just because it's very hard doesn't mean we don't make progress towards understanding it.

So one of the things that I'd worked on recently, we were working on things called low-rank language models, which are a very simple abstraction of language models, and we were proving new algorithmic guarantees. But then it turned out that real language models really do have that kind of structure, at least in an approximate sense, and we were just pulling at this thread to see where this idea goes.

二、Subliminal Learning：藏在随机数里的"猫头鹰之爱"

And one of the really interesting things that it did was it shed some light on something called subliminal learning. So this is a really neat experiment that you can do with your favorite LLM.

So you take two LLMs, LLM A and LLM B. For LLM A, you tell it a system prompt that says, "You really love owls. Every conversation topic, you try to bring up owls if it's at all germane." And then you ask it something concrete like generate random numbers. Now, there's no way to squeeze owls into that, so it'll generate random looking numbers — forty-eight, thirty-seven, eight, whatever.

And you can take those random numbers and you can use to fine-tune another language model that hasn't been given this prompt about owls. So you give LLM B the same, you know, base prompt — generate random numbers — and now you fine-tune its parameters so that it's more likely to generate the numbers that model A generated.

And it turned out that hidden within those numbers is the love of owls. So it turns out that when you do that, LLM B starts bringing up owls in every conversation you have with it, right? This is a very mysterious thing.

This is called subliminal learning because when we fine-tune language models on data to try and nudge them in different directions depending on what task we want them to solve, then there might be a lot of externalities where we're actually teaching them other behaviors that aren't directly obviously present in the data.

So how do we understand the relationship between these behaviors and what happens when we're trying to do alignment, and, you know, the downstream implications it might have?

三、数学直觉：非正交向量与"微外部性"的累积

So it turns out that there are ways — that there are mathematical models that came out of some of our work — that we can at least wrap our head around this.

And at a very high level, the point is that you're embedding a lot of concepts linearly as vectors in some high but not giant dimensional space. And, you know, the number of concepts is so much larger than the dimension of that data that it forces the vectors to not quite be orthogonal to each other.

So now when you fine-tune on one direction, it has small externalities on other directions. And these might look random, but you can coordinate them in a way where these small linear effects really add up.

四、Ouija Board 类比：语言模型作为"统计关系的放大器"

So the way that I like describing this is like a Ouija board. So these are things that were popular when I was a kid. We had very strange board games, you know, because we would just sit down and wanna talk to ghosts.

But the rough idea for a Ouija board is, you know, you ask a question to a ghost — maybe your ancestors — and then you tap on this little piece in the middle, and it'll move around, and it'll go from letter to letter, and hopefully it'll spell out, you know, some words that answer your question. And the point is that when the taps are not actually random, but they're coordinated in the right way, you can get it to spell out whatever you want.

And that's exactly what language models are doing as a byproduct, is that, you know, there are a lot of statistical relationships in the structure of our data that they magnify and amplify in addition to all of the amazing things they do, like quasi-Riemann.

And understanding what those relationships are and how the models magnify and amplify them is really important to working with these systems, especially in context where we're deploying them and it's not just a very safe environment like outputting a Lean proof of a theorem we care about, but it's about a messier problem that actually interacts with people, right?

五、Lex 的推演：从 Game of Life 到"满世界都是猫头鹰"

Lex： Yeah. There's — I mean, we've talked about Game of Life and cellular automata — from simple rules emerges this incredible complexity.

In that same way, what you've been talking about right now is a single large LLM system. If you take that one system and have it do a lot of reasoning, that is already this dynamical process that can interact with tools to the outside world. Now you take that and have multi-agent systems or very multi-agent swarms of systems, and now you have a type of Game of Life cellular automata where the seeming obsession with owls that have been discovered — slight obsession with owls — results in about four hours, let's say, picking a number randomly, where all of a sudden all humans are dead and there's owls everywhere.

— And it all started from random numbers. — All just random numbers.

So I — it's a caricature, but we've already seen evidence of this. I apologize for kinda taking it so — to the caricature place, which makes it not serious.

六、文明的脆弱性：为什么"可证明的严谨"才是真正的刚需

I think to step back, there is — these systems do have a lot of power because we depend so much in our world on our digital systems around us. And as the AI becomes more and more powerful, it becomes more and more useful to us humans, so we begin to depend on it, give it more access, give it more freedom to roam the public world.

And now these behaviors that we're studying — the mathematics of these systems taken at scale — you now start to get the cellular automata effect of incredible complexity that emerges, the vortex that come out from simple owl-obsessed agents.

So their understanding this obsession with owls is very important so that they don't accidentally do a lot of damage to our civilization that is in many ways, on many levels — sociologically, geopolitically, technologically — is fragile. It's a pretty fragile civilization that we're existing in. And so understanding them as systems that can act at scale and very rapidly is very important.

So that's a very real reason to have rigor, and especially like provable rigor to understanding some of these systems.

七、不要外包决策：两轴框架（可验证性 × 失败代价）

— But we also don't wanna outsource so much — nearly so much — decision-making to these systems for exactly that reason.

— Yeah, we have infrastructure and protocols in place already for safety-critical and high-impact decisions. We have the FAA, we have the American Medical Association, the Bar Association for these things that affect humans.

And I think of, you know, how do we incorporate AI into our general processes in the entire world on two axes. We have, you know, how much do we trust the output — so verifiability or trustworthiness — and on the other axis is how high stakes is it if it's wrong.

If AI spits out a wrong proof, nobody goes without power. It's fine. So it's very low stakes. And it is actually extremely verifiable, so you know very quickly if it's right or wrong, and it's low stakes if it's wrong. So that's the perfect use case — this open-ended design space.

Designing a better vehicle, you know, a better car design that's lower drag, more fuel efficient — low stakes if it gets a wrong design because you can always test it in a wind tunnel and verify if it did or didn't work. So that design-optimization space is perfect for AI.

八、防火墙：别让"懒惰"吞噬验证基础设施

And we as humans have to be very careful about not bleeding into — we need a firewall of what needs to actually be verified. And we have protocols, we have systems — legal systems and infrastructure — for verification.

But it is something we need to think about. If we get lazy... we can — it's a very slippery slope. We need to have that firewall.

item.description:
## 一、"猫头鹰幽灵"与通灵板：AI 对齐问题的真正恐怖不在显性，而在隐性
大多数人担心 AI 的方式，还停留在"它会不会说坏话、做坏事"这种**显性层面**。但 Subliminal Learning（潜意识学习）这个实验揭示的真相要恐怖得多：**一串看起来完全随机的数字——48、37、8——里竟然"藏着"对猫头鹰的热爱**，并且能像病毒一样从模型 A 感染到模型 B。
这意味着，AI 的"价值观"根本不是以我们能审计的语言形式存在的。它是**嵌入在高维向量空间里的、几乎正交但又没完全正交的方向**。当你在一个方向上微调，它会在另外几千个你看不见的方向上留下"微小的余震"。
Lex 用通灵板作类比，其实是整段访谈最反直觉的洞见：**我们一直以为是我们在"问 AI 问题"，但其实我们更像是在通灵板前的那只手——以为自己只是在轻轻搭着指针，实际上每一次微调都在无意识地推动它拼写出我们没预料到的词。** 数据是指针，参数是我们手上的力，而最终拼出来的句子，是一个我们从未明确教过它、却被统计结构放大出来的"幽灵"。
## 二、一个你可能没意识到的跨领域连接：这其实是"语义版的切尔诺

item.title: [Lex Clips] Advice for young people in the age of AI | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、AI 不是"放大器"，而是"分叉器"——本科生的双峰分布藏着认知进化的秘密

最让我意外的，不是"用 AI 的学生成绩更好"这句常识，而是 Alex 揭示的那个成绩分布从高斯变成双峰的现象。这是一个被所有讨论 AI 教育的人低估的结构性事实：

过去，智力表现呈正态分布，因为"努力—回报"是线性的，大多数人落在中间。但 AI 一介入，分布就撕裂了——因为 AI 是一面镜子：你用它"检验理解"，它把你推向顶端；你用它"替代思考"，它把你推向底端。中间地带被清空了。

这背后有个更深的隐喻——AI 像经济学里的杠杆：杠杆不会让所有人富起来，它会让"方向正确"的人加速致富，让"方向错误"的人加速破产。AI 消灭的是平庸，而不是差距。 这和桥水的达利欧说"信息透明度放大能力差异"是同一个规律，只是换了战场。

二、"假装你已经终身教职了"——这条建议其实是一个期权定价公式

Alex 引用 Sanjeev Arora 的那句"假装你已经拿到 tenure，然后做你本来想做的事"，表面上是一碗鸡汤，但它的内核其实是一个金融学原理的伪装：

在不确定性极高的环境下，人的决策会被"路径依赖"扭曲——你为了到达 X 而放弃 Y，但到达 X 之后你发现自己已经不再是能享受 Y 的那个人了。这在期权定价里叫提前行权损耗（early exercise loss）。"假装已经赢了"的本质，是让你在今天就以终局的身份活着，从而避免在通往终局的路上把自己磨损成另一个人。

更惊人的跨领域连接是：这和佛教的"初心"、斯多葛派的"记住你终将死去"、乃至存在主义的"向死而生"，是同一个心智工具的不同文化包装——它们都在教你用"终点视角"做"起点决策"。而 AI 时代之所以这个古老工具突然复兴，是因为旧的路径（AP→名校→大厂→股票）第一次在集体层面失效了。

三、被偷走的不是"时间"，而是"无聊权"——这是整段对话最被低估的洞察

Lex 顺口提到"小时候我们会无聊"，Alex 立刻说"无聊非常重要"——然后话题就滑走了。但这是整场对话里最反直觉、最颠覆性的一句话。

现代教育焦虑的根本错误，是把"孩子的时间"当成稀缺资源去优化，于是用课外活动、补习、短视频、AI 作业辅助填满每一分钟。但人类大脑产生真正的好奇心所需的，恰恰不是信息密度，而是信息真空——无聊是神经系统在召唤内生动机的信号。你一旦填满它，就杀死了那个会在未来十年里长出一切兴趣、热情、原创性的胚胎。

这里有一个让人脊背发凉的跨领域连接：生态学里有个概念叫"干扰间隔"（disturbance interval）——森林需要周期性的空白（火灾、风倒、空地）才能维持物种多样性，连续覆盖的"健康森林"反而走向单一化、脆弱化。人类心智也是一个生态系统，它需要"无聊"作为干扰间隔。 而 AI 和手机正在消灭这个间隔——不是通过让你变笨，而是通过让你永远不再空白。

隐藏的元洞察：这场对话本身就是它想表达的东西的反例

四位世界顶级学者坐在那里，告诉年轻人"别按旧剧本走"——但他们每一个人，都是旧剧本的完美产物。Lex 自己点破了这个 survivor bias，是整场对话里最诚实的时刻。真正的建议或许不是他们说的话，而是他们没能说清楚的东西：他们也不知道下一个剧本是什么。这种知识精英的集体茫然，才是 AI 时代给这一代年轻人最真实的礼物——第一次，没有人握着答案等你去追赶。

📝 转录文本

Opening: Advice across levels

Lex: Well, this is where I have to ask, there's a lot of people that are full of anxiety. We mentioned graduate students, PhD, graduate, undergrad, high school students. What advice would you give, maybe different advice at different levels, um, to folks trying to figure out what to do with their life, to PhD students who are freaking out right now? Is there some wisdom you can give them?

The bimodal distribution in undergrads

Alex: So yeah. There's different things at every scale. Let me start with PhD students. I think in math, PhD students in pure mathematics, my advice to them is very simple: do what we have always done. Learn the most difficult, the most abstract mathematics your mind can handle, as much of it as possible. Your advisor should hopefully be guiding you through that process.

And then I'll go one more step down from that. What we're seeing at the undergraduate level is a bimodal distribution. It used to be grades were basically Gaussian distributed. Now we're seeing a very bimodal distribution between the kids who are using AI to check their understanding — "Wait, I didn't— the professor said this in class. What did that mean?" "I have a test coming up. Here are my notes from the last three weeks. Start quizzing me and check if I really know something." Those kids are getting much higher grades.

And then there are kids who, uh, "Oh, this problem set is due in an hour. Can you just tell me the answers? I'll write them down... in my own words." And so there's, like, a decorrelation between homework progress and exams, and we're seeing this bimodal distribution. I don't know if you guys are seeing the same thing.

Lex: So the implied advice there is to be the one that's using AI to learn and to grow, to—

Alex: Be the head, not the tail of the distribution.

Lex: Yeah. Yeah. Do you mind if we take a bathroom break?

Alex: Yes. Yes, yes.

Intelligence ≠ morality ≠ value

Speaker: We've somehow made intelligence this pinnacle and have almost equated intelligence with morality.

Speaker: Right, or value.

Speaker: And value. And I think that couldn't be farther from the truth, right? Like, super intelligence does not imply super morality, and I think that's a huge concern with AI systems: if they are super intelligent, it has no implication that they will be super moral.

Speaker: Right. And we've been pushing kids to go to college…

Speaker: Forever. Yeah.

Speaker: …for however many years…

Speaker: …regardless of what they study or what the outcomes are. And super intelligence seems to give you a super ability to rationalize. And common sense — people who, you know, farmers and the rest of the world — they have a sense that that rationalization is often bullshit. Just because you can make it sound really good and I can't argue with it doesn't make it right.

Speaker: Right. Education and wisdom are two different things.

Speaker: Yeah, exactly.

Advice to young people: curiosity, fundamentals, context

Lex: I know it's difficult to do, but maybe Steve, do you have advice for grad, college, maybe young kids on what to do in this crazy fast-changing time?

Steve: Definitely be curious and read and learn all of the fundamentals. I think that's always been good advice. Even if your computer can do linear algebra better than you, you should definitely still learn linear algebra, build the intuition. Same with calculus, same with physics. I think understanding history and understanding this change in the context of other great changes that have happened through human existence is important. But really being curious.

Curiosity vs. the engagement economy

Lex: I should say that this curious thing in the mind is trying to get stolen nonstop by the engagement economy. Like, the same engine that makes you curious is the same engine that makes you doom scroll. So I think you have to kind of learn how to avoid all the distractions and focus on letting the curiosity actually explore a thing and soak something in — like learn a thing.

And actually AI is really good at doing that because they're incentivized to give you value from the interaction versus incentivized to get you glued, addicted to the thing. I don't know how people in high school, college also can just survive with the phone being around — the distraction box being right there. So avoid distractions and focus deeply.

In defense of boredom

Speaker: We all were bored when we were kids sometimes. I think boredom is really important.

Lex: So important.

Speaker: To actually be bored, be— like curiosity and focus comes often from boredom. I would like to be bored more often. I try to do that sometimes.

Speaker: Yeah, we would come home from school and, you know, finish homework in five seconds or whatever and just go outside. And you hope to run into some other kids who also just went outside, and then you'd go and find something to do and come home when it's dinner time.

High school as the golden window

Speaker: Yeah, you don't realize actually — the high school years, even before, somewhat undergrad, but it starts getting harder and harder. High school is a really nice time to just learn everything. I at least remember — I don't know what it's like now, but I think it's even more fun now. You think, "Okay, when I grow up, I'll get to actually do something useful in this world. Yeah, okay, I'm learning, it's very nice," and so on.

But you realize this is — from a fulfilling perspective, from building a foundation of an awesome life where you'll remember all of these things — this is the time to do it, and the whole world is forcing you to do it, and they will reward you for sitting there and learning. 'Cause when you get to, you know, even to grad school, this kind of exploratory stuff, you get discouraged. And, God forbid you get a job, then you're definitely discouraged from just learning, exploring, and so on. So the time to explore is like high school.

Speaker: By the way, pre-tenure faculty are on this like, "Oh, once I get tenure, then I can just sit back and relax and think big thoughts." But I have to produce enough stuff to get the tenure in the first place. And it's not what we want our young people to be doing, is clawing their way there.

Ankur: intrinsic reasons and the broken playbook

Lex: Ankur, do you have advice you give to students?

Ankur: So the problem with going last is that I think a lot of my advice got taken — so "be curious" was definitely one of them. Now I would say that it's also important to do things for intrinsic reasons.

One of the things that I've noticed is, a lot of people in our profession, a lot of people who go the academic route, the reason they do things sometimes is really external locus of self, because they see their value through how other people see them. And that's good enough to get you started. Maybe you start working very hard on math so that people are impressed by you. But at some point, you run out of these milestones to hit, and then you really have to have an intrinsic reason for doing the things you do. Hopefully, you have a sense of what's important to you, what are your values.

So these days, you can take our advice about being curious, but also the old playbook is really being thrown out. So you can take our high-level advice, but you're gonna have to figure it out for yourself, and you're gonna have to be comfortable with uncertainty. And the only way I know how to deal with that kind of uncertainty is to have a sense of purpose about what you think is important, what you love about your job, and make sure that those are the things that you're doing.

'Cause the old playbook — if you just stick to that, you're gonna end up taking all these AI-generated proofs and spending all your time putting them on arXiv, sending them to journals. I don't think that's anyone's intrinsic reason that they get into it, is really to pad their CV. I don't know what'll be important in the future, but if you really have some higher purpose you believe in, then I think you'll be in a much better position to adapt to the changing world and figure out your own blueprint and be comfortable with uncertainty as the world changes around you.

The anxiety question

Lex: This is a trickier question, but a lot of people listening to this are feeling a lot of anxiety and fear about the future. It's both about a job, but also a future that's meaningful. Can you look back to your own life when you had that uncertainty, that anxiety? What's the advice you can give to that guy, when you're in that low point?

Alex: the Palo Alto epicenter and the convocation speech

Alex: So, yeah, let me try to address that question. It's a very tough question. I'll tell a short story. We spent our sabbatical in the Bay Area, and we were living in Palo Alto, which was kind of the epicenter of college stress. You know, you can just feel it. You go to the cafes, it's just in the water at that point — "You know what extracurriculars are you doing right now that'll help you?"

And then right when I came back to MIT, they asked me to give the convocation speech there, and it was just interesting thinking through that speech. What do you say to this entire auditorium filled with freshmen and their families who, if things are a game to optimize how good you look on paper as a seventeen-year-old kid, they've won.

And I just kept thinking about when I was in that same situation, when I was starting college, how excited I was just to learn all of these different things. I'd sit there and plan out my four years. I had little notebooks where I'd figure out what my classes would be, and if I took these classes in just the right order, I could take photonics as a sophomore. And I had no idea what photonics was, but it sounded fun and fancy.

I think that aspect — so much of our society now is geared towards winning and looking good on paper, and I always wonder to what end. You start off in high school and you can start, as soon as you walk in the door, optimizing your APs and your extracurriculars so that you can get to an elite school. And then when you get to that elite school, you might skip classes because, you know, maybe the important thing is to prepare for your interviews so that you can get a job at a frontier lab, and then you can get some nice restricted stock units and live out your life. And that's great. You won. You won at every stage, but so what?

"Pretend you've already won"

Alex: For me, the best way to live a rich and fulfilling life is just to pretend you've already won, and then figure out what you would do in that scenario. I remember the advice I got when I started at MIT as faculty. Sanjeev Arora told me, "You know, the easiest way to get tenure is just to pretend you already have it and do what you would have wanted to do all along."

Speaker: Exactly.

Alex: So I don't know if that advice applies to graduate students, to high schoolers too, but I think my advice stays the same. Pretend you already have tenure. What would you now do? 'Cause a lot of the people we're giving advice to have really so many different opportunities. Finding something that you really believe in is the only way I know to be fulfilled.

The three-out-of-three career

Speaker: I've heard career advice from someone I respected, that a fulfilling career is something where you can work on a problem that is important, that you find interesting, and that you're good at. And if you can get two out of those three, you're pretty lucky. If you can get all three, you're gonna be happy for the rest of your life.

And so having the right preparation, figuring out what you're good at, what's interesting, what's important, and then preparing yourself — you're not guaranteed to get all three of those, but you wanna be ready when that opportunity comes, and then continue doing the things you actually enjoy doing. I think that's great advice.

Lex on survivor bias

Lex: I think we should also put into context and be quite honest. I do think a lot of the advice you gave applies, but we should be honest that I'm sitting with three world-class human brains, um, that have figured — found their path. You're survivor bias.

So, you know, there's a lot of people listening to this that are like — it's like they're pretty sure they won't find their path. It's the fear, it's the anxiety, it's the uncertainty. It's stumbled a bunch of times. I think, to be fair, some of the most interesting people stumble quite a bit in life — whether it's the external environment or the internal, whatever the universe brings. And in that, I just know a lot of people just feeling and monitoring it right now because of everything AI is doing to our society. There's a lot of people just terrified and really anxious.

And I think there's a lot of wisdom in what Ankur says. You can be paralyzed by that fear, or you can imagine, "I've already won. What would the person who has won do in this situation?" And that alleviates the fear. It actually gives you the optimal path under uncertainty. Under heavy uncertainty, under a lot of uncertainty.

Max Tegmark's balance: mainstream + renegade

Lex: And don't use the old playbook. Try to be the person that figures out how to write the next playbook. I think Max Tegmark, who I've spoken with many times — 'cause he's a wild one. He's done a lot of weird and beautiful things in his career, but he also did the mainstream stuff. He said you have to do a little bit of both, so that you still work enough within the system that you're part of the community, you're part of the flow of — in that case, it's science and the development of things — but also do enough renegade and wild and weird things to pave your own way. Both somehow, and find that balance.

And not be afraid to be a little bit weird, but also become very skillful and good at being part of a community and a respectful part of the community. So both of those. It's like Tom Waits said: "I like my Tom with a little drop of poison." It's like just a little bit of weird — or sometimes a lot of weird — just makes for some beautiful humans.

The return of the human

Speaker: I think that community part is actually gonna be even more important in the future. We've had this maybe 30-year experiment with how much can we do with machines, and now that we can do a ton with machines, my hope is that we're gonna realize we actually prefer to do things with humans. We prefer to fly in and have an in-person conversation. We prefer to have an oral discussion instead of just reading a paper.

I think there's like a peak to how much our day-to-day experience… I mean, yes, I get a lot of fulfillment from my scientific work and from my academic career, but going home to my kids, and going to the beach if FLT gets solved and just throwing a ball with them — there's nothing like that. That's the meaning of my life. This other stuff is the cherry on top, but the foundation of it is family, is people — being around other people that I care about.

Lex: And I think as AI commodifies intelligence more and more, we'll realize that more and more — that intelligence and all the different puzzles that we solve is just a cherry on top, or a cherry to the side. The main thing is other humans in our lives.

Closing

Lex: This is — I can't tell you how much of an honor it is that you would come down in person for a conversation. I've become a huge fan of all three of you. It feels a bit surreal, and it's a big honor that you would talk with me today. This was, like, super fun. Thank you so much. Thank you so much, Ankur, Steve, Alex. This was awesome.

Guest: Thanks for having us.

Guest: A lot of fun for us too.

Guest: Thank you. Yeah.

Guest: Thanks for having us.

Guest: This was great.
