item.title: [Lex Clips] What Grigori Perelman thinks about AI solving mathematics | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

Perelman 的 20 年时差：一个拒绝被证伪的预言

最出人意料的观察：Perelman 在 2006 年的"退出"，其实是对 2026 年整个数学界被迫面对的困境的一次提前演习。 他拒绝 Fields Medal 和百万美元奖金时，社区把他当成怪人；而今天 AI 把"解大问题"变成廉价商品，Lex 和嘉宾不得不讨论"会不会不再颁发 Fields Medal"——他们正在集体被迫走进 Perelman 二十年前就一个人住进去的那个世界。换句话说：Perelman 不是数学界的异类，他是数学界的时间旅行者。 他只是比制度早了一代人达到了"证明如果正确，这就是全部所需的信用"这一必然终点。

跨域连接：象棋给数学的一个不太吉利的脚本

嘉宾用"centaur math（半人马数学）"来安慰自己——人机协作仍然是美好的做数学方式。但这个比喻恰好指向了一个他似乎没有说完的历史教训：

  • 1997 年 Deep Blue 击败 Kasparov 后，国际象棋界也乐观地进入了"centaur chess"阶段，人加机器被认为永远胜过纯机器。
  • 到 2017 年，顶级 centaur 对局已经被纯 AI 碾压，centaur chess 作为竞技形态悄然死亡。
  • 国际象棋并没有消失，但它的价值维度彻底换了——从"谁算得最深"迁移到"谁下得最美、最人性、最有故事"。

如果这条曲线套在数学上，那么"centaur math"不是终点，而是过渡站。真正要问的问题不是"AI 会不会抢走证明的工作"，而是："当计算与证明都被外包后，数学作为一种人类活动，它的审美内核是什么？" Fields Medal 若还要存在，奖的可能不再是"解决了什么"，而是像棋王头衔一样——奖"你是一个什么样的人，在你的工作里留下了什么样的痕迹"。

隐藏的真相：数学论文从来不是逻辑结构，而是社交文物

嘉宾顺口说了一句极其重要的话：教学生读论文时，告诉他们跳过前两段，直接从 Lemma 3 开始，再反向回去理解整篇文章。这句话看似教学技巧，实则揭示了一件数学界讳莫如深的事：

数学论文的"困难"大部分不是逻辑困难，而是隐性知识（tacit knowledge）困难。

第一段里"非局部系统的扰动理论"之类的词汇不是在传递信息，而是在进行社群身份认证——它告诉圈内人"这篇文章属于哪个流派、该用哪套直觉去读"。研究生卡在第一段，并不是因为逻辑不够，而是因为缺少被圈内人默默传递的那层语境。

这里的意外洞见是：AI 加速数学学习的真正机制，不是它算得更快，而是它溶解了这套"社交密码"。 AI 可以同时持有数千篇论文的隐性框架，把第一段的"黑话"翻译成第 3 引理的"硬内容"。所以 AI 冲击数学界的第一波打击，不是针对"证明生成"，而是针对数学界几百年构筑起来的门槛经济——那些靠"知道该读哪本书、该找哪个导师、该在哪个会议上喝咖啡"才能获得的隐性知识，现在正在被公开化、商品化。

Perelman 当年之所以能独自完成庞加莱猜想，很大程度上就是因为他主动退出了这套社交密码系统。从这个角度看，他的工作方式本身，就是预演了一个 AI 时代的数学家：不需要圈子、不需要奖赏、直接与真理本身发生关系。制度曾经把他当成一个难以理解的苦行僧，而现在它要考虑的是：在 AI 时代，是不是每一个数学家都得多少学一点"像 Perelman 那样活着"？

一个更不安的类比：印刷术之于修道院

让我把类比推得更远一点。中世纪的修道院，最核心的劳动之一是手抄圣经——那是一种神圣劳动，既是工作也是祈祷。古登堡印刷术出现后，手抄圣经的经济价值在一代人内归零。修道院没有消失，但它们必须回答一个痛苦的问题："当我们劳动的产品被机器廉价复制后，我们劳动的意义还剩什么？"

数学界现在面对的，就是同一个问题。而 Perelman，是那个在印刷术发明前就已经说"我不是为了卖圣经而抄圣经"的修士。他是在提醒整个共同体：如果你的身份认同建立在"我能证明别人证不出的东西"之上，那么 AI 一定会摧毁你；但如果它建立在"与真理对视"的那个瞬间，没有任何东西能摧毁你。

📝 转录文本

关于 Perelman 的话题引入

Lex： You know, it's hard to think of a more iconic problem to say this is the hardest, you know, one of the hardest problems in mathematics. It's been around for so long and—

嘉宾： What do you think on that—

Lex： Uh, sorry, it just made me think of Perelman credit—like, uh, the Perelman… what did he say? He said, "If the proof is correct, that's all the credit I need." He famously turned down the Fields Medal. What do you think he would say about all this, the OpenAI drop?

Perelman 会怎么说？数学家的"怪"

嘉宾： I mean, I have a very hard time predicting what Perelman will do or say. I did not know he would decline the Fields Medal. I did not know he would decline the million-dollar Clay Prize, so—

Lex： What do you think about that in general, like turning down a prize? A few folks have done that in the history of prizes. They're all about prize—

嘉宾： He's the only one who has turned down a Clay Prize…

Lex： …and the million dollars.

嘉宾： Uh, what do I think about it? Mathematicians are weird.

Lex： Okay. Yeah.

嘉宾： We—To each his own. We love diversity of opinions and thoughts, and that's what makes the world of mathematics so wonderful: it's, there's so many different kinds of people, and we let them all in.

"进入 Perelman 的世界"：Fields Medal 还会被颁发吗？

Lex： I mean, these questions are kind of coupled with what the mathematics community is dealing with now and the value of prizes, because in some sense, what his particular way, world view is aligned with this new world view that the mathematics community is entering, which is, like, it doesn't even make sense. The Field—I don't know if there'll be ever another Fields Medal given. And so you're like, "We're entering Perelman world."

嘉宾： We were talking about that explicitly this summer when the Fields Medals, you know, the last round of Fields Medals was given out in Philadelphia, and there was definitely a question, you know, 'cause people were following the progress. There hadn't been this latest bit of progress that really puts the question in the most powerful way possible. But already this summer, we were thinking, "Is this the last time that a Fields Medal is awarded?" I sure hope not. But we have to figure out what that means, you know?

奖项究竟在奖什么？

The—You have to think more sociologically about what do prizes accomplish. Why have these prizes? The people who win these prizes are already, you know, tenured professors at top places, and they're gonna be doing mathematics for the rest of their lives. Well, Perelman being one very—

Lex： Yeah, exception.

嘉宾： …very well-known exception. So what do the prizes accomplish? They celebrate the activity. They celebrate. They say, "This is what we think is important. This is, you know, the highest instance of something."

And there will still be activities that we wanna celebrate. I don't know if right now they're given out for solving major problems. Uh, solving major problems is something AI systems can do. That's not something that will be rare, and hence, it won't be nearly as valuable as it was in the past.

Centaur Math：人与 AI 协作的数学

I would like to think that despite our earlier discussion about the solved axiom, again, I don't believe the solved axiom, and I believe centaur math will be a very—

Lex： Centaur math, okay.

嘉宾： …like, great way to do math. I mean, that's how I currently feel now. I'm constantly talking to AI systems, and I'm learning a lot of math a lot faster than I'd be able to.

如何读数学论文：跳到 Lemma 3

Because the way math is written, you know, I sometimes give a paper to a grad student to read, and they come back a week later, and I say, "So how far did you get?"

"Well, I didn't really get past the first page, to be honest."

"Oh, really? Tell me."

"Uh, well, actually, I didn't get past the first paragraph."

I say, "Okay, fine. Why not?"

"Well, the first sentence is 'by the perturbation theory of non-local systems' and I don't know what any of that means, so that's, that's kinda where I'm stuck."

I'm like, "Okay. You don't know how to read a math paper. You don't—You skip the first couple of paragraphs. Go straight to, you know, the Lemma 3. And that's where you can start working and work your way backwards to what the thing is doing." But…

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## Perelman 的 20 年时差：一个拒绝被证伪的预言
最出人意料的观察：**Perelman 在 2006 年的"退出"，其实是对 2026 年整个数学界被迫面对的困境的一次提前演习。** 他拒绝 Fields Medal 和百万美元奖金时，社区把他当成怪人；而今天 AI 把"解大问题"变成廉价商品，Lex 和嘉宾不得不讨论"会不会不再颁发 Fields Medal"——他们正在集体被迫走进 Perelman 二十年前就一个人住进去的那个世界。换句话说：**Perelman 不是数学界的异类，他是数学界的时间旅行者。** 他只是比制度早了一代人达到了"证明如果正确，这就是全部所需的信用"这一必然终点。
## 跨域连接：象棋给数学的一个不太吉利的脚本
嘉宾用"centaur math（半人马数学）"来安慰自己——人机协作仍然是美好的做数学方式。但这个比喻恰好指向了一个**他似乎没有说完的历史教训**：
- 1997 年 Deep Blue 击败 Kasparov 后，国际象棋界也乐观地进入了"centaur chess"阶段，人加机器被认为永远胜过纯机器。 - 到 20

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Anthropic S-1 Shocker, Greatest Business Ever? Google’s $500B Wipeout, Midterm Predictions
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"诡计"：Anthropic 的"末日论者不在场证明"

这期节目里最锋利但最被低估的洞察来自 Sax ——他捕捉到了 Anthropic 一个精妙的叙事结构：它一边喊着要"放缓竞速"，一边比任何人都更凶猛地在推进递归自我改进（RSI）。8 月的博客里已经承认 26% 的下一代模型任务由自家模型生成改进。

但真正值得玩味的是：这不是伪善，而是一种制度化的"不在场证明工程"（alibi engineering）。它和 20 世纪烟草巨头们一边在医学期刊上发警告、一边推广过滤嘴香烟是同构的；也和 Oppenheimer 在三位一体核爆后立刻呼吁国际管控、却继续推进氢弹研发是同构的。

关键识别点：当一家前沿技术公司主动呼吁监管时，监管的范围往往恰好画在它自己已经越过的那条线之内。Dario 的"pacing letter"不是刹车，而是一张提前写好的辩护状——"是你们不听我的，不是我停不下来"。

二、你可能没意识到的：这不是最大的 IPO，这是资本主权的转移

播客里反复提到 Anthropic 的债务和 AI 复合体占到美国国债同期发行量的 30%。所有人都把这当成"系统性风险"讨论，但没人指出背后更深的历史回声——

上一次七八家公司能和主权政府在债券市场正面抢资金，要追溯到 19 世纪的东印度公司和 1870 年代的美国铁路债券狂潮。那两次都以同一种方式收场：公司最终要么被国有化，要么反向把政府变成了自己的功能延伸。东印度公司最后拥有自己的军队和税收权，铁路巨头则在镀金时代直接写美国法律。

这里有一个让人毛骨悚然的跨界连接：七位创始人持有 50.1% 的 F 类投票权，其中 80% 的股份注入"非营利/利益公司"——这不是慈善，这是一个超越国家资产规模的、由七个人投票控制的准主权实体。沙特主权基金是 9000 亿美元，Anthropic 的非营利分支如果真的继承 80% 的股份，上市后将轻松超过。

我们正在实时见证的，不是一次 IPO，而是现代民主国家历史上第一次出现"由七人董事会控制的、规模超过中等国家 GDP 的准主权体"。而选民、监管者、甚至大多数硅谷人都还没意识到这一点。

三、Microsoft 图表揭示的"反鲍莫尔定律"：知识工作第一次被"工业化"

节目里 Jason 展示的图表看似普通：Microsoft 四年内营收从 1980 亿涨到 3320 亿，员工只增加 2000 人。但这张图是人类经济史上一个范式转折的早期证据。

经济学家 William Baumol 1960 年代提出"成本病"（Baumol's cost disease）：服务业和知识工作无法像制造业那样提升单人产出，所以医生、教师、律师的实际成本会永远跑赢工业品。这个定律统治了战后 70 年的经济学。

Microsoft 这张图可能是鲍莫尔成本病的死亡证明。更惊人的是：Freeberg 的"1 美元 Nvidia 成本→18 美元 Anthropic 收入"图谱里，每一层都保持高毛利，意味着这不是零和的边际替代，而是全链条的生产率净增。

跨领域连接：这和 1920 年代"电气化"进入工厂车间的那十年高度相似。电力一开始只是替代蒸汽机，产能提升有限；但当企业重新组织车间布局（从"中心轴驱动"改为"分布式电机"），生产率才真正爆炸。我们现在还处在"用 AI 替代单个白领任务"的阶段，相当于 1915 年的工厂——真正的爆炸要等到企业重新组织工作流。

而 Jason 说"每个员工都有五个 agent"的那一刻，就是 1925 年。

四、一个让 Sax 自己都没意识到的隐藏讽刺

Sax 本季多次强调"Anthropic 在搞 regulatory capture 不道德"，但他同时赞美 Anthropic 的"capital efficiency"。这两件事其实是同一枚硬币：

Anthropic 真正的护城河不是模型质量，而是它比 OpenAI 和开源阵营更早、更深地嵌入了联邦政府的 AI 政策制定机构——前拜登官员整批加入，现在开始挖特朗普政府的人。这种"旋转门套利"正是它能把 110 亿融资只花掉 9-10 亿、却估值 2 万亿的真正原因之一：监管优势让它拿到了别人拿不到的政府和军方合同、拿到了别人拿不到的能源审批优先权。

所以这不是"伟大的生意顺便有点监管捕获"——监管捕获就是这门生意本身的一部分。

📝 转录文本

All-In Podcast Ep. 295 — Anthropic S-1 Shocker, Google's $500B Wipeout, Midterm Predictions

Cold Open: Sax Returns, "Superintelligence" vs. "AI"

All right, everybody, welcome back to what is, of course, the number one podcast in the world, tweaking all the mid podcasters out there for five years running — the all in podcast. It's episode 295. And Sax is back. Sax is back. Sax is back. How you doing, brother? Good, good.

I saw some fake news that you guys had stopped using the term super intelligence, you're getting some shade for that. Oh, I listen. We're here for this week in super intelligence right now. I mean, the whole super intelligence. It was kind of ridiculous. Oh, are they? Maybe I shouldn't stride and it, but they were trying to say that we were using the term AI still instead of SI. Who was saying that? This is literally what the press is spending their time on. Yeah. This is why it's such fake news. They have a photo of me. I wasn't even on the October 23rd episode. You do look great, though. You do look very presidential there. Man, if only you were born here. Look at this fake news. I mean, the US is the most influential tech podcast. Well, that's good — but actually we're not just a tech podcast, we're the number one podcast in the world. Give us has cooled on the use of the term super intelligence, and then they tried to say that I somehow was defying the president's instructions.

All right, but I want to clarify: I was not on the October 23rd episode. So gotcha, I'll be keeping you guys in line on this from now on. Absolutely.

Freeberg's Week, Chamath's Sales Quarter

Well, we will get focused on super intelligence with us again this week — your favorite organic farmer, David Freberg. How's Ohalo doing? You've been pretty busy yourself. Ohalo in Kenya this week — lots of excitement, lines of farmers trying out true potato seed. Your energy looks pretty good, you look like you got some good energy.

And, speaking of good energy, man, we had a fun time playing cards last week. That was a blast — a great dinner. You didn't stop talking for seven hours. It's sort of like the podcast. Yeah, it's unbelievable. It's unbelievable. Just come on, that was a lot of talking. Affleck texted me after: "I'd never want J Cal in the game again." Affleck as a member of the group — it's gonna be Ben Affleck or you, and we pick him. So you're out. That's fine. You're never getting an hour. I mean, it's an upgrade. I mean, you just kept chirping for eight hours straight. It's unbelievable. He could have been at the game for a long time, had a lot of material. It was really fun. It was so much fun.

And Chamath Palihapitiya, everybody's favorite enterprise sales executive from the 8090 corporation. How'd you do this week? Did you hit? Did you ring the gong? Did you hit your quota? Or are you gonna have to work this weekend? Q4 is off to a good start, but I never want to count the chickens. Okay, that's good, considering you whiffed Q3. No, no, no — Q3 was okay. We whiffed Q2. Butchered it, butchered it. All my fault too, because I forced these poor salespeople — I forced these three poor salespeople to just only focus on the gigantic deals. You're learning. You're learning. I had to learn the hard way. You want to get those singles and doubles, and the people who pay on time and who start the projects on time. We'll see an Ancest one, but you can build a ginormous business with singles and doubles. Absolutely, you can.

Anthropic Drops Its S-1: The Headline Numbers

Speaking of gigantic businesses, Anthropic — Ant — dropped their S-1. That's the document that outlines the nature of the business for an IPO, an initial public offering. And got to ask the question: this seems to be the greatest business in the history of entrepreneurship.

Goldman and Morgan Stanley are going to lead the round, and they are targeting November 16th, right before Thanksgiving, for this IPO we've been waiting for a long time. It's been delayed. The ticker will be ANT — A-N-T — and they're aiming to raise, wait for it, 100 billion dollars. In other words, like three months of compute. And that would make it the largest IPO ever, surpassing SpaceX. They raised 85 billion back in June, if you remember.

And Polymarket says — our great partners at Polymarket say — 78% chance Anthropic raises at least 95 billion. The valuation: 1.5 to 2 trillion. Here's your Polymarket right now, it's saying between 1.75 and 2 trillion market cap — 31%. So, yeah, assume it's going to be slightly under 2 trillion.

The revenue is the story, Sax:

  • 16.3 billion in the first half of 2026 — 14x year over year. So, in other words, the first six months of 2025, one-fourteenth of what they did in the first six months of this year.
  • Q2 is going to be a whopping 11.6 billion, a 30x jump over the last five quarters and almost as much as they made in the first half of the year.
  • TAM — total addressable market — they say is 40 trillion. That's extraordinary. I don't know how they backed into that, but we'll talk about it.
  • Projecting 100 billion of ARR by the end of the year. Now, unspecified if that's annual recurring revenue or their annual revenue run rate, which is ARRR, like a pirate.
  • 112 billion in cash.
  • Unique ownership structure of seven founders — yes, they have seven — are going to hold 50.1% of the voting power through a single class F share.

Sax, is this the greatest business in the history of capitalism?

Sax: Fastest Value Creation in Venture History

It could very well be. I mean, I think this is probably going to be the biggest venture outcome of all time, especially given the time in which this was created. I mean, this is only a six-year-old company. I think the exit here is going to be on par with SpaceX's IPO, but SpaceX has been around for like 20-something years. So this is probably the fastest value creation of any venture-backed company in history.

And I don't know if you saw, but there was a tweet this morning about the distribution of wealth this is going to create among the employees. Hundreds and hundreds of employees are going to be making hundreds of millions of dollars, and then thousands of employees are going to be making $10 million plus. I mean, this is going to be an enormous wealth creation event like San Francisco, and maybe all Silicon Valley, has never seen before.

The "Phantom $80B Loss" Refuted

Now, there's a few other data points in this S-1 that I think reflected the strength here. Number one is that this $80 billion loss number that we've heard so much about — that the media has constantly been pumping and harping on as proof that Anthropic was either a fake business or that we were in this whole bubble — that narrative basically just got completely refuted. It turns out that that $80 billion loss is a phantom number.

It resulted from the fact that Anthropic had issued convertible notes — basically to their infrastructure partners like Amazon and so forth. And as Anthropic's valuation increased, those convertible notes got recorded as a loss on the balance sheet and that flowed through into the income statement. But it's not a real loss. If they had just issued equity, that loss wouldn't be there. So it was not a cash loss. It's basically a fake number.

And in fact, what was revealed in this S-1 is that Anthropic has been an extraordinarily capital-efficient business. They've raised something like, I think it was around 110 billion roughly, and they've only spent about 9 or 10 billion throughout the entire course of this business. And they still have, like you said, JCal, about 100 billion left of cash or cash equivalents on the balance sheet.

So everyone thought, based on the previous reporting, that this was a huge loss-making business. In fact, it ended up being a very capital-efficient business.

Margins, Compute Multipliers, Recursive Self-Improvement

Then the other thing you saw was that their margins have been improving. I think their gross margin is now something like 85%. And what you see is that for a given task or capability, they're showing roughly 10x improvement year over year in their ability to deliver that task — the cost effectiveness of that task gets 10x cheaper year over year. And that allows them to cut the cost of that model or that task by, let's call it, 50%. The consumer recognizes a huge cost savings, but they are able to realize an even greater savings because they're able to capture the rest of that efficiency in their margin.

That's what we basically saw: again, they're cutting the cost of their tokens significantly, but their margins are going up even faster, because they're able to produce these models that are more and more efficient. They call them compute multipliers. It's very interesting the way that Anthropic sees their business. The framework that Dario has is that there's raw compute, which is scaling very rapidly as a result of better and better chips and more and more of those chips. And then there's the compute multipliers, which are things like algorithmic improvements or better curation of the data, or it can be things like better architectures, more MOE architectures — things that make all these models more efficient. So they're able to give you the same answer for one-tenth the cost, or they can take those efficiencies and create greater capabilities.

This is what we're seeing: that business is actually improving. And I think it is a little bit of a refutation to all the people who've been saying over the past year that they're getting commoditized away, that open models are basically putting them on a hamster wheel where they're basically going to zero on gross margin, or that it's a business that only works because it's heavily subsidized by venture capital.

In fact, I think there's a lot of reasons to believe that Anthropic has a pretty big lead. And if you believe that recursive self-improvement has kicked in, as they are claiming it has, then their lead could actually grow.

Freeberg: The AI Value Stack — Everyone's Making Money

Freeberg, your thoughts on the impact of this massive deluge of capital coming into Silicon Valley, and then this corporate structure — 51% ownership — and what impact this might have on the technology industry, the venture capital industry, and on democracy here in the United States?

We've never seen this much capital flow through to a nonprofit organization, or whatever they're calling this anthropic nonprofit entity, but 80% of the seven founders' shares are going into this nonprofit entity of some type. Benefit corporation — who knows what it's going to be structured as. It's optional, but that's another interesting shoe to drop. So take it whichever way you like, in whichever order you like.

Can I just comment on the economic value that's arising from AI that, of course, kind of revealed a little bit in this? In the S-1, Anthropic shows how many customers they have that are spending 100k or more. If we take a look at the image here, it's a pretty remarkable ramp in customers spending 100k or more:

  • 200 customers in 2024
  • 1,500 end of 2025
  • 11,900 customers spending 100k or more at the end of September

So I asked the question: how many customers are there for which $100,000 annual spend is less than 1% of their total annual spend? And the answer is: in the US, it's about 200 to 300,000 businesses. Globally, it's a bit over a million. So if you just say, "Hey, look, Anthropic's customers that could spend 100k or more and have it be less than 1% of their total spend," the addressable customer base is about a million customers. So they're only at, call it 1% of total customer penetration potential.

The Dollar-to-Eighteen-Dollars Chain

Now the question is: is there real money to be made here? So I took a look at the AI value stack to try and identify who's making money where — and it turns out everyone's making money. What is this chart? Is this AI output? I had Claude make this for me as an image. Cool. Or I should just say, "my analyst made this for me in my shop" — your box.

I basically said: start with Nvidia. How much does Nvidia spend to make the chips, and how much do they sell the chips for? So for every dollar of COGS, every dollar that Nvidia spends, that turns into four dollars of revenue for Nvidia — 75% margin. It's obviously a baseline of compute spend, but 85% is the incremental gross margin. So at the end of the day, a dollar that Nvidia spends turns into $18 that Anthropic is making selling to customers.

And the question is: are customers making money? We're seeing the customer ramp as it is, and the spend ramp as it is, and the customers are making — call it — on the order of two to ten times the money they're spending. Across the whole value chain, there is such margin to be had, there's so much value being created all the way through to the customers.

And we're only 1% — or Anthropic is only 1% — penetrated on their customer potential, and probably less than 10% of the spend potential per customer. This really is what Eric Schmidt a long time ago, in the early days of Google, used to say: Google's total addressable market is global commerce. And I think for the first time ever, we're seeing a business actually potentially starting to realize that theory. That if you can create enough productivity gain for your customers, your TAM is commerce. Now you have the broad-base cost of borrowing go up, because every other part of the United States economy is levered to the 2's through 5's and 10-year complex.

What is the market risk? Explain it just crisply here as we wrap. What is the market risk?

If interest rates go up because the US Treasuries have to pay more for people to buy their bonds, then everything else in the economy has a higher cost of borrowing — that has negative implications. If the opposite is true, the AI complex has to pay more, and then there's a bunch of negative repercussions narrowly to the complex. The problem is: we're trying to buy an AI stock. Token cost matters, right? We're sitting here with the Token Max, and look what we're seeing — I mean, we keep seeing Jevons paradox play out at every level. As you cut the cost of tokens, more and more use cases, enterprises use it more and more, and the net result is that the total demand just keeps going up and the total revenue and market size keeps growing.

Freeberg, this is your alma mater. You witnessed the cost-per-click greatest business ever. This was the previous one that we said was the best business ever created, along with the iPhone franchise. I think the Google Cloud business is looking really tremendous. I mean, I don't know if you guys remember, it wasn't too long ago, and this thing was not making money. The question is: does Google actually have the models that sit on top of it? And in many cases they do — so they can make a higher margin on that piece of the stack.

So when I say it's complicated: I think there's a story you can build in the Cloud business that shows the next couple of years of really progressive growth in that business. Max Anderson's Viral Thread: The Vickrey Auction Shift

Typically, in a Vickrey auction, what happens is: Freeberg bids, I bid, if I'm the under-bidder, Freeberg gets filled at my price, because he was the high bidder. So it's a really great way of doing price discovery. At Facebook, when we built the first ad system, that's essentially what we copied — we copied Google's feature for feature. But if now what they're doing is they've abandoned the Vickrey auction, Freeberg's right: you're over-earning. And if the market starts to smell that out, they're going to start to wonder what's actually happening underneath the hood.

So these claims, which are now well syndicated, have been out there since July. And I'm not sure that Google IR has necessarily nipped these in the bud. I think what happened was the information war that happened post-earnings was recirculating Max's post here and saying this has been going on for a while. And when you look inside the comments, it's a bunch of other people seconding his analysis as accurate.

Without knowing the details, Jason — because they don't spend money in the Google ecosystem — I think it's really important for Google IR to get in front of this. Because if this momentum builds, this idea that this franchise is essentially robbing Peter to pay Paul — like pulling money from the future into the present to kind of smooth out earnings — the market will react badly to it. Then they do look like more of a structured conglomerate — now you have a YouTube revenue block, a GCP block, and other bets block, and a search block. None are dominant. But they'll have to go through this complicated process where a bunch of folks may not want to own that kind of a business. There's a different buyer pool. So you have to go through transitioning out the folks that wanted to own a single-stock bet on search or ads or whatever it was, and now have to move to this other kind of business model. And when you switch buckets like this, a bunch of folks say, "Oh, it's too complicated."

So problem number one is: if you were Google IR, please read this and refute it, or try to figure out how to get in front of it, because every analyst now will try to figure out whether this is true. The second, though, is very narrow: how do you keep Demis at Google? That's it. That's the only task. Pay Thomas Kurian whatever he wants. How do you keep Demis at Google?

I'm not going to be there. Where are you going to be? What do I need to do a midterm live stream for? Because you're going to lose. Your party's going to lose, so you're not coming. If we outperform, I'll pop in and spike the football. Otherwise, I'm not showing up. That's not cool. Wants to hear you come on. We can drink, we can drink some tequila, we'll have fun with the Sax. Come on, you can't cry. We should all be drinking, by the way. Maybe we should get together at Chamath's house and drink and do it live.

Sax's Closing Warning

I agree with a lot of your analysis about what will happen if the Democrats win, JCal, because they have not changed their stripes. Okay, people are just forgetting who the Democrats are and what they were like during COVID — all the lawfare that they perpetrated, all the crazy woke stuff. It's all there ready to come back. They have not really analyzed why they lost in 2024. They have not really changed or adjusted anything. If anything, they've become more extreme. The DSA is ascendant in their party, as even Gavin Newsom acknowledged. So I think that if the Democrats do take Congress, you're likely to see how nutty they are, and the American public will be reminded of that, and that will be really interesting to see. But that's why there's a pendulum in politics, right? There is a pendulum.

Um, I think we need a — yeah. I mean, I'm wondering who the champions are. If it's not JD and Rubio, I wonder who the champion on the right will be. I think it's going to be somebody we can't even name right now is going to emerge. And I think the same thing on the left.

Anyway, it's going to be exciting. We're going to get Sax to show up, and we'll see you all next Thursday night for our live stream. Love you besties. Bye-bye. Bye-bye.

Brain Man, David Sacks. Oh man. We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy, because they're all just like this — like sexual tension, but they just need to release them out.

item.description:
## 一、被忽略的"诡计"：Anthropic 的"末日论者不在场证明"
这期节目里最锋利但最被低估的洞察来自 Sax ——他捕捉到了 Anthropic 一个精妙的叙事结构：**它一边喊着要"放缓竞速"，一边比任何人都更凶猛地在推进递归自我改进（RSI）**。8 月的博客里已经承认 26% 的下一代模型任务由自家模型生成改进。
但真正值得玩味的是：这不是伪善，而是一种**制度化的"不在场证明工程"**（alibi engineering）。它和 20 世纪烟草巨头们一边在医学期刊上发警告、一边推广过滤嘴香烟是同构的；也和 Oppenheimer 在三位一体核爆后立刻呼吁国际管控、却继续推进氢弹研发是同构的。
关键识别点：**当一家前沿技术公司主动呼吁监管时，监管的范围往往恰好画在它自己已经越过的那条线之内**。Dario 的"pacing letter"不是刹车，而是一张提前写好的辩护状——"是你们不听我的，不是我停不下来"。
## 二、你可能没意识到的：这不是最大的 IPO，这是**资本主权的转移**
播客里反复提到 Anthropic 的债务和 AI 复合体占到美国国债

item.title: [Lex Clips] Computation in nature: Slime mold, fruit flies, and turbulence | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、果蝇的秘密不是"算得少"，而是"根本没在算"

视频里最反直觉的一点藏在那句"strain-sensitive neurons fire ... local computation is happening in that shoulder muscle"。表面上这是在说果蝇用更少的信息做出更快的决策，但真正惊人的事实是：果蝇的翅膀肩部肌肉在信号到达大脑之前就已经完成了"计算"——这意味着它根本没有把问题形式化为我们理解的那种"求解 Navier-Stokes"。

它不是在用更小的模型逼近同一个问题，而是把问题本身替换成了另一个问题：不是"预测气流"，而是"响应形变"。这就好比你问围棋 AI 怎么下，它却告诉你"我根本不下，我让棋盘自己震动，然后让石头落到低处"。果蝇把流体力学从"预测问题"变成了"物理反射问题"——这与现在最前沿的 neuromorphic computing / physical reservoir computing（物理储备池计算）惊人地同构：让物理介质本身承担计算，大脑只做读出。

二、Kamal Jain 那句玩笑话其实是宇宙级物理定律

"If my laptop can't find it, then neither can the market." 这句引用在视频里是作为博弈论的注脚出现的，但如果把它推到极限，它暗含一个让物理学家都会不安的命题：

计算复杂度，可能是和热力学第二定律同级的宇宙硬约束。

想想看——Navier-Stokes 的 blowup 之所以能通过图灵机构造出来（Terry Tao 的工作），恰恰说明"不可计算性"可以物理地嵌入在流体方程里。换句话说，宇宙并不会"替你"去完成 NP-hard 的优化。那么当一只椋鸟群在空中瞬间转向、当一个黏菌找到最短路径、当市场完成价格发现——它们都没有在"解问题"，它们都在用物理过程绕过问题。

跨领域连接：这与经济学里 Hayek 的"知识分散"命题、神经科学里 Friedman 的"自由能原理"、以及深度学习里 lottery ticket hypothesis（彩票假设）其实共享同一个骨架——可计算性决定了什么样的解会在自然中存活下来。

三、棒球外野手的曲线，是物理学里一次失传的发明

视频里一笔带过的那个外野手案例是整个对话里最深的宝藏。为什么外野手不走直线？Steve Brunton 的解释是"持续重估轨迹"，这当然对，但还可以更锋利：

外野手在跑一条让自己的视觉信息增益最大化的路径。 直线路径的代价不是跑得慢，而是在那条路径上，球相对于他的视角几乎不变，等于主动丢弃了传感器数据。曲线路径强迫球的视差持续变化，从而让每一步都在采样新信息。这其实就是机器人学里的 active perception / informative path planning，也是贝叶斯推断里"探索 vs 利用"的运动版本。

最意外的连接：这和果蝇翅膀的 strain neuron 是同一枚硬币——果蝇让翅膀的形变做"被动数据采集"，外野手让身体的轨迹做"主动数据采集"。两者都拒绝"先建模完整系统再决策"的 Laplace 式方案，而是把身体本身当成测量设备。

四、一个贯穿黏菌、果蝇、外野手、湍流的隐藏原理

把视频里所有例子并排看，会跳出一个被忽视的共同点：它们都不是在"解方程"，而是在"让环境替它们解方程"。

  • 黏菌：让化学梯度在物理介质中扩散，物理过程就是算法。
  • 果蝇：让空气在翅膀上留下压痕，形变就是答案。
  • 外野手：让自己运动，视差变化就是观测。
  • 湍流控制：让涡旋碰撞，流体自己完成了维度塌缩。

这其实挑战了视频里那个"好坐标系应该多小"的提问方式。真正的问题也许不是"多少个变量够用"，而是——哪一部分可以外包给物理本身？ PV=nRT 之所以好用，不是因为它压缩了信息，而是因为它承认了平衡态物理已经替我们完成了压缩。而天气之所以不可压缩，不是因为变量太多，而是因为没有任何自发过程愿意替我们做这件事。

所以 Alex 问的那个"涡旋碰撞能做什么计算"的问题，可能有一个让所有人都没想到的答案：它能做的计算，恰好是我们不愿意自己做的那种。

📝 转录文本

一、自然界已经在"解"哪些计算问题？

  • So one of the things I would wonder, you know, scientifically, I mean, these are really interesting problems, and that was a great explanation.

So I'm always curious about what computational problems nature can solve already, right? And there are a lot of examples of this. You know, there's a famous one with like slime mold finding shortest paths and mazes. In fact, some of the precursors to Navier-Stokes were, you know, like some of Terry Tao's work on showing that you can have blowup for Navier-Stokes-like equations because they can simulate Turing machines.

So I guess I would also wonder what sorts of computational tasks these computations with vortices colliding can do, and how that imposes limits on what sorts of coordinate systems ought to exist. 'Cause, you know, you mentioned PV equals nRT. That's an amazing dimensionality reduction —

... because you don't keep track of all of these positions and velocities of particles, but there's just, you know, a small list of numbers that describes a meta state, and that's it. But if I really had a tremendous reduction, you know, like that in the case of turbulence, then it would seem to me very difficult to compute very interesting things too.

二、Game of Life 式的类比与"算法透镜"

  • Could it be like the game of Life, where you have this very simple cellular automata system, and it's a universal Turing machine, and you can cook up whatever behavior you want in it?

  • Yeah, that's right. I mean, so game of Life, a lot of times people think about, you know, what are minimal rules to have all of these exotic behaviors, and it's really shocking how small the rules need to be to get that, right?

But I guess, you know, I'm a theoretical computer scientist. One of the biggest exports from our field is really the algorithmic lens. So it's not just about, you know, computation where you have a well-defined problem and a laptop and you wanna solve it, but it's also about, you know, computation in the natural world, you know, and what that teaches us about what the rules of nature might be.

So, you know, some famous examples of this are things like equilibria in multiplayer games, and Nash equilibrium is a great solution concept. But of course, the fact that it's hard to compute Nash equilibrium, you know, throws into question, is it really a universal mechanism that explains how people play games?

There was this amazing quote by Kamal Jain that I really like, which is, "If my laptop can't find it, then neither can the market." And, you know, to me, what's really exciting is the nexus of a lot of these different perspectives. When you were describing it, it sounded to me like there are very interesting computational problems under the hood, and that one can kind of get a dual perspective on these things by thinking about how that computation imposes limits on what a good coordinate system ought to look like.

三、两个极端：地球气候 vs 果蝇飞行

  • So I think that's a really nice way of framing the problem. Uh, and I would take two extreme examples.

So Earth's weather and climate systems are actually just complex. They — all the scales do matter. The weather in this zip code matters to me. Um, you know, everything matters. All the variables matter. And you're right. Like, if I over-reduce that system to, you know, five numbers, then I lose the descriptive capability of what I actually care about. That's one extreme.

The other extreme, let's think about how, you know, a moth flies or a butterfly or a fruit fly. They are proof by existence that you can interact with an extremely complicated turbulent flow and do very advanced engineering control. They can control their forces and moments in gusts, in rain. They can live very rich lives, and they presumably don't have a PhD in fluid dynamics —

... or know the Navier-Stokes. They're probably not running supercomputer simulations. There might be five or six numbers that actually matter to their daily life of maintaining a leading-edge vortex and, you know, stalling their wings to perch and to land.

And those are kind of two extreme examples, and I really want to be able to handle both of those. We want to be able to handle the full complexity of truly complex systems, and we want to be able to distill down the absolute bare minimum essentials for fast decisions in those kind of insect extreme cases. And biological flyers still dramatically outperform, you know, human-designed, fluid systems in many regimes, so we still have a lot to learn about, about these simple systems.

四、不确定性下的鲁棒解：外野手的曲线路径

  • So maybe we're, like, veering into research now, but, you know —

... to me, it's always amazing how nature not only solves very hard optimization problems, it seems to find very robust solutions. And I'm always struck by the fact that, you know, when we model it, we tend to model it assuming we have full knowledge, you know, about what the boundary and initial conditions are for things like Navier-Stokes. But when a bird flies, you know, it doesn't know all of that.

And to some extent, you know, modeling things with uncertainty is really how you reframe the optimization problem to get very, you know, rich and robust solutions. And it's kind of amazing to me how a lot of everyday examples sort of fit into this.

I remember, you know, I'm a big baseball fan, and I remember reading a math paper about baseball that when you've got an outfielder, you know, once the ball has been hit, a lot of stuff is known. You know, the velocity, the trajectory. You would think the outfielder would just take a straight-line path to where they expected the ball to be. But when you observe outfielders, they don't take straight-line paths. They take a slight curve to it.

So why is that? You know, at least one way to wrap your head around it is that that's actually a very robust strategy, 'cause when you're taking a curved path, you can continually reevaluate —

... the trajectory of the ball and then adjust as needed. So there are very interesting solutions that nature finds, but it's not always obvious what is the right formulation for the optimization problem in the first place, and sometimes modeling it in the case of uncertainty so that you can design solutions that are robust to the fact that you don't have full system knowledge seems to be an important piece of the picture.

五、果蝇翅膀上的"边缘计算"

  • So there's a fun aside related to this. Um, insects in particular don't have the ability to measure their full flow field. Um, they can react to gusts of wind faster than the information that hits their wings, goes to their brain and back to their muscles.

So researchers have studied this for decades in biology. And what they've found is that there are strain-sensitive neurons embedded on the wings, maybe a few dozen to a few hundred of these in very stereotypical locations. So brother fruit flies will have the same locations of these strain-sensitive neurons, and those strain-sensitive neurons fire when the wing bends in a certain temporal pattern.

So it gets hit by a gust of wind, the wing bends, neurons fire, and a local computation is happening in that shoulder muscle of this insect that goes directly back and corrects robustly based on partial information of a system it doesn't have equations for that is nonlinear and turbulent. So it's like, again, proof by existence —

... of exactly what you're saying is maybe the robust strategy of actually relying on partial information and uncertainty. They can do more than we can at this point, with way less information.

六、彩蛋：黑洞奇点与 Navier-Stokes 的玩笑

  • Yeah. I have a couple of — I apologize — pothead thoughts, 'cause Alex mentioned black holes. I have a fun thought that maybe the singularity observed with a blowup in Navier-Stokes equations comes into play when we're — as opposed to airplane wings on Earth — we're traveling through two connected black holes in a warp drive that we figure out, and then there's the flow control of spacetime, and that becomes relevant because now you're in a black hole, hence the singularity.

This is the — For people just listening to this, the look Alex just gave me, it hurts my soul. Okay. So moving on to the next topic.

  • But the forcing, you'd need the black hole vortex to also be forced at exactly the right —

  • The, yeah, the force. Where's the force? I mean, at that point —

  • How do you... Yeah. You could try to ride it. Yeah. There's a way — You can make something out of this.

  • There's some non-zero probability that future ass that will listen to this, that guy is the one time he said something that was actually correct. Okay. If it's okay, a quick bathroom break.

  • Yeah. Sounds good.

观看原视频 →
