item.title: [Lex Clips] The hardest physics problem in fluid dynamics: Turbulence explained | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这段对话真正讨论的，不是湍流，而是"可简化性"的边界

Brunton 丢出了一个被大多数听众忽略的炸弹：房间里的气体有 10²³ 个分子，比任何湍流都"复杂"，但它反而是湍流的反面。为什么？因为气体的所有尺度之间是解耦的——分子的疯狂运动在宏观上塌缩成三个数字（温度、压强、密度）。而湍流之所以是千年难题，不是因为它"复杂"，而是因为它的尺度彼此纠缠，不允许信息向上塌缩。

这是一个让人不安的洞察：复杂度不是问题，耦合度才是。一个有一万亿参数但层级清晰的系统，可能比一个只有五个变量却彼此反馈的系统更容易被理解。这解释了为什么大脑的 860 亿神经元可以被意识统摄，而只有少数几个变量的 2008 年金融系统却崩塌到无法预测——危机时刻，正是宏观与微观尺度突然"耦合"的时刻，正如层流转捩为湍流的瞬间。

二、意外的观察：物理学的所有重大突破都是"换坐标"，而不是"算得更快"

Brunton 说了一句很容易被滑过去的话："牛顿的 F=ma 出现在我们把太阳放到宇宙中心之后。"把这句话推到极致，你会得到一个颠覆性的历史模式：

  • 牛顿革命 = 日心坐标系
  • 相对论 = 时空坐标统一
  • 量子力学 = 希尔伯特空间
  • 傅里叶分析 = 从时域到频域
  • 深度学习 = 从像素空间到潜在空间（latent space）

AI 的本质工作，不是"思考"，而是在数据中寻找一组让问题变得平凡的坐标。 ChatGPT 的 Transformer 做的事情，和寻找湍流坐标是同一类事情——它找到了一个让"下一个 token"变得可预测的高维表示。所以当 Brunton 说"这是一个完美的 AI 问题"，他其实在说：凡是 70、80 年代被卡住的问题，本质都是坐标问题，而 AI 刚好是一台坐标搜索机器。

这也给我们一个可怕的启示：你人生中反复解不开的难题，很可能不需要"更努力"，而需要"换坐标"——换一个描述问题的变量，换一个看待关系的维度。

三、跨领域连接：鱼、章鱼、与"身体即坐标系"

Lex 问了一句很关键的话："可是鱼已经解决了（湍流）。" Brunton 轻描淡写地认同——但这里藏着一个更深的裂缝。

鱼没有解微分方程，鱼也没有大数据集。鱼是用身体本身作为坐标系解决了湍流预测问题。它的侧线、鳞片、肌肉张力分布——这些不是"传感器"，而是与流体耦合的物质本体。这呼应了 Rodney Brooks 的话："The world is its own best model."

把这个思想推到极致，就会撞上章鱼之谜：章鱼三分之二的神经元在它的触手里。它不是中央集权地"计算"湍流，而是让每条触手自己与水流共振、协商、决策。

于是产生一个异端的猜测：湍流也许根本没有一组"数学上的"简洁坐标，它只有一组"形态上的"简洁坐标——需要一个会流动、会变形的身体来表达它。这意味着未来破解湍流的，可能不是 Transformer，而是软体机器人 + 具身学习：让一个人工鱼在水里游一百万年，它找到的坐标，可能是任何方程都写不出来的。

这又反过来逼问一个哲学问题：如果一个解只能被身体表达、不能被符号表达，它还算"理解"吗？ 这正是数学与生命之间最深的那道裂缝。

📝 转录文本

The Big Puzzles in Fluid Dynamics

Lex: Can you speak to some of the maybe beautiful, fascinating phenomena in the space of fluids that you've been thinking about? You mentioned turbulence. What are the big puzzles to sort of solve in this space to understand? You've mentioned drag, like air, fluid. What are like the big Millennium Prize type problems that people are thinking about?

Brunton: I mean, there's so many. You can break them down into a few categories. So turbulence is very hard because it's multi-scale.

Lex: What is turbulence?

Turbulence as a Multi-Scale Phenomenon

Brunton: Turbulence is this phenomena that when you have a complex fluid roiling or mixing and moving — kind of like a Da Vinci's… he has these beautiful drawings of fluids at all of these different scales. All of the scales matter: the big vortices, and the medium vortices, and the little vortices — all of them actually matter to predict the lift and the drag and the thing.

So the gas in this room is a great counterexample. It's the opposite of turbulence. It is complicated — the molecules are all moving around in a very frenetic way, and there's a lot of molecules. But that, you know, ten to the twenty-three number of gas particles — all of those individual configurations don't matter. We know from thermodynamics (this is like the great success of classical physics) that there's a small handful of numbers that actually determine how this gas behaves — you know, temperature, pressure, density.

That simple description doesn't exist for turbulent fluids: for the flow over a wing, the flow inside your heart, for, you know, any — for the flow on a river. All of the scales actually matter. All of the numbers in that simulation actually matter to predict the next, you know, behavior — to predict what's gonna happen. And that makes it fundamentally challenging.

Is There a Coordinate System for Turbulence?

So this is actually a great AI problem: Is there a coordinate system? Is there a set of numbers just like we have for gases — you know, temperature, pressure, density? Is there a set of numbers or some representation of a fluid, of a turbulent fluid, that allow it to be simply described in a way that is useful for engineering — to build, you know, motors and engines — just like we have for gas dynamics?

Lex: So then the interesting question, if it's a problem for AI (and AI is listening, I'm sure)… um, the solution to that problem, would it — would the path lie through mathematics or through having the AI system sit there and watch some fluid for a while?

Brunton: I think yes to both.

Lex: 'Cause fish, they figured it out.

Coordinate Transformations as the Prelude to Breakthrough

Brunton: They figured it out. Well, so I think you have the right keyword — coordinates. And I — so that's kinda why I said both. And I'm not trying to be trite, but all of our great physics breakthroughs were predated by a coordinate transformation. So Newton's F = ma came after we put the sun at the center of the universe instead of the Earth, right? You had to do that coordinate transform first.

So I think what — the way I see it is: we need to take all of this data, these simulations, these observations of fluids, and what we're looking for is a simple coordinate system so that the description of that fluid becomes very simple and generalizable, beautiful in a physical sense. And that is both a brute force — you know, get a lot of data, try a bunch of different coordinate transformations and representations until you find the simplest one that generalizes the best. But there's also a lot of deep mathematics in what the form of that coordinate transformation might take.

In general, if you find a question that really smart people asked, you know, in the '70s and '80s, but they hit a wall computationally — that's very fertile ground right now. So like, we know what the form of these coordinate systems probably should take from some fundamental principles. We've just never been able to write them down. They're too complicated to write down. That's like a perfect problem for AI: you know, now let's give it a lot more data, a lot more compute, and see if we can start learning these transformations we know should exist.

Vortices: Structured Chaos

Lex: Just so I understand, the formation of vortexes — so that's like a, like, little, like, tornadoes.

Brunton: Little tornadoes.

Lex: Their formation is — is that part tricky to understand?

Brunton: Uh, yeah, absolutely. And it's beautiful too. Like, I love watching these videos of, you know, if you shoot two vortices together, they'll, you know, influence each other and then merge in these very interesting ways — that you have like a red vortex and a blue vortex, and you can see where they merge and join.

But they also stretch and fold, and, you know, turbulence is chaotic, so the trajectories get tangled like spaghetti. It's not random. There's a huge amount of structure — but it is very multi-scale, very, very tangled.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、这段对话真正讨论的，不是湍流，而是"可简化性"的边界
Brunton 丢出了一个被大多数听众忽略的炸弹：**房间里的气体有 10²³ 个分子，比任何湍流都"复杂"，但它反而是湍流的反面**。为什么？因为气体的所有尺度之间是解耦的——分子的疯狂运动在宏观上塌缩成三个数字（温度、压强、密度）。而湍流之所以是千年难题，不是因为它"复杂"，而是因为**它的尺度彼此纠缠，不允许信息向上塌缩**。
这是一个让人不安的洞察：**复杂度不是问题，耦合度才是**。一个有一万亿参数但层级清晰的系统，可能比一个只有五个变量却彼此反馈的系统更容易被理解。这解释了为什么大脑的 860 亿神经元可以被意识统摄，而只有少数几个变量的 2008 年金融系统却崩塌到无法预测——危机时刻，正是宏观与微观尺度突然"耦合"的时刻，正如层流转捩为湍流的瞬间。
## 二、意外的观察：**物理学的所有重大突破都是"换坐标"，而不是"算得更快"**
Brunton 说了一句很容易被滑过去的话："牛顿的 F=ma 出现在我们把太阳放到宇宙中心之后。"把这句话推到极致，你会得到一个颠覆性的历史模式：
- 牛顿革命 =

item.title: [a16z] Why AI Could Turn Small Law Firms Into Billion-Dollar Businesses
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被遮蔽的"影子劳动力市场"：软件市场的真实体积比任何人想象的都大一个数量级

最反直觉的观察藏在 Alex 的一句玩笑里："VC 以前会说原告律师的软件市场很小，他们都买 Microsoft Office。" 这句话揭示了一个被整个行业集体误读的事实——所谓"小软件市场"其实是一个被定价机制隐藏起来的巨型劳动力市场。

原告律师行业每年创造数千亿美元的赔付结果，但软件支出只有几十亿。为什么？因为真正的消耗品是人力。Eve 的本质不是在卖软件，而是在出售一个"每小时 0.12 美元的律师助理劳动力"——这个劳动力市场在物理世界从未存在过，因此也从未被计入 TAM。这与 Uber 当年打开的"愿意为私家车付钱但买不起黑车"的中间市场结构同构：AI 时代的 TAM 不是现有软件支出的扩大，而是"物理世界因价格而根本不存在的那部分需求"的货币化。

跨领域连接：这几乎复刻了云计算早期对 IT 预算的"小市场"误读。AWS 刚出来时，分析师看传统服务器市场觉得"也就那样"，结果真正爆发的是那些永远不会买服务器的创业者——他们过去根本不在样本里。

二、"专业化悖论"：AI 不会让律师变成通才，而是把 mom-and-pop 律所推向极致垂直

主流叙事认为通用大模型会抹平专家优势。但 Jay 不经意间说的那句话——"将来会有人专精于 soft tissue injury 中涉及 X 和 Y 事实模式的案件"——指向一个几乎没人谈论的方向：AI 不是让每个人都变成全科医生，恰恰相反，它让"专精到荒谬程度"的律所第一次具备商业可行性。

原因是三重的：(1) AI 把研究成本压到接近零，使得一个超窄垂类的客户获取成本第一次低于其 LTV；(2) 地理约束瓦解——你可以在 Phoenix 代理全美范围内的某类伤害案；(3) 积累的垂类数据会形成对该大模型本身都不可及的护城河，因为超过 99% 的和解案件数据永远不会进入任何可爬取的语料库。

这是对一个常见直觉的直接反转：很多人担心 AI 会让律师业"赢家通吃"。但 Eve 展示的未来恰好相反——它让 Long Tail 的尾巴变得极其肥厚。Chris Anderson 的 Long Tail 理论最初写的是零售（Amazon），而真正把它推到极致的，很可能是专业服务业。

三、保险公司 50 年前就在用 AI，只是没人注意——而现在信息不对称即将系统性崩塌

最被低估的细节是 Colossus——Allstate、State Farm 这些保险巨头用来给"断了一根拇指"定价的内部专家系统。它们事实上早在 1990 年代就在工业化地运行一种结果导向的理赔 AI。整个美国的伤害赔偿价格体系，在过去 30 年里是由单向持有决策数据的一方定义的。

Jay 轻描淡写的那句"deny deny deny 是保险公司的规则一和规则二"——这不是道德问题，是最优博弈策略在交易成本不对称下的必然结果。原告律师的边际时间成本太高，所以保险公司的最优策略就是对所有索赔施加一个"摩擦税"，让大量正当赔付因不经济而被放弃。

这里有一个让人毛骨悚然的推论：如果 Eve 把原告端的边际成本砍到接近零，那么过去 30 年保险公司支付出去的保费价格本质上是"被欠赔金额补贴的"。一旦这个补贴消失，保费必须上涨→保险市场的所有定价模型需要重写→可能触发监管重估。Eve 卖的不是软件，是在一个 30 年的信息不对称体系上凿第一个洞。

跨领域连接：这与高频交易出现后对做市商的影响惊人地相似。Citadel 和 Virtu 的崛起不是"更快撮合"，而是把过去藏在价差里的隐形税收强行可视化。原告 AI 对保险业的作用，可能就是法律领域的 HFT 时刻。

四、彩蛋式洞察：原告律师行业其实是人类历史上最古老的"AI 商业模式"

contingency law 的结构——事先投入高成本的"计算"（律师工时），押注一个概率性的 outcome 支付——与现代 AI 推理经济学完全同构。原告律所本质上是用蛋白质跑的推理集群，几个世纪前就在实践"按 outcome 收费"的 token 经济学。Eve 做的不是让律师变得像软件，而是把一个本来就是 AI 结构的行业，终于迁移到了硅基基础设施上。所以它比 SaaS 的"outcome-based pricing 革命"领先了几十年——它从来就没在 per-seat 的世界里生活过。

📝 转录文本

开场：被忽视的另一半法律世界

Historically, plaintiff law really didn't need more than a cell phone email address. That was kind of it. No software really solved their core problem, which is labor constraint. Most people think of AI is like, "Oh, you're going to fire everybody and cut costs." And it's like, "No, actually, like, if I use Eve, I make a lot more money for my firm. People can't pay $500, $600 an hour on a blank check for however long the case might take."

What Eve has aimed to do is really handle that whole thing end to end. One firm in LA went from managing about 100 clients per attorney to 500.

Wow.

That is a type of thing that is possible.

Why is Eve better than just kind of like raw intelligence?

If you drop Albert Einstein into a law firm today, he will not be productive for quite some time. That is a general problem that Eve is solving. And why won't that person be productive? Well, it's due to a number of things. One is—

Hi everyone. I'm Alex Rampel, partner at Andreessen Horowitz, and I'm very happy to be here with Jay from Eve, co-founder and CEO.

Everybody knows a lawyer, right? Everybody knows law. But most people, I think, especially in Silicon Valley, when they hear "law" and "legal," they kind of think about corporate law—like really big, you know, supposedly white-shoe law firms where you go to Harvard Law School and you bill $2,000 an hour.

But there's another side of law which actually is bigger, more distributed, and I guess we would call that plaintiff law. Every time you drive on 101, you see all these billboards. Maybe start off: what is Eve? What form of law and legal AI do you focus on? And maybe a little bit about the industry in general — because most Americans are familiar with it but they don't necessarily realize, especially people here in Silicon Valley, they've heard of Wilson Sonsini but they haven't heard of Morgan and Morgan. And Morgan and Morgan is probably a lot more profitable than Wilson Sonsini. What is plaintiff law, and explain Eve in your own words?

什么是 Eve：面向普通人的法律 AI

Absolutely. One, thank you for having me here, Alex — always fun to talk about Eve.

What Eve is, is legal AI for real people, right? Like people like you, me — not institutions, not in-house legal, not the people that already have all the resources. But how do we actually provide legal services to people that otherwise can't afford it?

This is how the plaintiff law industry really came about. What ended up happening was — you talked about how Wilson Sonsini might charge $2,000 an hour, and that's really the business model. Lawyers' time is expensive and you're trying to point lawyers towards more and more expensive time. The same is true for most lawyers. They have a lot of bills to pay and they need, today, legal work. The more work you put behind it, you can represent your facts better, you can get a better outcome. That is the state of the world we live in today.

To account for this, lawyers understand people can't pay $500, $600 an hour on a blank check for however long the case might take. So the plaintiff industry came about working on contingency law. What this means is: they only get paid when they win the case for the client. And this is what's allowed them to even have any sort of level playing field with people versus institutions.

What Eve is aiming to do is really handle that whole thing end to end — how do you represent a client all the way from the very first call to getting them a settlement? How do you do that end-to-end thing purely with AI and give that to the lawyers to then amplify the outcomes they can actually provide. That's what Eve is doing. We're really arming — you know, think about giving David a slingshot to take down Goliath. That's what we're doing.

市场失灵：供需曲线与被压抑的正义

So what I find fascinating about this is — I kind of think about Econ 101, where you have a supply curve that goes up and to the right.

Right. Price and quantity. As the price goes up, the quantity supplied goes up. If I can make $100,000 by doing something, wow, I'm totally in. But the demand curve is the opposite direction. Price goes down, quantity demanded goes up considerably.

If I think about applying this to law — what if I have $1,000 of damages? I can call a lawyer, even for contingency. They might not want to take my case because if they take a third of the outcome, they want a bigger case. It's going to require a certain amount of work.

AI really liberates these market failures to a certain extent. You mentioned giving David a bigger slingshot. If I have $1,000 of damages I certainly can't pay $1,200 an hour for a lawyer, so I'm out. Enter contingency law. The problem is the settlement might not be big enough. The lawyer might want to serve me, but he or she has paralegals they have to pay. But if the software can do the work, now the market opportunity is so much bigger. You can actually deliver justice for a lot of people that otherwise were priced out — because how are you priced out of contingency? It's not really in the interest of a lawyer. They want to serve a thousand customers, but they can't. They have to focus on the biggest ones to the detriment of the smaller ones.

That is exactly right. I think that is the actual market problem we have today.

If you go back to first principles — if you're a person, you deserve a great lawyer to represent your case. And usually you only need a lawyer when your back is against the wall. The best of us, the worst of us, comes out this time, and we don't have the skill sets to represent ourselves. That's why this whole profession exists. That's why the legal system is about a third of our government.

Today what's happening is: because lawyers still need to get paid, it's still bottlenecked on legal work. Today, if a lawyer doesn't make at least $5,000 in fees off a case, they do not take it on. That is the market dynamics today. And even at $5,000, they're losing money on a lot of cases. They're really banking on few cases paying out very large.

They're not even guaranteed to win, period. So they already take that — that's the contingency aspect. But it's kind of like, even if I win, I lose, because my costs of carrying the case are going to be higher than the actual potential outcome even if I win.

That's exactly right. Think about it — most people here have been in a car accident, a fender bender of some sort. If it's below the deductible, no lawyer in America will touch that case. It's just not economically worth it. Even if the deductible's $3,000, $4,000, to an individual, that is the difference between a paycheck being gone versus not. And there's no representation they can get for that.

为什么 96% 的劳动纠纷案件被拒绝

The same thing — and the reason is actually from their side. Let's say you've been getting harassed at work and your employer could stop it. In the hospitality industry, you could tell your customers, "Hey, don't harass my employees," and change processes to make that happen. Today that doesn't happen. Because when that person calls, the lawyer on the other side has to pick up a call, field that call — that's about 30 to 45 minutes. After that, go do legal research. In employment in America, pretty much everything's at-will, and you have to tie a problem to a protected clause — it's called causes of action.

That work requires them to go spend 10 hours to research case law, research the facts, go back and forth and ask them more follow-up questions, see if they qualify. And while they spent all that time, they might still realize, "Hey, this doesn't even make me $5,000." So that is why 96% of cases on the labor/employment side, for example, get rejected. You can never find anybody to represent unless you come out of pocket. In many cases, people don't have money to come out of pocket, so you just kind of take it, unless something really egregious happens.

That is the current state, and it's all bottlenecked on legal labor. This is what Eve is meant to do. How do you now take that 10 hours — now it's immediate with Eve? A call comes in, Eve actually answers the call and automatically uses its insights on the law firm to know whether or not this is a case the lawyer has to take on, and then hit the ground running with a demand or the initial preliminary work done. That completely changes the economics of that type of case.

We're still at the very beginning stages. Eve is getting more and more capable of handling outcomes end-to-end over a very long horizon. These cases take six months to a year, and probably a thousand actions, back-and-forths. As the accuracy of Eve is getting higher and higher, this long horizon becomes possible. The more this becomes possible, even more complicated work gets tied down to a constant case. So now all these people without representation get representation.

If you really ask yourself — how many times in your life, if asking for legal help wasn't a friction point, would you have asked it? That number is way higher than we think.

Blue Bottle 的那位 Trial Attorney

So it's a funny story. This is a true story.

I was in Blue Bottle, a little coffee shop in Los Altos, and I was explaining Eve to somebody probably nine months ago. Most people think of AI as like, "Oh, you're going to fire everybody and cut costs" — all about cost savings. And it's like, no, actually, if I use Eve, I make a lot more money for my firm. It's not because I'm cutting costs. It's because I can take on more cases. It's actually revenue expansion.

So I'm explaining this as an outsider investor can, not as well as you probably would. At the end of this — we were talking about many topics but Eve came up — and this guy comes up to me, he looks a little angry. He has a big dog, and I'm kind of afraid of big dogs. He was like, "What was that company you were talking about?" I was like, "Uh-oh, is he going to get mad?" He's like, "I'm a trial attorney. I want to try it."

Oh, great. So I got you a new customer there. Thank you.

律所经济学：从账单到结果

The whole point is that you expand the revenue opportunity. Everybody has driven on 101 or I-95 — the corridor that goes from Florida all the way up to Maine. Half of the ads are for trial attorneys, plaintiff law. They're obviously advertising there because they want to get called.

What do the economics look like? This is why Eve is so fascinating — I have to turn down 90% of the leads that I'm getting, I assume. I spend money on a billboard, I get lots of inbound. How many of those turn into cases? How many of those cases turn into revenue? Maybe kind of a before-and-after, because you're not a cost savings play for lawyers — you're a revenue expansion play.

That's exactly right.

When most people drive by, they see the face and they forget about the people behind them and the amount of work every single call actually takes. The math on the law firm side is very simple: the more people you represent, typically speaking, the more money you make. Because you can take on more people — and you honestly are denying and not taking on many cases because they're too expensive to take on — the demand from their perspective is not really a constraint. It's really the supply of labor.

Different firms are in different realms of problems, where the bottleneck keeps shifting. A small firm might just have one attorney with a case manager or office manager that fields the initial call and just notes it down, and then the lawyer responds back in their free time — kind of chaotically running around. Then there's a next level: they find a way to systematize it. They have an intake team, a call center that intakes it — now that becomes a new bottleneck. When you increase your marketing spend, let's say you looked particularly attractive on that billboard and a lot of people are calling in — suddenly that team is overwhelmed, and you're limited again by how many people you can represent.

This is the daily challenge these small businesses are dealing with. They're small businesses — they're not massive enterprises. They want to represent individuals, and everyone here went to law school, not business school. They want to be there for the people. We're basically consolidating all of that into the Eve platform, such that they are getting pulled in only for what they need to — their lawyer insights, their particular insights on how they take this case. Eve keeps raising the floor. How do I take it from this floor to the next level? That is where I believe all lawyers should spend time — talking to their people and helping get client outcomes.

洛杉矶那家律所：从 100 到 500

Well, this is kind of the market failure point. I could serve all 5,000 leads that came in if only I could hire a paralegal for 12 cents per hour. But there's no labor market that could actually function. With AI, now I can. Do you have anecdotes of just like a before-and-after?

Yeah. One firm in LA went from managing about 100 clients per attorney to 500.

Wow.

That is a type of thing that is possible. To their credit, they worked really hard to achieve this. They utilized Eve up to the max — all the way from intake, fielding the call, doing qualification, automatically removing all the relay problem of passing things from one attorney to another to a case manager. All that is now handled within agents in Eve. All the way to settlement, where it's actually briefs before they go to a mediator discussion that tells you: here's what you need to focus on, here's what the settlement outcome should look like for cases like this that we worked on, and here are the tactics you used before that got you here.

That is what the future looks like. It's truly moving the case forward continuously, and you're helping it do a better job than it could do by itself. That is, I think, the future of law — where you as a lawyer are really going to look more like a data scientist and engineer, engineering something to be better and better. That is a shift the top law firms on Eve mentally kind of go through.

被 VC 误读的"小软件市场"

Well, I kind of think of — if you look at your average law firm, they don't really know AI. This is kind of an interesting take on the world of AI-enabled applications in general. What was the software stack for law before? If you're a big firm like Wilson Sonsini, probably the most important thing is your time tracker, because you're billing by the hour. If you're in contingency law, your time matters but you're not billing your customers on that. You probably need to have — each case, here's how much money I'm spending on the case. But I imagine your primary tool was Microsoft Word.

This is how VCs would have gotten this industry wrong before: "Oh well, the software market for plaintiff law is small. They all buy Microsoft Office." Microsoft Office is kind of expensive, so therefore the software spend is in the tens of billions of dollars a year or something — seemingly comically small. But wait a minute — the outcomes that they deliver are in the hundreds of billions of dollars a year. They can't deliver more outcomes because they're really constrained on labor. And they can't hire labor for 12 cents an hour because it doesn't exist. So it turns out the software market is kind of like this shadow labor market, and it's massively bigger than anybody would have expected.

In order for me to go into business — I graduated from law school, I want to be in this particular subsector of the field — what was my software stack?

You know, this is the unfortunate thing about plaintiff law and institutions.

Historically, plaintiff law really didn't need more than a cell phone email address. Honestly, even Microsoft Word — some people on the solo side would not buy it for cost reasons.

It's because if you think about it, you actually don't do that much redlining. It's a trust-boundary situation. One side is kind of in opposition to the other side. So you're not really collaborating in the same way that you are when you're doing contract review.

So that was kind of it. No software really solved their core problem, which is exactly what you mentioned — their labor constraint. That is the core of how they do anything at all. Because they have labor and they're good at managing their labor, they found a way to solve every problem to them that looked like a labor solve. That's how they've grown up.

As a result, a lot of resources on software went towards defense/institutions, because that's where the budgets were — for Harvey, really any legal software company today. Vast majority of them are on the defense side because that's where the budgets are. That's what's easy to build for, easy to get money for.

On the plaintiff side, these are small businesses that are watching their pocketbooks every month. If you're not driving outcomes for them from day one, you're out. You're not getting renewed. They're going to curse you out. Anything they can do, they're going to come after you. That's what's made things so difficult.

But what we realized is: their core problem is — we know what their incentives are. They want to represent more people. They want to win. We can do that now. The beauty of software today is: once you do a task manually — even tasks that include crunching new pieces of data and transforming it, which is kind of what AI is really good at — you can now encode it as a process. That is a fundamentally new shift that has never happened before. That's what they were trying to do with people-operations, but it never worked because every single case is still different enough that you can't do it — it's still bottlenecked on hiring smart enough people to be able to handle it. Now one smart person can actually handle, like we talked about, 500 different cases of very different facts, very different situations. How do you even keep that in your brain? It's hard. But now you don't have to.

为什么单纯的智能不够：Albert Einstein 的悖论

One of the things a lot of founders are thinking about right now at the application layer is: uh-oh, maybe I'm roadkill from the big guys. The labs that produce the intelligence — maybe they're going to go tackle my space next and I'm toast.

There are many ways of defending against that, but defending kind of sells it short. If you have a network effect, or if you have data that actually nobody else has, you can deliver better outcomes. Who cares if everybody uses ChatGPT or Claude behind the scenes? Why is Eve better than just raw intelligence, and how does it get better because of the practitioners that use the product?

Yeah, we're betting on these models getting better and better.

Our value is exactly that. If you have a thousand Albert Einsteins to work with to do litigation — or the best attorney ever to do every single task — we would take it. The problem is: if you drop Albert Einstein into a law firm today, he will not be productive for quite some time. That is a general problem that Eve is solving.

Why won't that person be productive? It's due to a number of things. In plaintiff law, the vast majority of data is actually non-scrapable. Less than a percent of cases actually settle and get turned into case opinions. Vast majority settle pre-demand or pre-litigation, and some even before that — where it's actually just a negotiation of, "Hey, this is how I was wronged, please fix it."

To make that concrete: I'm in a car accident, I'm not at fault. The adversary — the other side's insurance company — is like, "Oh, you weren't that hurt, we'll give you a dollar." They always try to deny, deny, deny. Rule number one: if an insurance carrier is denied. Rule number two: denied. It just goes on. Those are the rules of insurance carriers.

So now I hire a lawyer to actually get what I'm owed, because I actually am injured and my car is actually totaled, and they just don't want to pay me. You get a settlement — doesn't go to case, doesn't go to actual trial. But Geico actually did pay $29,000. That's very useful information.

Insurance is the one that's dealing with 100,000 different lawyers. They have the shared community, they know all the cases. But because it's charted across all the different local firms, they don't know exactly Geico's every single move.

That's exactly right. They even have ominous-sounding software like Colossus, which tracks — they try to basically say, "A broken thumb, this is how much we think it's worth." Which, in their defense, is a hard thing to do. But they are also saying, "This is how much we can get away with giving them away for," irrespective of that individual's actual need. That's what the legal system is meant to fix.

跨辖区上下文：Eve 真正学到的东西

The interesting bit and the challenge: if you go and Google "how do you write an amazing demand letter for State Farm for soft tissue injury cases" — that today exists nowhere. Even for a new paralegal that is joining a plaintiff firm, this is something they have to learn. On top of that, it gets more complicated: when you're in a local jurisdiction, the local environment — the court system, your opposing counsel — they all behave a little differently, and that context matters too.

What Eve is doing is turning this historically incredibly difficult-to-utilize, multi-attribute, multi-dimensional information into: what is the best thing I can do at this particular moment to improve the outcome of the case? And that same question is repeated thousands of times during the case. A human brain is just not capable of keeping all of that in mind. But AI is. That is the type of data we help build for law firms, and they're seeing the immediate value from it. The first place where they see value is of course intake: who do I even take on? Who am I good at representing? And then keep getting better.

数据主权与共享：律所间的"旅行与分享"

I imagine — these aren't giant firms. If I'm a lawyer in New Jersey with a four-attorney practice, and over there is a lawyer in Arizona with a seven-attorney practice, but their counterparties tend to be State Farm and Geico. At the limit it's actually fine to share information. How do you think about data? I imagine this is always hard for companies when you're getting off the ground — "No, this is my data." But there's also a give-to-get.

We've largely followed the rules of engagement that already exist in this industry, but we've amplified it with software. The rules of engagement: for their own cases, they want to be very private — that is important by law. It's attorney-client privilege, and we don't train on that data, ever.

However, what attorneys also do, to share this knowledge — they actually travel. They attend CLE and they share tactics with each other on how they went up against State Farm's X and Y defense, because State Farm repeats that defense across the board. Not picking on State Farm — anyone is fair game here. That is what they're already doing.

So we hire our own attorneys and track success rates of cases for our platform. If you're using Eve, you should have more success. That's what we track. We have this product called Auditor, which actually analyzes every single case through every single page overnight and looks for situations that a perfect attorney would catch every time. Across the board, unfortunately, vast majority of cases — almost every single case — has missed information. Now that's no longer a thing.

法律的未来：对抗性博弈与 ADR

Maybe talk about the future of where things go. On the one hand, I can imagine a world where one of these days Geico is going to get a little bit smarter. "Deny, deny, deny" is how they got smart before, right — they realized it is an adversarial system. Each party is kind of fighting each other, but they're going to get superpowers.

You see this playing out a little bit with Muse and all the consumer agents — "I want a reservation at this restaurant that's impossible to get and they have a human answering the phone. I can DDoS them now that I have to pay one penny per hour." Eventually they're going to realize they're getting DDoSed and prevent it.

How do you think about your client's adversaries? How are they adapting? It was great for Geico when they could say "You have $2,000 of damages" — the consumer is like, "Yeah, I did have maybe $2,500 of damages." They never really had to worry about that before because of the quantum. Now, unfortunately for them, but fortunately for the Davids of the world, people that are actually aggrieved — now they can fight back. You mentioned long-horizon agents. What does the practice of law look like when a lot of the stuff can actually be done by AI?

My framework for thinking about this is: ultimately when you have an individual, they're going to need representation.

Whether that representation — who does the work on the representation — you can assume it's 99% AI, maybe 99.9% AI, there's always going to be that little bit that is the human touch. We do believe that people are going to make a positive difference to the outcomes of the case.

What you have on the defense side, or really the institution side, is what's always happened: they have more resources, more money, more time — which is actually another weapon they have, which is quite powerful when individuals are in debt to pay their fees. That is a strength they're working with, and they're relying on centralization and standardization. On the defense side you have an attorney fighting your case and pushing them to get to litigation.

I think a lot more cases are going to have teeth, and all the routine back-and-forths are going to happen through agents talking to agents. It's crazy future world, but I think that's where we're headed. The difference-maker is: what does the attorney understand about that client, that set of facts, and their local environment of who they're going up against locally in that defense firm? And they're using that insight to make a difference for their client. I don't think that ever goes away.

In fact, we're seeing already many customers on Eve are actually choosing to spend more time on their trial work. Because it actually enables that. Previously, going to trial took down your entire firm — suddenly you're just spending all your time doing trial prep, interviewing juries, you want things to settle. It's more of a settlement motion.

Instead, I think things are going more into real advocacy. How do I actually make our point known? My client is against the wall, they're doing bad things, doing good things — how do I represent them in what actually matters for them?

诉讼融资与数据科学化

I imagine this is kind of the data science side of what you're doing as well — with this giant data set that's probably never been accumulated before, because as you mentioned it's so bespoke. There's no communal repository for all of the settlement amounts.

I've seen this with litigation finance a little bit. If I'm a trial attorney, and I'm not getting paid by the hour by my client, where do I pay myself and my staff and my office rent? There are companies that will show up and say, "I will fund this case." They're counting on you winning it. They do all sorts of clever things — "Here's the judge, here's this." They're using data. Those guys have been very data-science forward. But historically this data just like never really lived anywhere. Now that it does, you can make smarter decisions as an attorney. Do I take it to trial or do I accept the settlement? Geico offered me $12,000 — should I push back and fight for 15? Should I take it to trial and try to win $100K? How do I make those decisions?

That's exactly right. We can help them make the best decision in every single case, and know when an optimal outcome has been achieved.

It's still the attorney's responsibility to push it even further. That is what I meant by "data-science-like work" — you're using the power of software to do work you never even thought to do, to improve the outcome.

法律系统的 5 年展望：ADR 与自动化争议解决

Where does the legal system go? I was having some trouble with Wells Fargo and I'm like, "I've tried for four hours to do this, I'm just going to sue them." I went to ChatGPT. I was like, "sue Wells Fargo." Four hours later, it had sued Wells Fargo. It actually found a process server. I got the notice — like, we're going to court — but the date is in February.

Another similar vein is happening with patent law. Before, it's so much work to go file a patent. Now it's less work to file a patent, but you still have the USPTO, which is the bottleneck. If you were to prognosticate — where does the legal industry go now that AI is becoming table stakes? If you fast-forward 5 years, what does it look like? What's similar, what's different?

Most likely, I think it's inevitable that you're going to have to create systems where not everything goes to the court system.

This already is a framework that is used in law. For some types of veterans' affairs cases, that goes through a different committee. For labor and employment, that goes through EEOC in a lot of cases before it goes through — and employers have figured out different ways to mediate and have arbitration that doesn't necessarily go through the court system.

This is the framework that naturally evolves. I expect that to happen more and more. The tweak that's going to happen is: for some pockets of it, we're probably going to go through some version of ADR — automated dispute resolution — where AI-enabled mediators, or central parties that have a neutral view of both sides, are going to use AI to really speed up how they come up with judgment. I don't think the judgment will really be replaced, but what they will get is a set of facts that shows historically here's how this happened, here's how this happened. It's up to them to remove the biases that might exist. I think we're just going to spend more and more time on that side of things.

小律所能变成十亿美元级公司吗？

Do you think the small law firms get bigger? If I could only handle 100 cases per attorney, now I can handle 500, but in the future maybe 5,000 — why do I limit my office to a very small New Jersey location? Maybe I should go more broad.

You could have larger, almost corporate-like law entities. The biggest trial attorney firm is Morgan and Morgan — they have billions of dollars in revenue — but your average firm is quite small. You could imagine, powered by Eve, the small firm could actually become a billion-dollar revenue business. It's kind of like venture outcomes versus what you'd call lifestyle business. (You were a VC once — how you know that term.) Somewhat pejorative term for "you make profits." But is that a reasonable take, that some of these small guys can actually... I mean obviously you can't go public as a law firm for now — maybe in Arizona you can — but is there a chance for some of these local mom-and-pops to become very very large institutions?

I think the transformation that's going to happen is: a lot of these law firms are going to look more like software companies.

I think they're going to finally participate in the software revolution that's been happening for the last 30 years that they've been left out of. If you deep-dive, you'll understand why. Let's say you have a $25,000 settlement. The attorney gets maybe a third of that — call it $8,000 for simplicity. Of that $8,000, about half of it goes towards labor spend, 30% goes to marketing, and the rest maybe is profit. Because of that business, it is so difficult to reinvest back into servicing your next client better. The only way you can really do that is by hiring a better attorney today.

What changes is: now they can actually accrue a database and data set that is unique to them, that gets them results that are better than their competitors for a subset of law. This is specialization. Historically this industry already went through that — 30 years ago, there was your neighborhood lawyer that handled everything, from employment cases to IP to what have you.

Yes, exactly.

Now what we have are specializations of practice areas. You have someone really good at IP, someone that's good at employment. Now it's getting even more specific — someone that's good at, let's say, nursery birth defects or something along those lines. I can anticipate that to go even another level, where now someone could get really good at soft tissue injury cases that involve X and Y fact patterns, and advertising for those cases might be a lot more cost-effective than some other larger firm like Morgan & Morgan just showing their billboard everywhere.

Get good at something locally and then expand across the entire country because you have such high competence around that one field.

That's exactly right. We're also seeing the opposite — working with some on the scale of Morgan & Morgan. Some are actually coming together. The ones that got so big are actually going around buying other law firms, because they realized with Eve they can very quickly consolidate what used to be a very painful reintegration process. Now it can be done on exactly what the client wants, which is: the client wants a legal outcome, and Eve is made just for that. By doing that, they get to largely work away from a lot of the change management, workforce changes, operations changes, because Eve handles a lot of that for them. They can speed up their time to making that acquisition worth it.

结果导向定价：原告律师从一开始就在做的事

Well, the funny thing is that there's this movement underway to outcome-oriented pricing. SaaS used to be per seat per month. I used to joke it was the "Tall Grande Venti" model of software selling. You go to any SaaS company's website — this is why Claude can clone them all so readily, they all look the same — "$79 a month, $99 a month, $129 a month." Tall Grande Venti. And it was per seat.

Look at a company like Zendesk, which had $2 billion of ARR when they were last a public company. They were taken private by Permira and Hellman & Friedman. Now they're like, "Uh-oh, how many seats do you need? Maybe zero. We need to deliver outcomes." So everybody in the software world, a lot of AI companies, "We deliver outcomes, we charge for outcomes."

The interesting thing is that the form of law that you focused on was always outcome-oriented from the very beginning. You have other types of law that are not outcome-oriented, where I guarantee all the clients would much, much, much prefer that it was outcome-based.

Sometimes it's tricky. Like I have a trust-and-estate attorney at McDermott Will & Emery. She's very very good. She's like so expensive. I guess my outcome is my death. So I don't know if I want that. But you would prefer to just say there's a fixed cost. There's often this data asymmetry — in their defense, the reason to charge by the hour is not so much to rip off the client, but there's data asymmetry between what I want in my head and how I articulate it. Maybe the scope of the project is changing over time.

Other forms of law — I would argue they probably should look more like plaintiff's law. They should have outcome-oriented pricing as well. Or immigration law — that should be outcome-oriented. Everything should be outcome-oriented pricing. But it's hard because there's a data deficiency, in terms of how will I win this case on behalf of the defendant. How do you think about other forms of law? You could probably expand well beyond plaintiff law. Plaintiff's law was ahead of everything we're seeing right now — everybody wants outcomes, nobody wants to pay for the ingredients. This was the only field, probably of business, where it was always outcome-oriented. But shouldn't other parts of law work that way?

That is our exact belief as well.

The hard part has been: it is hard. When you're on the defense side, or even the plaintiff side, the question around a new case: is it 10 hours of work, 100 hours of work? In many cases you really don't know until you take it on. For plaintiffs, that is why we had to go so deep into each practice area, into achieving outcomes. We were doing what is now coined "long-horizon agents" like last year — that's just what was needed to drive results. Now it's getting better and better to actually drive legal outcomes.

Ultimately I think what is needed for democratizing law is: from a set of facts, you need to know how much compute resources you need to arrive at an outcome. That happens through both aggregation of and better usage of data, and better usage of actually running the compute to achieve a set outcome. We're doing both. That is why we're laser-focused on outcomes.

Eventually this David-versus-Goliath thing is happening everywhere. It's not just in BigLaw or in-house legal — those are just where the budgets are. They actually can write basically a blank check for an intermittent period of time, and the forcing function around "how much is this actually worth in outcomes to me" is not known. You know this — like when you go fundraise you might get hit with a $100K check. What is the exact outcome of that? It's very hard to know what the value is. But that is the only way they can price today. That's because they don't know what the expected value of their work actually is.

That's the asymmetry as well. "Okay, you need to hire a lawyer for your Series C." What does that mean? It could be very very simple, or very complicated. So it's very hard to have a flat rate.

That's right. They could get burned in — well, they can't get burned in the low direction. "I charge you $25,000, I spent an hour on this." But they could get burned if "I have to now spend 4,000 hours of attorney time, I could lose money on this." Which, of course — every single firm — oh, well, actually, like as you know in corporate law, these are loss-leader products, and then you try to make it up on the M&A or IPO. Obviously a little bit different than plaintiff law.

Eve 自己的定价演化

How do you guys charge? I imagine you had — it's not like on day one when you started the business you knew exactly what you were going to charge for, what type of customer. I imagine your thinking has evolved on this as well.

Absolutely.

From actually, weirdly enough, from day one — we started probably with the "Tall Grande Venti" model, because we didn't know any better. As we dug into it, we realized what they care about is outcomes. What they care about is: how do I serve more clients? That actually forced us to be outcome-based from very early days — we're talking like a year and a half ago, which is pretty funny that's "early" in today's world.

AI time — like dog years times 100.

Exactly. There's so much room to grow. Now that we talked about that value diagram — a third goes to attorneys, half of that is labor — that is half they don't have to spend anymore. How do you actually turn that into something more useful? The best way to get more useful work is actually to spend it, weirdly, on more tokens — more work that Eve can do to make more money for your firm.

A lot of the market dynamics that is helping us is exactly this. We actually believe the billable-hour model — I don't think it's going to die completely, but I think it's going to be on the way of the seat-based pricing model. For some subset of law, that is probably the best way you can charge for the work, because it's very difficult to know value until an outcome many years later. But for a lot of it, that's not true anymore. For a lot of it, you actually know what the outcomes are. You should be able to take your work down to an amortized amount and deliver that back. That is what we are betting on. This is why we focused on delivering legal outcomes from day one, end-to-end, in such a way that it is as simple as a lawyer saying "Here's this client I got in, give it to Eve. Eve will pull you in when you're needed, and you're good to go."

增长的瓶颈：工程师

Plaintiff attorneys are supply-constrained, not demand-constrained. Many of them are, because they have this infinite influx of clients that they can't serve because the math doesn't really work in terms of CAC versus LTV. The old-fashioned thing for any business applies to them as well. Where are your constraints? What holds you back from growing faster? You're obviously growing incredibly fast. What are your rate limiters? What do you need as inputs to grow faster?

It's really fascinating.

A lot of the legal benchmarks — even benchmarks that are shared publicly, that Anthropic, OpenAI, many of whom we're working very closely with are working on — care a lot about almost a single outcome. Here's a task, did it kind of do mostly OK. The world is now moving into agentic work. For us, the only thing that ever mattered was the agentic outcomes. The end outcome here is: today we're still at the point with technology and processes where there's still a decent amount of human touches needed per case. But by doing more and more work, we've been drastically reducing that month over month.

In our industry, we need to do that per case type. For every single case, we're learning that like a science. How do you actually resolve this case? How do you build a mini attorney brain that is capable of crunching all these data points to that resolution, and driving it across the board, working with all the tools they have access to including Claude and whatnot to drive that outcome? That is a really hard problem. We're largely limited by engineers at this point. We have a limitless number of things to do to drive this forward.

The other fun part is: we have demand. The moment we are able to deliver on, let's say, moving vehicle accident cases end-to-end, the amount of value that gets unlocked for the world from that is in the hundreds of billions of dollars. And that's just one subtype.

一次完全自主的端到端案件：还差一点点

Actually, that's a great question. Have you had a fully autonomous end-to-end case? Answer phone, onboard client, get check from Geico — has that happened end-to-end?

Not yet, but we're close. That is why we need the engineers. To put things in perspective, a single case has probably 10,000 back-and-forths. Here's how you think about it: a client comes in, let's say it's a PI case. Now you have medical records. You have to actually outbound-call insurance companies and healthcare companies to get hold of the records that the clients already had. That actually takes two weeks today.

With Eve outbound agents — we actually have voice AI that can do the outbound call, and funnily enough that's an area where we're already seeing agents talking to other agents, and learning how to get past each other. Which is hilarious. That is one step that's needed. Then from there you have to create a document and actually have a conversation with the other side. All of these are tasks we are completing end-to-end. Today there's a little bit of touch required where someone makes an outcome better, or does something a little better. But exactly what we're building right now is: how do you actually drive this whole thing end-to-end? We're seeing early signs of that, where it's actually live in some customers.

对手方的反应：感恩节前夜的 Discovery

Have you seen — going back to the defense side and their Colossus of information — have you seen their reaction change in general? "Uh-oh, these guys contacted me with this. I always need to settle because they probably have pretty firm rules about this." They don't just randomly make it up as you go, I would assume, because they're dealing with this tens of thousands of times per year. If I'm Geico — "Oh, you demanded this much. Well, my first attempt is going to settle here. But if their costs go down, maybe that changes." Have you seen any change in reaction?

I would say largely the defense side very much still works on an hourly business model. They haven't quite caught up to the same pace as our attorneys. There's a lot of pricing asymmetry here.

What the defense used to do for this one law firm we're working with: they would wait and push out discovery request dates until a day before Thanksgiving or a major holiday. Then send discovery there, because they would know the person would go on vacation and be stuck with all this workload over that vacation, and they wouldn't do a good job at it, or would rush it.

Because it was such a repeated tactic, they created an agent on Eve to respond the same day. Next time this came through, they responded immediately with the responses — and the defense were like, "What is going on here?" The tactics don't—

There's so many variants of that happening now, which is causing the defense to realize: wait, is this what happens when the other side has resources? Oh, crap. And that's what's fun to see.

结语

Well, Jay, this is a fantastic conversation. I learned a lot. Didn't realize there were 10,000 touches every time you went through a case. Really fascinating and delighted to be your partner. Bring Eve to the next 10,000 firms.

Thank you. We still have so much more to go. We've probably helped a couple hundred thousand clients today, and we have hundreds of millions to touch. I would love to be making a difference in their life every day. If that's of interest, please come join Eve.

Awesome. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、被遮蔽的"影子劳动力市场"：软件市场的真实体积比任何人想象的都大一个数量级
最反直觉的观察藏在 Alex 的一句玩笑里："VC 以前会说原告律师的软件市场很小，他们都买 Microsoft Office。" 这句话揭示了一个被整个行业集体误读的事实——**所谓"小软件市场"其实是一个被定价机制隐藏起来的巨型劳动力市场**。
原告律师行业每年创造数千亿美元的赔付结果，但软件支出只有几十亿。为什么？因为真正的消耗品是人力。Eve 的本质不是在卖软件，而是在**出售一个"每小时 0.12 美元的律师助理劳动力"——这个劳动力市场在物理世界从未存在过，因此也从未被计入 TAM**。这与 Uber 当年打开的"愿意为私家车付钱但买不起黑车"的中间市场结构同构：**AI 时代的 TAM 不是现有软件支出的扩大，而是"物理世界因价格而根本不存在的那部分需求"的货币化**。
跨领域连接：这几乎复刻了云计算早期对 IT 预算的"小市场"误读。AWS 刚出来时，分析师看传统服务器市场觉得"也就那样"，结果真正爆发的是**那些永远不会买服务器的创业者**——他们过去根本不在样本里。

item.title: [Business of Sport] Man United’s Doom Spiral, Burnley on the Brink, & The WSL’s Reality Check
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

杠杆收购的"自噬"机制：资产用自己的血买下自己

伯恩利那笔交易最惊人的地方不是债务规模，而是结构的自噬性——俱乐部用自己银行里的 6000-7000 万英镑现金做"首付"，用自己的球场（Turf Moor）做抵押贷款，然后再让自己背上这笔新债。这不是传统意义上的收购，而是一场精心设计的寄生式所有权转移：买家没花自己的钱，被买方却成了融资主体。有意思的是，这个机制与某些跨国企业的反向并购，甚至某些高控制度组织的财务捕获手段，在结构上完全同构——目标主体为自己的被捕获出资。曼联在这个结构下还能撑住，是因为它拥有近似于"主权信用"的品牌等级（10 亿债务 vs 50 亿资产 + 6.77 亿年收入，杠杆率仅为营收的 1.7 倍）；而伯恩利的债务已经达到了营收的 7 倍（parachute 结束之后更惨），这不是风险，是一台正在慢动作内爆的机器。

曼联球迷的"剧场化支持"：一种被低估的抗议语法

Carrick 被鼓掌下场的那一刻，发生的事情比"球迷支持教练"要微妙得多。那其实是一种反向献祭——球迷用对边缘人物的爱，来放大对核心权力的恨。这与人类学家吉拉尔（René Girard）描述的"替罪羊机制"在方向上正好相反：传统的替罪羊是把共同体的焦虑投射到无辜者身上以恢复秩序，而曼联球迷是把本应给教练的愤怒"卸载"干净，再把总量全部指向 Glazer 家族与 Ratcliffe。这是一种成熟度极高的集体政治语言，但它的致命弱点在于——它没有释放阀。可以被赶走的人（主帅、技术总监），球迷不想赶；真正想赶走的人（股东），赶不走。于是鼓掌的声浪越大，系统的憋压越高。节目里 Charlie 说的"dog years"（俱乐部时间以狗年计）其实点出了关键：这种压力一旦累积超过某个阈值，会越过"更换主帅"这种便宜释放阀，直接撞上更昂贵的东西——比如整个管理层的信任链。

WSL 与 LIV 高尔夫的隐秘同构：被金融化的部落情感

这期节目最反直觉的观察是——女超的问题恰恰是因为它获得了"太多"主流媒体曝光。它跳过了"地下生长→部落形成→破圈"的自然演化路径，被直接空投进成熟男足产品的分发管道（大球场、黄金时段、国家电视台）。这与 LIV 高尔夫、Quibi、乃至某种版本的元宇宙叙事都是同一套模式：用供给端的资本密度去模拟需求端的有机热度。你把 VC 的"种子期—加速期—收获期"模型往女超上一套就看得清清楚楚：23/24 赛季场均 7600 人 → 26/27 赛季场均 5200 人，这是一条在"加速期"反而出现负增长的曲线。任何风险投资人看到这种图形都只会蹦出一个词：失败模式。而真正扎心的跨领域对照是女子橄榄球——同样的性别、同样的"小众"起点、同样是传统上男性主导的身体对抗项目——却在没有空降资本的情况下年年保持 25% 的复合增长，连在加拿大打的客场都爆满。这件事说明一个残忍的真相：部落忠诚度无法用 PPT 买到，只能用时间长出来。资本可以买演员、买球场、买媒体版面，但买不到那种"我爸带我爸爸的爸爸带我来过这里"的继承性情感基础设施。

一个被忽视的系统性模式：三个故事其实是同一个故事

你注意到了吗？曼联、伯恩利、女超——三个看似不相关的话题，共同指向的其实是同一个病症："叙事资本"对"物质资本"的强行扭曲。Glazer 的叙事是"全球品牌永远赢"；Alan Pace 的叙事是"数据驱动的中型俱乐部升级样板"；女超的叙事是"性别平权的下一个蓝海"。三个叙事都足够漂亮到吸引钱，但三个物质现实都在反过来嘲笑叙事。而最关键的是——叙事资本一旦被注入，就会产生"沉没叙事"效应：所有参与者都被迫继续讲下去，因为承认叙事错误的声誉成本，高于继续燃烧真金白银的现金成本。Velocity Capital 两年不交账目，本质上就是当叙事无法再翻译成数字时的沉默。所谓"We expect to make the necessary filings in coming weeks"，翻译成人话就是：故事还没编完。

Why Clubs Don't Fire the Manager (Until They Must)

Yeah, sure. I mean, one of them — look, very, very often football club boards don't really want to get rid of their manager. It's expensive, and you know that the risk of replacement is high, and that there's going to be a lot of friction in the short to medium term in that replacement. But sometimes, effectively, the manager's position becomes untenable because the relationship with the crowd's broken down. And that, in turn, makes it very difficult to actually win matches at home, because the atmosphere is toxic, the players can feel it, the players can sense it, and the players start to feel, well, probably the manager's not going to be here much longer, so they stop listening to him. And eventually, almost your hand gets forced by events.

I often say that football club time in a football club is like dog years. So it's like a pressure cooker where everything happens much quicker than it does in normal life. Because, you know, results — which are very public in a football club, whereas in normal businesses, results are something that you see when a company announces its results, you know, six months, a year later — in the football club, the performance is out there, right in front of people, every single week. And that just accelerates the pace at which that pressure intensifies to the point where you really can't do anything about it.

In the case of United, obviously they started the season with absolutely no intention whatsoever of getting rid of Michael Carrick. But... Obviously, the run of results and the trend of results and the trend of performances are such that normally you would at this point see a change. But in this case, they've in a way been able to stick with it because of the support the crowd has for him.

The Theatre of Supportive Protest

Ironically, that support is almost... being theatrically ramped up as a counterpoint to what they're saying about their lords and masters, the owners and directors of the club. So it's a very instinctive way of United, who historically have always been a very supportive crowd. They've not been a crowd who have called for people's heads all that much. It's a way of them saying — this isn't about us, we're a supportive crowd. This isn't about him, he's a good guy. This is about you guys.

Now, of course, the problem is that the release valve for that is an awful lot harder, right? Because changing the manager and changing the narrative from "we need change" to "now we're going to get change" — then fans start to become interested in who the replacement's going to be. That person then comes in. Often you'll find the players want to impress that new manager because they want to play, fundamentally. And everyone's attention then switches on to — is this guy going to be successful? I'm not just talking about United, I'm talking about any football club.

In this situation, it almost feels like the natural thing to do is to have a clear-out at boardroom level.

You know, firing a manager is painful, it's expensive, and it does cause short-term friction. But fundamentally, it happens. So I think there are two elements to it. On the one hand, one of the signs of a well-run and healthy club is when effectively discipline is observed at all levels. Because that discipline is redolent of a respect within the club for people, the jobs that they're doing, the challenges that they face, which are not always jobs and challenges that are necessarily all that well known by the outside world, but people inside them know. People inside these clubs know. So the players — particularly the senior players, and we are talking about senior players here — inside the club will know that Man United's hands are tied in the transfer market by the financial setup there. So when they start coming out and saying those things, that reflects two things, I think.

Why does that guy never get any heat, right? And I think there's a bit of that.

Internal Relationships at the Elite Level

So the second bit is internal relationships. And this is, I'd say, one of the biggest challenges of being a club executive, whether it be chief executive or technical director — whatever it might be — is trying to achieve the right working relationships with your senior employees or your senior staff, whether that be other less senior executives or players or whatever.

That is always a challenge, but particularly a challenge at Premier League level where you're dealing with people who are very self-confident and who know that even if they do get thrown out the club, that's not going to be the end of them. They're probably going to go to a club that's more successful that may even pay them more money. So that is, I'd say, a real challenge for clubs in general, particularly big ones, is — how do you get a grip on your senior staff so they all say, "Right, this is the direction we're going. I understand what role all of these different people play. I understand my own part of it. I'm respectful to the challenges that other people face. Let's all do this together."

But pressure plays havoc even with a plan like that. So what it does is it just strips away all of the veneer. If you go back to the start of the season and you look at interviews that were being done by players and staff for the start of the season — "we're all together, I've never known a dressing room more united, we're all right behind Michael, all the players believe, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah." That's not just United, that's all clubs. Two or three months down the line, a bunch of bad results, a lot of booing, a lot of external scrutiny — starts to strip away some of that shiny veneer. And you start to see where the cracks really are.

And I don't think that this reveals that the crack is necessarily that this person or that person is about their job. The crack is that you've got a whole bunch of people who are operating within an ecosystem, within a structure, financially — as you said — which... doesn't allow them to deliver on ultimately what the fans and the general public as a whole might expect. And therefore, as you say, it's always almost like everyone's got one hat, one hand tied behind their back all the time. That then invites more pressure, the cracks become more apparent, and it has a sort of agglomerative effect by which the thing just gets worse and worse and worse.

But as I said, I think one can speculate all day long about, quote, you know, whose fault it is. You know — could the players be performing better? Sure, they've still got some really good players there. And they've still got a lot of players there who, you know, would walk into most Premier League teams. You know — could the technical staff be doing better recruitment-wise? Sure, yes. It's more of an accumulation over a number of years. But also from a recruitment strategy, I think it was less about the players they brought in and more about the ones they didn't. It was just not addressing things that even the most average fan could sit there and say — you probably need some defence. This is the left-back situation, which is totally fair.

Burnley FC — previously looked on by many as one of the best run clubs in the country, definitely the Premier League, for the years that they were in it, sitting on pretty good cash reserves, you know, should we say relatively content moving in between divisions where…

These are basically the 2010s, aren't they?

2010s. We're talking about that decade between 2010 and 2020. They were owned by a group of local British people, Mike Garlick and a few others. Yeah. And they had Sean Dyche as their manager for most of that period.

The Leveraged Buyout, Explained

So what happened was, is that Burnley got taken over in 2020 by an American businessman called Alan Pace and his investment vehicle ALK. And this was achieved by what is known — and most people now, because of Man United, most football fans kind of do understand this, but I'm about to ask Charlie Jr. to explain it to you — it was achieved by means of what we call a leveraged buyout, Charlie.

A leveraged buyout, in this instance, basically used the assets that Burnley already had to secure the financing to buy the club. So ALK took a loan to buy Burnley. So they took a £65 million loan, and that was secured against partially Turf Moor. So the asset that is one of the most valuable things Burnley has, they secure it against that. Alan Pace, ALK, gets the money.

That's a high-interest loan from MSD. And it was reportedly around 8% to 9% a year. Yep.

We should also say Burnley famously previously was debt-free as a club. Not just debt-free, it had £60–70 million in the bank. In cash reserves, exactly. In the cash — in cash and bank.

So not only were Burnley's own assets used as collateral to buy the club — to make it even better, what then happened…

Well, yeah — I mean, from our perspective, £37 million of that cash from the cash reserve was actually used to complete the rest of the deal and then added into like a debt from the owners to the club. So the cash reserves of Burnley paid part of the deal. Yeah. A loan secured against the assets of Burnley paid part of the deal.

It's like, you know, they basically bought Burnley with a mortgage that was secured on Burnley, and then kind of they used Burnley's savings as a deposit for buying the club. That's literally what happened.

I mean, when you actually say that out loud — wow, okay, how on earth can that happen? We've looked at it from Manchester United's perspective previously at a much bigger level, but we can come on to why it's slightly different.

The Compounding Problem

This was not a great thing for the club at the time. This spent the cushion that they had and put them in a much worse position from a cash perspective. And that has only obviously got worse over the years, because what happens when you have big debts with high interests in a club? They generally get bigger. And not only do they get bigger, but increasingly, they will use — I mean, I saw the cash position is now, I think the net cash flows is minus £18 million, i.e. the club is spending £18 million more just in standard cash flow in the business than it actually receives. Therefore, it requires £18 million in cash injection from its ownership to keep going. And the problem is that the ownership has been finding that cash through more debt. Yes.

And the long and the short of it is they've ended up in a situation — and I always have to place a sort of cautionary note on these things, saying that sometimes when we read out numbers, they'll be from a football club's most recent set of accounts, and those are obviously retrospective, and by this time of the year, in some cases, very retrospective, right? So the last set of accounts received from Burnley FC was from 2024-2025 season, right? So this was the position as of summer 2025, but you can bet your bottom dollar it hasn't gone any better since, right?

And broadly what it revealed is that the club is — was... at that point and probably now is — more £150 million in total external debt, right?

Debt Done Right vs Debt Done Wrong — A Primer

So this is — I just want to make a distinction here, Charlie, because I know a lot of football fans get very concerned about debt. Understandably so. Somebody came to me the other day — and this is actually in relation to a football club I know very well — and they said, "Oh, we're really worried that we — with the, you know, the club owes X amount of money." I said, "Who's — oh, it to?" And they said, "Well, the owner."

I said — well, that's not really proper debt, right? That is simply that the owner has chosen to fund the club using his own cash in a way that means that when he then eventually comes to sell the club, he's minimizing his capital gains outlay, right?

So let's say that you buy the club for £50 million. You then spend £50 million of your own money improving the club, and you then sell it for £100 million. If you have not put that money in as debt, but you've put it in as equity, you're then going to pay capital gains tax on the £50 million profit that you've just made, right? You're going to pay 20-odd percent on that. So you're going to end up £10 million heading off to the taxman, and you're going to be thinking — how's that happen? I put £50 million in.

So club owners often inject money as debt to make sure that when that sale of £100 million happens, effectively, they receive £100 million from the new owner — the first £50 million of which is repayment of the debt, then the other £50 million is for the equity, which is the same as the £50 million they bought it for. So eventually there's no tax payment. So it's a matter of tax efficiency.

But that's not the case when a club owes money to third parties — second and third parties — because that debt is real. That is repayable. That's got nothing to do with a tax wheeze. That's absolutely money that is going to have to be paid. And particularly if it's money that's owed to other football clubs or relating or to footballers or to ex football managers or to whatever the hell it might be, right?

Administration and the Peculiar Nature of "Football Debt"

Because here's the rub. The safety mechanism for a football club, when it gets into desperate financial trouble, is usually to go into administration — which is the British term for Chapter 11 in the States. So it's effective for you to say, we can't pay our bills, we're basically bust. Then goes into a situation where it gets administered by a court-appointed administrator, who then basically seeks to sell it. And from the proceeds of selling it and its assets, whatever it might be, then seeks to return as much money as possible to the external creditors.

The exception to this is what we call football debt. So this is debt that the club owes money to on previous football transfers, to contracts it owes to players and all this type of stuff. That all has to be paid out in full, whereas the other debts, the creditors get the best deal that the administrator is able to give them. So let's say that they were owed £10 million. The administrator might come along and say, "Look, I can give you £2 — make of it what you will." Congratulations, you've got two. Sorry you made a loss of eight. I can't do anything about that.

The football debt is looked at differently. That has to be paid in full in order for a club to exit administration and keep its license.

And this has been the thing that's almost brought a few clubs down — Derby County being the most recent famous one. Sheffield Wednesday would have been, except that enough of the players had left by this point that they managed to slide out from underneath that particular one — is when your external debt and your external football debt in particular is worth more than the value of your club. The administrator then goes out, puts it on the market. Somebody says, "I'm willing to pay £30 million for that." And the administrator says — "I'm not sure that's going to do the trick, because it's got £50 million available of debt — of football debt. And unless you are able to pay the whole of that £50 million, this club is not going to be able to exit administration and maintain its license to play football."

The Relegation Scenario and the Bury Precedent

But what I would alert you to, Charlie, is this — is that whilst you are in the Premier League, you can be in superficially quite a lot of difficulty, but there are a lot of avenues open to you because you have at any one time the current set of TV distribution payments that you currently have. And then you know that you're going to get at least two further seasons of TV distribution payments, even in the event you get relegated. So as happened with Leicester City, you can start factoring that money forward effectively and say — "look, we know we're going to get that money" — and a bank will effectively lend you money up front against the security of that down the track.

Now, the problem is, is that not only are Burnley in this massive bind of having a huge amount of debt, massive interest payments, the ownership itself owing money to the club, no cash reserves, etc. — the problem they've got is they're also in the relegation zone of the Championship.

And you start to think about that balance that I've raised on this show before, between what the enterprise value of the entity is and what its unavoidable liabilities are. So if somebody was to say to me — right, let's just say that Burnley was mid-table in the Championship rather than in the bottom three, and it still had one more season of parachute payments left, and someone would say — "what do you think Burnley's worth in the market?" I'd say, "well, probably about £100 million quid, something like that." Okay, so there's £150 million quid in debt. The enterprise value of the thing is £100. So if you stuck into administration, the administrator could potentially attract in a bid of £100 million, out of which he could pay the football debt and could pay a certain amount of pence on the pound to other creditors, and it could exit administration in an orderly way.

The problem comes if Burnley are relegated. Well, sorry — the big problem, the real potential existential problem — comes if Burnley are relegated from the Championship to League One, as has happened in the last two seasons to Leicester and Luton. It's happened twice recently, where clubs have come straight from the Premier League into the Championship and straight from the Championship then into League One.

So if somebody then said to me — "okay, imagine Burnley are in League One, and they're into their final season of parachute payments. So there's no more beyond this. So they are basically now a League One club. What is Burnley worth then?" The answer would be about £25 million. So you've got a club then with liabilities of £150 million, including a big chunk of them being unavoidable football liabilities, where the enterprise value is £25 million. And where the main asset that they have is the debt that is owed to the club by its own owner, right? Which in this case effectively is now Velocity through ALK.

Now, if Velocity and ALK themselves were also to go into administration and would say, "we haven't got the money, I'm sorry," that also disappears off the balance sheet. So then you've got a situation where even if somebody came along and said, "here's £25, £30 million pounds," the administrator would say — "that doesn't cut the mustard. That doesn't get you out of administration because it doesn't pay the football creditors, which means you can't exit."

This is what happened to Bury. This is why Bury went bust — is that the total amount of their football liabilities in the league which they were in was greater than the value of the club itself. And this is... why so many Burnley fans are so worried right now. It's not one thing. It's about three to four things, all of which are happening at the same time. Sky-high interest payments mopping up all the current cash, very poor performance on the pitch, massive debt, the only debt in its favour by the owners who don't seem to have any money. Otherwise, why would they be borrowing all this money at high interest rates, etc.? You just look at the whole thing and you go — ooh, if that, it's almost like a perfect storm if all that came together.

The Regulator Enters — Plan A, Plan B, Plan C

What does the regulator do about this?

Well, the regulator has confirmed that they are now investigating it, and they have been demanding further information — not a surprise there — regarding the structure and financial stability of the club.

Now if you look at Burnley — what happens if relegation happens while they're in the bottom three in the Championship? That's a very relevant question.
