Why Now

Okay, well, I guess a good place to start would probably be why we want to talk about it right now. When we talked about it before, I think it was very important to say that the issues that we had were with the structures, the approach taken to existing tournaments. It was nothing about opportunity, it was about business. And what makes sense to support and give a product the best opportunity to succeed has to be the fundamental aim and goal.

Think back to our conversations that we've had in recent weeks around men's football with the football regulator and how many clubs would be insolvent without 30 days of funding from the owner — to the WTA spending growth capital on the prize money of players.

What we have in women's football right now — and we'll use the WSL — I think has been a concerning trend, focused on, and we can use attendances as the grounding of this, of a drop-off in interest in the product. But that drop-off in interest in the product goes hand in hand with this continual discourse of growth and success and everything's going really well — "look the other way" type stuff. The attendances suggest otherwise. And the attendances don't just suggest otherwise in a small pocket, distilled little category of numbers that have come out of a few weeks. This is now something that has been going on, I would say, towards the later part of last season and it's continued into this season.

There was something I heard the other day, Charlie, and it was the two very senior people in women's football having a conversation — and you actually sent me the article in the Telegraph. But it really highlighted to me part of that issue of — I mentioned the discourse — we were being fed this kind of narrative of success, and only at the end of this article did the comments come that attendances in many of the biggest games or reportedly the biggest games in the WSL were down. But it wasn't spun as a negative. It was spun as a development point. And it was a footnote. It wasn't a key part of the conversation. But guess what? It is the conversation. Because what we're talking about here is an entertainment product. We're talking about something that is now in the most competitive attention economy, as we say all the time, in history.

Getting people into your stadiums is a key part of that. Women's football has seen a move over the last year or so of a number of its teams in the WSL go from small grounds to big grounds. Use Chelsea as an example. They have left the Kingsmeadow, which is, let's say, 5,000, and they've gone to Stamford Bridge, which is 40,000. Now, normally you'd think, "OK, they would do that because demand was so high at Kingsmeadow that Stamford Bridge is the natural step up because they could capitalize on all of the cash they were leaving on the table from the fans unable to get tickets in there. They could bring more into the event and everyone wins. We start making more money. People like you and I can stop sitting here criticizing them for not generating enough revenue and you guys go, well, we'd love to, but we don't have a big enough stadium. Well, here's your big enough stadium."

The problem is that the first game of the season with Chelsea women at Stamford Bridge was against Aston Villa and it was 7,000 people in there. That's a 20% occupancy rate in Stamford Bridge. 20%. And that, by the way, is pretty consistent across all the grounds. About one-fifth of the seats are sold when clubs are playing in a bigger ground.

Moments vs Tribes

That's a problem, not just for the revenue that comes in on the day, but it's a problem for the overall product, because how bad does it look for a sport, for a concert, for anything, when you're tuning in and the main thing that you see as a fan, supporter, maybe just a first-time watcher, is empty seats. To me that suggests that there's a lack of interest in this product. It means that — why should I care? Clearly actually other people don't care. Stamford Bridge is, you know, a fifth full. Maybe this isn't a very good game that I'm watching. No, no, it's actually one of the big games. It's the opening game of the season.

But really if you look at the raw data, you see a product that is very much a moment's product and not a tribal product. And a moment's product is built very specifically around the key times in a calendar in a year where there's a bounce off the back of the Euros and people are interested for a few months. What football is — men's football — it's a tribal product regardless of what is going on. People will go and turn up for their team most of the time. Old Trafford was still full despite the animosity that was being thrown at the club. And this isn't a tribal product yet. And yet it's being treated like a tribal product. And that is an issue that has gone now much deeper, I think, in product women's football.

The "Startup" Framing — Debunked

Right. So, I hear it said by people in women's professional football — "we shouldn't be judged as if we're a mature sport, we're a startup." Yeah. That's a more recent type of excuse, or reason I should say, but it's one which is being given quite a lot at the moment.

I just want to put that in context. Women's elite football in this country, in a league format, started in 1991. Um, it moved to um a sort of more tiered and professional basis in 2018 when it was still under the aegis of the Football Association. It was then spun off by the Football Association four years ago — three to four years ago, okay? So it certainly isn't a startup in concept. So as far as the paying punters concerned, they've been able to watch women's elite league football for almost all my life — and more than yours, than your life span. We're talking about pushing on towards 40 years of women's elite football.

So this whole thing of "well we were never allowed to play" — it's like that's in the mists of time now. I mean, that is so long ago that the vast majority of people weren't even alive when women weren't allowed to play proper football. Was it '71? Yeah, yeah, until '71, right? So we're talking about 50, 55, 56 years ago. But even at the elite level, it's been in place for almost 40 years now. This is not a startup.

Even if you really stretch a point and say that what we're talking about in startup terms is the point at which the Football Association spins off the Women's Super League to become the Women's Super League, which happened three years ago. And you say, okay, that's the startup — okay, from a business perspective. And that's when things go into startup phase.

VC Phases Applied to Football

Now, I want to ask you a question as somebody who is a senior person within a venture capital business which backs startups. When you invest in a startup business, how many years would you regard the pure startup phase as being before you move into what we call accelerated growth phase?

Really? Three years, obviously. So you'd expect loss-making for the first couple of years, let's say. At that time, you would have expected to see something that got them close to on the initial pitch, hitting the revenues that would have then justified that initial investment. But obviously growth. But growth. But then what you could well have seen is recognising that upside. Then they've gone back and gone — right, we've seen the opportunity, we need more, and that's growth. That's the real growth phase, right? If you're saying that you have a venture fund, you need the businesses that you're investing in to return within five to seven years. And anything beyond that is long.

So basically, just to summarise what Chas has said there, which is that the first couple of years might be looked at as the pure startup phase. Years three to five are the accelerated growth phase, when things should really start to motor and really start to look like it's going to become a really successful business — so that in years six, seven, eight, you're able to exit those investments. Why? Because they've achieved so much more than they had done five years previously that there are other people coming in who go — "wow, that's amazing. I want to buy into that." Okay.

So the FA spins it off, in sort of whatever it is, two to three years ago. Okay. So if you were to make the argument that all of women's professional football started in 2023, whatever it might be — I don't accept the argument, because they'd already been professional since 2018, and they've already been playing elite semi-professional since 1991. But let's just say that you say, okay, that was startup, right? So 24-25, 18, and 25-26 become the startup phase when you start to iron out a few of the issues, but you're already seeing growth. And then you move into 26-27, which is what we're in now, and more money comes in and you start to see accelerated growth when the whole thing really starts to rip and go upwards from there. And you see that happen for two to three years because there's obviously a lot of clear blue sky to aim into because you've spotted a big opportunity — a big TAM, as we would call it, Total Addressable Market. And during those two to three years, people start to get super excited about it so that in year six, seven, people say — "wow, okay, we've really got something here."

The Numbers Don't Lie

Okay — this is the problem with women's professional football. Is that we are now entering, or have entered, what should be the accelerated growth phase. And what we're actually seeing is massive reductions of attendance. Which is the only metric we can use here because their TV deals are tiny. And also last year were very disappointing as well. But leaving that to one side, let's just stick on attendance for the moment. Well, you can't actually do it just because total revenue is £90 million for the whole league. Right. So you can't even look at revenue. So we're actually being kind here in saying that bums on seats is the metric.

So in 23-24, which was the start of their startup phase, the average attendance in WSL1 was 7,600. Okay. The average attendance this season, 26-27, which is the accelerated growth phase, is 5,200.

Right. So what you've seen here is a product being brought to market, the market having a couple of years to look at that product, and then just at the moment when it's meant to take off like a hot air balloon, that's been pricked — it just sinks back to earth and then goes into flames on the ground. 5,200 down from 7,600, right? Yeah, that is an absolutely colossal drop.

Now the average of 7,600 was largely built off — as Charlie says — certain showpiece games, the big ones, the ones that, you know, even casual football fans might take a bit more of an interest in because it's between famous men's clubs and it's their women's arms. So you get a bit of transference of rivalry. You get a bit of brand relevance and all this type of stuff.

So let's just take, for instance, Arsenal against Man U. 24-25, 46,000. This season, 29,000. Right? So 46,000 to 29,000. Chelsea-Arsenal, big London derby, 34,000 in 24-25, down to 19,000 now. Liverpool versus Everton, the Merseyside Derby, 24-25 — again, startup phase — 15,000. 26-27, two years later, 9,500. Arsenal Women, which is the one successful club, the flagship, which, as of last season, was accounting for 41% of the total spectators in the entire league — last season, average attendance of 34,000; this season over its first three matches, 24,000.

So that is a massive, massive percentage reduction. Now we have to say this is after three to four rounds of matches. As I said in the beginning, I think the reason you can have this conversation is because it's the continuation of a trend that was being seen last season. Yes, because attendances last season were lower than they have been in 23-24 as well. So it's not like this is a sort of one-off situation we're seeing. We are seeing a downward trend in general.

Holding Myself to Account — Fair Apples-to-Apples

So what I then wanted to do, I wanted to then ask the question of myself, because I have to be fair. First of all, I took a look at direct comparative numbers for all these matches across the league. And it is probably true to say that the way in which the matches have fallen, it means that whilst it might look like a headline attendance reduction of about 25%, I think the actual number is more like 15% reduction, if you actually look at it on a pure apples-for-apples basis.

In what way?

Well, just in the way in which the fixtures have fallen. So in other words, we say it's 5,200 per fixture, but that can be heavily conditioned by which teams have had more home fixtures than other ones, and which those home fixtures have been, and all this type of stuff. So probably on a normal basis, that 5,200 would be more like 5,600. Right. So I might expect over the course of this season that that number might not stay at 5,200. It might be more like five and a half, 5,600, something like that. But it's still miles down from 7,500. And during a phase when the whole thing's meant to be growing like topsy.

The European Comparison

The second way in which I wanted to hold myself to account is I want to try and work out — is this a WSL problem or is this a problem with the professional women's product full stop?

So I went and looked at the European women's leagues to see if they've got similar issues. So we're looking at obviously the big five leagues of Europe, England being WSL, but then you've got La Liga Femenina, you've got the Frauen Bundesliga, you've got the Première Ligue in France, and you've got the Serie A Femminile in Italy. I think that sounded good. Does that sound okay?

Right. So La Liga Femenina in Spain has got an average attendance of about 1,700 people. Okay. Frauen Bundesliga, which is, as you'd expect from German clubs, they've been a bit smarter about it. It's a mixture of professional and semi-professional. They've been much more careful with their cost bases, as you'd expect from fan-owned clubs, rather than what we have here — 3,300. Right? Bear in mind, WSL is 5,000 or so at the moment. Okay. Première Ligue in France, 2,200. Okay. And Serie A Femminile, as far as I could tell, about 1,600.

Okay, so it's pretty consistent. Across the major European leagues, you're looking at average attendances of about 2,500, right? And then in WSL, more like 5,000.

A Product Problem, Not a Stadium Problem

So this is the product that's been in the marketplace for — whether you call it three years, four years, five years, six years, 10 years, or 20 years, depending on when you take your start point from — it's been out there a while now and it's received a totally disproportionate amount of mainstream media focus.

If you think about other disruptor sports, new sports, new products, whatever it might be, and we've discussed many on this programme, and you say — "okay, how much real serious attention does the Baller League get from mainstream media?" Answer — almost zero. They have to create it all for themselves. How much real attention does, you know, we're talking earlier on about sort of, you know, disruptor products and things like, you know, show jumping and that stuff — how much mainstream media projection do those types of sports get? Zero. McZero. Nothing, right?

Women's professional football has been given vast amounts of mainstream media projection, being free to wear on national broadcasters, going on the main pay TV suppliers, being housed in the best facilities that sport knows — major men's professional football stadiums. Don't forget originally they were in smaller stadium than — "we were all told the reason that's not doing as well as it should do is because the stadiums they're in aren't all that great." Okay — transfer them into the great new stadiums. Oh shit, the attendance goes down not up. Christ, what was going on here?

But I wonder actually — if there's this constant desire, understandable, because a lot of people have got massive vested interests in this product. There's this constant desire to try and find reasons and excuses. "They're not playing in good enough stadiums. The matches aren't at the perfect time of day." They've actually been changed this season. "This season's scheduling is meant to be much better" — again, hasn't happened. "The players aren't paid enough" or "we need bigger stars," whatever it might be. And again, the WSL has been able to attract almost all the bigger stars because they play so much more than other European leagues and even American leagues.

At what point do you actually say — this is a product problem. This is not actually about which stadium it's played in or what time of day it's played in, this type of stuff. This is being demonstrated across multiple geographies that basically, not to put too fine a point on it, almost nobody wants to pay to watch it. It's a fundamental problem. It's the same problem that LIV came up against over the course of three years, which is you can throw as much money at it as you want, but at what point do you actually listen to what the market's telling you?

The Cadence Problem — Comparing with Rugby and Cricket

Do you remember when we've had chats around men's club rugby? Yep. And the power of international, and when fans really turn up versus did they turn up every single week at scale to the extent where they are actually viable businesses as well, continually growing, not just maintaining. It comes up a lot. We've had it in cricket — club cricket, county cricket — 3,000 to 5,000 at the biggest counties over four days.

You then flip it really and just say — well, what we see suggests that men's professional football is the only sport that can maintain the consistency across the cadence of matches on supply, i.e. one, two matches a week, fans will turn up 80% of the time. That is an incredible product to try and base yourself off.

In this way, I think, there's this presumption that because it's football... it will sell and attract people. But it's not — because, as we've talked about before, men's football, rightly or wrongly, has been grounded in 160 years' worth of history and is ingrained in the fabric of communities in ways that very few things are. Can any sport match the consistency that we see in men's sport? And in trying to create...

Men's football.

Men's football, sorry. And in trying to replicate that in the women's game, you're just setting it up to fail.

Now your argument, Charlie, is... I don't disagree with it, but it is vulnerable to what proponents of the women's game would say is — "yes, so give us the time. Give us the time to grow tribal values. Appeal — it's gonna take a long time, you're gonna have to wait for this. And in the meantime, we're still gonna have to pay the players gazillions of pounds, because that's just what we do, because it's football, and because they deserve to be paid like men's footballers are." That — but it's men's football. I'm paraphrasing.

But my point is — I just wonder here that everything that you're saying is true, I agree. The bit I don't quite agree with is that men's professional football is the only viable professional sport. And with the cadence — cadence being the consistency that the product is served up to you with — that it can sustain selling out a 40,000-seater stadium.

I'm not even talking about selling out. I don't care about sell-outs. What I care about is revenues. 80% occupancy. Yeah, but revenues, as you said, come from... total attendance, revenues, whatever it might be.

Now, we can say about the Prem Rugby, we can say — has it hit a ceiling? But others might say, but the ceiling's... reasonably high. I mean, you know, they're getting 15,000 a game, right? And then the question comes is — okay, right, 15,000 a game feels like there should be enough there in and around that to be able to pay a group of players. Now, there are challenges around that because rugby squads are very big and their current substitutes rules, which are totally crackers and I don't get, on a business perspective, why they allow them at all, but it requires basically to have at least 30 full-time professionals, whereas you don't need those in football clubs. So if I was rugby, I'd be looking very, very hard at how many professionals do we really need to be able to play this game. Another story.

But you instantly think — any sport that can get 15,000, 16,000 on average coming every week to each individual event, not just one but each individual event, kind of feels like it's earned its right to exist as a professional sport. And I would say the same that, you know, I've got huge criticisms of this country's second biggest sport, which is horse racing, but there are 30, 40, 50, 60 times a year when you have 25,000, 40,000, 60,000, 80,000, sometimes even more coming. And you go — okay, this is now a question of structuring. This is now a question of trying to make sure that all of this revenue that is coming in, we make sure that we fiddle around with the backroom operation to try and make sure that we don't end up sort of overexposing ourselves.

The Market Is Telling You Something

The challenge I've got here with women's professional football, and the reason I wanted to broaden it out from the WSL to the other European leagues is — it's not the truth staring us in the face that people don't want the product. No one wants the product. Well, nowhere near enough people want the product to make it a viable professional sport under any circumstances, right?

So who's currently filling the hole? I just want to get to this crucial point. I know that various friends of ours won't forgive me if I don't. The gap between the current level of interest and the amount of money that's being paid to pay these professional footballers — a lot of money — is currently being filled by owners.

Now, I know from my own bitter experience that the reason they do that is because owners attend these conferences where they are told by panelists at these conferences — experts, i.e. people normally playing with other people's money, not their own — that the next big growth thing is women's football.

So when I say to an owner of a football club that I'm involved with, "I'd be very careful here, right? You know, you could end up spending a lot of money on this in the next five years. And where you end up at the end of that five years might not be where the people at that conference were telling you. You might just find that's disappeared down a black hole." — "Oh, no, no, no. You know, in five years' time, I'm told all of these things will be worth £100 million pounds." Now, once you believe that all of these franchises or clubs, whatever, are going to be worth £100 million, then spunking £5 to £10 million a year on them feels like a sensible thing to do. You say — okay, so if I spend £5 or £10 million for the next five years, but at the end of it, I end up with something that's worth £100 million, that makes sense.

I'm not asking you to comment on it. But what happens when you cease to believe in the big story? What happens when you cease to believe in the £100 million at the end of it? Do you not end up in the same situation that those LIV golfers were in when they were told by Scott O'Neil, "your franchise is worth £100 million"? We've heard it all before, mate. We're not buying it this time.

I completely agree. But you said that maybe my points were vulnerable to those saying — "But come on, give it time. It needs the time to grow." What would you then say to that?

Where's the Growth Profile?

Well, I think as a venture capitalist, you'd be well within your rights, as you did do a little while ago, to say — hey, where's the growth profile? I can believe in your story about time if it's heading in the right direction.

So if, let's just say — because I think this is broadly the market expectation — the broad market expectation was 23-24, they did 7,500 average attendance. And let's just say that over the following three years, it had gone 7,500, 8,000, 8,300, 8,900. And we were sat here right now at 9,000 rather than 5,000. Okay. That wouldn't to me demonstrate explosive growth. And it definitely wouldn't to you. I imagine it didn't show explosive growth, but you would then listen to the person on the other side of the table. He said — "look, it's a slow burn. It's going to take a while, but look, it is heading in the right direction. And if we carry on like this, in 10 years from now, we're going to end up with 12, 13, 14,000. And at that point you are towards the Prem men's rugby and you are starting to justify your place in the professional sporting world, et cetera. So yeah, look, I fully get it. It's going to take a while, but please bear with me. It will be worth it in the end."

When things start heading in the wrong direction, you then start getting into discussions about throwing good money after bad. Which is — okay, at what point do we actually seriously have to start looking at our product here? Because in any normal business, if you're in the startup moving into the really aggressive growth phase and your audience and your revenue started bombing backwards in the wrong direction, that would not be the moment at which everyone started doubling down, would it?

No, but that's kind of why I want to go back to my point. And I hear you, you're right. Taken in the context of me just saying — a sport is successful based on whether it fills the bums and seats of a stadium — then rugby has a very good justification. But if we're talking about men's football being a good revenue generator and poor in its cost controls. My point really around it being the only sport that could do that — actually it does consistently stand with rugby, because rugby is a very poor revenue generator even though it fills its stadiums. It has a media deal that pays its clubs £3 to £4 million a year.

The WSL needs to fill its stadiums, part one. But, you know, we've let them, we've gone very lightly on the revenues, right? On the financial side. But really there's a much, much bigger issue here, which is the broader business of the WSL needs to be far, far better than it can. We're just going very gently on the thing which is the most obvious signifier of how you could measure engagement.

The media deals need to improve, the commercial deals need to improve. You've got — well, the media deals are so — you've got the media. No, of course, no, of course it went. But I'm just saying — as a — which again brings me back to, you know, if we're just trying to model things off the men's football game, you are forever going to come up against blockers that may not — you may not want to accept to there, but are absolutely there.

The Fugazi Problem

And we'll spare them the blushes — if even if they care, I don't know. But remember we recently — I can't remember who produced it — we read that report. And I think this is where why we want to talk about it right now, because there's just been a few things around the narrative that have made us feel stupid for questioning whether this is successful. "Women's football has arrived — how could you look at this as being something that isn't going to be successful?" And the more of this you read, the more conferences you go to where you're just being told — just like with LIV saying, "come on guys, £100 million franchises." That isn't the case. It's just a fabrication of reality.

But also, Charlie, if this is going to work — the reason things work, the reason things are able to develop and change is because you recognise there's a problem. Yes. So for as long as we sit here listening to conferences, to reading those reports, to reading that Telegraph article and say — "Hey guys, the sun's all shining on us." I'm sitting here going — "Oh, great."

Now if I'm in the position to — if I realise the issues that actually exist for the women's football product, for the WSL, and I get to grips with that based on the comms of the people actually in it, and they go — "Look, you know, we think we have something, but, and there is a big but, this is what we need to do." I can go — right, okay, well, do you know what? Firstly, there's a self-awareness in the product there that shows me that maybe with a bit of my support and understanding of how to structure it, the right people around it, we could try and make something out of this, because it is something in theory that could work. Then that's great. But I'm never going to get to that if everyone keeps flogging this narrative, this — as you said — Fugazi, of "well, nothing, nothing to see guys," almost an upwards — almost an upwards — "let's keep on playing — let's pay the players more and more, let's pay a million bucks for to bring a player in" — not a million bucks by the way on a transfer fee, in wages. But that's also — you're talking about a league, the WSL1, with revenues which are the equivalent of a large Championship club. Sorry — total revenues of the entire league — one large Championship club — that's then spending a million in wages on one player, and they're not just not just doing it, but then celebrating it. Absolutely. As a sign of progress.

What's the Answer?

So here's the question. You know the sporting landscape as a whole really, really well. I did start pointing this problem out three years ago, but I've never, other than saying that they really need to look at product innovation, I've never really come up with an answer. So I'm not sitting here saying that was an easy thing to do.

The Carney Report, that was the preface of all this stuff off, was a crashing mistake. It should never have had two professional leagues. That was an absolute disaster. The franchises or clubs needed to be better geographically spaced. They had to have a cost control. There are lots of things wrong with it, but that's — none of those things are the reason why attendances are at 5,000. Yeah, right? Attendances are at 5,000 because people aren't hooked on the product.

The Michelle Kang Caveat

Yeah, and that's okay. Can I throw in a — a caveat? Yeah, what do we think of London City Lionesses and Michelle Kang?

What's the caveat?

The attendances have increased at a smaller level. There's been, should we say, through an incredible amount of self-financing, owner financing. Awful from a structural perspective, again, if you're trying to regulate an industry. But she's put in like £22, or was it £22.4 million, I think, to this project. And the rest. That was as of last accounting. I think you'll find it's up at more like £40 now. But they're on revenues of £1 million. They bought some... top talent, as in, well, actually the Ballon d'Or winner, Alexia Putellas. That was who I mentioned earlier on, who's on a million a year.

Yeah. But okay, so my point is there you've got someone that almost maybe has a slightly different incentive structure. She's a very rich person who is building something from scratch as well, not attached to a men's club. So it's an independent asset, clearly and unashamedly almost spending a huge amount of money to try and elevate this, but at the same time existing in an ecosystem which is exclusively...

Okay, right. I totally get your point. You have a very rich person spending a vast amount of their own money on a professional sport which not many people really care about. Polo is like that. Polo, right? Big rich guys come in and they will spend £10, £20 million on their polo team. They themselves get to play in the polo team. They get to play with three Argentine professionals and they play at Windsor or at Cowdray Park and 5,000 or 6,000 people turn up because it's a nice day out and they sip champagne and they watch the whole thing and this type of stuff. And the whole thing goes on and no one ever stops to say — does that deserve to exist? Yes, absolutely fine.

If there were 10 Michelle Kangs and they all decided that they wanted to fund to a ridiculous level their football teams and didn't really care that almost no one wanted to turn up and watch — it just is what it is because "I've got a passion for it. I've got a mission about it." I've got no problem with that whatsoever. Please don't expect the rest of us to be interested. Don't have acres and acres of coverage in the mainstream media and on national broadcasters telling anyone who is not passionately interested that they're a dinosaur, an idiot, don't get it, etc, etc.

The market will tell you what the market needs you to understand. And if the market doesn't turn up, it's not because the market's an idiot. Right? So I've got no problem with what Michelle Kang's doing. She should knock herself out. She's not just doing it there, she's doing it at Lyon as well. Okay? She's a billionaire and how she spends her money is totally up to her. If she wants to pay a female professional footballer a million a year to play in front of 3,000 people at Bromley FC, that's totally her prerogative. But can we all please recognize within the industry that this is not the next big thing?

Honest Comparison — Women's Rugby

Pretty conclusive but it is to me. Yeah. Um — how do you reckon that's going to go down with whom? People that listen? I'd imagine you guys will have, you know, a few views on this. I think we can recognize that it's a very sensitive topic, but I I hope that any conversation — it's an educated approach or a reasonable, at least, fair, grounded in the type of critique that we would level at lots of other and have levelled at lots of other sports organisations. And if this was a men's product we would go in gangbusters.

As I said when we covered this the first time, I always balance this out by saying I'm checking across on the numbers with women's professional rugby — or semi-professional rugby, as it is — 27% up attendances. 27%. When England played against Canada recently in Canada — England — right? So this is in a country where the sport is still amateur — rammed stadium here. They sell out Twickenham. The Red Roses do. Right. But they're rammed out stadium even in Canada.

This is a sport which every single year is beating records, beating records, beating records whilst keeping pay under control. And that's a sport. If someone came to me and said — "how far do you think it could go?" I'd be like, "well, I don't know. It's growing so fast. Who knows if it carried on growing at 25% a year for the next five or six years, that could become something really investable."

So this is not about men and women. It's nothing like that. You know, what this is about is about looking at the metrics, looking at the trend graphs, looking at the amount of capital invested for the return on capital invested, looking at people's medium-term horizons and asking ourselves the question — is this working or is it not working? And having, frankly, the honesty to call it out when it's not.

Sign-off and the Substack Tease

Okay, brilliant. A lot in there. Obviously, there's things that people will be incredibly passionate about, I'm sure. But in all seriousness, we encourage the conversation with us. Please come and give us your thoughts on this. Not just thoughts, but new facts. New facts. New insights, stuff that you think we need to know or haven't taken into account, please. Exactly. Exactly.

And speaking of that kind of stuff, there has been, Charlie, can you believe it, even more happening in the world of our favourite topic — LIV Golf — this week. As today, when this is releasing, the new deadline, the final deadline for players to sign up to LIV 2.0 — well, the transfer window slammed shut, for want of a better phrase. To use that old favourite.

So I think we should probably have a look at that. But also there has been some news this week about some pretty extraordinary payments that have been given to some of the executives at the top that based on our enthusiasm for this topic over the last few weeks, we probably should explore in detail. So we're going to go and do that on our Substack.

So please, please join us on our Substack. I promise you — if you have not seen my Viking comrade here ever get angry and excited, he's normally a very equitable chap, come on to the Substack to see what really gets him going. Because this has really sort of made him rage. Yeah, it's good, isn't it? It's good.

Anyway, guys, for now, thank you so much. And we will see you next week. Thank you, Charlie. Thanks, Charlie.

item.description:
### 杠杆收购的"自噬"机制：资产用自己的血买下自己
伯恩利那笔交易最惊人的地方不是债务规模，而是**结构的自噬性**——俱乐部用自己银行里的 6000-7000 万英镑现金做"首付"，用自己的球场（Turf Moor）做抵押贷款，然后再让自己背上这笔新债。这不是传统意义上的收购，而是一场精心设计的**寄生式所有权转移**：买家没花自己的钱，被买方却成了融资主体。有意思的是，这个机制与某些跨国企业的反向并购，甚至某些高控制度组织的财务捕获手段，**在结构上完全同构**——目标主体为自己的被捕获出资。曼联在这个结构下还能撑住，是因为它拥有近似于"主权信用"的品牌等级（10 亿债务 vs 50 亿资产 + 6.77 亿年收入，杠杆率仅为营收的 1.7 倍）；而伯恩利的债务已经达到了营收的 **7 倍**（parachute 结束之后更惨），这不是风险，是一台正在慢动作内爆的机器。
### 曼联球迷的"剧场化支持"：一种被低估的抗议语法
Carrick 被鼓掌下场的那一刻，发生的事情比"球迷支持教练"要微妙得多。那其实是一种**反向献祭**——球迷用对边缘人物的爱，来放大对核心权力的

item.title: [Lex Clips] The death of GitHub: Why open source maintainers are burning out | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

当"维护者"成为系统的单点故障

有一个被忽视的事实：GitHub 的真正瓶颈从来不是服务器带宽、不是存储、不是算力——而是人类注意力的生物学上限。开源运动表面上是"去中心化协作"，但每个仓库底部都藏着一两个人类的神经系统，他们的睡眠、情绪和自我价值感构成了整个数字公地的真正基础设施。AI 可以无限生成 pull request，但不能替一个精疲力竭的 maintainer 感受"被看见"的快感——而正是这种心理代偿机制在过去二十年里补贴了整个科技行业的创新速度。

出人意料的观察：GitHub 的"死亡"并非死于代码过载，而是死于反馈的通货膨胀。当 AI 让提交 PR 的边际成本趋近于零，而审阅 PR 的认知成本仍然是人类的——这不是扩展性问题，这是宏观经济学问题。它和 1920 年代德国魏玛共和国的恶性通胀同构：当生产货币（PR）的成本坍塌，而需要用稀缺资源（maintainer 注意力）来"兑付"每一张货币时，整个系统的价值体系就会崩溃。

跨领域连接：Perelman 的黑板与数学期刊的"慢变量"

Lex 把 GitHub 的危机和数学期刊并置，这个类比比表面看上去更深。Perelman 把 Poincaré 猜想的证明丢到 arXiv，然后花数年在全世界的黑板前被人追问"第 247 页引理 412"——这不是低效，这是人类认知带宽的生物学定价。数学社区默认了一个被开源社区遗忘的真理：真理的产生速度不能快于验证的速度，否则知识就只是未经消化的噪音。

把这个洞见横向迁移，你会发现一个惊人的模式： - 营养学：人体吸收的速度不能快于消化酶的催化速度，否则再多食物都是毒素； - 森林生态：倒木必须被真菌分解回土壤，否则森林会被自己的"生产力"埋葬； - 城市规划：道路建设速度一旦超过社区形成速度，就产生 Robert Moses 式的空心城市。

开源项目的 maintainer 其实是数字世界的"真菌"——他们负责把 PR 这种"倒木"分解回代码库的"土壤"。而 AI 正在以不可持续的速度制造倒木。

隐藏的系统性真相：开源与学术的共享脆弱性

你意识到 Lex 和 Terry Tao 都把"开源 maintainer 的倦怠"与"数学家的退出"放在同一个精神拓扑结构里了吗？这两个看似不相关的生态系统共享一个秘密架构：

它们都是用"内在动机的无偿劳动"来补贴"外在客观价值的生产"的系统。

一旦这种内在动机的河流被 AI 污染——不是因为 AI 本身邪恶，而是因为 AI 让"输出"变得廉价而"验证"仍然昂贵——两个系统会以完全相同的方式崩溃：不是爆炸，而是维护者悄悄离开，留下 zombie repos 和 zombie journals。

更深的洞见：也许 GitHub 的下一代形态不是"更智能的 CI/CD"，而是认知成本的透明定价——让每一个 PR 的提交者必须先承担一部分审阅成本，就像生态系统中的"反向循环"。这其实在生物学里有一个精确的类比：所有可持续生态都有闭环的物质循环，而不只是单向的生产。GitHub 从一开始就是一个开环系统，这才是它真正的病根。

📝 转录文本

一、GitHub 的危机：开源维护者的崩溃

Lex： Can you comment on your view how everything's changing? Even just observing the insane evolution of even arXiv, which is similar in some ways to what's happening on GitHub, for example. A lot of people in the open source movement are really struggling to know what to do. Some are predicting the death of GitHub.

嘉宾： Why? Just 'cause there's so much code being added to GitHub—

Lex： —that it can't sustain the growth?

嘉宾： So one of the things that makes the open source movement successful is there's a kinda one or a few folks that really manage each repository, the human beings, and they are, um—psychologically and on many levels are becoming overwhelmed by the, all the pull requests.

So it becomes impossible to manage and they get exhausted and there's this whole feeling. The open source movement, maybe similar to the academic environment, requires the humans to be motivated. And if you get worn out by the just similar the ideas that Terry Tao mentioned, that you just quit. And so that's a failure mode that you want to kind of avoid.

二、与数学期刊系统的类比

Lex： So journals were already in math under very, very severe strain from the number of things before AI, having nothing to do with AI, just there was, you know, more people producing more knowledge, sending it to journals, and journals had to referee it, and referees are exhausted and being asked to, work really hard to understand these theorems and check them.

The only thing worse than that system, I think, is not having that system. Because the way that, like, our mathematical epistemology, the way that we arrive at truth, is deliberately slow and careful and precise.

三、Perelman 与 Poincaré 猜想：缓慢验证的典范

Go back to Perelman's solution of the Poincaré conjecture. He puts these papers on the archive, and then people around the world are, you know, shocked by this, and so they invite him to come give lectures. He gives he comes to Stony Brook, he comes to NYU, he comes to Princeton.

He's going all around the country and the world, and he's giving three-hour long impromptu explanations of, of, you know, maybe an hour is, is him explaining what he's doing, and the next two hours are people saying, "On page two hundred and forty-seven, Lemma four hundred and twelve, I don't understand how you do this." And then he goes to the board and gives them a half-hour lecture on how he does that.

So the entire thing lives in his mind. He's done the best he can to communicate it on paper, and then it's up to us, the community, to go back through it very carefully, very in a detailed and precise way and agree, yes, this is a real proof of the Poincaré conjecture.

四、结论：解决方案只是第一步

And that took years to do and a whole lot of human effort. So coming up with a solution is only the first step in the process, and that process has to be deliberate, and it has to be community-driven. And so that's what the journal system is trying to accomplish.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 当"维护者"成为系统的单点故障
有一个被忽视的事实：GitHub 的真正瓶颈从来不是服务器带宽、不是存储、不是算力——而是**人类注意力的生物学上限**。开源运动表面上是"去中心化协作"，但每个仓库底部都藏着一两个人类的神经系统，他们的睡眠、情绪和自我价值感构成了整个数字公地的真正基础设施。AI 可以无限生成 pull request，但不能替一个精疲力竭的 maintainer 感受"被看见"的快感——而正是这种**心理代偿机制**在过去二十年里补贴了整个科技行业的创新速度。
**出人意料的观察**：GitHub 的"死亡"并非死于代码过载，而是死于*反馈的通货膨胀*。当 AI 让提交 PR 的边际成本趋近于零，而审阅 PR 的认知成本仍然是人类的——这不是扩展性问题，这是**宏观经济学问题**。它和 1920 年代德国魏玛共和国的恶性通胀同构：当生产货币（PR）的成本坍塌，而需要用稀缺资源（maintainer 注意力）来"兑付"每一张货币时，整个系统的价值体系就会崩溃。
## 跨领域连接：Perelman 的黑板与数学期刊的"慢变量"
Lex 把 GitHub 的危

item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、藏在指引里的"记忆体回旋镖"：一次没人说破的产业链反噬

管理层把 PC 第四季度 miss 的 15–18 亿美元几乎全部归因到"客户在最近几周说市场严重放缓"，归咎到"Memory 价格上涨"。但真正值得玩味的是：内存涨价本身是 AI 军备竞赛的副产品——HBM 吃掉了 DRAM 的产能，大云把 SK 海力士、三星、美光的高端产能锁死，溢出的价格压力顺着供应链"回旋镖"打回了消费 PC 市场。

于是你会看到一个诡异的因果链：英伟达拿到的订单越凶，联想戴尔惠普越造不出便宜笔记本，英特尔的 CCG 业务就越惨。英特尔同时站在 AI 盛宴的受益端（数据中心 CPU + 代工）和受害端（PC 内存成本）——它既是赢家又是输家，而市场却只允许一家公司有一个故事线，这就是今晚 -20% 的更深层解释。

二、分析师的"线性外推陷阱"与一个物理学家都会笑的毛利预测

视频里罕见地把 27–30 年的毛利预期全列了出来：44% → 46.6% → 51.9% → 53.9%。你看着这组数字，是不是觉得像教科书里的"合理增长"？

这是典型的 Spherical Cow（球形奶牛）谬误——物理学家笑话里那种"假设奶牛是完美球形"的建模方式。华尔街的 DCF 模型需要可微分的曲线，所以它把一个本质上非线性的产业周期，强行捏成了平滑斜率。但半导体产能爬坡从来是阶梯函数：18A 良率跨过某个阈值前毛利纹丝不动，跨过之后一夜扩张 5–6 个点。

视频博主其实暗示了这一点——"一旦这个线性外推被证伪，承压的时间跨度会比较长"。换句话说，接下来真正的风险不是基本面变坏，而是模型本身坍塌。这是定价机制的危机，不是公司的危机。

三、Andy Jassy 的"沉默告白"：当亚马逊承认落后谷歌一年

这期视频里被低估的一句话：亚马逊自己说，Trainium 外卖要到 2027 年底才开始。博主前几天还预估"落后谷歌两三个季度"，被官方正式延长到整整一年。

把这个信号跨界放到更大的图景里看——它呼应了一个和医疗板块跨界打通的隐藏规律：所有"全栈垂直整合"的公司，在新技术拐点都会面临同一个两难——守住自家闭环 vs 开放外部变现。谷歌 TPU 当年只内用了近 10 年才开卖，亚马逊现在也在走同样的曲线，而博主把目标仓位从 8% 拉到 19% 的医疗板块，本质上押的也是同一个赌注——那些把 AI 真正"下沉"到特定垂直场景的玩家，才是 2027 年的真需求。换句话说，博主在亚马逊/英特尔上收缩的仓位，与在医疗/软件上扩张的仓位，底层是同一个判断：通用算力的边际收益开始递减，垂直落地的 alpha 才刚开始。

四、一个值得记下来的意外彩蛋：20% 的 Token 会流向网络安全

Andy Jassy 几乎是顺口提到的——未来可能有 20% 的 AI token 消耗在网络安全。这个数字如果成立，就解释了今年网络安全板块（CrowdStrike、Palo Alto、Zscaler）的离谱强势：市场在 Agent 大规模部署之前，就已经提前为"AI 攻防战"定价。

这里有个反直觉的推论：Agent 越强，网络安全的 TAM 越大。因为每一个具备自主行动能力的 Agent，都是潜在的攻击面；每一次 LLM 调用，都是一次新的权限边界检查。这不是软件行业的常规增长，而是AI 自己制造出来的新品类支出——类似于汽车普及后保险业的爆炸式扩张。

📝 转录文本

开场

各位观众大家好。今天这期视频一定会录的，只是录的时间会比较的晚。为什么？

首先第一点，今天非常的忙。但是英特尔的财报我看了，看了两遍。第一遍我怕漏了，且第一遍听完之后我的感受不是非常的好；第二遍我听完之后，把很多数据带进去、把管理层对于 27 年的这一个展望带进去之后，其实我觉得 OK。那么稍后我会把一些数据和大家分享一下。

然后我还听了亚马逊的这个财报，亚马逊的财报我也会去做一个总结。那最后，就是经过现在盘后下跌完之后，我所有持仓的一个百分比全部总结出来，和大家分享一下接下去操作上的一些分享。

那么因为很多人可能比较好奇的是，这一次跌完之后接下去会怎么操作，比起这家公司的一个基本面，现在到底在什么的一个位置，可能大家会更加的关注。好吧，那我就废话不多说，直接开始。

一、英特尔财报：盘后 -20% 是否合理？

那首先先聊一下英特尔。那英特尔为什么盘后出现下跌？盘后的下跌是不是合理？

首先盘后的下跌一定是合理的，但我个人认为盘后下跌的这个幅度——现在看到盘后下跌 20% 到 23% 左右——这个幅度本身我认为是过了。但是整个市场就是这样的，再加上现在短期之内市场的情绪面不是非常的好，相对会低一些，有这样的一个财报，特别是有这样的一个指引出来之后，导致盘后出现了 20% 这个下跌。

那为什么盘后的指引没有达到市场的预期？首先先从结果去看，单凭这个数据的话，我当时看完数据的时候也让我挺意外的。因为通常来说，我以前和大家分享过，一家公司的 IR（Investor Relations）和华尔街的这些分析师，他们之间都是有联系的、有沟通的。所以通常来说，经过这个沟通，我们很难会看到最后财报出来这个结果和市场的这个预期差得非常的多。

而这一次从指引这个角度去看，确实差得比较的多。刚刚过去第三季度其实比市场预期是高了不少、也好了不少，但是第四季度这个指引差得比较的多。

为什么指引会 miss？

为什么会差？如果你去听财报会的话，你能找到这个答案。首先我们先把以色列那边工厂受到的影响剔除，你即使把这个影响给加回去的话，利润率、包括营收也是比市场预期要低了不少，利润率比市场预期要低了 2%。

那背后主要的一个原因是：如果我们去看英特尔的业务，除了它方具（Foundry）这一块，它的产品（Product）这一块总共有两个业务——一个是和数据中心相关的，现在增速非常的好；另外一个就是和 PC 相关的。

那 PC 这一块，现在整个市场里面，在刚刚过去这个第三季度，特别是第三季度的后面两个月——八月份和九月份，包括刚刚过去的十月份——整个行业在进行去库存，且去库存的一个周期非常的厉害。

所以第四季度营收指引上的这个 miss，比市场预期要多了将近 1.5–1.8 个 billion（15 亿至 18 亿美金左右）。这上面的一个 miss，几乎全部是来自于 PC 端这一块——个人电脑。

那为什么会出现这种情况？管理层说到，个人 PC 端这一块，在最近的几周，客户开始说市场是严重放缓，用了非常严重的词。因为 Memory 价格的这个上涨，过去两个月 PC 的放缓在加速，未来几个季度会继续承压。

所以管理层预计整个今年 PC 市场的一个 TAM（Total Addressable Market）会下降 12%，明年会继续下降 10%。那这明年下降的 10%，我会带入到稍后和大家分享那个数据里面，所以这个 10% 我们可以先记下来。

顺风与逆风的"量化"难题

那我这边打了一个星。因为一开始你就指引低于市场预期、大幅低于市场预期的时候，分析师在问问题的时候，基本上都会围绕着"你为什么会低于市场预期？到底是什么样的一些原因导致你低于市场的预期？"

而英特尔本身，它有很多个业务，有很多的产品又在一个量产的一个过程里边，又有很多的产品刚刚推出来。所以英伟达的财报——啊，英特尔的财报会里面，不知道为什么我老是要立英伟达——所以英特尔的财报里面其实有很多个：有些是逆风的，有些是顺风的。最后把逆风和顺风全部加在一起，管理层给了一个比较明确的一个指引，无论是营收端也好、还是 margin 这一块也好。

当我第一次听财报的时候，当管理层先解释到 PC 端这一块今年会比较严重地放缓，现在整个行业里面在去库存，渠道里面在去库存，然后明年还会继续放缓，然后分析师就问（因为分析师也带着一个比较负面的态度去问这些问题）："明年是不是投资的一年？因为看起来你们明年那个 CapEx 好像会比你们的现金流要赚得多。"

所以管理层也说到：明年是投资的一年，所以明年的自由现金流是负的。听到这边，我在听第一遍的时候，就感觉好像不妙。因为管理层——我以前说过——市场不是非常喜欢这一类进入投资周期的公司。所以这些是相对比较负面的一些消息。

相对正面的消息（1-7 点）

然后相对比较正面的一些消息就是我这边写的第一点到第七点：

  • 暂时来说，现在英特尔还是受到产能这个限制。
  • 新推出的英特尔现在也推出 GPU 了，为什么要去做 GPU？他们主要是做 Inference（推理）这一块的 GPU。有了 GPU、有了 CPU，整个 AI factory 是全部的一个输出了。
  • 方具（Foundry）这一块的良率在持续上升，18A 两位数的这个增长，所以管理层非常的有信心，18AP 会成为外部客户的一个选择。
  • 14A 就是他们再下一代的一个技术，也公布了 0.9 PDK，这是一个非常大的一个里程碑，为未来风险量产去做一个准备。而且现在已经有好几个潜在的客户，管理层说名字等客户自己去公布。那我个人的推测，现在市场里边大家基本上已经知道了背后的一些大云，可能都是未来潜在的客户。
  • 方局（封装）这一块明年的封装业务营收也会出现一个大幅度的加速。
  • 数据中心主要的一个核心还是来自于 CPU。管理层的一个预期是未来五年整个 CPU 市场的一个 TAM 会从 40 个百分点涨到 20 个百分点，今年 30%，明年会继续 30% 的一个增速。

把基本面"量化"进模型

但其实，即使我聊了一些比较利好、就为 27 年可以期待的一些利好和现在短期之内所遇到的一些逆风情况，可能大家对于数据上感官不是那么的直接，就像华尔街的分析师也是一样。我觉得有一个问题问得非常的好：他说，你们真的有很多的一些逆风和很多的一些顺风，那我怎么把很多逆风和顺风加在一起？

因为最终还是看数据嘛——还是看你的营收增速，还是看你的一个 margin 会不会扩张。这就是华尔街所关心的。为什么这些人关心？是因为你和我聊了那么多基本面，如果我没有办法把这些基本面去量化的话，我没有办法把这些数据放到我的模型里边。模型里面如果没有更新的数据，我就没有办法对于价格去做出一个预估。

所以我们就来看一下数据。

2027 年 PC 业务：市场高估

首先我这边的一个方框里边所圈出的，我们看的是 2027 年的这个预期。前面我聊他们 PC 端这一块，PC 端市场现在预期 2027 年是 33.4 个 billion，和 2026 年的一个同比增速是几乎没有任何的增速。但是前面已经说到了，27 年和 26 年做对比的话会下降 10%。

那在这个基础上，如果整个行业下降 10%，但是管理层又聊到我们产品端这一块的一些 mix，因为会有一个新产品上线，新产品上线之后这个 mix 会抢占一部分的市场份额。所以从英特尔这个角度去看，他们在 Client Computing（PC 端）这一块可能下跌的幅度比市场的预期要小、比整个行业的幅度要小。

但我还是按照整个行业下跌这个幅度去算：同比增速如果放缓 10% 的话，对于营收端这一块的影响差不多就是在 3.3 个 b 点左右。所以我这边画了一个向下的箭头：明天、后天，包括下周，华尔街的分析师对于 2027 年 PC 端这一块做出一个指引之后，33.4 这个数据会被下修。

2027 年数据中心：市场低估

然后另外一块就是他们业务增长最快的那一块——数据中心。数据中心现在市场预期明年 2027 年的营收是在 35.2 个 billion。

但是在财报会里面有一位分析师问了：你们在第四季度给的这个指引一个季度是在 8.5 个 billion，我能不能把你 8.5 个 billion 去年化？8.5×4 就是 36 个 billion，把这 36 个 billion 当做你明年数据中心这一块营收的一个最低点？管理层肯定了这样的一个想法。

然后之后有另外一个 follow up：从 Quarter over Quarter 这个角度去看，有没有可能每一个季度环比都会出现增长？你想一下，我这边 8.5 乘以 4 是今年的第四季度，如果 Quarter over Quarter 都有成长，那明年随便怎么样一定会超过 36 个 b。管理层自然在第三季度财报会的时候，他不会给你一个 27 年的这个指引，只有到明年的 1 月份再公布第四季度财报才会给。但是基本上给了一个方向：上半年你要扩的话可能会有些难度，下半年的话是一定会扩的。

那我们即使假设上半年环比增速不扩——四季度 8.5，一季度 8.6、8.7，二季度 8.7、8.8——和今年的四季度可能不会有太大的差别。但是下半年随着产能进来之后，下半年明显是会出现一个非常大幅度的一个增加。

所以在这种情况下，现在市场预期明年数据中心这一块 35 个 billion，我认为是明显低估了。我个人一个预期是起码在 40 个 billion 以上。

一来一回：对利润的净影响

数据中心这一块市场是低估了，然后 PC 端这一块市场是高估了。一来一去，PC 端这一块可能高估了 3 个百分点，但数据中心这一块可能低估了 3–4 个百分点。其实从市场接下去会进行的这个调整对于营收这一块的影响去看，我认为可能加在一起的话是差不多的。

那另外一点，对于 bottom line、对于 operating income 这一块的一个影响：因为 PC 端这一块的利润率相对会低一点（30% 不到一些），而数据中心这一块的 margin 会高一些（40% 多一些）。所以一来一去，其实对于利润端这一块的影响，如果数据中心往上修的话，利润端这一块可以抵消 PC 端这一块的一些下修。

2027 年毛利率：市场的"线性外推"

前面我们讲到了营收，这是华尔街比较关心的一组数据。那另外一组数据华尔街比较关心的就是整个 2027 年的利润率。你的毛利润率在今年比如说 42% 的这个基础上，还能不能继续扩张？

有一个人就问得非常的直接：明年毛利润在今年这个基础上还能不能继续扩张？管理层说：只要我们明年还是增速的一年，我们的一个期待是毛利润还会继续扩张。

现在市场 26 年市场预期是 40%，差不多最终就是停在 42% 左右；27 年现在市场预期是 44%。那我认为从 42% 到 44% 的这一个市场的预期基本上是可以做到的。

那这边有一个风险就是：管理层对于 27 年 PC 端这一块放缓的速度是否低估了？管理层预期是 10%，有没有可能高于 10%？说实话，这个谁都不知道。类似于 22 年——我记得 22 年年初的时候，当时整个芯片板块进入一个周期，当时 AMD 苏妈其实也低估了整个行业去库存的过程，苏妈一直对于行业见底的时间点是过于乐观了，后来其实是从财报里面去证明苏妈是过于乐观——起码提早了 3–6 个月左右。

所以站在这样一个时间点，我很难去做出自己的判断：管理层对于 PC 端放缓这个速度到底是乐观还是悲观的。我只能说存在一定的风险。

但是 PC 端只是英特尔 Product 这一块里边的一部分业务，而且这一部分业务本身就 stagnant（停滞），本身它的增速就非常的小——26 年同比是负增长的，27 年同比再负增长。而英特尔在产品端这一块的一个增长主要就是来自于数据中心这一块，那数据中心的环比增速每年是在 30% 以上。

小结：两点可确定

全部加在一起，然后把这些数据带进去之后，我觉得有两点：

  • 第一点比较可以确定：数据中心在整个 27 年，华尔街对于数据中心 27 年营收的预期是低估了。因为根据他们第四个季度数据中心 8.5 个 b 这个数据去做一个线性外推，管理层也给了一部分的指引，所以数据中心端市场是低估了，PC 端市场明显是高估了。根据管理层的预期，明年还会放缓 10% 的话，那起码是高估了 3 个百分点左右。
  • 最后一个问题就是利润率。华尔街最关心的就是你利润率会不会持续扩张。现在市场的预期是：27 年 44%、28 年 46.6%、29 年 51.9%、30 年 53.9%。华尔街明显做出了一个非常明确的线性外推。一旦这个线性外推被证伪的话，短期之内就会承压，承压的时间跨度可能会比较长，因为市场一定要找到你的转折点到底在哪。

但起码我觉得这一点比较好的是，管理层给了华尔街的分析师一部分的安慰：就是从 margin 这个角度去看，和 26 年去做对比的话，会继续扩张。

二、亚马逊财报：资本开支的"故事线反复"

OK，然后来聊下亚马逊的财报。我听完亚马逊的财报之后，其实我没有觉得亚马逊的财报很差。但是市场又在聊："哎，亚马逊的投资过多了"，所以盘后下跌。这不又跑到了两个季度之前市场所交易的这个故事线吗？

所以我就说，到底是加大资本开支好呢，还是放稳资本开支好？这个问题我在昨天直播的时候就聊过——我们必须要思考的，因为你会发现在不同的时间段里面，市场对于加大资本开支这个反馈都是不一样的。

但我觉得最重要的就是：我们既然投资 AI 的话，你必须要看清楚整个 AI 的这个趋势，必须要退后一步去看，而不要去关注整个市场交易这个逻辑，因为这个逻辑随时会变的。上一个季度的财报，当两家大科技去证明了它的 ROI、它的投资是有回报的时候，市场马上给出了一个正面的反馈；然后这个季度难道又回到了一个"你投资的话你就应该被杀跌"吗？

所以我不可能去猜测市场在某一个时间段到底交易什么样的一个逻辑线。从投资这个角度去看，我们需要关注的是：你以前投资下去这个资本开支是不是有回报？这个回报来自于哪？这个回报来自于未来营收的增速、来自于未来利润率到底会停在什么位置。

罕见的 27–28 年指引：AWS north of 40%

而且在这个季度财报里边，Andy 可能也知道市场到底需要什么。因为很少亚马逊会对 27 年——前面英特尔它不会给 27 年的指引，它只是给你大概的方向，没有给非常明确的指引——但是今天 Andy 给了非常明确的指引：AWS 的增速在 27 年和 28 年 north of 40%，都会在 40% 以上。

我说，当管理层给出这样的预期的时候，他告诉你这个增速只是一个底部、只是一个最低的区间。因为管理层能够给你 40% 加，就说明他们能够做到比 40% 加还要好。

那亚马逊是三大云里面最大的这个体量，它都能够增长 40% 以上，你想想对于微软、对于谷歌来说意味着什么？微软刚刚过去这个季度 48%、49%，AWS 增速也是 40% 以上。所以这三家云，我认为几乎是一个明牌：就是明年 27 年、包括 28 年，他们的营收增速在现在的基础上只会继续增加。虽然他们的体量已经非常的大。

为什么？是因为他们过去这一段时间，他们资本开支这个增速匹配了未来云的这个增速，因为订单都是确认的。

那 Andy 所给的这个指引，市场的预期在多少？市场的预期在 27 年 AWS 的营收增速 38%、28 年的话是放缓到 31%。我在前段时间付同木请我去做的一个线下当时我分享的时候，我就说我认为市场对于 AWS 这块的增速是低估了。市场认为它会出现一个 deceleration（增速放缓），但我认为增速不会放缓，我认为是一个明牌。

可能市场某些时候就是一个默认的假设：当你体量到了非常大的时候，它默认的假设一定是你的增速会放缓。但实际上从数据中心这个角度去看，因为这些大云，他们都是有订单进来之后，才会去造、才会去花这个资本开支。不要看他们的资本开支和去年做对比增长了 100%，明年可能在今年这个基础上再增加 60%、70%。为什么他们敢这么去做？是因为他们看到了未来的订单，他们有这个 visibility（可见度）在那边——Andy 前段时间接受采访的时候说到——所以他们才会那么激进地做资本开支。

所以第一点，我认为就是这一次财报会议里边重中之重：它罕见地给了 27 年和 28 年 AWS 这个增速。而在这个基础上，他有很多的 on demand token——他留了一部分的 on demand token 就是给短租这些需求。如果 token 的价格持续保持在高位，这一部分短租的需求进来之后，42%、43%，甚至于 45% 以上都不见得是做不到的。

智能体对广告业务的影响

然后第二点：智能体对于广告营收这一块的影响。我看到没有人去聊这一块，这是 Andy 主动去聊的。Andy 说到，暂时来说是看不到智能体对于广告营收的这块影响，到现在也没有多少人去用智能体购物，这个体验并不好——并没有比你直接去商家购物体验要好。

那这个回答本身相对是比较主观的，因为他从亚马逊的这个角度去出发。从亚马逊的角度去出发，他绝对不会告诉你说"哎，我认为广告业务会受到影响，但是我们仍然坚持不和 OpenAI 之间进行合作"——我们不可能听到这样的一个答案嘛。所以这个答案本身相对会比较的主观。

第三点：网络安全可能吃掉 20% 的 Token

然后第三点，第三点也挺有意思。他说实际上市场里面有一部分的人预测：未来 20% 的 token 可能全部会花在网络安全上面。他说网络安全可能将会成为 coding 之后另外一个非常大的场景。

这样的一个观察可能解释了：在过去这段时间网络安全的个股——今年到现在为止网络安全的个股做得那么强——背后的一个原因，可能市场真的在提前定价。

第四点：Trainium 外卖时间线

那最后一点，就是亚马逊自己的 training 到底什么时候向外部客户进行兜售？就像谷歌现在已经开始卖 TPU 了，且在 27 年的话会有个 ramp up。亚马逊聊到我们和谷歌之间可能有些差别——它其实不是和谷歌之间有些差别，而是从卖 TPU 的想法的时间点上去看的话，亚马逊没有额外的产能在那边，包括成熟度也没有 TPU 做得好，效率也其实也没有 TPU 高。

所以从这个角度，我昨天在视频里说，我说亚马逊卖他们芯片的时间点可能落后于谷歌两三个季度，这个时间区间可能过于乐观了。从这个角度去看，他们说 2027 年底会开始卖，那就是落后谷歌差不多一年左右。

三、仓位更新：跌完之后的回顾

好吧，最后对我自己的仓位做一个更新。

这个仓位本身是已经算上了现在盘后所出现的这个下跌，差不多晚上 9 点、10 点、11 点左右那个跌幅，当时跌幅英特尔的跌幅已经是 20% 以上了。那所以经过跌幅之后——包括亚马逊也出现了下跌——跌完之后，我的 YTD 差不多 21%、22% 左右，接近于今年 7 月份的水平。

今年 7 月份的时候我最多跌到了 YTD 18%，这是今年 7 月底的时候。然后现在这一波的跌幅，从体感上我觉得这一波的跌幅因为比较的快，而且英特尔又是出现了非常大幅度的跌幅，从体感上可能比 7 月份还要严重，这是我体感上的一个感受。

但其实从结果去，因为整个 8、9 月份反弹得比较好，所以当时我其实从 7 月份跌完之后 8 月份去破了一个新高，当时 YTD 最高到了 44、45，经过这一波跌幅之后可能从最高点要回调 18%、19% 左右。那我是可以接受的。即使今年我如果在 One point 跑输了这个市场，我认为我也可以接受——这个没办法。

这就我今天在 X 上所说的：我说我如果能够接受它发布完财报之后涨 20%，那我必须要接受它发布完财报之后跌 20%。这个没有办法，我不可能保证它每一次财报都一定会超出市场预期，且市场都会给出正面的反馈。而且公司本身它不可能每一天、每一周、每一个月都在出现上涨。

那可能回过头我在今年年底做总结的时候，我再对于这段时间的操作去做一个回顾，看一下以后有没有什么地方可以进行改进。

四、宏观：10 月与 9 月的完全反转

好吧，但是今天我想分享的主要是：如果左边所有的百分比都是已经经过下跌完之后的百分比。那下跌完之后，我这边有个目标。因为我说，接下去 11 月份和 12 月份整个——

首先我们有一点需要明白的是：整个 10 月份到现在体感非常的差，因为大科技跌得比较多，半导体跌得比较的多，和 9 月份完全反过来了。但其实你去看整个标普 500 的参与度其实是比较高的，我看了一下标普的参与度去到短期 20 均线要去到 76、77 了。

为什么？因为价值股走得非常的强。而价值股走得非常的强——我们要把这个分开——很多价值股走得非常的强不代表这家公司本身非常的强，只是因为现在整个行业、整个价值股就是走得强。那为什么走得强？是因为利率出现下跌了。这是一个非常大的宏观背景在背后。

所以我们要把宏观的走势和个股的走势还是要区分开来。然后再加上一些个股上的走势，可能一些标的就会走得比较好。比如说像伊莱利利，整个医疗板块在 10 月份走得非常的好，但 9 月份跌得非常的多；那 10 月份走得非常的好，然后又加上伊莱利利发财报，所以比如说在今天的话就走得比较的好。所以这一块我们要稍微区分开来。

整个 10 月份的走势和 9 月份是完全反过来：因为 9 月份利率上涨，利率上涨价值股下跌，但是半导体板块、芯片板块和大科技走得相当的强；10 月份是完全反转。

但是我们千万不要去做一个线性外推，认为 11 月份和 12 月份就一定会延续 10 月份的下跌，然后持续下跌。你要再这么跌下去的话，半导体会变得非常非常的便宜，那个大科技也会变得非常非常的便宜。

然后你再退后一步去思考一下：整个，如果你认为 AI 这个趋势没有结束的话，你去思考一下现在很多价值股的标的，比如像可口可乐——现在估值是在 25 倍、26 倍静态市盈率，动态的话 24 倍，动态的话也在 24、25，未来 EPS 每年这个增速就是在 7%、8% 左右。而且利率未来又是会长期保持在一个高位。反过来你看这些大科技，可能 Forward PE 就是在 18 倍、19 倍，且它这个 EPS 的增速又非常的高。

到那时候，我们要自己问自己：到底哪一类的标的是我们未来想去布局的？

五、目标仓位：医疗板块的"大手笔"

所以我今天分享这个，我主要是说因为接下去利用接下去的两个月，我们要准备为 27 年去做一个准备。那我想了半天，可能还不是我最终的 target，但是这边先想一下，然后和大家分享一下，之后我可能会做调整，但是这个调整如果再有调整的话，可能也是一个微调。

医疗：8% → 19%（最大的调整）

这边有一个目标仓位，然后有一个年底目标仓位，这一块和年底我做了比较大的一个调整——主要是在医疗板块这一个调整。我在前天的那期视频已经说过，接下去我的期待是 2027 年在医疗板块这一块可能会有很多的落地，所以我把医疗板块的目标从 8% 上调到了 19%，非常大幅度的一个上调。

软件、硬件、大科技

那我聊到医疗板块、软件板块、硬件：

  • 软件板块：我从 16% 上调到了 18%。
  • 硬件板块：从 20% 降到 14%。
  • 大科技：会从 10% 降到 5%。

大科技背后的一个思考是：我亚马逊可能会持续减仓，然后剩下一部分大科技——因为我现在大科技里面算作什么大科技？算作大科技的仓位是亚马逊加特斯拉。特斯拉是 3.9% 这个仓位，特斯拉我说我是愿意想去加特斯拉的，所以我把大科技仓位放在 5%。那亚马逊的仓位我可能会慢慢的减，去到哪里？可能会去到医疗板块。

硬件下调的权衡

那硬件板块的这个下降，我思考了很长时间。因为我本身其实把医疗板块放到 20% 的，差不多 20% 的医疗板块、20% 左右的软件。但是实在没有办法从其他仓位给调出来，所以我把医疗板块下降到 19、软件 18% 目标仓位，硬件板块只能从这边去减一些。

但是即使硬件板块减完之后硬件 14%，你看一下我这边还有缺点板块，缺点板块里边的 7%（从 8% 降到了 7%）。你把硬件和缺点加在一起还是有 21% 左右的仓位。因为缺点板块里边我有的两个标的，一个是 VST、一个是 BE，这两个标的本身其实也是偏硬件的，所以还是在半导体硬件和 AI 相关的。那这两个板块本身加在一起（缺电和硬件）还是 21%。所以 21% 硬件板块加缺点，然后医疗板块 19%，软件板块 18%——这三个板块基本上还是并驾齐驱的。

AI Agent 板块

另外一个 theme 就是 AI Agent。AI Agent 里边我现在只有谷歌和 Qualcomm 两个标的。AI Agent 本身我的目标仓位 14%，未来我可能加，但是加的话到底来自于哪里，我还要去思考。但是你想一下，AI Agent 里边两个标的——谷歌、包括高通——这两个标的其实也是受到一部分 AI 的影响。那所以整体加一起和 AI 相关的一些标题，这些仓位还是比较大的。

国防与稳定币

然后国防的话，我是没有任何的改变的。国防仓位最近这段时间国防走得相对会强一些，GE 也出现了一些反弹，所以国防现在被动仓位现在已经来到了 15.3%，高于目标仓位的 14% 了。然后稳定币板块和缺点板块我相对都减了，目标仓位相对都减了 1% 左右。

六、英特尔跌 20% 要不要加仓？

那这边年底的一个目标仓位，这是我思考完之后所列出来的百分比。那接下去，在年底之前我有没有可能改变？有，但是改变的幅度可能不会太大。

那之所以我分享的目标仓位，是因为我知道很多人会问我一个问题：英特尔跌了 20%，70 块钱应不应该加仓？我会不会加仓？

从价格走势去看，其实我非常想加仓。因为正好把两个季度之前财报那一波上涨的一个缺口全部给补掉了。

但是如果根据我明年的这个目标仓位，医疗板块我要拉到 19%——因为我想过医疗板块如果 15% 可不可以？我觉得不是那么的够。所以我没办法，我把医疗板块拉上去，把软件板块也拉上去，必定要有其他一部分的地方稍微腾一些仓位出来。

所以我这个思考是：因为我现在现金仓位里面还有 NUGT 那将近 4% 左右的仓位，对于黄金这一块 NUGT 这个标的我是这么去思考的——黄金如果跌破 4000 的话，确认跌破 4 千的话，我会止损出局。如果没有确认跌破 4 千的话，那英特尔这块我可能会去做一个交易，找到机会的话可能会去做一个交易，那交易的仓位来自于哪？可能就是来自于黄金这一块短期上的仓位。

好吧，所以接下去还是看机会。然后这边目标仓位主要是在年底之前，我会尽量往这个目标去靠。

结尾

好吧，那这就今天的全部内容。如果大家有问题的话，我们可以在留言区里面继续交流。那下期见。

## 一、藏在指引里的"记忆体回旋镖"：一次没人说破的产业链反噬
管理层把 PC 第四季度 miss 的 15–18 亿美元几乎全部归因到"客户在最近几周说市场严重放缓"，归咎到"Memory 价格上涨"。但真正值得玩味的是：**内存涨价本身是 AI 军备竞赛的副产品**——HBM 吃掉了 DRAM 的产能，大云把 SK 海力士、三星、美光的高端产能锁死，溢出的价格压力顺着供应链"回旋镖"打回了消费 PC 市场。
于是你会看到一个诡异的因果链：**英伟达拿到的订单越凶，联想戴尔惠普越造不出便宜笔记本，英特尔的 CCG 业务就越惨**。英特尔同时站在 AI 盛宴的受益端（数据中心 CPU + 代工）和受害端（PC 内存成本）——它既是赢家又是输家，而市场却只允许一家公司有一个故事线，这就是今晚 -20% 的更深层解释。
## 二、分析师的"线性外推陷阱"与一个物理学家都会笑的毛利预测
视频里罕见地把 27–30 年的毛利预期全列了出来：44% → 46.6% → 51.9% → 53.9%。你看着这组数字，是不是觉得像教科书里的"合理增长"？
**这是典型的 Spherical

item.title: [Lex Clips] Limits of AI - explained by mathematicians | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"证明成立但我不懂为什么"——这是数学家的坦白，还是宇宙的隐喻？

Terence（第一位发言者）说出了一句乍听平常、细想惊人的话：我能证明定理，但不理解证明为什么有效。这句话常被当作谦虚，但它其实是数学家的"语言学时刻"——就像我们都能说母语却说不出语法规则，证明的"合法性"与证明的"可理解性"是两个独立维度。

一个出人意料的连接：这正是Ramanujan悖论在当代AI时代的回声。拉马努金从梦中得到公式，哈代用严格证明把它们追认下来——而今天，AI成了"反向拉马努金"：它给出严谨得无懈可击的证明，但没有梦，没有直觉，没有"为什么"。换句话说，数学家一直在和两种神秘主义打交道——过去是神，现在是神经网络。而他之所以不相信 Solved Axiom（"一切定理终将被解出"），恰恰是因为他知道：解出 ≠ 理解，而数学真正的推进力一直是后者。

二、对抗样本的真正含义：AI 不是在"看错"，而是在"看另一个宇宙"

Ankur 讲到 Alex Madry 的那个实验——给猫图加上"狗的扰动"再标成狗，训练出的网络居然在正常图上也能工作——通常被解读为"AI 有漏洞"。但他引用的论文标题才是真正的炸药：Adversarial examples are features, not bugs。

这意味着什么？意味着在图像的高维像素空间里，存在一套人类视觉系统完全盲视的、却同样有效的"猫狗判别特征"。AI 没有作弊，它只是在和我们不同的维度里完成了同一个分类任务。

跨领域的类比在这里非常锋利：这就像蜜蜂看紫外线、蛇感红外线、鲨鱼感电场——同一个"猎物在哪里"的问题，不同物种用完全不同的物理通道去解。AI 之于人类，不是"更笨的人"或"更聪明的人"，而更像一个新物种的感官器官。更出人意料的是：这个观察反过来质疑了"可解释性"研究的前提——我们追问"AI 为什么这样决策"，可能相当于要求蜜蜂用人类色觉描述它看到的紫外线。翻译注定失真。

三、"简单而可推广" ——数学家心中的黄金标准，可能正是 AI 最擅长的

Ankur 提到一个被低估的事实：用程序自动蒸馏物理定律（从观测重新推出 F=ma、Navier-Stokes）今天已经在发生。这件事如果展开，会把"人类将永远是提问者"这个浪漫叙事撕开一个口子。

一个没人愿意正面讨论的推论：数学家所推崇的"美"——简洁、普适、优雅——恰好是最容易被机械枚举算法逼近的审美维度。换言之，人类对"深刻"的判断可能一直在无意间向"低描述长度"（Kolmogorov 复杂度低）靠拢。而压缩，正是现代机器学习的本质。

一个更挑衅的跨领域连接：这与进化生物学的"最小基因组"研究同构——Craig Venter 团队用算法剥离细菌基因直到找到维持生命的最小集合（JCVI-syn3.0，只有 473 个基因）。生物学在找"生命的最简内核"，物理学在找"自然的最简方程"，数学在找"定理的最简证明"。三个学科在用三种语言描述同一件事：宇宙似乎奖励压缩。而如果这是真的，那么"人类负责问问题，AI 负责算答案"这种分工可能是暂时的——因为"好问题"本身也往往是一个高压缩率的对象。

四、Centaur Math——真正的隐喻其实来自国际象棋

Ankur 最后提到 "centaur math"（人机半人马数学）作为未来方向——这个词的来源其实耐人寻味。它出自 1997 年深蓝击败卡斯帕罗夫之后，卡斯帕罗夫本人提出的"高级象棋"概念：人+机的组合，在相当长一段时间里击败了纯人类和纯机器。

但这里有个被普遍忽略的结局：到了 2017 年前后，顶级的 centaur 组合开始输给纯 AI。半人马范式有一个保质期。

所以当两位数学家谈论"centaur math 是机会而不是恐惧"时，他们在描述的可能是一个有明确窗口期的过渡态——人类数学家的真正角色，或许不是在这个过渡期扮演好"骑手"，而是在这个窗口内弄清：当 AI 不再需要人类提问时，数学作为一种人类活动，剩下的意义是什么？Terence 已经在给答案了："价值不能只是'我问了一个好问题，我证了一个漂亮定理'"——这句话里藏着整整一代数学家将要面对的身份重构。

📝 转录文本

关于 Solved Axiom 的怀疑

Terence: By the way, and so to — sorry, to go back to your point — I don't actually believe the Solved Axiom. I don't think we're there.

I can prove a theorem, but I don't understand why the proof works. There's some magic that happens over here, and until I generalize somehow the phenomenon and understand it more deeply, then I'll see why the proof works the way it does.

Maybe that's one of the reasons why I don't actually believe the Solved Axiom: because the things that we do are much more exploratory. And what constitutes a good question beyond just, "Here's the Riemann hypothesis, make some progress on it"?

美、简洁性，与"谁在提问"

Ankur: So I think you also brought up a really important point — this generality and generalization of our concepts.

So related to beauty and mathematics, I think one of the gold standards has always been: how simple can your result be, and how much does it generalize? And, you know, out of this infinite space of theorems that could be proven, finding some structure that is simple and generalizes — that is, I think, still the gold standard.

And unless I'm mistaken, humans are still asking the questions. So, like, we prove existence-uniqueness of Navier-Stokes with AI, but humans are guiding this. Humans are still asking the questions. And I would love to see the next breakthrough: if you had a machine that can prove any theorem you pose, I want it to start telling me what questions I should be asking.

机器自动发现物理定律

Lex: Do you think it's possible that that machine just does a for-loop and finds all the simple and generalizable — basically all the E = mc² ?

Ankur: That's happening today, actually. So there are absolutely research programs that are systematically, automatically discovering kind of minimal physical laws. So this is less mathematical theorems, more physics governing laws and equations.

Lex: So observing natural systems and trying to see in those natural systems if there's simple physical laws that model how they operate.

Ankur: Yeah, distilling it down to the basics. So you can kind of recapitulate known theories. If you observe balls dropping, you can deduce gravity and F = ma. If you observe fluids, you can deduce Navier-Stokes.

And then, taking that to data, we haven't written down simple equations: weather, turbulence, solar flares, things like that. And I'm assuming similar things are happening in math, where there are probably these, like, minimal pieces that can be deduced.

"我能贡献的，它也能贡献" —— Terence 版本的 Solved Axiom

Lex: Do you think there's a large space of simple and generalizable things in math that could be discovered automatically?

Terence: So my version of the Solved Axiom is that anything that I do as a human mathematician — I've tried on several occasions to sit down and say, "Okay, LLMs will never do this that I do." And I'm like, "Well, why not? I can ask a question. I can ask it a question." I can ask it, "What questions should I ask?" Right?

Because it's such a generalized system — I'm not saying that it's good at all of those things now — but my version of the Solved Axiom is: anything that I can contribute as a human being, it could also have contributed on its own.

And so what I really mean by that is: in terms of value, what do I bring to the community? It can't be I asked a great question. It can't necessarily be — in this world of the Solved Axiom, which again I don't believe — but even in that world, it should be something other than I asked a great question, I proved a great theorem. And even in that world, I think you need mathematicians, people with human mathematical expertise.

Ankur 的回应：拟人化的危险

Lex: Ankur, do you believe in the Solved Axiom? Where on the spectrum of how close we can get to it — and in that spectrum, what's the role of the human, do you think?

Ankur: I guess I don't really believe in the Solved Axiom. I think — you know, maybe it's half true in some ways, and figuring out which half of it is true will be very interesting and challenging. So I think there'll be major surprises and more to come in terms of what AI can solve.

But, for me, when you're facing a new technology that's really, really good, the danger is that when you try to conceptualize why it's working, you do so by anthropomorphizing it.

深度学习的教训：对抗样本是"特征"而非"漏洞"

So, you know, maybe one of the earlier lessons here is from deep learning. There are these amazing examples: you can take neural nets, and you can do human-level or better object recognition. But in general, the way that it succeeds is less robust than how a human does — because there are all these examples like adversarial examples, where you can add very slight patterns to natural images that can completely fool these object-detection systems, but not a human.

I had a former colleague at MIT, Alex Madry, that had some really nice work which I really enjoyed. I think the title was something like Adversarial Examples Are Features, Not Bugs. So they did the following cool experiment:

  • Take a bunch of natural data — maybe pictures of cats and dogs.
  • Train a deep network to identify them very well.
  • Add some adversarial perturbations to them that, to the AI system, make a cat look like a dog and vice versa — a small little pattern that changes how the object detector works.
  • Then create a totally fake dataset: pictures of cats with dog patterns on top, labeled as "dog," and vice versa for cats.

And amazingly, when you train a deep network on this with all the wrong labels, it's going to learn something that does well on natural data.

So somehow, when we recognize what a cat and dog is, we do it in a way that we can articulate in terms of its legs and its tail and its shape in general. But a lot of times, when deep networks or AI can do things, they might be able to find trapdoors or backdoors to solving the problem that use a lot of statistical relationships in the data that a human doesn't.

边界、Centaur Math，与保留的谦卑

So to me, it's important to not draw this boundary very sharply between what you can do and what AI can't do — because you're going to be wrong.

But that doesn't mean that I don't believe there will emerge some kind of boundary, if only for the fact that I think we over-anthropomorphize the way that they solve problems. And when I'm looking through the OpenAI solutions, they just don't look like a human has solved those problems.

So to me, there still seems to be a very big qualitative difference — and that's an opportunity, really, for collaboration and centaur math more than it is dread about the AI overlords. But, you know, who knows? Could be wrong next week.

item.title: [Lex Clips] The $1 trillion dollar problem - Navier Stokes expert explains | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：这个"反例"不是在否定物理，而是在揭示方程比现实更"极端"

AI 构造的那个无限细化的涡丝，像花样滑冰收臂加速一样把自己拉成一根近乎零维的线——有限能量，却在局部长出无穷大的涡量。这里真正令人震撼的不是"方程可能爆破"，而是：Navier-Stokes 方程里藏着现实从未允许发生的解。 真实流体里黏性是慷慨的，它把每一次欲望般的集中都及时抹平；而方程作为一种"纯数学造物"，却保留了这种病态自由。

换句话说，这不是数学去追赶物理，而是数学暴露出：我们日常依赖的方程，描述的世界比真实世界更宽广也更危险。 这几乎是柏拉图式的——理想原型里住着现实中被禁锢的鬼魂。15 年前数学家才开始相信反例可能存在，正是因为需要先放下"物理直觉即数学真理"这个潜意识前提。

二、一个让人意外的跨领域连接：金融闪崩、癫痫与涡丝其实是同一类事件

把这段话从流体力学抽离出来，你会发现同一个结构反复出现：

  • 闪崩（flash crash）：全市场总能量（流动性）有限，但在毫秒内集中到某几个标的，形成"波动率奇点"。
  • 癫痫发作：大脑总电活动稳定，但突触放电在局部神经集群内相干同步，形成"放电涡丝"。
  • 黑洞形成：总质量有限，曲率在一点发散——所以广义相对论才需要"宇宙监督假说"来挽回体面。

这些系统共享一个数学灵魂：守恒的全局量 + 失控的局部集中率。 流体里负责"兜底"的是黏性耗散，大脑里是抑制性中间神经元，市场里是做市商与熔断机制，相对论里是事件视界。Navier-Stokes 的千禧难题，本质上在问一个远比流体更普世的问题：在怎样的方程结构下，自然必定会自动安装一个"审查员"？

嘉宾说这"物理反直觉"，其实不是——现实世界里到处都有这种被压制的奇点倾向。只是我们习惯了看到审查员工作的结果，而忘了审查员本身的存在。

三、"百万 vs 万亿"这个比值，是整个科学共同体的隐秘诊断书

嘉宾那句俏皮话值得停下来咀嚼：解决百万美元的数学问题，几乎不触动那个万亿美元的工程问题。 这不是谦虚，而是暴露了一个结构性错位——

数学家在证明"解是否存在"，工程师在问"解长什么样、算得多快"。前者是关于方程内在生命的问题，后者是关于方程对外行为的问题。这就像语言学家证明一种语言在形式上无矛盾，与一位诗人用这门语言写出能让人落泪的诗之间——相关，但近乎正交。

更深的洞察是：人类知识市场的声望结构，与它的效用结构严重脱钩。 Clay 研究所的七大千禧难题闪闪发光，而真正能让碳排降低、让心脏泵更安静、让飞机更省油的那些"脏兮兮的"模型降阶、湍流闭合、逆向设计问题，几乎没有同等的智力荣耀供给。这是一种学术市场的流动性错配——有限的智力能量集中在少数"奇点问题"上，而广袤的工程相空间里，许多可解但不优雅的问题长期无人问津。

有意思的推论：如果未来 AI 真的开始主导科学发现，第一个被重新定价的，可能恰恰是这种"百万/万亿"错配。AI 不懂声望，只懂梯度。

📝 转录文本

From Vortex Coalescence to a Mathematical Singularity

Coalescing into medium vortices, coalescing into bigger vortices. But so the AI proof of this kind of counterexample — that you can have finite blowup — basically creates this very, very specialized vortex that in the third dimension is stretching out and thinning it, so that it can essentially become, uh, infinitely thin. The radius gets smaller and smaller and smaller as it stretches out.

Kind of like a figure skater doing a spin — you pull your arms in, you go much, much faster. And there's this very specialized kind of rate of contraction of this vortex, so that the energy in the fluid still remains finite, but at this localized filament the flow kind of blows up and you get infinite vorticity.

A Recent Shift in Mathematical Intuition

I was surprised when mathematicians, before the AI proof, started thinking it was going to be possible to find this counterexample.

— Which only started maybe 15 years ago.

— That's right. It's, like, relatively recent —

— ... in the grand scheme of things.

— Yep. Instead of looking for a solution, looking for a counterexample, yeah.

— Yep. 'Cause all of our physical intuition tells us diffusion does solve the problem, and so it is, like, very physically counterintuitive.

The Engineer's Perspective: Important, But Not Transformative

— In the mathematics world, that's a really hard problem. Impressive to construct a counterexample. What does it teach you as an engineer who's stared and studied at a lot of different natural systems that are fluids? And maybe take that as a step towards: what are the equivalent kind of hardness, and harder problems yet to be solved, in fluids?

— So it's a very important math result.

— Uh-oh.

— I'll say, like —

— But —

— ... day-to-day engineering fluids and applied-math kind of analysis of fluids is almost completely unchanged. Fluids are just as hard to simulate and predict today as they were a month ago or two months ago.

And so when I'm trying to actually solve an engineering problem with a fluid — I wanna design an airplane wing, or an artificial heart, or whatever it is — I'm still having to simulate and predict and manipulate this flow in a very practical way that's expensive in terms of supercomputer time and wind-tunnel resources.

And this mathematical theorem and proof are very interesting, but it operates at a regime that's so non-physical that it doesn't really affect my day-to-day engineering.

The Million-Dollar Problem vs. the Trillion-Dollar Problem

There's still — I don't know, this is very pithy, but I like to say: you know, we solved the million-dollar math problem. There's a trillion-dollar engineering problem, which is, like: how do you predict these things in a fast, efficient way, and do this inverse design? That's a much harder problem.

— And you say it's a trillion dollar because that literally —

— Literally —

— ... if you solve some of these problems, that's how much money you'll make — not 'cause it's a prize, but, like, there's industries.

— Yeah. And we could say, you know, trillion dollars of possible benefit to humanity of, like, better, faster solutions, lower drag, less emissions, you know, all of it. We have, like, transportation, defense, health, energy — all of these have, you know, fluids at the very core technology.

Why the Math Still Matters — As a Baby Step

And so I think those problems are still very hard. And this math result is important in the sense I was talking about earlier: that we don't know the fundamental character of what is possible in these equations. We don't even know if the solutions exist. That's, like, so fundamental. This is, like, a baby step towards a much bigger human goal of understanding what's in an equation in a more practical sense.

item.title: [All-In Podcast] WHOOP CEO, Will Ahmed: 50B Hours of Health Data, a 4 Million Member Data Moat, & the FDA Fight
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、订阅制不是"收钱方式"，而是公司灵魂的手术

Will 讲到 2018 年从 500 美元买断转向订阅时，大多数听众会把这当作"商业模式优化"。但真正惊人的点藏在他一句轻描淡写的话里："it changed our DNA."

这是一个被严重低估的因果链： - 买断制 → 公司激励是让你换新，所以每 12 个月必须发布新硬件（哪怕没有真正创新） - 订阅制 → 公司激励是让你不走，所以 18 个月前买的硬件现在还能用上 ECG、血压、Healthspan 这些后发功能

反直觉之处在于：订阅制让 Whoop 变成了一家"反苹果"公司。苹果的商业模型逼它每年制造"你的旧设备不够好"的焦虑；Whoop 的商业模型逼它制造"你的旧设备还会变得更好"的期待。同一个硬件生意，收费节奏一变，整个公司的伦理走向就反转了。

跨领域连接：这与 Rolls-Royce 把喷气引擎从"卖发动机"改成"按飞行小时收费"（Power by the Hour）是同一种 DNA 手术。一旦收入和使用时长绑定，公司就从"推销员"变成了"守护者"。订阅制的真正革命从来不在财务报表里，而在工程师每天醒来时问自己的那个问题里。

二、23.6 小时 ≠ 可穿戴，而是人类身上诞生了第二个心脏

Will 轻飘飘地提到一个数字：平均每位会员每天佩戴 23.6 小时。

请停下来品一下这个数字。它意味着——用户只在洗澡的几分钟和换电池的几分钟里把 Whoop 取下。Apple Watch 的平均日佩戴时间大约在 12-14 小时，Fitbit 更低。23.6 小时是一个相位转变的信号：这个东西已经不是"你戴着的设备"，而是"你身体的延伸器官"。

这里有一个被所有人忽略的隐藏结论：Whoop 不是赢在产品，而是赢在"去掉屏幕"这个看似倒退的决定上。

  • 有屏幕 → 你会主动看它 → 它变成任务 → 你取下它休息
  • 无屏幕 → 你忘记它存在 → 它变成皮肤 → 24 小时数据流不中断

这是一种"反注意力经济"的产品哲学。整个硅谷过去 15 年都在抢夺你的屏幕时间，Will 做了相反的事：让你忘记这个产品存在，以便获取你所有不在屏幕前的时间。

跨领域连接：这与婚戒的进化路径惊人相似——婚戒从"炫耀的装饰"演化为"忘记它在手上的符号"，恰恰是因为它的意义不在被看见，而在持续在场。Whoop 做了同样的事，只不过把符号变成了数据流。

三、HRV 的真相是一场医学哲学的静默政变

Jason 讲到两次救命经历：一次 COVID、一次肺部炎症压迫心脏。Will 则讲了棒球运动员的霍奇金淋巴瘤、另一位十年老用户的睾丸癌。所有这些病症彼此毫无关联——却都被同一个指标提前捕捉到。

这里藏着一个被主流医学系统还没消化的爆炸性事实：HRV 不是在诊断具体疾病，它是在检测"系统性偏离"。

传统医学的范式是：特定症状 → 特定检测 → 特定诊断。 Whoop 揭示的新范式是：系统性偏离 → 定向探查 → 发现任意异常。

这是从"命中式诊断"到"预测性维护"的根本范式迁移。

跨领域连接：这与波音、劳斯莱斯几十年来在喷气引擎上做的事情一模一样。他们不会去"诊断"引擎某个具体零件会不会坏，而是在引擎上埋成百上千个传感器，持续监测振动、温度、压力的偏离基线的程度。偏离到某个阈值 → 不等故障发生，直接检修。

人类医学正在从"修理工模式"迁移到"预测性维护模式"，而 Whoop 可能是第一个在消费级规模上实现这件事的公司。这解释了为什么 FDA 和 Whoop 的冲突不是"合规问题"，而是监管体系的本体论危机——FDA 的分类框架（"健康 vs 医疗"）建立在旧范式之上，一个本质上拒绝分类的技术必然撕裂它。

四、彩蛋：一个让人脊背发凉的推论

Will 提到他们已经能"通过生理信号预测某项生化指标偏离正常范围，而无需测量该指标本身"。

这句话的技术含义被大多数人错过了：这意味着在未来某个版本里，抽血检查可能会被反向定义——不再是"定期全套体检"，而是"Whoop 告诉你哪一项该查"。

更深一层的哲学意味：可穿戴数据正在吞噬实验室检测的市场定位。50 年来血检产业建立在"你不知道自己哪里有问题，所以我们查一切"的前提上。当这个前提被打破时，整个诊断行业的商业结构都要重排——而 Whoop 作为"分流器"将坐在上游。

LeBron 11 年不签约却自愿佩戴——这不只是营销美谈。它是一个信号：顶级身体的持有者比医生更早意识到了这场范式迁移。他们在用自己的身体做早期研究。

深入解释 HRV（心率变异性）

Will: HRV stands for heart rate variability. It's the amount of time between successive beats of the heart. And it's a little counterintuitive, but the more variability in time between successive beats of the heart, the healthier your overall system is operating.

And it's this lens into your autonomic nervous system, which consists of sympathetic and parasympathetic activity. So sympathetic activation — heart rate up, blood pressure up, respiration up. It's what happens when you have a thought like "there's a lion in the room," or when you start to exercise, or you're thinking about something stressful. Conversely, parasympathetic is all the opposite. Heart rate down, blood pressure down, respiration down. It's what helps you fall asleep. If you exhale for a long period of time, that's parasympathetic.

And what you want is for sympathetic activity and parasympathetic activity to be coupled. So your body's kind of constantly regulating its environment. And when that's the case, it means you have a higher heart rate variability — that the measurement will be higher. And we're measuring heart rate variability 24/7. It was really one of the key innovations in founding the company. I did all this medical research when I was a student at Harvard and heart rate variability was a thing that like jumped off the page to me because there was really interesting research on it, but it couldn't be measured 24/7. And so that's where part of where Whoop was born out of.

Anyway, heart rate variability is something that we use for stress monitoring. It's something we use for our recovery score. We baseline everyone on Whoop and then we're able to show you every day: are you within your baseline? Are you a little higher? A little lower? And when you look at trends of this over years, you start to get a sense for: is someone getting healthier over time or less healthy. It's a really important longevity indicator.

Typically speaking, as you get older, your heart rate variability will drop. So, people who are in their 20s, their heart rate variability will be anywhere between 80 and 100 on average. 30s, you start to drop to 70. 40s, you start dropping to 50. 50s, 60s, all of a sudden you're in 30s and below. And so if you can fight that trend — those averages — and keep your heart rate variability even just flat over years, that's actually a sign of good fitness, good longevity.
