This is a good point to explain what the journal is.

Will: Yeah. The Whoop Journal is essentially a 100+ different behaviors, lifestyle decisions, supplements, drugs — you name it — that someone might want to log. Popular things that people log every day are: did I drink alcohol last night? Was I hydrated? Did I travel? Did I meditate? Was I happy? Was I sad? Was I stressed? And all of this anecdotal information also builds on these data sets. If you wanted to come up with an algorithm for predicting whether someone would be happy, you would actually need a fair amount of data from someone on their overall mood as an example. So anyway, we're excited about bringing all these different types of data sets together, and it's one thing that we feel uniquely positioned to do because not that many companies have people opening their app eight times a day and 80% of their member base interacting with the AI.

The journal was a major unlock for me. Here's from a user perspective — since we're doing a whole user session here. What's really interesting about it is you get these behavioral insights. And I think you get into behavioral insight when you've used it 10 times — five yeses, five nos. As an example, if you're doing creatine, somebody's paying attention at Whoop. And I guess you got a lot of — how many people working over there now?

Will: 1,200.

Whoa. That's grown significantly.

Will: Yeah, pretty grew.

Yeah. Wow. So when you pull up your behavioral insights — in the morning it will ask you and prompt you, because in the mornings when everybody opens this to check their sleep score, recovery, it prompts you. You can start to figure out after this "five and five" what impact that behavior has on recovery.

洗热水澡 +7%：令人惊讶的个体化发现

So it turns out for a warm bath — which was never my thing. I hate baths. Not my thing. Like, I'm a guy going in a bath, hanging out in a bath, I have no interest. I'm like a guy from Brooklyn. Kind of feels weird to be in a bath with the candles.

Will: Any salts in the bath? Are you adding frag—?

I did add the — yes, you got me. I'm adding salts to the bath. Yes. And that's now also tracked.

Will: It helps.

It helps. Warm bath — plus 7% on my recovery. Have you ever heard of something like that?

Will: That's very high as a response. For folks who are trying to figure out what we're talking about — essentially, when you log these things, Whoop then will tell you what's positively or negatively affecting your recovery score. A big wake-up call for a lot of people ends up being alcohol, because it'll show you that alcohol has this hugely negative effect.

Disastrous.

Will: On your recovery.

It's poison. I don't drink, so I never even log it. But—

Will: You have a couple of beverages now and again.

Will. And then what impact has — I feel like I've got a good relationship with alcohol, although it's got a negative 9% for me. So I'm now looking at my behavior insights. Here's a sneaky one —

Will: Wait, have you considered having that drink while you're in the warm bath?

Yeah, right. Maybe I should start adding more baths. But I do steam room, I do cold plunge — those are more neutral, but I like the way they make me feel. And there's a lot of longevity research on saunaing and contrast therapy.

晚餐时间与维生素 D 的相关性

So second to alcohol for being the most negative for me is a late meal. Eating within 3 hours of bedtime, we've now seen across the entire Whoop population, is really detrimental to your sleep and your recovery.

Will: It's because your body is still digesting for those first few hours that you're in bed. And as a consequence you're not getting quality sleep.

So you get high stress during the sleep, I would assume. Yeah, that whole high stress thing. Here's mine. For some reason, vitamin D — minus 3. I don't know if that's accurate or not, but I was putting a little vitamin D in. Maybe that's a false positive.

Will: It could be that the days you took it were days that you were traveling. There could be something else going on.

There's a correlation here that we're not seeing yet.

Will: You can ask Whoop that. "I'm seeing vitamin D minus 3 — does that make sense? What could be going on?" And maybe it'll look at your travel alongside that.

Okay, this is a modest difference and it's a correlation, not evidence, that vitamin D caused the change. Your recent recovery has ranged 27% to 87%, but you haven't logged vitamin D in this 14-day stretch. So there's no recent complication. Okay, so I got a little more work to do on that one.

But plus 5 strain is minus 5 on recovery — that makes total sense.

Will: Yeah. When you work out, your body needs to recover.

Plus 1% of the day in high-stress zone — minus 9% on recovery. So through my — what does the stress score come from? Temperature, heart rate, HRV?

Will: Primarily HRV, but it's also using other sensing.

Got it. So that's kind of your special sauce — proprietariness in the stress score.

Will: The stress score itself is something that we invented. Of course, we based it on physiological research. And I would say that's one of the hard things about this space — which is: how do you take medical research that's credible, and then a lot of data (because you're going to be getting data from consumers), and then great design? Because at the end of the day, you have to design something to ultimately have a score that people want to look at. So there's a lot of science to it, but there's also art to it. And I think it's something Whoop has been very good at. The recovery score — and now our Healthspan score — is the most screenshotted page in the app.

Makes total sense. When you share that — consistent bedtime plus 4, caffeine plus 4, creatine plus 4, morning sunlight plus 3. Now that I have this, I also do some meditation with the Calm app and with Waking Up, or on my own — that also, I don't have enough data in there yet because I keep forgetting to log it. But it does log my skiing. So I use Slopes.

Will: Yeah.

So slopes — you're a skier, Will, or—?

Will: No, I ski but not — it sounds like you ski more than I do.

I mean, I try to get to 30-40 days a year, but two hours a day. So it's like executive skiing — CEO skiing, if you catch my drift. Do a podcast before, a little more —

Will: You're doing it in Japan.

I do 5-10 days in Japan — is the goal. The rest are at my ski house.

Will: That's elite skiing.

Yes. So you can come with me and Tucker Carlson if you're into it. It's a really weird trip.

Will: Great.

The other nice thing is it pulls in my Slopes data and puts it as an activity. So you have an activity tracker. The activity tracker is really great. I do these long walks in Japan or when I'm in New York. I love to do long walks my age. Long walks, and rucking, and farmer's walks are like the key to longevity, I'm told. But the great thing is, now it knows that, and it's making a training program for me around that. And it asked me — the AI — "What's my goal?" I said, "My goal is to not get injured and ski better, and these are the exercises I know are going to help." It's now the AI understands my goals, kind of coaching me and setting up plans.

GLP-1 追踪：药物与可穿戴的融合

And then lo and behold, one of the things I had asked you for maybe on DM somewhere on Twitter or something — you know, I take a GLP. So I started tracking it. I take a light GLP. Lost 43 pounds on it.

Will: Look at that, man. That's awesome.

Well, yeah. And I mean — let me tell you, that makes a difference when you're 213, you get to 170 — skiing, sleeping, everything. I wish I had Whoop during that journey.

Will: Did your resting heart rate go down a lot?

You know, I wasn't fully on Whoop for the majority of that. So that would have been so cool to have. You know what? I'll gain the 40 pounds back and then lose it. But now I'm on a maintenance dose. And you just released a GLP tracker that has in it all the cohorts of things you want to make sure you're doing when you're taking GLP, including protein consumption. So maybe you could talk a little bit about that and how GLPs are kind of making their way into the ecosystem here.

Will: Well, in general, in line with this theme of — we want to have a lot of data under the Whoop umbrella so that we can actually give you the right insights. If you're taking a GLP-1, that's a pretty meaningful shift to what's going to happen for your body. And one of the challenges with GLP-1s is that typically speaking, about 50% of the weight that someone loses is fat and 50% is muscle. So that's how sometimes people can end up getting quite frail even though they've lost a considerable amount of weight.

And so it's good for Whoop to know that you're on a GLP-1. And then in turn, it's really going to push you to get some activity and hopefully a little bit of strength training — even if it's just body weight — so that you don't end up losing that muscle. And I think that's also where the appropriate diet with protein, and — we've heard some anecdotal success around people taking creatine while they're on GLP-1s — I think is super important.

And just to say: we have all this data and we take it very seriously and we want it to be secure and private. We've actually gone through—

Oh, here we go. Yeah, I'm just — you know, I mirrored my phone. Here's my actual Whoop. You can see my resting heart rate, all that. But I added my GLP there, and it said, "You got to get to 9,800 steps now. You got to do two strength activities a week. Hydration 7 days a week. Protein." And then just check off that you took your GLP. And it took me through a little script to say, "How often do you take it," etc.

Will: And there would have been a process here, I imagine, where the AI was asking you about some of this, and you ultimately confirmed you wanted to do these things and have a plan, right?

Yeah, absolutely. And I'm at 300 days on my streak here.

The other thing you added — you added badges, a little bit more kind of like Peloton has an insane number of badges, and so you get to see where you're at. And I am a rucking machine. I'm in the top 1% of people doing rucking and farmers. So that's like a little competitive thing.

Will: Yeah, there you go. You got to maintain that now. You got to keep rucking every day.

FDA 之争：Wellness vs Medical 的分类战争

Okay, so let's talk about you and your relationship with the FDA. Little controversy here. It's been covered over and over again. All these devices, I guess, are not under medical devices. And maybe you could explain to us how the FDA looks at you versus other medical devices, and how that's changed over time.

You have blood pressure insights (BPI), and you launched it. The FDA was a little bit like, "Hey, we're not happy here." And then you have the ECG heart screening stuff. All of these devices — whether it's my Apple Watch — medically cleared.

Will: And that's medically cleared.

So, and when you do these things, you always get this disclaimer: "Hey listen, we're not in the heart attack business." So when I had those things, it's up to me to interpret that, or a doctor.

But talk to me about the tension and how it's been going across the two administrations. Because now you've lived through — President Trump is like all-in on disrupting, and he put a Kennedy in there to do that, and he's a bit of a disruptor himself and he's very pro-business. And then Biden — obviously maybe a little more regulation, less pro-business, definitively less pro-business — but I don't know in the medical space how that happened. So talk to me. It's not a politics show, but you're all running into regulation now.

Will: Well, just to say: it's been certainly a long process for Whoop in working with the FDA, and we've worked with them in a lot of different contexts, which I'll talk about here in a second. The history of very innovative technology with somewhat dated regulatory policies is a history that has controversy from time to time. So I'm not surprised that we've had some challenges or disagreements along the way. But I'm actually really happy with our relationship with the FDA today.

Now, four years ago, I really wanted to be able to do blood pressure monitoring. And historically, you needed a cuff for that. And it was really a pretty difficult signal processing problem. There was no product on the market that could measure blood pressure accurately from the wrist. So we set out to see if we could do it.

One of the ways that we collected a huge data set on it was in a collaboration with our members — we asked members if they wanted to participate in a stress, sleep, and blood pressure study, and as part of that we actually had 70,000 people enroll. So think about the ability to generate studies at huge scale fast. People were actually uploading their blood pressure readings every single day for a number of weeks. And what that allowed us to do was to build out a pretty powerful data set on blood pressure monitoring, and also to be able to train that alongside all of the physiological data that we were already collecting.

Anyway, fast forward, we get to a period where all of a sudden we've got a very powerful algorithm for measuring blood pressure. And that's one of the things that we do, I think, very well at Whoop: we pick a hard physiological signal, and then we say we want to be able to measure it as accurately — or within a similar accuracy — as a medical device. And then we look to bring that to consumers.

And there was controversy around blood pressure monitoring before we launched. Because prior to launching it, historically, blood pressure had been under the category of physiological signals that needed to be a quote-unquote "medical device." And just as some background for our listeners — the FDA is really supposed to evaluate products that have a medical diagnosis. And then if you're not providing a medical diagnosis, then it falls under a category called "wellness."

There's a pretty good history for this with heart rate monitoring, for example. If you do heart rate monitoring for exercise, that's wellness. If you do heart rate monitoring for sleep, that's wellness. If you do heart rate monitoring for AFib detection or heart attack prediction — okay, that needs to be regulated. So the FDA in the past had a pretty clear distinction for heart rate: this is wellness, this is medical.

With blood pressure, they said that if you're measuring blood pressure, it has to be medical. But the problem with that is there's an avalanche of research that supports that — not surprisingly — blood pressure affects your stress, it affects your sleep, it affects your overall well-being. And we felt like there was a pretty clear lane for us to introduce a blood pressure feature that was a wellness feature.

So we launched the feature. The FDA came back and said that they felt like it needed to be regulated. They actually sent us a warning letter. There was a big disagreement that played out that was quite public about it. But we stuck to our guns, and I ultimately really believe in the way that we approached it. And through a long process, the FDA actually has since updated their guidelines — I think based on our case, but also based on feedback from the industry — that supports that blood pressure can also have wellness applications. So our blood pressure insights feature is still available for consumers.

And just to say it: we have these conversations with the FDA across a lot of different categories. Whoop also has medical clearances from the FDA. So our ECG feature — where you can literally do an ECG from your wrist by just putting your fingers on the Whoop — that's an FDA-cleared product, 510(k). So in some cases we're going through a process of clinical trials to get FDA approval. In other cases, we want to bring a product to market faster, and we also believe it's a wellness application. And so that's kind of a healthy process for innovative companies like Whoop to be pursuing with the FDA.

为什么不自己做血压袖带、体重秤？

Why don't you guys — I know you guys have some sort of integration with this Omron blood pressure cuff. I was like looking it up. Why don't you guys just make your own blood pressure cuff? Or listen, we're at a $10 billion valuation here. We got four million members, 250 on average a year, let's say, or got a billion in revenue. Like, let's just buy this company, Omron, or let's get in the blood pressure cuff business, and let's get in the scale business while we're at it. Like, I trust the brand. I just want the Whoop scale. I want you to be the person who puts the features in. I want you to control it. I want it to work. I don't want to have to go through Apple Health and the back door to get my Fitbit scale uploaded. I just want a Whoop-branded blood pressure cuff and a Whoop-branded scale.

Will: Well, I appreciate you saying that. In a lot of categories, we are debating: do we want to build this ourselves, do we want to partner with someone, or are we going to make an acquisition? And often we've defaulted to either building or acquiring versus partnering. In the case of blood pressure cuffs, we felt like that was a fairly commoditized technology, and there is medical efficacy there. So if people want to do a calibration with a cuff to set up their Whoop, which will then measure it without the cuff — because at the end of the day, we kind of want to replace the cuff — that feels like a fairly healthy system.

And it's also worth saying that we feel like we've earned the right to accumulate all this data because we have very strong data policies. So we do not sell data. You are not the product, Jason. The membership is the product.

And that's a huge, I think, distinction in this space, especially when you have big technology — Apple. Yeah, let's just call it what it is. You may not want to say it, but — I can. They make their money advertising, and Apple's a pretty good steward of data, I'll give them that, but they make it on really expensive hardware. So you are unique in both cases — in terms of business model, you're in our corner, which I love.

Apple's going to make a competitor, huh? They know their watch kind of sucks and their software sucks. Like Apple Health is terrible.

Will: The Apple Watch is the most successful smartwatch in the world. So I think in terms of the category that they built to own, they've been successful. I think it's an important product for them. It's a product that does a lot of things. So if you want text messages and emails and to be able to call—

Too much. But they're going to make — you worry to keep you up at night that they're going to make a Whoop competitor.

Will: Well, I have enormous respect for Apple. I think they're one of the best in the world at hardware and software. I think a lot of companies have entered our space and had challenges with the screenless wearable or other wearable products. It's interesting — 10 years ago, there were more competitive products in the market than there are today.

That's true, actually. Yeah. You had a lot of people trying this.

Will: People forget the whole Jawbone kind of Fitbit era. There was a whole class of Nike and Adidas and Under Armour.

Yeah. I mean, how dumb was it for Nike to stop pursuing that? My god, it was such an obvious smart thing for them to do. They had a good start and then they gave the business to Fitbit, I believe, and then they just got out of it.

Lightning Round（闪电问答）

All right, listen. It's time for lightning round.

Will: Lightning round. Lightning round with Will.

Yeah. You got to be honest here. Here we go. Brian Johnson or Andrew Huberman? Pick one — for podcasting.

Will: Huberman.

Who's making a bigger contribution to the science and technology?

Will: I think Huberman has a wider audience. I think Brian has pushed people's imagination of what they should be measuring. And I think both of those are really helpful.

Cold plunge or cold shower? Make a difference.

Will: I'll say cold shower, because it's very accessible and it's something that people can do every day. And you do it for even 30 seconds, 60 seconds — you're just going to feel a lot better.

Yeah. Wakes you up. Red light therapy or just the classic hot sauna?

Will: I like the hot sauna. Old school.

Yes. It gets hotter. I think the red light thing is just marketing nonsense.

Will: Yeah.

Okay. Zone 2 cardio or lifting? This is for our age. I think you're 40 now, Will. Are you 40 yet?

Will: 37.

  1. All right. So I'm rounding you up to 40, I'm rounding myself down to 50. Zone 2 cardio or lifting? What do you think? You got to pick one for my age and for your age.

Will: I think this depends a lot on what someone's goals are. But in general, I think that everyone should be lifting more weights, and probably doing — if they have an hour to exercise, they should spend more time lifting and less time on an elliptical.

Love it.

Will: Because your muscle mass is such an important test for longevity.

The alarm in Whoop is quite sophisticated. You can wake up based on recovery, sleep score, or with a hard 6 a.m. — pick one of the three.

Will: If you're on vacation, you can go with recovery or sleep. But if you're trying to run a tech company, you better pick an exact time.

Okay. Coffee first thing in the morning, or wait 90 minutes? Which one?

Will: I personally drink the coffee.

Yeah. Let's go. All right. Strength score, sleep score, recovery score — which one do you obsess over most? You can't say they're all your children. You love them all equally.

Will: Recovery. I mean, I wake up every morning waiting to see that color of that dial.

大新闻：LeBron James 成为 Whoop 全球大使

I love it. All right, listen. There's your hour with Will from Whoop. Great product. I give it my highest endorsement. 8sleep I'm an investor in — I love that product, too. Those are my two favorite health products.

And hey — at the time of this recording, you have a little announcement about the king. No, not President Trump. Gotcha. Not King Trump — but LeBron James, now playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. Big announcement.

Will: Well, we're announcing today LeBron James is now a global ambassador for Whoop. He's been on Whoop, interestingly, for 11 years. And we never had any formal relationship with him. We loved that he wore the product. Frankly, it was really important in the early days that he did wear the product, because he was one of the first 100 people to ever wear it. And so it was incredibly validating that this incredible athlete was willing to try a technology from an unknown company called Whoop. And it gave us a lot of hope that we were on to something.

But it's been extraordinary to see his career over two decades plus. And he's really the pinnacle of performance and longevity. And so he joins a roster of ambassadors like Cristiano Ronaldo and Patrick Mahomes and Lewis Hamilton and Aryna Sabalenka and Nelly Korda, and so on. So it's a great group.

Now you had a philosophy though early on — we talked about this in our previous discussions — that like, you're not going to pay athletes to wear it, and you're not going to beg them to wear it, because they're the customers. They're the ICP, the ideal customer profile. So, is this maybe a change in thinking, or is this a unique one-of-one case? Hey, he's been on the product for 11 years without a formal relationship, and he's in that era now — he's going to retire in a couple of years, and hey, man, he's probably going to go into this Kobe/Shaq post-playing era where he gets in deep into business. So what's the thinking here, and how do you think about athletes at large?

Will: I think in general, if your business is pre-marketing, so to speak — like, you're not in a stage where you're doing big television advertisements and so on and so forth — you should be really careful paying anyone to use your product. You want people to love your product authentically. And in our case, it just so happened that early on our target market was these professional athletes. So we needed them to organically love the product. And by the way, because you have to wear it 24/7 — there's no amount of money I'm going to be able to pay an athlete to wear something 24/7 if they don't like it, right?

So on the flip side, it was like, "Well, if it actually works and it's measuring their sleep and recovery and they play better, they should want to pay for it." That was our attitude for a long time. And we had a number of these individuals who are best-in-class of their sport — global people — that wanted to invest in the company because they loved it so much.

Amazing.

Will: And from there, we also developed relationships where we could use their name, image, and likeness, which has a value associated with it, that we recognize — to be able to do advertising. So they've been amazing partnerships, and I'm very grateful that LeBron James is part of the Whoop roster.

Whoop 能否在比赛中佩戴？

Wait — are the players allowed to wear these during games?

Will: That's something the NBA is still looking at.

Got it. Yeah, because they're not allowed to wear jewelry. They got to take all that off because of injuries. But they could put it — because you could wear it on your armband. They could embed it in like a wrapper. So maybe some of them have snuck it on the court. Who knows?

Will: You probably saw the Australian Open stuff.

No, I didn't. Tell me.

Will: Well, at the Australian Open — the tennis tournament—

Yeah, I don't watch tennis.

Will: A number of players were asked to take their Whoop off while they were playing. And it was, I think, in part because the Australian Open didn't know what they were wearing — but they were just wearing it under their armbands and everything else. And the ITF, which is the International Tennis Federation, actually had approved Whoop to be worn in matches. So the Australian Open was kind of out of line. And then next thing you know, the other majors have come forward saying that wearables can be worn. So I think there's this sort of natural evolution of—

Resisting it, safety checks — and by the way, they're right to want to be restrictive about what can be worn. It's not a — I don't think it's a safety thing. If you're wrapping it around your armband or something like that — I'll tell you.

Will: I mean, obviously, I agree.

I'll tell you what's going on in the background. Your marketing department's probably getting shaken down. They're probably like, "Hey, you know, we'd love to have Whoop involved. It'd be terrible if something happened to an athlete wearing 1.2 oz. But if you were to put a logo behind them for $10 million, well, we might have a different opinion."

Will: You know all the ins and outs.

I — it's not my first time at this rodeo. I know the shakedown when I hear it.

结尾闲聊：Jason 的 Launch Fund、晚期二级市场的乱象

Will: How are things for you in early-stage venture? Are you starting to lead these billion-dollar seed rounds, or you're staying true to the accelerator model?

You know — nobody wants to do year-zero work. So I am leaned into that.

Will: Great.

But then at the end, we have this syndicate and we have 4,000 members of it, and we would syndicate our early-stage seed deals. "Hey, if you want to get involved in this — Jason's putting in 100K, you might want to put in 5K." They kept asking me, "Can you get me into Zipline? Can you get me into Whoop? Can you get me into SpaceX, Anthropic?" — whatever it is. So we started a late-stage practice that we just started this year at the syndicate — thanks for asking.

Will: Great.

We did Zipline. We did Icon Homes — 3D printed homes. These are all billion-dollar companies, $5-billion companies in fast space. So when I know the founder, the CFO gives its approval, because you have to deal with this, right? People doing off-the-books transactions and SPVs and buying out early employees and other early investors. You have to deal with some of this SPV madness.

Will: I'll say this: it's complicated when your business is failing, and it's complicated when your business is winning. So it's always complicated. My advice to everybody with these SPVs — off-the-books, whatever — is just build a relationship with the CFO of the company and just get their blessing for it, and let them know what you're doing. And if they really don't want you to do it, then you're going to have to accept that, right? It's their company. I don't like this idea of going behind the back of the company.

And the other thing to be wary of are these secondary brokers who claim they've got shares from someone at a price.

Will: Yes. And they go around saying that, but they're really just trying to create a market.

Happens to me all the time.

Will: Yeah.

Because I literally — I'm on the board of a company that's worth a couple billion dollars, and they come to me, and I say, "Okay, great. Who's it with?" Because I gotta — I'm on the board of the company. I got to talk to the CFO, and I can help coordinate with you. And then crickets. And I'm like, "Hm, they're fishing. It's always a fishing expedition."

This thing didn't really exist 10, 15 years ago. The only time I ever saw it was Facebook. And then Uber when Masayoshi came in — he was like, "Hey guys, I need you to sell some of these or I'm going to invest in Lyft." And we were like, "Okay." I gave him 10% of my shares at the time. I was like, "Sure, I'll take a little 10% off the top just to keep Masa from investing."

Will: What a run that business has had. But congrats.

Yeah. I mean, and right now like trading at an all-time low P/E and they're surging. It's really weird to watch what's happening — like the anti-AI trade. DoorDash, Uber, Figma — a lot of these companies getting taken to the woodshed a bit. And some of them are just not impacted by it. But hey, AI is going to change everything. Lots of great investment opportunities.

We'll see you all next time on the All-In Interview program. Go get a Whoop! Get yourself a Whoop! Perfect Christmas gift.

Will: Thank you.

Appreciate you doing it, Will. Love the product.

Will: I'm going all in.

## 一、订阅制不是"收钱方式"，而是**公司灵魂的手术**
Will 讲到 2018 年从 500 美元买断转向订阅时，大多数听众会把这当作"商业模式优化"。但真正惊人的点藏在他一句轻描淡写的话里：**"it changed our DNA."**
这是一个被严重低估的因果链： - 买断制 → 公司激励是让你**换新**，所以每 12 个月必须发布新硬件（哪怕没有真正创新） - 订阅制 → 公司激励是让你**不走**，所以 18 个月前买的硬件现在还能用上 ECG、血压、Healthspan 这些后发功能
反直觉之处在于：**订阅制让 Whoop 变成了一家"反苹果"公司**。苹果的商业模型逼它每年制造"你的旧设备不够好"的焦虑；Whoop 的商业模型逼它制造"你的旧设备还会变得更好"的期待。同一个硬件生意，收费节奏一变，整个公司的伦理走向就反转了。
> 跨领域连接：这与 Rolls-Royce 把喷气引擎从"卖发动机"改成"按飞行小时收费"（Power by the Hour）是**同一种 DNA 手术**。一旦收入和使用时长绑定，公司就从"推销员"变成了"守护者"。订阅制

item.title: [Bits + Bips] 'Who Are You Really Protecting?' Jim Bianco on Banks Blocking Agents
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"懒惰税"是整个金融业的底层操作系统

Bianco 这段话最辛辣的地方不是"银行自私"，而是他无意间揭示了一个结构性真相：现代消费金融的核心产品不是"金融服务"，而是认知摩擦。银行真正卖的不是账户，而是你意图和行动之间的那道鸿沟——你知道该把钱转进货基，但你今天不会去做；你知道该最大化积分，但你懒得研究。这道鸿沟每年价值 4 万亿美元零息存款。

这里出现了一个非常微妙的供需倒置：传统认知中，银行提供便利，客户支付费用。但真实的商业模式恰恰相反——银行售卖"不便利"，客户用无偿存款作为支付手段。所谓"方便存取"只是广告语，真正的产品是"方便到不足以让你每天去管它"。AI Agent 的威胁不是技术层面的，而是存在论层面的：它第一次让"意图"可以直接执行，中间那条利润带被整段蒸发。

二、跨领域连接：这是"健身房模式"的全行业崩塌

有意思的是，这个"摩擦即利润"的商业模式并非金融独有，它弥漫在整个经济中：

  • 健身房：假设 80% 会员不来，否则跑步机根本不够用
  • 订阅服务：假设你忘记取消自动续费
  • 航空里程：复杂到让多数积分永远失效（"breakage" 在会计上是明确的收入项）
  • 退税/报销：假设你嫌麻烦不去申请
  • 保险续保：假设你不会每年比价

AI Agent 不是在颠覆"一个行业"，而是在同时拔掉所有"懒惰税"产业的插头。这是一次横跨经济的摩擦套利清算。更深的洞察在这里：富人其实从来不交这个税——他们有财务顾问、税务师、助理、私人银行家。所谓个人代理人的崛起，本质上是代理人阶级（agency class）的全民化。这不是一个科技故事，而是一个阶级再分配的故事，只不过用算法重新包装了。

三、一个出人意料的反转：AI Agent 可能让系统性风险变大而非变小

节目中一句话被轻轻带过，但我认为它藏着整段讨论最危险的盲点。嘉宾说：2023 年 SVB 的挤兑是社交媒体驱动的恐慌，而 AI Agent 只是个体优化，所以不会引发系统性风险。

这个判断可能完全错了，而且方向正好相反。

社交媒体挤兑之所以危险，是因为情绪传染快但不精确——有人逃，有人观望，有人反向抄底。但当数百万个 AI Agent 共享相似的优化逻辑（都从同一批模型蒸馏，都读同一类数据，都调用同一组 API），它们会在同一毫秒对同一组阈值做出数学上一致的反应。这不是"羊群效应"，这是确定性共振——比恐慌更快、更同步、更无情。

换句话说： - 社媒挤兑是心理学问题，有迟疑、有噪音、有缓冲 - Agent 挤兑是代码问题，是无情绪、无延迟、无异议的集体行为

银行真正该担心的或许不是"Agent 把客户的钱扫进货基"，而是哪天凌晨三点，一个新闻事件触发了几百万个 Agent 的同一个 if 分支。他们现在以"安全"为名封锁 Agent，恰恰是在用错误的方式回应正确的恐惧——而真实的风险正在他们看不见的地方积累。

四、"你到底在保护谁"这句话的真正威力

Bianco 这句反问的政治能量远比它表面上更大。因为它迫使银行承认一个事实：金融业从未对散户真正履行过受托责任。而讽刺的是，一个基于大模型的 Agent，可能是普通人此生拥有的第一个真正意义上的 fiduciary（没有佣金、没有关联销售、没有月度 KPI）。

当银行说"AI Agent 不安全"的时候，它其实在说一句更尴尬的真话："一个真正站在你这边的东西，正在打破我们过去几十年赚钱的默契。"

这不是技术监管问题，是代理关系的所有权问题——而所有权之战，历来是经济史上最血腥的那一类。

📝 转录文本

Banks Are Quietly Blocking AI Agents

We found this out last week that a lot of the banks screaming the word "safety" have now blocked AI agents from accessing — you know, I can't access with an AI agent my Chase account as of this past week or so. And today in the Wall Street Journal, now the same thing is happening with credit cards.

The Business Model of Laziness

Let me bottom-line it for you. A lot of financial services — you know, TradFi financial services — business model is based on laziness. There's $4 trillion in zero-yielding money and zero-yielding bank accounts. You don't want to log in every single day and sweep that money into a money market fund. You wanted to have an agent do it.

The banks — a big part of their profit is they'll sweep your money out and they'll invest it for themselves out of your zero-interest account. Now that you're able to do it, the banks are afraid they're going to lose that revenue stream.

They offer credit cards with points and other perks. There's a whole cottage industry of people using Reddit subthreads and using AI agents to try and maximize points. No, no — I want you to sign up for my credit card and pay the $300 a year, but not actually use the points or maximize the points. So, they're blocking that.

So much of our business model in finance is based on frictions and laziness. And AI is now threatening that — we're pushing up against how the banks, how the credit card companies make money, and they're obfuscating it by saying, "I'm trying to protect you. You can't move your money every day and make a couple extra bucks in interest because I have to protect you."

Who Are You Really Protecting?

And really, the question I ask is: "Who are you really protecting? Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?"

They're pricking themselves. I mean, the agents here are acting as fiduciaries of the customer.

Right.

So, I understand why the banks denied access to Plaid something like 10 years ago when they wanted customer data. Plaid was not acting in the interest of the customer. Here, these agents are acting on the interest and request of the customer. So, I don't think that is going to fly, and it's going to hurt banks that — to your point, Jim — are benefiting from that spread. Banks like JP Morgan, really, that have a lot of zero-interest deposits.

Direction of Travel: Dig In or Break Ranks?

So, what gives, fellas? How do we know the direction of travel? A couple of things either happen: the banks dig in, they create regulatory moats, which is something that they can do very effectively, and they try to preserve and prevent. Or some of them break ranks, become tech companies — maybe some of these neo banks. How does this play out? I mean, there's the obvious friction. What gives?

Well, let me — more regulation, unfortunately. We're going to get more regulation. I think that's one —

I don't think so. And then it's going to run up against — you know, pushback on this if you want, but what do most people not really concerned a lot about, in general, when it comes to technology? It is privacy and safety.

We give away all of our private information. We vomit all of our opinions on social media. We don't care that our phone or our browser is looking at our private data to basically serve up ads of our interest. Why are we going to put our foot down about this now?

If all of a sudden an AI agent can make my life easier, can save me a couple bucks by sweeping my money into a money market fund, then I'm not going to lose sleep over safety. I haven't lost sleep over safety on anything else over the last 10 years. Why would this be the tripwire?

I think that while the banks will put up the regulatory moats, I think the public is going to start demanding more and more of this — you know, the freedom to do what they want to do with their, as you said, their fiduciaries, in the form of an AI agent.

Lessons from the 2023 Mini Banking Crisis

Yes, we saw a preview of this in the 2023 so-called mini banking crisis, when SVB and First Republic went down. You had these mini runs on the bank. So it was far more severe then, and you also had wire transfer on social media involved.

Here, you don't have a social-media-driven kind of bank run activity. It's really agents that are finding these optimizations. And there still are frictions — like new bank account opening is a major friction. So I wouldn't overstate the risk, but it is creating a tension with these legacy business models — to your point — that benefit from spreads.

Opportunity and Threat: The Consolidation Risk

So it also feels like an opportunity and a threat. The opportunity is that the great disruptor has arrived. If you're a community bank and you get in front of it, maybe you can have a go and you can drive scale in a technology-centric way. Austin talks about this often on the show.

But the risk, I think, is that — let's just say the agents have their way and margins get compressed. What does that mean? It means incremental consolidation to a point where there's additional pricing power that's brought back. That's my concern here.

Why Community Banks Will Push Back Hardest

You're right. You're right that the community banks are going to look at this as a threat, and it's because it's going to collapse their margins. I mean, a lot of those zero-yielding balances are more at the community banks than they are at the big warehouse banks like JP Morgan or Citibank.

And so they're going to be looking at: what's our business model if we have no zero-yielding balances? What's our business model if everybody tries to maximize their points on whatever credit card that we issue?

Right now, their business model is a bet on friction leading to laziness. And if that goes away, they're going to have to rethink their business model from the ground up. So they're going to be pushing back harder than anybody else.

Show Outro

If you like this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bips and Bips, along with my friends Ram Ahluwalia and Chris Perkins and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds, covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing — we've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes, it's anonymous, and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

[music]

Sponsor

What if your crypto could do more than just sit in your wallet? Nexo is a digital assets wealth platform where you can generate daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds against your assets. Today, Nexo serves more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com.

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why High-NA EUV Pays Off for Intel but Not TSMC
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、同一台机器，相反的结论：技术价值的"关系性真相"

这段访谈最反直觉的地方不在于谁对谁错，而在于同一台 4 亿美元的机器，对 Intel 是"值得"，对 TSMC 是"不值得"——而且双方都没算错。

这揭示了一条经常被忽视的产业规律：一项技术的 ROI 不是它自己的属性，而是它与你其他选择之间的夹角。High-NA EUV 的价值取决于你是否先搞定了背面供电；背面供电的价值又取决于你的制程节点、良率曲线和客户组合。这就是经济学里讲的"互补性陷阱"——单点先进没有意义，先进只在整个配套矩阵中成立。

一个让人惊讶的推论：Intel 之所以能"吃下" High-NA 的高价，不是因为它更有钱，而是因为它更早做了另一项看似无关的架构赌注（背面供电）。领先者并不是在每一步都领先，而是在"决定下一步选择空间"的那一步上领先。

二、跨领域连接：芯片布线 = 城市基础设施 = 组织通信结构

把这段技术解释翻译成另外两个系统，意外对称得惊人：

维度 芯片 城市 公司
粗线路 电源线 水电气管道 决策/预算流
细线路 信号线 街道/行人/绿化 日常沟通流
挤在一个平面 传统正面布线 架空电缆城市 所有事都走周会
分层解耦 背面供电 地下管廊 异步文档 + 同步决策分离
换来的红利 可以用更贵更锋利的刻刀 可以种更密的树、拓宽人行道 可以引入更高带宽的协作工具

真正值得停下来一想的洞察：很多公司引入 Notion、Linear、AI copilot 效果平平，不是工具不行，而是"信号线和电源线还挤在同一个平面"——所有信息仍然竞争同一个会议时段。他们缺的不是更贵的工具，而是一次"背面供电"级的架构重排。High-NA EUV 对没做背面供电的厂来说"不划算"，和昂贵协作工具对会议过多公司的"不划算"，是同一道题。

三、最不易察觉的反转：让 Intel 伟大的东西，正在阻止它伟大

访谈后半段讲 PDK 的部分，表面上在聊"工艺设计套件的成熟度"，实际上藏着一个几乎没人明说的组织悖论：

Intel 过去几十年之所以能领先，恰恰是因为它没有正式 PDK。作为 IDM，设计团队和晶圆厂团队"就坐在隔壁"，晶体管数据直接口口相传、互相啃原始数据。这种"没有文档"的亲密感，是它的护城河——沟通成本几乎为零，迭代速度拉满。

但当它要变成一家 foundry 的那一刻，这个护城河瞬间翻转成天花板：你无法把一个"靠默契运转的系统"交付给外部客户。隐性知识的最大问题是——它不能被打包。

这不是芯片独有的现象。它和以下三个场景结构相同：

  • 家族企业规模化失败：老板一句话顶十份 SOP，于是永远写不出 SOP。
  • 开源项目维护者困境：核心贡献者脑中跑得通的东西，新人需要三周才能复现。
  • 顶级研究实验室转公司：PI 一瞥就懂的数据，产品化时需要重建一整套度量体系。

Intel 现在在做的事情，本质上是在给自己 50 年的"口头传统"做反向考古——把每个工程师脑子里的默会知识，一条条翻译成客户能读懂的 PDK 1.0 文档。这是一场对自己过去成功原因的清算。

最意外的结论：TSMC 之所以能当好 foundry，可能不只是因为它更擅长服务客户，而是因为它从一开始就不被允许依赖隐性知识——它和设计团队天然分离，被迫把一切写下来。它的"劣势"被结构性地转化成了它的核心能力。Intel 现在要补的，不是技术课，是"失去默契"的课。

📝 转录文本

What High-NA EUV Actually Is

For 14A, Intel is using a new kind of lithography machine, high NA EUV. It uses the same extreme ultraviolet light as today's UV machines, but changes the optics.

NA, or numerical aperture, is a measure of how wide a cone of light the machine's mirrors can focus onto the wafer. The wider the cone you can focus, the smaller the spot that your light can carve. Standard EUV machines have an NA of 0.33. High NA widens it to 0.55. So, high NA can print features about 1.7 times smaller in a single pass.

Why "Single Pass" Matters Economically

When features are smaller than the lithography machine can print, chip makers have to split the pattern across several passes, each printing a different set of features. The most tightly packed patterns can require two, three, or even four passes. Each traditional pass takes up valuable time on a machine that costs around $200 million, and it introduces another opportunity for defects.

High NA machines cost about twice as much, but they can reduce the number of passes that are needed. So, the question which determines whether they justify their higher price is how much more time they save, and how much they reduce the risk of defects.

The Interview: Why Intel Says Yes and TSMC Says No

Now, you guys are using high NA EUV tools for 14A, whereas TSMC has said that they don't make economical sense yet for them. How do you decide whether the next litho tool is the one that is ready to adopt or not?

Yeah, and you know, high NA is a good example of where, because of the architecture of our technology versus TSMC's, we make different conclusions off of the same tool set.

We use backside power. That means that you actually alleviate some of the pitch requirements you have on the front side, and that allows you to print that directly with high NA. TSMC has to run very tighter pitches because they don't have backside power, and they can't do that with high NA, so they have to use double patterning EUV. So for them, it's not very helpful. For us it is very helpful.

Now at 14 we've left it as an option and it's something that we'll have a discussion with the customer on because there's some value proposition of it. There's some complexity that it adds.

What Backside Power Actually Does

Chris is referring to a feature called backside power. A chip has two different kinds of wiring:

  • Power lines deliver electricity to the transistors and they need to be thick.
  • Signal lines let the transistors talk to each other. They're much thinner, but they need to be spaced apart so that the signal from one wire doesn't interfere with the signal from another.

In the past, all of these power lines and signal lines had to be crammed together on top of the transistors. Intel's newest process moves these power lines below the transistors to the back of the wafer. This frees up space on top so the signal lines don't have to be packed as tightly.

This change makes high NA worth it for Intel. Without backside power, the wiring is so tight that it would require multiple passes to print even with high NA. With backside power, a single high NA pass is enough.

The PDK Question: Intel as a Foundry

Outside companies can now commission Intel to manufacture chips that they've designed. They follow Intel's process design kit or PDK, the menu of what a given process can build and the rules for building it.

Do you need to lock that into your PDK right now for customers who are planning on developing on 14A?

It's an option in the PDK today and we're handling it as a customer by customer discussion that we have as to whether or not they want to go down that path or not.

So, for 18A, there's public reporting that there were delays and or issues with the PDK such that some instructions didn't work and it was difficult for people to use your foundry to build their chips. Tell me about the process of Intel becoming a foundry and then having a PDK that other customers can use to make whatever chip that they're making as well.

There's definitely a learning curve to how you become a foundry and that's something that our competitors have gone through as well. PDK is a good example of that.

For decades we've been an IDM and we've gone to our product teams and we've shown them our transistor data and we share that data back and forth and we haven't had a formal PDK type process. So, that's a new process that we've had to go implement on 18A.

And 18A started out not having a PDK. And so, there's definitely a lot of feedback we've got from the customers as to what they expect for quality and maturity of the PDK, what sort of information that they want to see in there. And so, we've tried to incorporate that into making sure that hey, we have a PDK that meets our customers' requirements.

And I think that's where we've ended up — that we're starting to get PDKs that have this. And 14A will have that from the get-go. It has very high-quality PDKs. Again, there's maturity metrics for what is a PDK: .5 versus a .9 versus a 1.0. And we're constantly going through and taking customer feedback and incorporating that into the quality of our PDK.

Closing Observation

For most of its history, Intel's fabs made only Intel's chips. That could be part of what allowed TSMC to gain an edge. Serving many customers gave TSMC more wafers to learn from, more revenue to reinvest, and more pressure to hit deadlines.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here, and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
