这段访谈最反直觉的地方不在于谁对谁错，而在于**同一台 4 亿美元的机器，对 Intel 是"值得"，对 TSMC 是"不值得"**——而且双方都没算错。
这揭示了一条经常被忽视的产业规律：**一项技术的 ROI 不是它自己的属性，而是它与你*其他*选择之间的夹角**。High-NA EUV 的价值取决于你是否先搞定了背面供电；背面供电的价值又取决于你的制程节点、良率曲线和客户组合。这就是经济学里讲的"互补性陷阱"——单点先进没有意义，先进只在整个配套矩阵中成立。
一个让人惊讶的推论：**Intel 之所以能"吃下" High-NA 的高价，不是因为它更有钱，而是因为它更早做了另一项看似无关的架构赌注（背面供电）**。领先者并不是在每一步都领先，而是在"决定下一步选择空间"的那一步上领先。
## 二、跨领域连接：芯片布线 = 城市基础设施 = 组织通信结构
把这段技术解释翻译成另外两个系统，意外对称得惊人：
| 维度 | 芯片 | 城市 | 公司 | |---|---|---|---| | 粗线路 | 电源线 |

item.title: [YC Root Access] Building AI for the $650B Home Services Market
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、身份降级作为渗透技术：从"AI 创始人"到"学生"的权力反转

最惊人的细节藏在那个奥克兰的停车场里。他们穿着"硅谷创业者"的外套上门——零对话。换一件"学生来请教"的外套——每天 8 场对话。这不是销售技巧的调整，而是一次完整的身份降级（status downgrade）操作。

美国蓝领服务业对"穿西装带 AI 的年轻人"有系统性的免疫抗体——过去二十年里，每一个来敲门的"数字化方案"都从他们口袋里拿走了钱、很多没留下价值。于是行业演化出一套防御反射：进门即逐客。而"学生"这个身份触发的是完全相反的脚本——分享、炫耀、怀旧、"我爸当年也是从这干起的"。

跨领域连接：这与人类学的"参与式观察"（participant observation）惊人同构。马林诺夫斯基在特罗布里恩群岛做田野的核心方法论，就是刻意放弃"研究者权威"换取"学徒资格"。Broccoli 的创业史，本质上是把人类学田野方法论误打误撞地嫁接到了 B2B 销售上。真正的洞见是：在任何高度戒备的行业做早期发现，你的学位和创投简历都是负资产。

二、"工作周围的工作"：被忽视的 15% 才是真 TAM

视频里一个被轻轻带过的数字其实是整个商业模式的罗塞塔石碑——承包商把营收的 2% 花在软件上，却把 15% 花在办公室人工上。Service Titan 这类传统 CRM 公司打的是那 2%，年收入已经能做到 10 亿美元级别。而 Broccoli 打的是那 15%——这意味着它的理论天花板不是"再造一个 Service Titan"，而是吃掉传统 CRM 市场的 7-8 倍。

这里有一个大多数 AI 投资人至今还没算明白的会计换轴：过去二十年 SaaS 的 TAM 公式是"软件支出 × 替换率"，现在变成了"人工支出 × 自动化率"。前者是百亿级游戏，后者是万亿级游戏。Broccoli 之所以能从 0 做到 60M ARR 不眨眼，是因为它在"人工预算"这个池子里游泳，而不是在"软件预算"的鱼缸里游泳。

出人意料的推论：这也解释了为什么他们的 AI 比 BPO 外包商第一天就打赢了（3 单 vs. 2 单）。那些 $5000/月的呼叫中心员工并非能力低下——而是因为他们处于一个经济系统性低估的岗位上，训练、激励、工具都长期欠配。AI 不是在替代"顶尖人类"，而是在替代"被结构性低估的人类"——这才是 AI 真正的早期红利区。

三、代码的地理学与"精巧想法"陷阱

两个被访者说过一句被播客轻轻放过、但其实应该被刻在创业博物馆门口的话："We never wrote a single line of code in San Francisco. It was in a plumber's shop."

这是一句深度空间社会学。软件的质量不仅由写代码的人决定，还由代码被写出来时周围的物理环境决定。在 SOMA 的联合办公里写的"水管工 AI"，和在萨克拉门托 Marcel 店里一边听电话一边写的"水管工 AI"，架构会不一样、边缘案例会不一样、提示词会不一样。甚至——它们对"什么是成功的一通电话"的定义都会不一样。这是代码的产地标签（appellation d'origine contrôlée of code）。

而反例，就是他们在挪威的那次失败。技术上无懈可击的 EV 智能充电方案，经济上死于一个 Kahneman 式的事实：每年省 50 美元低于"行为改变心理阻力阈值"。消费者不是在和"50 美元"做比较，而是在和"明早上班车没充电"做比较——后者的心理成本可能是前者的 20 倍。

跨领域连接：这与医疗依从性研究里的"每日服药经济学"是同一回事——降压药省下的"未来心梗概率"远超每日服药成本，但依从率依然只有 50%。所有需要用户持续承担微小认知税的方案，不管技术多精巧，都会在行为经济学的墙上撞死。创业者最该学的不是编程，而是识别"自己正在爱上的那个想法，是不是一个只有在 Excel 里才成立的想法"。

四、彩蛋：三次 YC 被拒的真正含义

一个被低调带过的事实：他们申请 YC 三次被拒，第四次才进去。而这家公司今年 ARR 要做到 6000 万。这里的隐藏模式不是"坚持就是胜利"的鸡汤——而是早期筛选系统本质上是在筛"持续尝试的生物"，而不是在筛"第一个想法的质量"。

真正的推论令人不适：如果你是一个只有一个 idea 的创业者，YC 的拒信其实在告诉你一个事实——你被拒的那个 idea，和你最终会成的那个 idea，大概率没什么关系。拒绝的信号指向的不是"换方向"，而是"保持结构，换目标"。他们始终是三个人，始终服务承包商生态，始终用 API 思维——变的只是 API 后面的那个物体从 Tesla 变成了电话。这不是转型，这是保留身体结构、更换器官的生物进化方式。

📝 转录文本

开场：第一次公开谈 Broccoli

主持人：I'm really excited to talk to you guys because this is the first time you're talking publicly about what you're doing and you're a very very successful YC company. I've been looking forward to this conversation for a long time. I've known you for over four years and I've seen what you've been working on in those four years and how incredibly impressive Broccoli is. The truth is nobody else knows — been very much under the radar compared to other companies. So I'm just like really stoked to be part of putting this out in the real world.

Maybe we can start with — before we get into all the details and the long story — just tell me about Broccoli. What is Broccoli today and where is your company today?

创始人：So Broccoli today automates their entire front office. The AI answers all their customer calls, follows up on leads, schedules those appointments, and we do this across voice, text, and SMS. Today we serve over 500 customers, and we just got this stat last week where the run rate for our AI-booked jobs is at over a billion dollars for our customers. So Broccoli is booking that much revenue for our existing customers today, and the growth has been phenomenal. We are going to end the year at over 60 million of ARR. So we're accelerating — the last two years we were at 0 in revenue, and we'll end the year at over 60 million.

主持人：Wow.

起点：大学里的三次 YC 申请

主持人：Basically we'll talk about how this all started. You moved to the Bay Area in 2024 and there's a pretty clear straight line from when you settled on this idea, but there was a long journey prior to that. Let's just start from the very beginning. You guys applied to YC three different times, interviewed three different times with different ideas. And then you finally got accepted with Telmatica. Tell us what Telmatica was and how did you guys get started with this?

创始人：We met in college. We had our dorms right next to each other and we have been working on different ideas right from our second year in college — like sophomore year in college. We started out with a very simple local delivery app inside the college campus itself. Just a classic idea. We got banned, FYI. We could not take payments, we could not do a lot of things because they were just deemed illegal outright. But that just gave us a quick start — like whatever he was trying I was involved in that, whatever I was trying he was kind of involved in that every time. So right from 2017 we have been working on one or the other ideas.

主持人：Which college did you guys go to?

创始人：We are from BITS Pilani in India.

疫情中的 edtech 尝试与第一次相见

So we worked on something for the first three years, and then when COVID struck, I was stuck in Spain for some time because I was there for a research internship. During that time, we decided to work on this edtech idea together and we ran that for about 3 years. That's where we met Gustav for the first time.

主持人：I remember having a follow-up phone call from the interview and just being like, you guys are great but are you sure you work on this idea?

创始人：Exactly. I was like, trying to hint that maybe not. Yeah. We worked on that for one and a half years, and Gustav's words — or Oracle's words — came out to be true: we could not scale it. It was just very hard to scale. So we decided to shut that down. Spent a good 3 months taking a break.

But we were very determined that we would start something for sure. So we had this amazing framework that there is no losses as such for us. Let's pick an idea, work on it for 3 months, if it does not work out — perfect, move on to the next idea. We can keep on doing that for the next 10 years. We don't care.

Telmatica 的诞生：EV 的软件 API

So surprisingly the very first idea that we chose was Telmatica, because EVs were just starting to become a thing back in India. And we were just good at software. So — what is the intersection of something which is very hardware driven but we are good at software? It was just APIs for electric vehicles.

So we started out with that. We established some use cases and applied for YC in the first 25 days of the inception of the idea and we had a conversation with you. We got in, and that's how we came across Telmatica.

主持人：Got it. But EVs were still very small in India — in the US it was still kind of growing but still small. Was India the right place to build Telmatica?

创始人：The short answer is no. Because as soon as we got into YC, after like four months, we moved out and we moved to London. India was a great starting point but the market was still not big enough, and the use cases that we were trying to build just did not exist. So India was not the best market for us to start.

搬到伦敦，奔赴挪威

主持人：How did you decide to go to London? That's a long journey.

创始人：Yeah. And I never had traveled outside the country before we started this company. What happened was — we announced that we were part of YC and then people started reaching out to us from across the world. We had a lot of European energy companies reaching out and telling us: "Hey, can I use your API to connect to a Tesla or a BMW?"

We were like, that's pretty interesting, tell us more about this. So we made our first trip just as soon as demo day ended. We raised a seed round and we traveled to Norway for 2 months.

主持人：Wow.

创始人：We met over 20 companies there and then we were exposed to their use cases, which we thought were much more interesting as they were trying to figure out a solution over the last 2 years — versus back in India, no one was thinking about the use cases that we were trying to build towards. So we decided and came back after two months, and within a month we took the call that we were going to shut down operations. Operations was basically us staying in an Airbnb in Bangalore, and then we moved to London and were spending majority of our time traveling.

挪威的 EV 洞见：电网级需求响应

主持人：It seems like a pattern — moving to Norway, which is at the time (and still is) the number one EV country in the world, highest penetration of EVs. What kind of problems were people describing to you in Norway that they wanted your help with?

创始人：Yeah, several. And the biggest problem was that they were not just adopting more EVs, but they were also adopting renewable energy and clean energy sources — and you can't store energy on a grid level. So it was a very challenging problem to manage the energy supply with the energy demand.

The use case was more around demand response. So based on how much energy is being produced through wind and solar, you want to also manage your energy consumption, and our APIs could help these companies shut down EV charging for, let's say, thousand vehicles in a particular district if you don't have enough wind that night.

主持人：So basically, dynamic EV charging based on when energy is cheap.

创始人：Correct. The consumer gets the benefits of using energy when it's favorable for the grid, and the utility companies are going to compensate the consumers.

为什么没成：$50/年不够痛

主持人：Why did this not work?

创始人：That is a great question. Even today this idea sounds brilliant — like this is world class. But if you look at the economics from a consumer point of view, you're saving maybe 50 bucks a year. It's not exciting enough when somebody's going to remotely control your charging — then you want to go to office next day, but turns out there was not enough wind energy, so your Tesla is not charged and you need to miss work. That's much more painful than $50 a year.

So there was not enough adoption from the consumer level. None of our customers who were these energy utilities could get any traction with these programs — which in turn meant we never saw the usage for our APIs because of the business use case not being there.

承认失败：投资人让我们"回去找真工作"

主持人：What do you guys do when you realize this pain is not severe enough in this market, and you have to do something else?

创始人：That's a very interesting point — in hindsight I can talk about it like, yeah it was pretty obvious. But when you're doing it, you feel like maybe the next big deal is going to solve all of this if I get this big utility company. And then also you've raised capital — like we went through YC — so it makes you feel like oh, the investors have seen something in this space. So it forces you to pursue that idea. But now we know that investors are giving you the capital to you as founders to learn about this market and figure out the next steps, instead of trying to make the initial idea work.

主持人：How did it feel to realize the thing you've been pursuing for a year and a half, 2 years, wasn't going to work?

创始人：Two and a half years, actually. We were quite lean. One of our learnings was this from Telmatica: you have to see how important the problem that you're solving is to your customers. Of course, it will be the most important problem to you, but is it the topmost priority for your customers? If it's the fifth top-most priority, probably it's not something that you should be solving. Ask what are the top three. That was one of the guiding principles for how we chose what to work on for Broccoli.

It is really challenging — I still remember a moment when one of our initial angel investors had called us during the pivot phase and said, "You should just return capital and get real jobs, and then maybe you should come back and do this." We had to take a break for two days where we were like, are we the best people to build a business? Maybe we've never done any real work in our lives — we don't have any personal problem, because all our personal problems were college-student problems.

It was really stressful. But perseverance around — it's not us, it was the market, and if we focus on solving our customers' most painful problems, maybe there's light at the end of the tunnel. That was the initial mindset that helped us go through the pivot phase.

为什么选承包商：三种客户里挑一种

As Adi mentioned, we were very focused on the customers we were still serving. So we were not doing like an AI CRM — that's a completely different idea. During the pivot phase, we focused on the customers we were serving. There were three types of customers: energy utilities, electrical contractors, and fleet operators.

Out of the three customers that we were serving, we chose contractors as the market we wanted to go after — because I personally loved selling to owners and contractors versus a product manager at a 5,000-person P&L kind of a company. That was my personal bias, like, I would love to sell to this customer base.

And then we had two criteria before we chose the next idea — all of these were learnings from Telmatica:

  1. We wanted to go after a massive market from day one. Not a market that's potentially going to grow. Of course, the market should grow, but it should be big enough from day one.
  2. We wanted to solve our customers' most painful problem. Not the third, not the fourth — the most painful problem.

So we chose contractors as that market because it's a massive market. Service Titan is a leading CRM company in the space — they do over a billion in revenue and have recently gone public.

奥克兰停车场：换上"学生"的身份

But then the next thing was: now what's their most painful problem? This was May 2024. We had our office hour, and we were just talking about what we were doing next. We shared, "Hey, we're thinking about this market and I'm reaching out to people on LinkedIn to do some customer discovery."

And then you had told us: "Guys, what kind of contractor hangs out on LinkedIn? I would just go door-to-door and speak with all the contractors in the Bay Area within two weeks, and then you'll figure out if there's something worth pursuing or not."

We're like, "Sounds good." And we did this for the next 2 weeks — and guess what? We had zero conversations.

主持人：What happened?

创始人：It was just so crazy. You had told us within 2 weeks we should have spoken to everyone. We were sitting in Oakland. We were in a parking lot Monday 1:00 p.m. — like, why are we not getting these conversations?

Then I realized we were acting like salesmen. We were coming in hot, saying: "Hey, we're startup founders in San Francisco, so we're going to build AI solutions for you." And this plumber literally had a couple of things in his hand and he literally was like, get the f* out of this office right now. Somebody had shut the door on our faces as well — this had just happened that day.

主持人：Do they get bothered by salespeople a lot?

创始人：Oh yeah. Because this industry — people are selling, and two years ago in the service industry AI was like — you don't see that. If you bring AI in my business, like, get out. This is a family-run business and all of this.

So we were getting zero conversations, and I was sitting in this parking lot — and even on LinkedIn I used to never say that I'm selling something. I used to say, "Hey, I'm trying to work on this project, I'd love to get your insights and advice." That was our initial outreach.

We maybe underestimated a contractor and thought they loved talking to an AI founder. So what we did was we pivoted. We dropped our bags in the car, did not take a laptop, anything. Went to the next plumbing shop at around 3:00 p.m. We shook hands with the owner and introduced ourselves as: "Hey, we are students, and we're here just to learn a bit more about family-owned plumbing businesses. Do you have a minute to talk to us?"

And everyone's like, "Welcome!" Everyone wants to talk about their lives — how their dad started this business, how they went through the pandemic, everything. Since that conversation, we were getting eight conversations every single day.

140 场水管工对话

We did that for the next two months. We went and visited and spoke with 140 contractors throughout the Bay, and we were learning so much. We had zero customers but we were so excited. We were sitting with their technicians doing training sessions. We were going on jobs with them. We were joining them on jobs — as students, everyone trusts a student. That was our two-month journey during the pivot phase to figure out our customers' most painful problem.

主持人：Tell me about these conversations. What did you guys learn from all these owners that were just like, come and talk, I'll show you around?

创始人：We learned everything about their lives. Our first question used to be: "What are you thinking about when you're driving back home post 5:00 p.m.? What's going on in your mind?"

And one of the biggest problems was them losing money after hours. After hours basically means they have their office employees in the office till like 4 or 5 p.m. — 5 p.m. there's no one in the office, but guess what, emergencies occur 24/7, and customers call them. They were using BPOs and third-party answering services that are outsourcing it. And all of us know they are terrible — they suck. But they're super expensive.

主持人：You need them, otherwise, like when someone has a broken water heater, you just can't — the alternative is voicemail…

创始人：Yeah. And if you don't answer the call, the customer is just going to call the next plumber on Google or Yelp. If you don't answer the call, that lead is gone — you'll never be able to recover that opportunity.

So our customers were truly trying to solve this problem. They were spending an extraordinary amount of money on answering services. If they were just using voicemail at scale, maybe it's not a painful enough problem. About 80% of our customers we were talking to had this option and they were spending around $5,000 to $10,000 a month on this service.

不提 AI 的 AI 销售

主持人：Even after hearing this, you can't come in and tell them "use AI." That's even more crazy to tell them.

创始人：They don't even realize what that means. And all of our customers are in the customer service business — there's nothing more valuable to them than how the customer feels interacting with them. And it starts with the phone call.

So we did not ever present a solution. We did not want to come in because we had learned the lesson: AI is not welcomed in this office. So we were like, "Okay, cool, tell me more about the solutions you're trying to…" and everyone said, "I don't have a solution."

And then we used to come back home at like 7–8 p.m. and tinker with voice agents. So what we did was — 60% of the times, we used to come up to the answering services topic. Before that, we had asked, "Have you used any AI solutions? Have you used ChatGPT?" And they were like, "Yeah, I use it to write emails." Great — they've used some kind of AI.

So we used to present: "We're engineers and we actually play with AI all day. And I came across this AI voice which actually blew my mind. Would you want to listen to that?" They're like, "Yeah, yeah, sure. Let's play a recording." They were like, "That's magical." And I was like, "Do you think you can use this in your business?"

They were like, "Yeah, yeah, yeah — I can see there's a use case where the AI can call my customers to confirm an appointment, 'cause that's the lowest priority use case."

主持人：The lowest risk from —

创始人：Lowest risk. We're like, "That's pretty incredible. Do you want us to come in and do something for you?" They were like, "Yeah, that'd be amazing if you can come in and build this for us." We're like, "Sure." And that is how we got our first set of customers — where we never presented this as a potential solution we wanted to sell.

第一个客户 Marcel 与萨克拉门托小店

Our first customer was basically a company in Sacramento, where we then embedded ourselves for the next 3 months. We used to daily commute from San Francisco to Sacramento, work from her shop, and that is where we wrote the first line of code as well. We never wrote a single line of code in San Francisco — it was in a plumber's shop.

主持人：And she was the owner of that?

创始人：Yes, she was the owner and CEO of that plumbing shop. Marcel Flowers.

主持人：Marcel. And now she's joined Broccoli?

创始人：Yes. She does hundreds of things. She's basically a great evangelist for the company, helps influence product, she's influenced our brand as well, and now she's helping us across the business.

两周上线：第一次胜过人类

主持人：So basically you would go back and forth to her office for a long time to build out this first version. How did it work when you launched it?

创始人：I used to sit in her office and just talk to her all day. And Adi used to sit in another office just building the first version of the product. We had something ready within two weeks. We had connected to their CRM Service Titan, we understood the scripts and everything that their actual call center employees were doing, and we launched within 2 weeks.

We were answering calls from like 5 to 7 p.m. only. And we used to monitor every single call. It worked — the customers did not hang up. Of course there were edge cases, but it worked. We booked three appointments that same day. The maximum appointments they had ever booked throughout the night was I think two, and we had just booked three in two hours.

主持人：So you did better than the humans?

创始人：The humans that they were paying $5,000 a month. Next day, Marcel was like, "I'm going to cancel the answering service." And I was like, "That's too soon, maybe we need to build…" "No no no, figure it out — month end I'm going to go live with Broccoli." (It was not even called Broccoli back then, but — "I'm just going to go live with the AI.") We spent another week and went live for the whole weekend, and we booked around 19 appointments. Previously they had maximum five appointments over a weekend.

So that truly made us believe AI might actually be a 10x better alternative than what they were using. And then she basically helped us go from our first customer to the next 20 just through her referrals and word of mouth. So we never had to go door-to-door again.

PMF 的真实感觉

主持人：So now basically all of these years since the beginning of starting a company — maybe this is the first time you're getting the real taste of product-market fit. A lot of founders watching this channel are thinking "do I have PMF?" Was there a moment where you thought "okay, this actually is working — we're going to build a really big company"?

创始人：I think the day we met Marcel, post that till today, I don't think we've ever taken even a 10-second pause to figure out where the next set of growth is going to come from. Because we are just being pulled into conversations — pulled into bigger, more use cases. So I think that is maybe what product-market fit feels like. And then you need to keep on finding it at every stage of the business.

24 小时工作制：印度 + 旧金山的时差团队

主持人：When you were in Sacramento, was it still just the two of you? Or do you have one more person in the company?

创始人：We had our founding engineer join us during Telmatica, and he's still with us after 4 years. He has been through everything with us — the pivots. He would stay awake at night because this was in Pacific time, so he would stay awake at nights and we were all anxiously waiting for these calls to go through, and then we'd see what happened on the call and then fix the thing. So he has been with us since then. Back then it was just three of us who started.

Marcel was confused — she was like, "You were here till 9 p.m. and then you come back next day at 9 a.m. and you fix that problem — do you guys not sleep?" And we did not tell her anything until maybe 2 months, and then we showed her Sahil — he was working in India, fixing things. We were working as a 24-hour team.

主持人：When you were $2 million, how many people worked at the company?

创始人：Around 15 people or less than 15.

市场规模：$650B 家政服务 + 15% 办公室人工

主持人：You've grown a lot since then. More or less been the same product — the voice agent that answers phones, books calls — scaled to 500 customers. But the HVAC owners use a bunch of other software too.

创始人：If you look at our customers today, they spend roughly 2% of their topline revenue on other software systems like Service Titan and QuickBooks, and they spend 15% on office labor — out of which Broccoli today automates 2% in the front office.

主持人：Wow. So basically you're making each of these companies much more efficient, which leads to them growing faster. How big is this market — home services, HVAC, plumbing, electricians?

创始人：The trades as a whole is massive — they spend roughly $1.5 trillion a year, and home services is basically a $650 billion market. US population spends $650 billion a year on fixing our homes.

主持人：People used to say the enterprise software market is a couple hundred billion dollars — and just this one is close to a hundred billion dollars.

当下最关心的事：从 15 人到 75 人

主持人：What's top of mind for you guys right now? You mentioned you'll end the year at 60 million in revenue. What are the things that you guys think about as you go into work every day?

创始人：For me, the number one thing I've been thinking about is building the leadership team in the company. We are at around 75 people today.

主持人：For people that join the engineering team — Adi, what are you telling them is going to be the hardest problems or most exciting things to work on right now?

创始人：When you are small, you have this superpower of being able to do anything just by will. You want it the next day — it should be possible — because you have these five people who can move very fast. But as you grow and have more customers to serve, you have to build structures around it.

So the thing we have been working on is: how does the engineering culture affect our velocity? We want to maintain the same engineering velocity and product velocity while retaining the culture. We want to be the best product still once we grow to 20 engineers and to 50 engineers and to 100 engineers. Broccoli should be the team that defines what is the future of trades.

That involves a lot of things — building the team culture, building the principles. I used to think the 14 Amazon principles just came out of nowhere, but you also have to think very deeply about how things would change with AI — like, everyone has those superpowers now.

How do you mentor new folks in the company? How do you teach them to think like a customer? The easiest way is to embed with a customer. Anyone who joins us in India or anywhere remote, they are required to visit us in SF and spend some time with our customers in plumbing shops, in HVAC shops — because that way they start thinking like a customer. So that's a huge culture shift for scaling that mentorship, that first-principles thinking, which we are currently actively working on.

技工职业的未来：15 年经验压缩到 2 年

主持人：I'm assuming the job of a plumber or electrician is about to change. You are going after the things they either don't like to do, or that people in the back office / front office are doing. But the job of the technician itself — fixing things for us — how do you think that job is going to change?

创始人：Today Broccoli is basically automating the work around the work. But the main work is for a technician to show up at your home and fix the things. The future technician is not going to look anything like what they're doing today.

Today they need to diagnose the issue, and you need like 10 to 15 years of actual field experience in order to become a trained pro. I think AI is going to reduce that gap to maybe 2 years of field experience — because you're going to have the intelligence of a 40-year-old pro in your ear, in your eyes. You're going to see things and the AI is going to help you diagnose that issue as well.

We're already seeing a lot of help for at least 20% of the issues. Even some of the frontier models that are not even trained on actual data are performing really well. More young technicians are going to be able to come into the field without having to spend 10 years — because that's what you have to do right now. It's a pretty skilled trade and you need to go through certifications.

主持人：Just a technical question — why are the models good at this? How do you think OpenAI or Anthropic or others are training their data sets of being good at diagnosing issues with home devices?

创始人：I would say most of it is just operational work. Whenever one of your appliances fails, there's no magic to it. It's literally just knowing what the serial number of that appliance is, looking up the right documentation for that appliance, and then knowing where to look. That's most of the knowledge-work part.

For a technician to do that while they are on field, maybe without internet — it's so hard. They have to know where to find the right things. That's why you have this operational inefficiency: they have to contact the back office, whereas a service manager would sit and walk them through what has to be done. But what if everyone had the knowledge power in their phones? That's what AI is unlocking for them. They still are the best at doing their job — which is plumbing. You have to go in and do the plumbing. But you now have this amazing suite of tools that help you with all of these operational tasks in a much more efficient way.

给七年前的自己：搬到旧金山，走向你的客户

主持人：If you look back on your life six, seven years ago when you were still in school — let's say I'm in your shoes watching this and I'm where you were seven years ago. How should I think about my life? What decisions should I make?

创始人：The simple answer is: you just need to move to San Francisco, and apply to YC. That's my simplest answer.

The more serious version is: you move towards your customers. That's it. If your customers are here, you come here. If your customers are in Norway, you go to Norway — and you're going to get all the answers.

内在动机：解决真实问题 + 和朋友一起做

主持人：What's your intrinsic motivation? What motivates you guys to do this when things are hard? Things are probably hard but in a good way right now. What motivates you? You seem on track to build a very large company with thousands of employees. Someone will go back in a couple years and look at this YouTube video — this is the first time you're talking to the world really about what you're doing. How would you answer that question?

创始人 1：For me, the intrinsic motivation comes from solving a very real-world problem. Anything that we decide today or do today, I can really see the effects on the field in the hands of a technician, like the next day. That's a very satisfying feeling — that you are helping someone do their job in an efficient way, in a physical, real-world scenario.

The second thing is just building something with friends. That's a great motivator for me, because you might have bad days, but the next day you wake up with the long-term picture that we are doing this, and the end state of this is going to be such a much better world for everyone. And you get to do this with your friends. What's a better way to do it than that?

创始人 2：I agree with both these points, and the friends thing is actually the most important thing. And the second thing is — I don't see myself doing anything else. There's literally nothing else I can do. So even if it's shitty hard, I don't want to wake up and — there's nothing else. Can I go and work for Adobe or Meta again? Like hell no. So the answer is very simple. There's nothing else for me to do. So we're just going to keep on doing this.

主持人：Adi and AJ, thank you so much. This is a great conversation.

创始人：Yeah, thanks for having us.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、身份降级作为渗透技术：从"AI 创始人"到"学生"的权力反转
最惊人的细节藏在那个奥克兰的停车场里。他们穿着"硅谷创业者"的外套上门——零对话。换一件"学生来请教"的外套——每天 8 场对话。这不是销售技巧的调整，而是一次完整的**身份降级（status downgrade）操作**。
美国蓝领服务业对"穿西装带 AI 的年轻人"有系统性的免疫抗体——过去二十年里，每一个来敲门的"数字化方案"都从他们口袋里拿走了钱、很多没留下价值。于是行业演化出一套防御反射：进门即逐客。而"学生"这个身份触发的是完全相反的脚本——分享、炫耀、怀旧、"我爸当年也是从这干起的"。
**跨领域连接**：这与人类学的"参与式观察"（participant observation）惊人同构。马林诺夫斯基在特罗布里恩群岛做田野的核心方法论，就是刻意放弃"研究者权威"换取"学徒资格"。Broccoli 的创业史，本质上是把人类学田野方法论误打误撞地嫁接到了 B2B 销售上。真正的洞见是：**在任何高度戒备的行业做早期发现，你的学位和创投简历都是负资产**。
## 二、"工作周围的工作"：被忽视的

item.title: [Odds on Open] Ex-Goldman Oil Derivatives Trader: Every Trading Strategy Is Momentum or Mean Reversion
item.dc:creator: Odds on Open
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：这个交易员其实在卖"油的触觉"，而不是油

Simmeran 随口说出的那句"you can't touch an interest rate curve, but you can smell a barrel of oil"（你摸不到利率曲线，但你能闻到一桶油的味道），表面是导师语录，骨子里却是他整个职业路径的隐藏主线——而他自己可能都没完全意识到。

重新审视他的轨迹： - 高盛油桌：优势来自非洲岸边装驳船的人、北海的货船路由——物理嗅觉 - GSR 加密：失去嗅觉，于是用链上账本作为合成嗅觉器官（谁的钱包在动，钱流向哪里） - Monaco 交易所：想交易电力、算力、水——重新把金融拉回"可嗅闻"的物理标的

他真正在做的事，是在反复逃离纯符号市场，回归可触摸的世界。 加密的 memecoin 让他焦虑（"没有基本面要收敛"），而电力让他兴奋——因为电力有物理终局。这是一种心理学上罕见的交易员类型：对"幻影资产"过敏的衍生品交易员。市场上大多数人在往符号化更深处走（代币化万物），而他的事业曲线一直在反向——从符号往物理走。他做的 Monaco，本质上是给那些同样对"纯符号"过敏的下一代交易员建的避难所。

二、跨领域连接：Theta 衰减与中年焦虑是同一个公式

Simmeran 转述导师那句"everything in life is an option"，然后机械地讲 theta decay。但有意思的是——他本人正活在一个 theta decay 极其陡峭的时间窗口里：

  • 他离开高盛是因为"最坏情况我还能回去做大宗交易员"——这是在低 theta（下行有限）的时候买入高 gamma（加密上行）
  • 他现在创业 Monaco，又是同一个结构：凸性对冲时间衰减

把这个框架挪出交易桌，会发现一个令人不安的真相：人类所有"趁年轻去闯"的建议，本质上是在描述 theta 衰减。你的可选性（optionality）每天都在变少，不是因为你失败了，而是因为时间本身在吃掉保险的时间价值。你 25 岁时持有的"换行业"看涨期权在 45 岁时值很少钱——不是因为内在价值变了，而是到期日逼近。

更深的连接：佛教的"无常"和期权定价是同一件事的两种语言。无常说"一切都在流失"；期权说"theta 永远为负"。前者让你放下执着，后者让你立刻行动。两个结论相反，但描述的是同一个数学结构。Simmeran 用它来合理化职业选择，但这个模型其实能解释——为什么他 4am 回办公室还要问团队"你们的 why 是什么"。那段独白不是鸡汤，是他在集体对冲 theta。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：他说"一切交易都是动量或均值回归"，但他漏了第三类

Simmeran 的这个论断听起来漂亮且 reductive，但他自己讲的三个故事都不符合这个框架：

  1. 2020 年 4 月负油价：既不是动量也不是均值回归。那是模型崩溃——对数正态假设失效。真实的交易动作是"打电话给 quant 加小数精度"。
  2. 墨西哥 Hacienda Hedge：这不是在赌方向，而是结构性义务流——国家预算需要锁定收入，和市场观点无关。
  3. Producer 3-way 的解体：客户不是因为"均值回归 vs 动量"而解除对冲，而是流动性危机——需要现金，不管公允价值。

真正的第三类是"流动性/义务驱动"——市场里 50% 以上的交易量来自于"必须交易"的参与者，他们的交易动机既不是看涨看跌，也不是回归均衡，而是不交易就死。央行、生产商、ETF 再平衡、保证金追缴、国家外汇储备、养老金久期匹配——这些流在他的叙述里反复出现（"客户现在就要现金"、"产油国必须对冲"），但他的框架却把它们排除了。

这里有一个跨领域连接：生物学里有"义务流"vs"兼性流"的区分——义务厌氧菌、义务共生、义务迁徙。它们的行为不是"选择"而是"约束"。市场参与者也是这样分类的。一个只用动量/均值回归两分法的交易员，相当于一个只研究"自由意志下的鸟类行为"但忽略了"候鸟因激素水平被迫迁徙"的鸟类学家——你会漏掉可预测性最高的那部分流量。

而讽刺的是，Simmeran 的下一家公司 Monaco，整个商业模式（traders 提议市场 + 承诺成交量 + revenue share）正好是在货币化"义务流"——他让 trader 的"indication of interest"变成一种半约束性承诺（不达标会被 slash activity score）。他在产品层面上发明了第三类，但在交易哲学层面上还没有把它纳入自己的世界观。

这就是最深的洞察：一个人经常会在产品里实现他理论上不相信的东西。 他的两分法是遗留的叙事，他的产品是真实的世界观。

📝 转录文本

Ex-Goldman Oil Derivatives Trader: Every Trading Strategy Is Momentum or Mean Reversion

开场金句

"You can't touch an interest rate curve, but you can smell a barrel of oil."

主持人： It's April 2020. Oil is negative. You're on Goldman's oil desk. What's happening?

Simmeran： Something that is not a once in a lifetime, but a once in a history kind of event happening. The price of WTI 1 day before X-ray on April 20th goes negative and settles 3763. You have to price something that's 300 400% ball in annualized terms.

Every form of trading strategy in the world arguably is some form of either momentum or mean reversion. My two favorite kinds of trades in the world are my size your price or your size my price. Even when you are pretty confident of over a long enough period of time this thing will converge to fair value and fundamentals. You have to be able to weather the mark to market.

主持人： What's the most amount of money you've lost in a single day?

Simmeran： $3.12 million.

主持人： How'd it feel?

Simmeran： Awful. Very awful. Very, very awful.

一、2020 年 4 月：负油价那天的交易桌

主持人： Simmeran, thank you so much for coming on the pod.

Simmeran： Thank you for having me.

主持人： It's April 2020. Oil is negative. You're on Goldman's oil desk. What's happening?

Simmeran： Uh, people are running around wondering what the risk in P&L is. Uh, just for context, right? Something that is not a once in a lifetime, but a once in a history kind of event happening. Russia and Saudi are launching into a price war. You have a global pandemic. You have demand destruction where no one's flying anywhere.

And all of the sudden a landlock form of oil, WTI, which is often traded, uh, has nowhere to go because suppliers and producers have produced so much oil, but there's no place to put it because of this demand destruction. And so, for the first time in history, uh, something that's never happened before, the price of WTI, one day before XRE on April 20th goes negative and settles 3763.

And this wouldn't really be a problem if you were just trading regular uh financially settled futures, right? Where you don't have any exposure to the underlying uh physical oil. But when you're on an options desk and volatility or pricing an option assumes that this thing that you're trading can't go negative, all of the sudden all of your models begin to break and you have to figure out what's my risk, what's my P&L, and what do I tell the head of commodities when he calls to ask, "Hey, how did the desk do today?"

模型崩溃下的应急操作

主持人： How did you figure those things out?

Simmeran： Uh, with a lot of patience, with a lot of uh double-checking, with a lot of talking with our quants on the desk and saying, "Hey, I've made these assumptions. Can we assume uh log normality, can we run this risk report?" Uh, and also getting pricing in the broker market and figuring out how do our marks, what we have on our balance sheet compared to where the market is pricing things, and then making sure that we're being conservative in our assumptions for how much any particular futures contract can move between now and let's say the end of the year.

主持人： I mean, it just seems so crazy like—

Simmeran： Yeah. I mean, this was one of my, you know, earliest years on the oil desk. I like to joke that I got the first white hair in my beard, uh, when oil went negative. The rest have pretty much come from later chapters in my life.

Uh, but yeah, I mean, the amount of like P&L swing that you saw, the amount of news headlines, uh, the amount of people that were sending me memes to say, "Hey, if I just have an empty swimming pool, can I take delivery and get paid to hold oil?" uh, is actually higher than I care to admit.

Uh, but but I'll never actually forget uh, one of my friends sent me this like screenshot of CNBC saying, "Hey, WTI suddenly negative. did you hear about this?" And I'm like, man, I'm literally on the on the desk trying to price an option uh with markets going absolutely haywire with very few market makers, if any, willing to provide any liquidity uh into the order book because no one wants to enter into risk that they can't get out of.

And so, this is one of the few times where it was actually easier to enter and exit options positions that were one year out compared to something that was expiring 1 month because you don't know how crazy this thing is going to get, right? You have to price something that's 300 400% ball in annualized terms. Uh, and I'll never forget having to actually call up one of our quants to say, "Hey, can you increase the decimal precision so I can mark the value of our options correctly?" Because these things are just absolutely crazy.

【赞助商插播：Onyx Spot Return Crude Oil ETC】

Most oil ETFs don't actually track the price of oil. They hold futures contracts, and many of them track oil for delivery up to 4 months from now. So, when you buy an oil ETF, you're not betting on today's oil prices. You're betting on where the market thinks oil will be next season. That's not the kind of trade you meant to make.

Which brings me to today's sponsor, Onyx. They're the world's biggest market maker in oil derivatives, and they built the solution to this problem. The Onyx Spot Return Crude Oil ETC tracks dated Brent, the price 78% of the world's oil deals are based on, and it reflects barrels shipping in the next 2 to 3 weeks. That exposure used to be reserved for oil majors and trading houses. Now you can buy it on Interactive Brokers. The ticker is OIL.

二、市场如何平复：CME 规则改写

主持人： Walk me through how did that get resolved? You know, how did how did everything quiet down? Um, everything's going haywire like you said your models are breaking. Um, annualized 300 400 V. What do you like how did things actually get sorted out?

Simmeran： Yeah. Yeah. So, uh, interestingly enough one week before uh this actually happened the CME allowed one of the first and actually the only like negative strike options to actually trade on the exchange. Uh, which means that effectively the CME was saying, "Hey, there is a possibility futures might go negative. We're fundamentally going to allow it and hence we'll allow options to uh trade with that strike."

And the other thing the exchange was doing was effectively shifting their margining methodology. Uh, because most people when they price options on things like oil, right, presume log normality which means that hey oil cannot go below zero. This was the time that they actually shifted to a normal model. And as people who have studied statistics or financial mathematics will know a normal distribution allows prices to go negative. And so the way they were thinking about margining also had to adapt accordingly.

Uh, and so effectively what we did was follow a similar model uh to be able to price our options and then over the course of let's say the next month or so markets began to kind of quiet down uh concentrate and then obviously we began the slow grind and rally back that the rest of 2020 and early 2021 saw.

三、高盛油桌是怎么赚钱的

主持人： How does an oil derivatives trader at Goldman make money?

Simmeran： Uh, a few ways is the short answer. Uh, right, the primary way that any bank trader will make money is facilitating client flow. Uh, the two major sources of client flow are producer flow uh or just corporate flow we'll say and then the other is more speculative or hedge fund flow.

I would say 80 to 85% of the flow that we saw uh on the desk was oil producers hedging. And that tends to be by far orders of magnitude bigger than uh any airline or any refiner that's hedging. Right? When the country of Mexico needs to hedge its production, that's not just the country of Mexico hedging its production. It is one of the largest sovereign hedging programs in the world. Right? Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal, any major uh financial media outlet has actually written quite a few articles about what's called the Hacienda Hedge, which is when the finance ministry effectively says, "Hey, we're producing a lot of mine crude. We need to hedge this." And so they'll go out to a bunch of physical major shops, a bunch of banks, and try and get prices on what they think are respectable hedges accordingly.

Right? So that's like the uh dominant source of flow. And then you have kind of what's happening in today's markets right where you have a lot of speculation on macro events. What's going on in the Middle East? Will the Strait of Hormuz close or not close? Uh, and that tends to drive a lot of more hedge fund macro uh I would say uh options-oriented flow which is viewed less as a hedge and more as a technical entry and exit point.

自营色彩与客户信息

主持人： How much discretionary trading is stacked on top of making money from client flow? I mean obviously you're seeing what's happening on such a granular level that you can make— I imagine there's points where you can make bets based on that. What what was it like while you were at Goldman?

Simmeran： Yeah, I mean at the end of the day our job is client facilitation. So at some points would we have to accumulate inventory in order to best facilitate liquidity uh which is called reasonably expected near-term demand? Yes. Uh, obviously like were we allowed to do anything that is untoward or illegal or uh goes against any regulatory guidelines? The short answer is no.

But I do think sitting in a seat like Goldman where you got to see hedgers, speculators, um, you know major hedge funds all across the world entering and exiting these positions but then also talking with players who are in the physical market, right? Uh, I think the most interesting oil traders in the world are those who uh not only are trading the financial derivatives and primitives that sit on top of the market but are actually trading the underlying spot market because at the end of the day the thing I love about commodities uh which is true now more than ever is that all of these financial instruments have to converge to the underlying physical value.

Right? So I think the greatest source of wealth when it came to information was talking to people who pad barges off the coast of Africa or who were trading uh Brent North Sea crude uh because they're like, "Hey, we we have cargos I need to go somewhere," or they were trading the price of freight right which is like, "Hey, how much will it actually cost me uh to get a cargo ship from point A to point B and what does the cost of that route look like?"

And so at Goldman, you were speaking to these producers all the time and getting a very good feeling for where the market was um being sitting in the center of it.

Sales–Trader 分工与 Aramco 突袭案例

主持人： Yeah.

Simmeran： So I would say because I cut my teeth there, it was probably more talking with the relevant sales folks who were then talking with the relevant clients. Uh, right, and obviously there was a clear bifurcation of responsibility where it was our job to be risk managers. It was our job to understand what the market is doing. Uh, and it was working very closely with a very strong salesforce to understand, "Hey, what is the client perspective on this and what are the needs that they need met that we can structure products around?"

Interesting—right someone who's trading volatility via variance swap or structured products on the options desk is very different than someone who just says, "Hey, I have a bunch of oil that I'm about to pull out of the ground uh and I want to sell it at a particular price. What's the best price to do so?" Right? And and you see this whenever for example uh Aramco happened in se— I want to say was in 2019 when there was a massive attack on a refinery, oil gapped up $20 over the weekend. And I remember the entire oil desk came in, called our salespeople and said, "Hey, we better reach out to our producer clients because they're going to probably want to lock in hedges at these attractive prices that they might not get a chance to do one week from now." And that's exactly what happened.

四、Swaptions、Producer 3-way 与整部银行机器

主持人： Can you give an example of any one particular trade that printed lots of money for Goldman's Oil Desk?

Simmeran： Yeah, I mean given uh that most of our business was was client facilitation, uh, a lot of it was really just uh creating very specific structured products uh that allowed people to enter into swaps, right? Uh, one of the things that I traded uh quite actively was uh swaptions, which is the option to enter into a forward starting swap, right?

And the beauty of this or what made this quite attractive to trade is that there weren't that many people that were honestly willing to warehouse the risk, right? Pricing the options and understanding all of the risks and nuances that go into even though it's not a standard vanilla option. If you go through a masters in financial engineering program like you will learn the necessary ingredients to be able to price these things but then actually warehousing that risk on your balance sheet is kind of reserved for people who want to one be able to do so, two actively know how to manage the risk uh and three are able to actually offload it into the market.

And so me pricing swaptions uh was one of the things that like we we were able to monetize quite well uh things like April 2020 whenever there's massive volatility in the market right on average dealers tend to be long convexity or long optionality. So whenever the market is moving around a lot, whether it's rallying or falling, uh, dealers or banks tend to make a fair bit of profit from that.

对冲的极限：客户信用变成银行问题

主持人： How does Goldman hedge away all of its risk? Uh, you know, those moments like April 2020, do the hedges actually behave as they're supposed to?

Simmeran： That's a that's a very interesting question. Um, so I'll I'll answer that in two parts.

It's impossible to hedge away exactly all of your risk, right? Um, otherwise you wouldn't get compensated to enter into a trade, right? The beauty of working at a dealer is, "Hey, you're willing to provide a price on something that could be very standardized or something that could be very bespoke." And when you are creating something that's very bespoke and very OTC and very structured for the country of Mexico or someone out in Southeast Asia, right? Uh, that's very tailored, it's very bespoke and so you have to figure out what is the most liquid hedge instrument that I can use as a proxy.

And what you're getting compensated for at a bank is really warehousing that basis warehousing that bid offer of like, "Hey, this is this spread is a risk that I'm willing to take on my balance sheet to facilitate it." So I would say it's impossible to like fully hedge out but that is the risk that you're getting compensated for.

But it's interesting to say like how you know how well do your hedges work because one of the most common structures that oil producers would trade uh is called a producer 3-way. Producer 3-way is you're long a put spread and you're short a call option in order to finance it. Right? So what that does is say, "Hey, I don't want to pay you any dollars upfront to buy this insurance. What I will do is buy a form of insurance that says hey if if oil comes off I'm protected up to a certain level right and in because I don't want to have to pay you for that insurance I'm going to sell upside convexity against it."

The challenge with this is if oil had sold off and was a slow grind down right producers would be quite happy because they said if oil goes below 60 if oil goes below 50 I'm quite happy. The thing with the put spread is it caps how much money you make as the market sells off. So if you're trading a $10 wide put spread, if you're trading a 60/50 put spread, right, the most you can make is $10 a barrel times the number of barrels you traded. When you have a very sharp move down that is much larger than $10 a barrel, uh, the amount that you make pales in comparison to the potential losses that you incur on the other side of the trade because no producer is hedging 100% of their production, right?

And so one of the most challenging and interesting things to navigate is, hey, there are a bunch of little oil producers in, let's say, emerging market countries that had these hedges on. They had put these threeways on and they were in the money on their hedges, but they were bleeding a lot more cash on the actual underlying oil because now they would have to sell it at a lower price. So what did they do? They unwind their hedges, right?

And so this actually became less of a market risk trade and more of a credit and financing trade to say, "Hey, these guys need the cash now. Do they have to unwind the hedges so we can they can lock in and crystallize the positive mark to market or do we give them structured financing? Do we work with other teams on the desk to figure out a more creative solution so they can still have these hedges in place?" Right?

And this is what really gave me an appreciation for the broader machinery uh that comes along with working at a bank because any risk that you think you might have in silo is really not really in a silo because now I have to call the CVA desk. Now I have to call the rates desk. Now I have to call the structured financing desk and say, "Hey, you know, so and so counterparty needs this. Can we facilitate this?" Right? What does the cost of capital look like? What is the embedded credit risk like? And I think that was a unique experience that I wouldn't have gotten to have if it wasn't for being on the oil desk at Goldman.

六、一个大胆断言：所有策略都是动量或均值回归

主持人： I, you know, before we did this podcast, you had a take about um all of trading strategies being one of two things. Can you lay that out for the audience?

Simmeran： Yeah, sure. Uh, I still stand by this belief. I'm happy to be shown counter examples. Uh, but I tend to believe that every form of trading strategy in the world arguably is some form of either momentum or mean reversion.

Right? An example of this very well is if you're a market maker, it doesn't matter if you're uh trading options, if you're trading single stock, if you're trading interest rate products, right? If you're a market making, you are arguably betting on mean reversion. I'm willing to buy at $99, I'm willing to sell at $101. If someone trades and buys from me at 101, I either need to skew my market and be a better buyer so I can be delta flat or risk flat, or I'm hoping that, hey, someone will come in and sell to me at 99 and then I collect the $2 bid offer, right?

And so any form of trading whether you're a long short relative value trader even if you're trading volatility you're you're trading volatility with either some expectation that V is cheap compared to what right compared to some sort of historical trailing average or V is trading incredibly rich compared to some other baseline right and so no matter whether you're trading linear products volatility products structured products at the end of the day you can really decompose it down to I'm betting on some form of this trend will continue to trend in this direction (momentum) or this thing is over/under extended and is going to snap back with some sort of probability (mean reversion) at the end of the day.

Right? Now this seems like a very simplistic view and and um reductive but at the end of the day that is fundamentally true. Now the question is what are the things that are going to trend and what are the things that are going to mean reverse. Now you start talking about factor models. Now you start talking about technical analysis. Now you start talking about coming up with neural nets and machine learning to be able to encapsulate it. But the underlying behavior that you're trying to capture is still momentum versus mean reversion.

七、期权视角作为人生操作系统

主持人： Yeah. At a place like Goldman, there are so many different desks on the trading floor. Um, and because you have this take, I would love to hear your thoughts on what you think what patterns come up in traders who dip their toes first in oil versus in rates versus in called delta one um equities hedging. Uh, give me the rundown. What sort of traders what sort of lessons do you think your typical oil trader pulls from sitting in that seat for 2 years in with regards to how they view the world?

Simmeran： Yeah. So I I view it as actually kind of agnostic of asset class. I think the beauty of trading options is that it gives you a framework for viewing the world. Right.

Uh, my first manager, the one of the first things he taught me is everything in life is an option. The moment you begin to realize that makes decision a lot making simpler. Uh, and then the second thing he said is everything is relationship based, right? And I think those two things have been fundamental guiding principles for everything I've done afterwards.

But going back to everything is an option, right? Uh, there's this concept in options called theta decay which means every day if you are long an insurance policy you're long an option right you're paying one day's worth of time value. A year's worth of insurance should obviously be more valuable than a week's worth of insurance so over time even if nothing changes the value of that insurance should decay right.

And so every day whether or we go about our lives doing X Y or Z right we're paying some sort of theta. Now the question is how do you monetize it or how do you optimize for it? That's the gamma, right? Gamma is this convexity gamma is the sense of like what is the embedded risk/reward uh for pursuing one option versus another right otherwise if everything was equally profitable you should buy every option in the world. Now we don't have infinite money lying around to pay that much option premium but that's a separate problem to have right.

And so I think the thing that you learn and begin to appreciate more than anything else when you're an options trader is viewing life through this risk/reward framework and being able to say, "Hey, from an EV perspective, from an optionality perspective, given the fact that I'm still going to be paying one day's worth of theta, right? Is this worth the optionality and convexity I'm getting from it?"

And that kind of is what led me to go to GSR. That's kind of what led me to later futures and and coming to build Monaco Exchange, which is what my team and I are currently working on, right? Which is, "Hey, there are very few things that let you build uh in a particular space that is relatively uncompeted or still nascent ground for developing new and interesting technologies." Right? And I think it's worth the convexity uh, or it's worth the theta decay to have that kind of convexity.

十、一个具体案例：Funding Trade

主持人： Can you give me an example of a strategy you were running that used to make money just so that our audience and myself can get a flavor for this sort of stuff you were doing?

Simmeran： Sure. Just to address something you said which I find quite interesting. It's like I find very few things are truly truly truly proprietary in terms of what the strategy is. The secret sauce is really what is your input, what is your output and how you connect the two, right?

I could tell you I'm running a momentum strategy, right? Momentum is a very well-studied phenomenon in every market, but momentum cross-sectionally, right, across a bunch of different things. Momentum from a time series perspective of, "Hey, this thing is moving more now in this direction. It's it's trending," right? And so like I think it's always interesting when people are very protective of of certain things that they're working on because I'm like the the secret sauce is maybe not what you're doing, it's how you're doing it.

Uh, but but to address your question like one very basic low-hanging strategy uh which isn't really discretionary or proprietary nature is the funding trade, right? The funding trade is a is a very prime example of something that anyone can do but very few people can do it in a size that matters. Uh, and that's because of balance sheet constraints, right?

What is it from from first principles? The funding trade is, "Uh, I want to enter into a delta-neutral position that lets me earn yield or carry." So how do I do that? If you go long a spot instrument, right? Let's say I go long spot bitcoin and I want to sell perpetual futures against it. Uh, I can do so and I'm risk neutral. I'm delta neutral. But because of how these perpetual futures trade, I can collect funding whenever funding is incredibly positive.

Right. Now the natural question to ask is, "Well why is funding positive?" Well, funding becomes positive when candidly there are more people that are buyers than sellers, right? The purpose of this funding rate instrument is to effectively balance the order book and say, "Hey, the market has this fundamental demand to drive flow one way versus the other," right? And so, we need something to balance the flow between longs and shorts. How do we do so? We create this funding mechanism that trues up the mark-to-market uh pretty much every hour, every 8 hour, every exchange has their own convention.

So whenever you have a massive bull run, right, think early 2020, 2021 or when you have a massive election event like 2024, right, where everyone is long to the tits, pardon my language, right? This leads to a massive funding trade opportunity, but there's very few people that can actually optimize uh and be able to monetize it to a massive extent. Why? Because it's very capital intensive, right? Not only do I have to go out and buy the underlying spot, but now I have to independently collateralize my margin position on on the perp side.

And interestingly, you even saw this in traditional markets where a bunch of people, Millennium is one of them, right? And a few other funds were buying uh a bunch of IBIT uh ETF contracts, right? They were buy they were buying BTC uh ETF and then they were selling CME futures against it because it was so capital intensive to actually be able to post status margin. Very few people could do it and so you needed a large enough balance sheet to do so. But even on the CME, you could earn 15% just from this carry trade alone.

And so that's a very low-hanging fruit that like, "Hey, when the opportunity lines up and you have the balance sheet you can go and do it." It's not very proprietary but it is a market observation that only people who understand why people are trading in these markets uh will be able to put on.

质量交易与"流入垃圾堆"的风险

主持人： What sort of other strategies are running right now that you think are printing in this regime?

Simmeran： Yeah. Uh, I think anything that is uh relative value is probably a good trade. Uh, in this case relative value I mean uh just long short linear one products.

Uh, and so one of the strategies that we had on for example was uh what we call the a quality trade, right? What is that? It's, "Hey, when things are going absolutely crazy and people need a flight to quality you want to go long the thing that will serve as that quality. Uh, and otherwise you want to go short things that on average over a long enough period of time tend to underperform or carry negative," right?

And so one of the first things that we did uh was look at kind of like the perpetual futures landscape and say, "Hey, how do these assets tend to move together over large periods of time?" right? Can I come up with buckets or cohorts for how certain assets move? And now you can look at factors based on that. You can say, "Hey, do these things tend to have correlations and covariances that we can put together uh and effectively trade accordingly?"

And so one of the things that would work quite well now uh and tended to work quite well in 2024 and similar regimes was this kind of quality trade where you would go long high quality liquid assets like Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and a few others and you would short a long basket of long-tail assets uh which tended to on average carry negatively.

The problem or the challenge with this is what happens when the market tends to be overly extended and exuberant and the thing that you think is a pile of trash now all of the sudden is 10x-ing or 20x-ing, right? And so that tends to be more of an art rather than a science of when you short, make sure that you can bear the mark to market uh when there are very idiosyncratic moves in that market.

十一、链上透明度：双刃剑

主持人： As a quant, are there any methods for sort of extracting what other people are doing? Um, call it figuring out their strategies. Um, what are some ways to do that?

Simmeran： Yeah. So I think there's two things, right?

Uh, one is repeat flow in the market, right? So for example, there were a bunch of people that developed yield products uh such that every Friday they would come in and sell covered calls. And so you would see this consistent phenomenon where volatility would come off on Fridays and then kind of rally back over over the weekend back on Mondays. And so being able to uh price that in and be proactive in that flow is one very cheap source of uh alpha.

The more interesting thing actually uh and this kind of led me to the next chapter of my career as head of DeFi was looking at on-chain analytics. Right? The thing with uh all these trading activity uh being on-chain is that you can kind of figure out, "Hey, person with wallet X is now moving funds from this place to this place or this is what their P&L is or this is what they're trading this is how they're trading it."

And so uh having this additional transparency of having a public ledger where all trading activity is fundamentally revealed now serves as a dual-sword because now you can have things like front running right or people call it MEV. You can you can call it whatever fancy technical terminology you want. But at the end of the day uh the transparency and scalability of DeFi also poses the question of how do we prevent people from being uh bad actors or taking advantage of asymmetric information that comes from all of these things being publicly disclosed.
