And so even when you are pretty confident of, "Hey, over a long enough period of time, this thing will converge to fair value and fundamentals," right? You have to be able to weather the mark-to-market and I think that's what trading on your own kind of fundamentally teaches you.

Maker 和 Taker：两种心态

主持人： Was it easy to grow into the buy side seat from sitting doing sellside stuff quoting as you said?

Simmeran： It's not easy, but it's also not the most challenging thing in the world compared to sitting in the buy side seat.

主持人： What was that transition like?

Simmeran： Yeah. So, um, the gear you have to switch from when you go from being a maker to being a taker is quite interesting, right? Where previously I would be market making and if someone wanted to argue about a penny that would actually be a legitimate argument if these things trade on the order of pennies right. If you're quoting an option someone's like, "Oh someone's like 3 cents tighter than you," that actually can be quite big or quite small depending on uh what the trading size of that market is.

When you're a taker, right? You're mostly trying to say, "Hey, how do I minimize my market impact?" uh, and then you begin to appreciate a different side of that puzzle where you're like, "Okay, well if no one else is willing to give me a price do I take this rather egregious price because my research and my conviction tell me that this is still a right trade uh or do I put not put on the risk because the transaction cost is too high?"

Right? And this actually takes me to another uh little quote that my friends and I would say which is my two favorite kinds of trades in the world are "my size your price" or "your size my price". Right? Because if it's your size my price, I have the balance sheet to be able to take on your risk. And so I might give you a you price but you'll take it because you have massive size that you need to get off. Right? And if it's my size, your price, it's saying, "Hey, I have such conviction in this thing. I know you're going to gouge me a bit offer, but I'm still willing to take on this risk because over the horizon of the trade, I have enough conviction that we're going to monetize orders of magnitude bigger." Right?

So, for example, when you have large corporates hedging, it's relatively their size, your price for the most part. And when you are now a taker, when you're now a speculator, it begins to be the opposite.

十三、Edge 的本质：石油 vs. DeFi

主持人： Contrast oil and um and and and DeFi for me. What is the foundation of edge for two of those things?

Simmeran： Uh, the foundation of edge on the oil side is really just the physical market. It's it's having friends in Saudi Arabia. It's having friends in the uh oil fields in the North Sea, right? It's having a deep understanding of what large physical shops are doing. Uh, and understanding that no matter where the financial contracts are trading, these things at expiry have to converge uh to the underlying physical market, right?

And that was a huge divergence from things like altcoins, right? Or random memecoins where there is no fundamentals, right? There's an arbitrary magic internet money that is trading at a ridiculous valuation because someone controls the supply and then they ran it up and no one really knows who controls the supply. And so you can have all these idiosyncratic uh phenomenon happen that are not tied to an underlying physical commodity.

Right? When I when I used to tutor interns at GS, one of the things I used to say is you can't touch an interest rate curve, but you can smell a barrel of oil. Unfortunately, in crypto, you can't smell the barrel of uh barrel of crypto coins and you can't touch them, right? And you can't do any of these other things.

And so I think going from a very fundamentally tied market which yes was stacked on top of it uh you had macro events you had speculation all these things but at the end of the day there is something physical that reality has to converge to rather whether you're talking about oil power a you name it right. On the other side you have very interesting uh market phenomenon. You have a different set of actors whose incentives might not be hedging aligned right they might be purely, "Hey, we want to be predatory or we want to launch a token that we control 90% of the supply of." Now, obviously that's a very interesting market and different dynamic to trade in.

主持人： I still love the the this thing about sizing and pricing. I think that's that's funny.

Simmeran： Um, I mean those genuinely are my two favorite kinds of trades, right? It's like either like you really have to get this risk off, right? And so you're willing to take whatever price someone gives you because you need to unwind your hedge, right? If you're an oil producer and you need that cash up front and you don't want to wait 3 years to lock in the P&L of your of your hedge that crystallized, you need that money now. You will take whatever exit price a dealer gives you because you need that cash today, right? Versus like someone is like, "Hey, I'm going to trade a market that's relatively illiquid, but my size is going to move that market." That's a very different conversation.

十四、当下的机会：AI、电力、Agentic Trading

主持人： From trading oil and from being a DeFi, you've seen, you know, many different parts of the market, buy side and sell side as well. Um, where do you think the opportunities are today? What sort of shops do you hear on the street doing really well? What sort where you know where is money being printed at the moment?

Simmeran： Yeah. So I think anyone at least on the sell side anyone who's facilitating uh trades as part of this like AI complex I think is like incredibly interesting right. If I could have gone back and traded another commodity I feel like power would probably uh be it right. You keep hearing about power, compute uh, nat gas, all of these things I think are are quite interesting uh especially with the rise of uh memory stocks becoming so popular. The fact that like SK Hynix a 43-year-old company you know just launched one of the world's largest ADR offerings for 23 and a half billion today just tells you how big this narrative is getting, right?

And so anyone on the sell side who's facilitating hedges or even speculation in this rather emerging OTC based opaque market, I think is printing a lot of money. But on the other side, when it comes to like buy side things, this I think it's a bit harder to distinguish necessarily where the edge is.

But I will say anyone who has access to the level of LLMs and AI that you're seeing today has unparalleled access compared to like 10 years ago, right? You have people that are like single single people that are launching their own firms that are running a few million dollars on the same scale as what would have taken like 5 years or 10 years to build 20 years ago, right? And so the access to frontier models has fundamentally changed who can access markets, how they begin to access markets, uh and also what kind of flows are going through.

And I suspect agentic trading and anything as part of uh anything that helps you systematize trading from first principles is just going to be absolutely massive over the next 10 to 20 years, right? You see this with Robinhood uh evangelizing their own agentic trading models. You see this with um a bunch of trading platforms that have begun to emerge uh where they don't own the matching engine, they don't own the risk engine. They simply own the routing layer where a lot of this flow ultimately goes and I think that is going to be what ultimately moves the needle over the next 10 years.

Garbage In, Garbage Out ×10

主持人： Do you think these frontier models democratize opportunity call it within markets or do you think they concentrate within the people spending billions on compute? You know your thoughts?

Simmeran： No, I definitely think they help democratize access uh in a way that was previously unparalleled, right? Um, in order to run a statistical regression, you don't need that much. In order to run a decision tree, you begin to need more and more compute. Now, do you need to spend billions of dollars?

主持人： Billions is a is a yeah, it's a figure. I've just, you know, checked it out.

Simmeran： But I think all these frontier models have the same thing. Actually, every LLM model probably suffers from the same thing where it just amplifies what you put into it, right? So if you put in shit out, it's going to amplify that shit by 10x. If you put in good trading knowledge, if you give it very good structures and rationale that it can easily iterate on right now, like you have this massive compute that's at your fingertips, what you input it can it'll just 10x that. So if you put good things in, it'll 10x the good things. If you put shit in, it'll 10x the shit. Right?

So now the question is, what are your x's? What are your y's? And then how do you construct that mapping? Right? If I want to forecast returns, okay, well, should I be forecasting one day returns or three days returns? Right now, I can just iterate on testing these things much quicker than I otherwise could have like 10 years from now.

Right? So, the the the thing that's giving you is just more horsepower. It's not necessarily making you smarter in the sense of it's giving you what the secret sauce of alpha is. It's just letting you try a lot more things in a much more scalable way. And I think for anyone who's intellectually curious and has the effort and persistence to actually be able to learn trading from first principles and then apply it in this accelerated way is the one who's going to likely win.

从第一性原理学交易

主持人： Our audience is very broad. There's a lot of different people. Um, but just to double tap on that, if you had to learn trading from first principles today and you want to run buyside stuff, call it in your PA, whatever that may be, what would be your approach?

Simmeran： Uh, I would probably go from first principles and think about, "Well, why do people trade?" right? People fundamentally trade because they either want to speculate, they want to hedge, or they're getting compensated for it right either as a market maker or as a sense of utility.

So if I start with those first three principles I would say, "Okay, well, what fundamentally moves markets?" right? Uh, are markets fundamentally still fully efficient? Probably not. Where do these inefficiencies lie? Well, you can launch agents to look at quarterly filings. You can see what sectors are actually growing or shrinking, right? You have access unparalleled access to data. The question is what can you glean from that data that you can then turn into a signal, right?

And so if if I were to go from first principles, I would say, "Okay, well, what are the sectors that ultimately will be the most impacted with this AI narrative?" right? Is it is it the energy complex? Uh, should I be looking at metals? Should I be looking at downstream effects of neoclouds? Should I be looking at semiconductors? Um, right. Like what are the different sectors that I can decompose any thesis into or any narrative into and then within those narratives right who are likely to be the biggest winners right.

I that's fundamentally I think like how you should be thinking about trading in general which is if I understand the why then I can figure out what is the best expression of that risk right the hardest part is figuring out like what is the risk I should be taking right and then two is like how do I monetize in the best way possible right are are is trading linear products the best way is trading options the best way that is a much much like later downstream question than what is the thing I probably should be trading, right?

What is probably the most interesting narrative that's exploding now? Why is copper trading at all-time highs? Right? Why has orange juice come off from like 5-year highs over the past like two years or something like that, right? There's all these like little things that you can begin to ask and that's now driven by intellectual curiosity on top.

十五、Monaco Exchange：市场准入的下一场革命

主持人： The reason why I asked that question as well is that—and I'm sure you agree with me on this. You look at the world today and there is just this explosion of people who want to trade. Um, and every single tailwind is on that side. Um, you look at the social contract that exists today. Um, leads to people wanting to make it call it independently um, want that freedom. Uh, and the explosion in access to information plus the excitement especially in the US public markets is just unfathomable right. The amount of vol makes it even more call exhilarating right. And you're in a unique spot where you were a trader um, both on sell side by side um, oil to defi and now you're building Monaco. What is your thesis?

Simmeran： My thesis is that market access is due for an unparalleled revolution and we want to build a key cornerstone in that right.

What does that mean more more explicitly? If someone in India or someone in Korea or someone in Turkey for example where you have massive hyperinflation right wants to have access to one of the greatest capital markets in the world how do they do so right? It's it's quite hard. If they do exist instruments for them to do so if there do exist brokerages for them to do so the bid offer and the conversion and all these additional costs erode so much of what they would otherwise be earning.

And so the question becomes, well how do we give them unparalleled access to markets that already exist? That's phase one, right? There might exist mutual fund instruments but they don't actually allow you to trade like single-single stock equity exposure right. So how do we give people in India how do we give people in Turkey how do we give people in relatively emerging markets where their currency is being eroded away access to something that arguably is a better value than what they currently hold.

The second thing is how do we give people access to new markets that were otherwise previously inaccessible to you, me and Joe off the street, right? And one one prime example and I think we talked about this uh even before we started rolling was was compute was one of them and computes obviously now taken over right you hear about it from or you hear about it from Compass and various other providers. You hear about the indexification uh and the OTC market that's emerged around it.

For me the the layer that I find more interesting is really power right. There's no venue in the world that lets you and I access markets or access instruments that let you either hedge or speculate on the price of power whether it's PJM whether it's whether it's a grid in the Philippines right. Whatever you whatever you consider right electricity is the input to everything whether you're charging your phone whether we're sitting in a lit lit studio we all have exposure to it. Then how why why can't we speculate on it why can't we hedge against it and if you if you game this out and look at the AI complex right people are talking about memory people are talking inference, compute, neoclouds. Very few people are actively talking in very vocal terms about well energy is an input to all of these. Power is an input to all of these, right? Do we expect massive power hedging? And the short answer is is yes, right? That's the other area where where you were asking, "Hey, where are people on the sell side and buy side making money?" Is anyone who's facilitating it? Right now, that market tends to be very OTC and opaque. We want to democratize access to a key input like electricity, which no one has previously been able to do.

Monaco 的差异化：Trader-sourced Listing

主持人： What differentiates you as a per se exchange? Because I hear of a million different ones, right? What's different?

Simmeran： Yeah, sure. Uh, I could talk from a technical angle about latency and order matching. I think that's less relevant because the numbers speak for themselves, right? I think this is one of the few venues that's built by traders who sat in both a buyside seat, a sellside seat, a traditional seat, and a crypto-native seat. Right? I have I have colleagues that have come from Hudson River Trading, from Jump Crypto. uh, one of our core engineers was one of the youngest grant recipients from NASA. Uh, he's literally a rocket scientist, right?

And so it's it's one of those things where like we have a very keen appreciation for the market that we're building for and the user base that we're building for it. It's us. We are the user base that we're building for, right? Someone who's a bit more prosumer.

But even more so, I would say the way we think about market access, the way we think about how what market should be listed uh is arguably unparalleled. And I can and I can go into details about what that market listing process looks like, but at the end of the day, this is a design space that very few people have decided to actively take on where a lot of venues when they want to list a market, right? They either charge massive listing fees or they have to go and convince market makers to provide liquidity.

We have a solution where uh we effectively have it be sourced directly from traders, right? If a trader says, "Hey, I want this market listable or I want this market accessible," we incentivize them to one propose that market and then we also give them long-term incentives if that market is successful. And this is something that I'm a bit surprised because it's a very elegant and simple solution what we've constructed but has yet been unaddressed uh by broader adoption.

上市流程细节

主持人： So the listing process um, yeah, you can go like even deeper into how that works.

Simmeran： Yeah sure. So right now, right, if I look at uh Hyperliquid, a leading decentralized exchange, you have to have 500K HYPE uh in order to be a deployer as they call it. If we had $80 million lying around, this would be a very different conversation in a different podcast episode. Uh, so not everyone does, right? And so that tends to be a barrier to entry for a lot of people.

If I want to list something on a centralized exchange, I have to go take a listing manager out to dinner, maybe buy him a Jeep, promise him that he'll get some kickback, right? And then I still have to go to a market maker and say, "Hey, this is worth your cost of capital. Please quote." Right? Each of those three sounds incredibly painful candidly, right? And I'm like, this is crowding out a lot of people.

So, let's take a step back. We're building a platform. We're building a venue that is built for traders by traders with traders. What ultimately moves the needle for us? Well, what is the thing that I find most attractive? Revenue. At the end of the day, where does the revenue come from? It comes from trading fees.

Well, why don't we say anyone uh who trades, right? As they trade, they generate revenue for the platform that maps to what we'll call an activity score on the exchange, right? Think of it as a credit score, if you will. If you have an activity score beyond a certain threshold, you can propose any market completely for free. But when you propose a market, you also give publicly what we'll call an indication of interest for how much activity you expect to do in that market over, let's say, the next 60 days, right?

We take all of these indications of interest together and anyone can co-propose with you because it's a public proposal. We take all of this indication of interest together. Uh, once it crosses a certain threshold, we work with our network of market makers, Oracle providers to facilitate it.

Now, a few key things.

  • One, when we consider your indication of interest, we weight it by how much activity you've done over the last 60 days, 90 days, you name it. Because someone who was active more recently tends to carry a lot more weight than someone who was active a year ago, but hasn't traded at all since then, right? And so we we factor that in on day one.
  • Number two, what is the benefit of proposing a market? Well, if you propose a market and you deliver that indication of interest volume that you said you were thinking about doing over the next 60 days, we give you a revenue share from the taker fees of that market in perpetuity. Even if you don't trade after that 60-day period, unless the market gets delisted. Why? You were early. You delivered your end of the bargain. The market is clearly of interest to other traders. Otherwise, it would have been delisted. We want you to partake in driving that volume and driving that revenue for the platform forward.
  • Three, I can take this indication of interest and say, "Hey, market maker X, Y, and Z, you were worried about justifying your cost of capital or is, hey, is there even going to be any trading activity on this?" Now, you have certified demand that you can count against when you're quoting this, right?
  • Four, how do I hold people accountable? Well, if you say, "I'm going to trade X million in this market over the next 60 days," and you end up trading not that, right? We effectively slash your activity score. And the only way to improve your activity score is either generating more fees on the platform or by proposing another market.

So, there's no mechanism of locking up a token in order to be deflationary. There's no, "Hey, you have to pay me a million dollars to get a market listed." We want this to be sourced directly from traders and have them drive what the listing roadmap should look like, right? And because we restricted to two proposals at a time, no one party can come in and say, "Hey, I want to list the next 100 markets," right?

But what this also allows is, "Hey, listing a market on Nvidia perp straightforward," right? Listing a market on orange futures now begins to get interesting. Listing a market on onion futures is actually illegal in the US. But but but but there's all these little interesting things that begin to emerge where people want to trade water, people want to trade power, people want to trade compute. We want to give them a platform to be able to express that interest and then work with them to be able to create a market around that and have them reap the rewards of facilitating. There's no Ponzinomics. There's no like you know there's no archaic uh market infrastructure. It's very much we want this to be driven by traders and disintermediate the need for brokers to be able to like consolidate trading groups and cabals.

But now what's interesting is this, right? Who who is the most active uh trader on any venue?

主持人： The market makers.

Simmeran： A market maker. A market maker is notoriously agnostic of what they trade. An apple is an apple. A widget is a widget. If I can price it and I can hedge it, I'm happy to quote it. Right? So, a market maker can work with institutional clients who want to have access to markets that they don't otherwise have access to and then can propose those markets and enter into rev-share either with institutions or other distribution networks. And now this creates all these interesting secondary markets that begin to emerge. Right? So, not only are we incentivizing traders uh to come in and trade with revenue share rebates, but we're also allowing people to be able to uh develop layers on top of the core technology that we've built to drive broader adoption.

举例：橙汁和洋葱期货

主持人： Give me walk me through an example. Let's say I want to list orange futures. How do I hedge that?

Simmeran： Uh, well, right now you can actually trade orange futures on ICE or orange futures are actually uh actually trade on the intercontinental.

主持人： I didn't know that.

Simmeran： Yeah. Yeah. Okay. You can trade uh, you can trade coffee, you can trade uh concentrated frozen orange juice. Uh, you can't trade onion futures unfortunately for now, but maybe we'll see.

主持人： Why is that?

Simmeran： Uh, in the 1950s, someone tried to corner the onion market. Uh, and so then the US government passed a rule that said you can't trade onion futures, but the US Department of Agriculture does publish a daily fixing for the price of onions uh in different regions. And if a data provider were to convert that into a daily price feed, I'm not saying that someone could make a perpetual future around it, but they very well could.

十六、Monaco 的目标客户、上线节奏与远景

主持人： Who do you envision being the people at trading on Monaco? Is it institutions? Is it everyone? What are your thoughts?

Simmeran： Yeah. Uh, I would say I'm my ideal customer profile, right? Someone who's maybe not thinking about trading in the trenches, as they say in crypto, right? Uh, someone who thinks about things from a portfolio perspective, someone who does want to run long and short strategies, uh, who wants exposure to 24/7 markets, someone who uh might have an agent that they want to connect, right, and can do so programmatically uh very seamlessly through our API stack, someone who's thinking about a world that is more and more moving towards 24/7 markets and wants to say, "Hey, as price discovery happens, I want to be a part of that process," right? Or I want to be able to trade a thesis that other venues wouldn't allow me to trade because they can't list those markets as easily. That I think is far more interesting.

Right? When I think about the first, you know, 100 or 200 traders on Monaco, it's likely going to be colleagues, friends, people who've who've obviously known the team that's built it, uh, and have wanted to be in the space for for a very long time. Beyond that, I think once you build a track record, once you show that you can handle liquidations, uh, and very, you know, adverse market scenarios similar to what happened one year ago on 10/10, right? Then I think you begin to see broader adoption in the form of institutions uh as you build that trust.

主持人： When are you launching?

Simmeran： Uh, next month. So uh, I'll be flying out to Token 2049 to visit quite a few trading groups uh and folks who've wanted to connect for for a while. Uh, it'll be a long flight, but I'm hoping to make the most of it. And then as soon as I come back, we're in the final stages of launching uh launching mainnet.

深夜拷问：Why?

And the the beauty of this also uh and if I can share a short anecdote, I was in the office a few weeks back uh Wednesday night until Thursday morning, 4:00 a.m. And I went home from the office at 4:00 a.m. I went to the gym, I showered, I got an egg and cheese burrito, and I was back at the office at 8:30. And I was the second person in.

And the thing that kept nagging my mind is what is my why, right? Like why why why the heck am I doing this? And we have a daily team standup and I went down the list and I asked each of my colleagues like guys like no no no fluff, no— Why are you here? Right? Why are you doing this?

And some folks said, "Hey, you know, this is a very interesting opportunity. We like the vision. We like the team. We like the opportunity. Uh, we get to grow. We get to learn. Um, obviously you know we want to build a business."

And I said candidly, if you're not here to build one of the best exchanges in the world, then we probably shouldn't be here, right? There's plenty of ways to make money. Like, you can go to a trading firm, you can cure cancer, you can go be an educator. There's like plenty of ways to to solve this. Uh, if the problem that you're trying to solve is simply how to make money.

But I think there are very few industries that let you compete with the best of the best on day one. Right? If I want to swim against Michael Phelps, I don't just get to randomly swim against Michael Phelps. If I want to compete against Hikaru or Magnus Carlsen, I don't just get to play with them on day one. Right? But this is one of the few industries where you get to go head-to-head with the titans of this industry uh and really give it a shot and build a business that has a chance to change the world. Right? And thinking about market access, thinking about how do we give people access to markets and instruments that they previously just were completely unable to do so or unable to access I think is a very interesting problem and one that deserves the the attention of the people building.

十年后的 Monaco

主持人： Let's say we do another podcast in 10 years. What do you want Monaco to look like then?

Simmeran： That's an excellent question. Um, I would say Monaco 10 years from now should still be a small team, building more and more products, building more and more markets, and unifying more and more institutional access.

Right? There's $15 trillion of value that exchanges hands between buyers and sellers every day. Half of that is about rates, right? A third of that's probably FX and the rest is scattered throughout. This is not a billion dollar market. It's a trillion dollar market, right? So carving out a piece and place in that trillion dollar market and building the infrastructure that can handle that is is a pretty momentous task and is a task that I want to spend the next multi-year horizon of my life building towards.

主持人： I love it. Thank you so much for coming on Odds on Open. This was this was awesome man.

Simmeran： It's a pleasure. Thank you for offering me.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：这个交易员其实在卖"油的触觉"，而不是油
Simmeran 随口说出的那句"you can't touch an interest rate curve, but you can smell a barrel of oil"（你摸不到利率曲线，但你能闻到一桶油的味道），表面是导师语录，骨子里却是**他整个职业路径的隐藏主线**——而他自己可能都没完全意识到。
重新审视他的轨迹： - 高盛油桌：优势来自**非洲岸边装驳船的人**、**北海的货船路由**——物理嗅觉 - GSR 加密：失去嗅觉，于是用**链上账本**作为合成嗅觉器官（谁的钱包在动，钱流向哪里） - Monaco 交易所：想交易**电力、算力、水**——重新把金融拉回"可嗅闻"的物理标的
**他真正在做的事，是在反复逃离纯符号市场，回归可触摸的世界。** 加密的 memecoin 让他焦虑（"没有基本面要收敛"），而电力让他兴奋——因为电力有物理终局。这是一种心理学上罕见的交易员类型：**对"幻影资产"过敏的衍生品交易员**。市场上大多数人在往符号化更深处走（代币化万物），而他的事业曲线一直在反

item.title: [a16z] Why Founders Are Betting Big on Factories, Mines, and Energy
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让人意外的观察：这不是"制造业回流"，而是"消费者补贴国防"的历史性反转

过去 80 年美国的技术扩散逻辑是：政府出钱做第一代（阿波罗、互联网、核能），然后"长尾"溢出到消费市场。但这期对话里埋着一个几乎没被明说的、方向相反的新模式——国防买单，但消费者最终定义质量上限。Aaron 那句"美国最大的礼物是美国消费者的挑剔"，和 Conor 讲的"国防承担前 100 件的高单价 CapEx"，拼在一起等于说：

政府不再是技术的定义者，而是技术的融资者；真正把东西逼到便宜又好用的，是消费电子级的客户纪律。

这其实是把一个军工复合体，重新组装成一个由消费者精细度反向驱动的、以国防订单做种子轮的通用工业栈。DJI 的轨迹（消费无人机 → 国防 → 人形机器人执行器）不是巧合，而是这个新物理定律的第一个经验数据点。

跨领域连接：这波"美国动能"的底层结构，和 Y Combinator 早期的 Silicon Valley 像到诡异

Aaron 自己在最后半不经意地说出了关键隐喻："人们嘲笑 YC 公司互相卖东西，但生态就是这么起来的——朋友之间容忍度高、愿意一起把东西搞坏再搞好。"

把这句话放到 Anduril / Saronic / Hadrian / Mariana 的供应链上，你会发现它们正在复现 2005–2012 年 SaaS 生态的拓扑：

SaaS 早期（2008） 今天的硬核工业
Stripe 的第一批客户是 YC 朋友 Hadrian 的第一批客户是 Anduril / Saronic
AWS 让"不用自建数据中心"成为默认 国防 CapEx 让"不用自建铸造厂"成为默认
开发者从大公司离职创业 Palantir / Anduril / SpaceX 的工程师离职做"中间层"
App Store 定义了可容忍失败的最小单元 低混合高产量 → 高混合低产量，车间技术员用 Claude 20 分钟改线

换句话说：我们正在见证硬件版的"API 革命"。过去钢铁、PCB、执行器、着陆架这些东西是像 Oracle 一样卖的——定制、慢、锁死；而 Hadrian 这类"制造业中间层（manufacturing middle）"本质上是在给工业基座做"REST API 化"。一旦接口变得可组合，组合爆炸就会压过中国的规模优势——这才是跟中国新能源曲线那张图真正相关的论据，而不是补贴额度。

隐藏的系统性真相：瓶颈不在技术，而在"美国人的意志（American will）"——这其实是个心理学问题，不是工程问题

Aaron 回答"怎样追上中国的能源曲线"时，有一个几乎被略过去的句子：

"这不是技术问题。这是我们美国人需要做一些灵魂拷问——我们到底还想不想造东西、还想不想增长。"

这是整期访谈最反资本主义话术、也最深刻的一句。它意味着：资本市场、Elon 式工程文化、国防订单，这些都是充分条件，但必要条件是一种"社会愿意忍受物理世界的噪声、灰尘、征地、噪音、变化"的集体心理状态。

这里有个几乎没人提的跨领域连接——和日本"失落的三十年"的真正病因是同一个诊断。日本 1990 年之后的问题从来不是技术断层（他们的材料、半导体、精密制造至今顶级），而是社会集体选择了"稳定 > 变化"。美国如果赢不下这一轮，不会是因为缺芯片、缺矿、缺电——会是因为每一个数据中心的选址听证会、每一个铜矿的环保诉讼、每一次电网改造的 NIMBY 投票，把 Aaron 说的那个"滚起来的雪球"一粒粒摩擦没了。

所以这期播客真正该让人警觉的信号是：Conor 在最后用了"it's ours to lose"。这是一句投资人很少说的话。它翻译过来就是——赢面已经发到手上了，但历史上手里拿着赢面还输掉的国家，数量远多于靠努力翻盘的国家。

开场：工业基座的觉醒

You don't have a defense industrial base without an industrial base. It's been a real wake-up call that we need to get building again.

AI will be a phenomenal tool that can be used in the physical world. The reality is AI cannot turn a wrench yet.

10 most valuable companies in the world, like the majority of them are hardware companies.

What's it like to visit one of these sites? You're building a physical thing. You're not sitting at a desk on your computer. You're out in the world. It sounds kind of sexy and romantic, but when you're actually doing it, it's rough.

When you show up at Mariana, when you show up at Hadrian, when you show up at Castellana, you literally get people who are so passionate about what they're doing. That produces really good results.

There's that very famous chart of like US power production versus China new energy production. What would it take to close that gap? I don't think that that is a technology problem.

一、为什么美国工业基座重新成为主题

主持人： Connor and Aaron, thank you so much for joining the podcast today. We're here to talk about AD 50 and this year's list. And let's just get straight into things. I know a big theme of this year was the American industrial base. Can you talk about what we've learned this year and why that's such a big important theme right now?

Connor： We've been saying for a while — you don't have a defense industrial base without an industrial base. And I think this year really put that into perspective. With conflicts going on in the world, and realizing that the hollowing out of our industrial base that's happened over the last several decades actually has real consequences on the battlefield for soldiers — both American soldiers and our allies — it's been a real wake-up call in the United States that we need to get building again.

Aaron： It's also not just one factor, but multiple factors happening at the same time. World conflict, continued evolution of the capital markets (we'll talk about capital flowing into this ecosystem later), and — one of the bigger things — you actually have an entrepreneurial base right now who is effectively raising their hand and saying, "I'm going to build in this ecosystem." That's incredibly important not just for our nation, but because you can build really valuable companies in it. It's a conglomeration of geopolitical factors, capital markets, and entrepreneurs all coming together. A really interesting time to be building, and a good time for us to be investing.

Connor： When we looked at AD 50 this year, we thought about where we're at in the history of American dynamism. We're still early, but one theme that has evolved is that you really need to start looking at American dynamism companies as a totality from end to end — from the input that comes out of the ground, to the factory that makes the thing, to the end system. That's how we set up AD 50 this year: three lenses. Each pillar is uniquely important to the end product or system, but people don't usually think that way. Many companies in our portfolio have thought from an inputs perspective, from a factories perspective, and now from a systems perspective.

二、从国防到民用：工业基座的溢出效应

主持人： One theory a person could develop after looking at the list is: okay, we built out this industrial base for defense — missiles, drones — but it's actually a tailwind now helping a lot of different industries in America. Energy, robotics, AI. Can you talk about how all these fit together?

Aaron： If you look back in history — 70, 80, almost 100 years ago — a lot of times technology development in America came from the government. Going to space, developing the internet, developing nuclear energy — the government said, "We are going to do this for the purpose of the government." Then the long tail of that technology was super valuable for everyone else.

What's different now, to some extent, is that private industry and private capital are saying, "We're actually going to be the impetus that develops something." Many of these markets are to serve the federal government, to serve the Department of War in some way. But when you build an industrial base — either down the supply chain or in end systems — it inherently has many use cases.

The term "dual use" gets talked about a lot in investing. Focusing on too many things at once is not good for a startup. But it is 100% true of what's happening with any factory being built today, any neo-factory, any energy production, anything we touch in minerals and materials in the ground — it's not just going into a defense system. It's going into my uncle's car. It's going into my kids' future toy. The tip of the spear is focused on the government; but in the long run, these systems will be used in the Waymo we took today, or anywhere else.

案例：DJI 的三段式路径

Connor： A good example is actually DJI in China, which has gone through multiple arcs. Started building consumer drones, recognized in the late 2010s there was a large market for drones in public safety and national defense, built out a real high-scale drone production business for defense. And now the company is behind the largest producers of robots in the world — because what is very similar to a drone motor is a robot actuator, which is the hardest part of building a robot.

So you have a company that, over the course of growing a large defense business that itself spun out of a consumer business, is now the world's leading expert on how to build and produce hardware for the next wave of physical AI — both consumer and industrial.

This technology transfer and process-knowledge transfer between military and non-military use cases is really important and has always been how it works. It's great to have the federal government be a subsidizer for figuring out this process knowledge and new technology. Then — our greatest gift in the United States is the discernment of the American consumer. We are going to push things to be more capable and cheaper than the government ever will. That symbiotic relationship in the industrial base is really important. We're seeing it on the energy side, the electronic side, across the entire industrial stack.

第一件事总是最贵的

Aaron： When you build the first of a kind of anything, it's quite expensive. Building a bespoke military system or consumer product —

主持人： Zero to 100, it's going to cost a lot.

Aaron： It's going to cost a lot. The beautiful thing right now is we have a federal government and a Department of War saying, number one, we're going to try to actively rebuild this industrial base. By doing that, they're changing the unit-economic decision from the start for these companies. Instead of building 100 things, you can say, "Okay, maybe build 100, but we're willing to pay a cost that the consumer or commercial market wouldn't pay." That means more machines in your factory, more CapEx that the government is helping pay at the start. Then that leads to things that are physical, financially viable, and at a scale that can actually touch the consumer.

Connor： If you're building a new PCB fab in the United States, that's a pretty expensive operation — expensive pieces of machinery. If you have a defense buyer as the first buyer to help you pay for or subsidize that CapEx investment, that's great, because — you know what else has PCB boards? Robots. You know what else has PCB boards? Hearing aids. The ability to pass on some of that CapEx to the defense industrial base will be really powerful as we rebuild industrial capacity in the United States.

三、创业公司如何压低成本、加快节奏

主持人： So what specifically are you seeing startups do to drive down costs and move faster?

Aaron： We can look to Elon for a lot of answers. The few modern-day companies that have built anything at scale are probably SpaceX and Tesla. If you look at how Elon and his team built those businesses, it's been very vertically integrated. I take the ideology that you shouldn't vertically integrate everything. If you're building a super exquisite system like a missile that is doing something very unique, you kind of have to — you have to control the exquisiteness, control the cost.

Connor： SpaceX and Tesla were doing first of their kind. There didn't exist an industrial base in the US to support them. They had to build it themselves. Where there are high-quality suppliers, you should use suppliers.

Aaron： The learning is: if you don't have an industrial base you can rely on quickly and reliably, then you have to do it — and inherently, that is a hard journey. Saying "I'm going to focus on the end system, build the most cost-effective, effective system I can — and oh, by the way, I also have to go figure out the ball bearing, the solenoid valve" — that's a lot. In the case of Tesla and SpaceX, the auto industry was a bit different because there wasn't a battery supply chain. Elon had to recreate it.

Connor： The whole power electronics, the whole drivetrain — they had to really build completely from scratch. Based off papers published in the '70s that had been collecting dust for 40 years.

案例：Mariana Minerals — 不只是更会挖铜

主持人： In terms of companies in the AD portfolio, there's Mariana Minerals, which bought a copper mine and is kind of reinventing things. Would they be a good example?

Connor： They recognized that existing players in the mining industry just were not going to pick up technology fast enough for it to make a difference. They also wanted to actually own the entire value chain to be able to put their money where their mouth was and capture the end value of the new technology they were bringing. They do everything from acquiring the asset, developing it, mining it, operating it, and refining the material themselves across multiple different minerals, and they sell a final product in the market. That's another trend I'd point to: how much founders and entrepreneurs building in these spaces are leaning into AI and software as a huge component of their build.

Aaron： When you look at the physical world, applying software and AI will look different than what has happened in legal or customer service. To Connor's point, many times you have to own the asset in order to really change the asset. Not every time, but a lot of times — showing is believing in the physical world. Whereas when you're purely a digital AI product, it's very easily transferable.

What Mariana is doing with this copper mine is really impressive. It's not just "we're going to be better at extracting copper." It's rethinking everything — the entire end-to-end process of how you plan, operate, mine, and refine materials. Once you own that process end to end and are using software at every stage, you capture that data and it feeds back.

Hadrian 与"没有银弹"的工厂

Connor： This is an important point — not just Mariana. If you look at a business like Hadrian, it's a perfect example of how to utilize software. But more importantly, there's no silver bullet that suddenly makes a factory or a mine perfect. It's actually 15 or 20 different things.

Look at what Chris has done at Hadrian — yes, it's what it takes to quote and even take an order of a part. It's the actual physical making of the part. It's how you inspect it and transfer it. There are all these different interim steps that exist within a factory. The beautiful thing — when you start from a fresh slate like Chris has in building his factories, or in Mariana's case, when you own the thing and take it over — is you can look at every single node from a first-principles perspective and say, "Was this process that's been done the last 100 years the right process?"

That's what's happening across every layer of the physical world right now — not just mines, not just factories. AI will be a phenomenal tool that can be used in the physical world. The reality is AI cannot turn a wrench yet. It will at some point, but we're far off. We can maybe have a discussion about the robotic models and autonomy we see in the physical world — we're getting closer. The nuance is: the physical world is not about putting a silver-bullet shiny AI product forward. It's a deep understanding of what a process looks like, how to physically manipulate it, how to change something happening in the world.

低混合高产量 vs. 高混合低产量

Connor： Maybe a specific example — low-mix / high-volume versus high-mix / low-volume, and how AI can change the game. Historically, if you're spending a lot setting up a line with automation, you really need to be producing a lot of one single thing to get the cost down and justify the investment.

In the US we do a lot of low-mix / high-volume manufacturing, which is very hard to automate because it's very expensive when you have to change the line all the time. But what we're seeing across our portfolio is that manufacturing technicians themselves have the intuition and now have the software tools to change the economics of what it looks like to produce low-volume / high-mix on the line.

You can have a manufacturing technician — this is not someone with a college degree, not necessarily someone who's studied software engineering — now able to use these tools to reprogram and reconfigure manufacturing lines on the fly. They understand the manufacturing process; they know how to do what they're doing in the physical world. Now suddenly they have tools so you can retool a line, instead of having to call a system integrator and it takes 3 months and hundreds of thousands of dollars to reconfigure a line. You can have a manufacturing engineer use Claude and do that in 20 minutes. That's been a real game-changer across lots of companies we've seen.

为什么"可调线"对系统公司至关重要

Aaron： Why that's important: when you look at how we've articulated AD 50 this year, there are three categories. A lot of times what we focus on is just the systems companies — Anduril, Saronic, Castellion. The list goes on. But if you can't iterate on the design and the prototype, not only do you not get a better end system, you also just move at a slower pace. By the time you finally fix a production-level missile or plane, you then have to go back and build up all these subsystems to meet the scale. If you have a more transferable, more adjustable line, you can build the prototype faster, and set up each component in a way that it can get to rate production quicker.

Connor： You're designing for manufacturability from the outset.

Aaron： Exactly. I keep going back to learnings from Tesla and SpaceX. They had to make those choices because they didn't have any other option. In the end, it's that mantra of "design for manufacturing" that now exists within all these systems companies. We are now in the age of seeing them produce. Go look at what Anduril's built in Ohio and now on the East Coast in Baltimore. Go look at what Saronic has built with the Shipyard. These are massive facilities that are, very soon, going to be producing thousands, tens of thousands, hopefully hundreds of thousands of systems. We haven't done that in America in a long time.

Connor： This is no longer an on-paper theoretical exercise. This is happening in the real world, and real stuff is coming off the lines.

四、国防采购的新逻辑：资本在政府之前出手

主持人： Something I think is special about AD founders is they make any problem an Elon-sized problem. I'd love to hear that applied to the different industries we're talking about.

Aaron： Defense specifically has historically been one of the hardest sectors to just build the thing you think the government needs. Unfortunately — and I experienced this when I served in the Army — the buyer is not the user, and the appropriator of the dollars for the buyer is completely removed. You have all these disjointed decision-makers who matter.

Back then we didn't really have neo-primes or AD companies. What you had was primes who would sit there and listen: "Tell me what you want. I'll develop the thing after you give me the money." The age-old problem is you get a system that's not technology-forward, that was developed for 10 years ago, and the end soldier gets something that's not super valuable to them.

What's different now — the "Elon-sized problem" lens — is you can ask, "What does the military actually need?" The beautiful thing is venture capital, American Dynamism, and the rest of the capital markets are saying, "We will fund that in advance. You can build in advance of the government saying, 'Here's the thing for you to build.'" The outcome: the soldier gets a better product, something that fundamentally changes the battlefield and helps with deterrence or security or safety. And you get a time frame of a system actually aligned with the requirement of the market and what technology can do today.

Instead of sitting and waiting for the government to tell you what they want, the government signals, you see it, and you build in advance using private capital. That just has not happened in the history of defense. Castelion is building a hypersonic missile that doesn't do a super exquisite thing, but it's really hard to build a missile that goes that fast and is reliable. The government has given them contracts and bought missiles — but if you look at the last 3 years of that business, it was private venture capital, entrepreneurs taking the risk and building the thing in advance. You see that again and again in defense: you'll just get better products, and the neo-primes and new companies will take a lot of that market share.

It's not just a defense thing. Aaron sees it in energy as well. We're rewriting our entire energy grid right now. We are on the one-yard line. We are just starting that process.

五、创业者的特质：这事儿值吗？

Aaron： Another part of it is a little more intangible: these are really hard companies to build. Really hard problems. When I talk to Turner, the CEO of Mariana Minerals, he's flying all over the world — middle-of-nowhere places. He's out where there's no cell phone signal, no electricity, touching dirt, spending weeks and months away from his family. It has to be worth it.

You're building a physical thing. You're not sitting at a desk on your computer. You're out in the world. It sounds sexy and romantic, but when you're actually doing it, it's rough. The travel is hard. The people you're engaging with — you're not calling up suppliers who operate in the same time scale and culture as you. These are really tough people to negotiate with and work with, who have a very different culture. If you're going to put yourself through that, it better be damn worth it.

People really gravitate toward problems that feel huge and enormous because these are real missionary founders we see building in the space. Even as it's heated up and there's more capital and it's gotten cool — it's still brutal.

从"重要"到"也最有价值"

Aaron： The biggest thing that has changed in American Dynamism land in the last few years: we always knew the companies being built in this category were really important to the fabric of America. Defense systems, energy, widgets that go into everything — that stuff is really important. It affects our safety, how we live our life.

But the biggest change is: those companies weren't just the most important thing to us. Now they can also be the most valuable companies. That's a big distinction. It's not just solving a problem for safety or security — it's solving that and those can be some of the largest companies in the world. That's what technology has changed in these industries. Mining has always been a big industry. Defense has always been. Energy —

Connor： It hasn't been economically worth it for a young, smart, ambitious person to go after these categories. But companies like Palantir, Anduril, SpaceX have proved you can build a really big business operating in these categories. If you look at the top 10 most valuable companies in the world right now, the majority are hardware companies. They're building a physical product. We've kind of come full circle.

So you get the most ambitious founders of our generation, who want to run toward that hard problem and know it's going to be worth it.

Aaron： The beautiful thing about many of these industries — mining, Rio Tinto has been around a long time; Boeing's been around a long time; good companies building good products — is when you take a first-principles technology approach about what the audacious thing to be built is, and then you get entrepreneurs like the folks on this AD 50 list — "yeah, I'm going to rebuild the American energy grid, that sounds fun" — that didn't exist 50 years ago. That didn't exist 5 years ago. America's best and brightest are building toward this category for the first time. And the opportunity is there.

As someone who served in the military, you always think of what you do as something greater than yourself. The capital markets exist to make money — this is a capitalist society, not a charity. But a lot of the companies on this AD 50 list are doing something that's going to be large and valuable and really inherently important to the fabric of America. That's pretty exciting.

六、工地现场是什么样

Aaron： Connor and I have the best job of all time. I do own steel-toe boots now, because of the number of site visits I've been to where they're like, "Yeah, you've got to show up in steel-toe boots."

Connor： It's not all sexy, to be honest. These are locations that are a lot of times —

Connor： Hard to get to, in the middle of nowhere. We're talking about real physical things that require earth-moving. 七、"美国制造"的传染效应

主持人： Is there a contagion effect to things being made in America — like, "oh, because that actuator is made here, now we can make this, now we can make that," and when you're able to compress one timeline you can compress multiple timelines?

Aaron： I don't think it's just timeline — I also think it's cost and quality. When we look at defense autonomous systems — what Saronic's making (a lot of boats), Covenent's making (a lot of missiles), Castelion's making (a lot of missiles), Anduril's making (a lot of things) — when you build many systems, you also require many subsystems below that.

Back to the comment we had earlier: by building toward defense, you also build for a different industry. We actually don't have a lot of humanoids or robotics in the world today — maybe thousands. When you think about the subsystems that go into some military systems, it's the exact same subsystems that are going to go into future robotic systems — actuators, motors, valves, switches. When you can build those to quality and to cost, you make other markets that maybe weren't viable suddenly make sense.

That's going to happen in the robotics world. We're going to spend time showing development of all those sub-components we're going to build for military systems — which is good, we need it for security and safety and deterrence. But then you're going to have this robotic wave in America. As I said, AI can't turn a wrench yet; it will eventually. That will be enabled by all those actuators and switches and subsystems we built. It's going to serve a different market, make it financially viable, and we're not going to have to rely on factories in China.

As you build an industrial base, an industrial base can be used for many things. Down to the component level — we just don't have enough of it in America. Talk to a robotics company today that wants to build some robotic deployment: there's a 99% chance the majority of what they're buying is coming from China. And so much of that is —

Connor： For many reasons — not just geopolitical. You want to onshore that purchasing for quality, cost, speed of iteration, and geopolitical reasons.

Over the last 3 years, it's remarkable how much of a supplier ecosystem has developed. One company in our portfolio, 3 years ago, would order two times the number of PCB boards they needed because they assumed they'd have to throw 50% away for quality issues. They'd get the batch from their supplier, do the testing, and 50% wouldn't pass a quality test. Then startups emerged in this category: "We're going to fix this problem. We're going to use software and modern technology to redo the way PCBs are manufactured in the US. Faster, cheaper, and — guess what? — better." That same company now buys PCBs from new suppliers, and they're keeping 70, 80, 90% passing quality tests. We underestimate how much the close co-location and co-development of this technology with the end customer and their suppliers really matters to drive quality higher.

八、"制造业中间层"：共同工程的新一代供应商

Aaron： Something really interesting is happening in the industrial base. You get this top-down demand signal from these new systems companies. We're building new military systems — but also, Joby and Archer are building new planes. Cars are being built differently, planes are being built differently, military systems are being built differently.

When you build these new systems, inherently the inputs to those systems need to change as well. Look at the industrial base in America today: historically, Boeing makes the 737 by picking up the phone and calling Honeywell, and Honeywell helps them build all the subcomponents. It's not Honeywell's fault, but what Honeywell does is say, "I don't want to build a new landing gear again. We have this landing gear that meets the spec and does the thing. Let's just keep going." It's rational. They're going to build more 737s and get paid the same way whether it's a 50-year-old landing gear or a new landing gear.

The problem: when you keep iterating on new requirements for end systems, at some point the 50-year-old subsystem just doesn't work. Maybe it physically meets the requirements, but it's been designed and developed in a way where we haven't innovated on it. We've developed new materials — physics hasn't changed, but the inputs to the physics and to the design have changed.

What's happening — the opportunity for a lot of these manufacturing companies — is what I call co-engineering. The long tail of sub-tier suppliers have been in "receive mode" for the last 40 years: Honeywell picks up the phone, "I need another landing gear, go make that landing gear," and they execute on specs with that IP in building it. When you want a new requirement, that middle layer cannot think on behalf of Honeywell and change the requirement, because they're not in a position to do it.

In the future, you're going to have this middle layer of supply companies that effectively become co-engineers with the end OEM — rethinking not just what the end system can do in terms of speed, weight, or mass, but the individual subcomponents will be rethought, re-engineered, and rebuilt. The end system will change from the top level; the individual parts and components will change. That just hasn't happened in the last 40 or 50 years.

You're going to see a completely new wave of what I believe will be called the "manufacturing middle" that will co-engineer and push design and development upward in the supply chain, as opposed to just being in receive mode and saying, "Okay, I can build the same thing I built 40 years from now." I think that's an opportunity. We're creating the American manufacturing asset class right now. Private equity has been playing in this ecosystem for a long time — looking at an asset, buying it, improving the cost, selling it off. That's not fundamentally changing the things we build. Right now, companies will change the things we build.

电网与电力电子：同样的架构性机会

Connor： A good example is the grid — the electronic stack. We're about to go through a huge step-change in how we manage and transfer power on the grid. Moving from static and mechanical systems deployed at large scale in the US in the '70s and '80s, to modern power electronics and battery storage architectures that are much more software-native and flexible.

When you have such a complete step-change in technology — where the technology replacing the previous thing is completely different — you have an opportunity to rethink the entire supply chain behind it, and the way all that design and engineering work happens.

Aaron： In the energy world, it's the same thing that's happening in the defense or commercial systems world: you have massive demand for data centers, new factories, new build. When you get this top-down level, you have the ability to innovate like Aaron's talking about and rethink the entire architecture.

Connor： Because it's a completely new architecture.

Aaron： Exactly.

Connor： You can't rely on components that worked in the previous world to just reconfigure. You actually have the opportunity to rethink from the ground up.

Aaron： Another important point: you could be pessimistic and say, "Okay, all these new military or end systems — not all of them will be adopted. That top-down demand, or Aaron, we're not actually going to increase energy by four times. There's not going to be that much demand."

I actually don't think it matters, because once you start the snowball of the demand cycle moving one way, even if you deliver half of that requirement — you're not going back. It doesn't make financial sense. When you rethink something first-principles and make the new design, new engineering decision — a lot of times with better cost, better efficiency — you're just going to buy that thing going forward.

Connor： Serviceability, easier to manufacture. You're never going back.

九、第二代创业者：从 Anduril、Palantir 出走的工程师

主持人： What are you seeing in terms of founders being second-generation Anduril or Palantir — maybe they see the learnings and the opportunity to be the middle-layer supplier in something that hasn't been touched since decades ago?

Connor： For sure. A great way to light a fire under an entrepreneur is for them to be banging their head against the wall on an engineering or supply-chain problem, and they're like, "Well, okay, I really care about this. This is a pain in my ass. I know it's bothering other people. I know it's a problem I don't just have here at Anduril or SpaceX or Tesla. It's a problem more broadly. I'm going to go solve that more generally."

The lineage of founders who have lived and breathed this on the manufacturing floor — and not just founders, but engineering teams who are like, "I saw this problem. I solved this within Anduril or Saronic. I'm going to go out and build this as a company. I know everyone in the ecosystem, so I have automatic access to a captive customer base."

We certainly see that trend. This is how ecosystems get built. People make fun of YC for all YC companies kind of selling to each other — but that's how it works. They're your friends. They're tolerant. They're understanding. They're willing to work with you and put up with something breaking because they're working on their own really hard problem, and if the thing you're doing is not the most existential thing to them, they're very willing to outsource it to you. That's beautiful. That's how Silicon Valley was built. What makes me really optimistic is the extent to which we're starting to see that in these physical-world ecosystems and supply chains.

Aaron： The few companies you mentioned — SpaceX, Palantir — weren't overnight successes.

Connor： Overnight successes that took 20 years.

Aaron： Exactly. The learning point — and we invest in a lot of entrepreneurs on this list who come from those ecosystems — is you learn this relentless focus to do one thing as well as you can, down a path, until you've succeeded. I've seen this with the guys at Castelion, for example. They focused for two and a half, three years on the first hypersonic missile — really hard to build. Other people showed up and said, "Oh, be multi-product. Go build this small drone here." And they said, "No, we need to do this one thing really well."

That comes from the fabric of SpaceX. At SpaceX the concept of being a responsible engineer is: "If this thing doesn't work, it's my ass. I'm going to obsess over this again and again." That's what it takes to build really hard things. There will be different derivations of success — not everyone will think just like the SpaceX mindset — but in the physical world you need to do that to build something really hard.

Connor： What you do by doing that is learn the process knowledge. Thing two, thing three, thing four are a lot easier. You've developed a supply chain. You have your relationships. You've developed design-for-manufacture processes. You've learned how to build a factory to a high quality, high spec. You've learned how to build trust with customers. If you can do that one thing really well, that sets you up to do other things really well — but it doesn't work unless you deliver on that one core thing.

十、美国资本市场的独特性

主持人： We talk a lot about competition. China — what does the United States do uniquely when it comes to our capital markets that really enables these startups?

Connor： This arguably is one of — Brian Shimp, the founder of Anduril, was talking about this a couple of days ago. We have literally trillions of dollars of private capital in our capital markets that follow success — technology success and production success.

Number one, we do not have a top-down directed industrial policy that says, "The state will put this amount of money into this." To some extent that's a good thing, because the money will follow the entrepreneur, follow the success. We've always had good capital markets in the United States. The distinction now is the capital markets have said, "You know what? The category of AD is really interesting." Aaron and I have been living and breathing this for a long time, but if you go look — not just up and down Silicon Valley and Sand Hill Road, but go to the major banks — JP Morgan has committed trillions of dollars toward investing in the physical world, not just defense, but factories and other things. And you see that again and again — not just venture capital firms, but private equity is starting to play in this category in a big way.

Aaron： Big credit firms.

Connor： Big credit firms. That's so important because many of these companies in the AD world require a lot of capital. When you build physical systems — a Falcon 9 rocket, a CCA, a Black Grid missile — it's so expensive to build up those lines and that physical system.

Capital markets speak with where the success happens. The reality is our capital markets are not top-down driven by our government, unlike China's. That allows us to be far more flexible — to follow success, as I said. And more importantly, to fund things in advance of it being obvious. We talked about building in advance of the requirement and the need. Maybe we're a little bit late on the energy side. Maybe a little late on some defense systems. But the capital markets have woken up, and we're putting hundreds of billions, if not trillions, of dollars toward this category for the next 10-plus years.

Aaron： If you look at just the first half of 2026, more risk dollars went into the defense ecosystem than all of last year combined — which was many times what went into the defense ecosystem in all of the previous year combined. Historically in defense, there's been a narrative around the "valley of death": how do you get the government contract to propel you through this period of needing to build out CapEx? What's really exciting is that's starting to disappear with the support of capital markets and risk capital. That's extending beyond defense to energy, robotics, critical minerals, and other important sectors.

十一、能源曲线、意志力与"it's ours to lose"

主持人： One question — maybe too much of a tangent. There's that very famous chart of US power production versus China's new energy production. America's line is basically flat, China's is up and to the right. What would it take to close that gap, or how fast can we build new power?

Aaron： I don't think that is a technology problem. I think that's — we need to do some soul-searching about our will as an American people. Do we want conforming projects to be built? Do we want to grow? If we do, the technology and the capital will follow.

Connor： It's not just an energy problem — it's an everything problem. We're optimists inherently. I do think that snowball has started to roll. The question, back to our discussion on capital markets, is: will there be emergent winners in these categories that then fuel more capital to flow into the ecosystem? It's a self-fulfilling prophecy. "If you build it, they will come." But at some point there needs to be a pot at the end of the rainbow. If there is for a few companies, capital will flow, like I mentioned.

The last thing I'll say briefly: anything in the physical world takes time. To set up a factory at a scale where it really affects our power generation or military systems — you can't take a couple of engineers, throw them in front of servers and computer screens, and come up with an answer. It's moving dirt. It is physically understanding a supply chain. These things take years. There's a little bit of patience we need to have on the capital-market side. I'm optimistic. It's happening. To some extent, it's ours to lose. It's ours as a government and a nation to mess up and to get in the way of this. That's a risk — don't get me wrong — but...

Aaron： Another long-term benefit of capital markets, even if short-term painful: people need to feel — you mentioned these are physical things, they take time. They also have a physical manifestation to the people and communities around them. The most important thing is that American society at large feels like they're participating in the economic growth coming as a result of this development.

Software had this ability to be siloed. It existed in just a few cities, was virtual. You experienced it in the way your interaction with digital services got a lot better over the last 20 years, but it was a little more abstract. In the physical world, someone's building a data center, a power plant, a mine in your backyard. You need a say and a stake in that. You physically see it. It affects your life. If you don't feel participation in the economic upside, it's hard. I do think capital markets long-term will solve this really well, because companies will figure out how to bring communities along for the journey and make it financially and economically worth it.

Connor： There are good examples on the AD 50 list — companies that build real things in their communities and show up the right way. There are also bad examples from the last few years. If you look at what AMCO does, they show up to these really small machine shops that exist, partner with them — they don't cut management and fire people. They say, "How can we build new products and grow the business you have today?"

It's that concept of working with communities as opposed to against them. We still need to wrestle with that a little bit in the tech world and understand that just because we sit in Silicon Valley, we don't understand everything happening in the world. Fundamentally, a lot of these AD companies will build stuff that touches Middle America. It will physically exist in Middle America. I think that's net good. More jobs, more prosperity, more energy and an abundance world — a safer America, and —

Aaron： Less concentration of wealth in these elite pockets on the coasts. It's a good thing.

Connor： Yeah.

Aaron： But it will take time.

Connor： Yeah.

主持人： Well, Aaron, Connor, thank you so much for joining. Everyone can check out the AD 50 list today.

Aaron： Awesome, thanks.

Connor： Awesome, thanks so much.

item.description:
## 一个让人意外的观察：这不是"制造业回流"，而是"**消费者补贴国防**"的历史性反转
过去 80 年美国的技术扩散逻辑是：政府出钱做第一代（阿波罗、互联网、核能），然后"长尾"溢出到消费市场。但这期对话里埋着一个几乎没被明说的、方向相反的新模式——**国防买单，但消费者最终定义质量上限**。Aaron 那句"美国最大的礼物是美国消费者的挑剔"，和 Conor 讲的"国防承担前 100 件的高单价 CapEx"，拼在一起等于说：
> 政府不再是技术的*定义者*，而是技术的*融资者*；真正把东西逼到便宜又好用的，是消费电子级的客户纪律。
这其实是把一个军工复合体，重新组装成一个**由消费者精细度反向驱动的、以国防订单做种子轮的通用工业栈**。DJI 的轨迹（消费无人机 → 国防 → 人形机器人执行器）不是巧合，而是这个新物理定律的第一个经验数据点。
## 跨领域连接：这波"美国动能"的底层结构，和 **Y Combinator 早期的 Silicon Valley 像到诡异**
Aaron 自己在最后半不经意地说出了关键隐喻："人们嘲笑 YC 公司互相卖东西，但生态就是这么

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller: Turning Stranded Energy Into Intelligence
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Bitcoin 不是"旧业务"，而是一台把电子变成现金的套利机器——AI 真正到来之前的融资工具

大多数人把 Crusoe 卖掉比特币业务读作"转型 AI"。但 Chase 自己把这段历史讲得很清楚：比特币从来不是业务，而是现金流泵。

真正的论点一直是——"用计算把搁浅能源变成市场"。油井旁被点燃的伴生气、冰岛过剩的地热、北欧低价水电——这些都是没人愿意要的电子。比特币挖矿恰好是人类发明过的最流动、最 24/7、最不挑剔的"电子变现引擎"：它不要求你有光纤，不要求你有客户，只要你有瓦特。

于是真正发生的事情是：Crusoe 用一台金融抽水机，把世界各地无人问津的电子抽成资本，再在 ChatGPT 这个历史时刻来临时，把积累的能源头寸转化成 AI 工厂。

这几乎是一个"打井是为了造油轮"的操作顺序倒置。类比：亚马逊早年卖书不是终局，而是训练仓储肌肉；SpaceX 搞 Starlink 是为了资助去火星。比特币对 Crusoe 的角色属于同一个物种——用一个成熟市场为一个尚未诞生的市场做财务预热。

二、他爬珠峰的方式，就是他建数据中心的方式——意外的"随机风险 vs 自觉风险"二分法

这是整段访谈里最被低估的洞见，Chase 自己都没有说破：

2014 年珠峰雪崩之后，他和搭档没有按商业队的标准路线走——因为标准路线要在最危险的昆布冰瀑穿越 8 次。他们重新设计了方案：到附近的山上做适应性训练，把冰瀑的穿越次数从 8 次压缩到 4 次。

他的原话是："我愿意承担的是我能通过训练管理的风险，我不愿意承担的是冰柱随机掉下来砸到我的风险（stochastic risk）。"

现在把这句话原封不动地搬到 Crusoe 的能源策略上：

  • 建在电网背后（behind-the-meter）——减少对电网互联这一随机变量的暴露（少过几次冰瀑）
  • 用天然气、SMR 核能、地热、小型模块化发电——自己可训练、可管理的风险
  • 不对单一技术路线下重注——类似他在珠峰上同时携带多套适应方案

绝大多数能源公司和数据中心公司对"风险"的定价是单维的（成本/收益）；Chase 的定价是风险的来源结构——这个心智模型几乎可以肯定来自雪崩那年。那场雪崩杀死了 15 名夏尔巴人，也许同时塑造了一家公司的架构。

三、他是在做"极端环境资本主义"——跨界到生物学的隐藏结构

你注意到了吗？Crusoe 建数据中心的地点有一个共同点：都是其他生物不去的地方。

  • 北达科他州巴肯油田（燃烧放空的废气）
  • 冰岛（火与冰的无人区）
  • 挪威（过剩水电）
  • 爱达荷国家实验室（SMR 实验堆旁边）

这在生物学上有一个精确的对应词——嗜极生物（extremophile）。它们不与主流物种竞争阳光和温带，而是寄生在深海热泉、火山口、永冻层。它们的生存策略不是"更强"，而是"去没人想去的地方，吃没人想吃的能量"。

Chase 的公司在做的事情，本质上是嗜极资本主义：在能源价格为负、甚至为负负（排放责任）的地方，长出一个计算物种。

这个框架同时也解释了他为什么对竞争几乎零焦虑——嗜极生物从不卷。热泉管虫不与珊瑚竞争，它们的生态位根本不重叠。当他说"我们更多的是在互相帮助而不是互相竞争"时，这不是公关辞令，这是生态位几何学的事实陈述。

四、一个让人不舒服的隐藏命题："人线性成长，公司指数成长"

他引用的 First Round 的一句话，是整期播客里最接近热力学第二定律的论断：

People scale linearly, companies scale exponentially.

这意味着什么？意味着即使你的每一位早期员工每天都在进步，他们在数学上注定会落后于一家真正在爆发的公司。 这不是品格问题，不是努力问题——是成长曲线函数形式的不匹配。

这解释了一个所有 CEO 都私下承认但很少公开说的残酷事实：你和创业初期最忠诚的战友，大概率要在某个时点分开——不是因为谁背叛了谁，而是因为公司生长在指数函数上，而人只能活在线性时间里。

这跟进化生物学里的一个概念几乎同构："红皇后假说"——你必须拼命奔跑，才能停留在原地。但 Chase 的版本更冷酷：即便你拼命奔跑，公司跑得比你更快。

五、最意外的观察：他的整个职业生涯是在系统性地反转自己的舒适区

量化基金做的是什么？保密、技术、不公开说话、不告诉任何人你的 alpha。 CEO 做的是什么？公开、政治、不断重复、把自己掏空给媒体和社区听证会。

Chase 从一个最反社交、最隐秘的职业，走到了最公众、最沟通密集的职业。他承认公开演讲"从来不是自然的事"，承认他需要教练来撬开自己。

这是一个比"从量化到创业"更深的身份反转——他把自己整个认知操作系统做了相反方向的刷机。而他的教练 Shane 扮演的角色，和他 2018 年在珠峰 8,600 米处的搭档扮演的角色，是同一个：在你准备放弃的那个海拔，有一个人让你继续走。

Crusoe 公司的核心价值观里有一条叫"think like a mountaineer"——现在你知道了，这不是比喻。这家公司的组织文化，字面意义上是从昆布冰瀑搬下山来的。

📝 转录文本

开场：垂直整合的复杂业务

We have a complex business because it's vertically integrated and it spans like a huge scope of different work streams. Everything from energy generation and bringing electrons online, building power plants, working with independent power producers and utilities to building data centers, operating at scale very large scale AI factories to very small scale AI factories and then building and operating a managed AI cloud platform with managed AI services.

What's made me very scalable as a leader is that we have these critical areas of domain expertise where I can move around and I can go very deep with any individual but I trust them a lot to be making the right decisions as we're sort of scaling things and everybody has a broad perspective of you know what we're doing at the macro scale and how each individual leader contributes to that vertically integrated AI infrastructure platform that we're building here at Crusoe.

嘉宾介绍

Okay, everybody. Today we have on Chase Lockach Miller. Russo is building so many of the data centers that power the age of intelligence. He's a very professional CEO and he talks all about the road from zero beginnings to a $31 billion valuation that he just closed. He gets into the nuts and bolts of scaling a very operationally intensive business. I think you're going to like it.

Chase, welcome to the long strange trip. — Brian, thanks for having me.

一条非线性的职业轨迹

We call this the long strange trip because my journey as a CEO was a very long strange trip. Kind of tracking your career. You've had a long maybe not strange but interesting trip like you were on track to become a professor. You became a hedge fund trader. You became a mountaineer climbing Mount Everest among other things. You're kind of an energy entrepreneur at least through my lens when you first got going and now you're the world's best data center builder. Is there a through line in all of this?

Chase: Um, as a person, I've always been uh attracted to trying to solve hard problems. That's I think that's been the throughline of my career. Take on big challenges, solve hard problems that are exciting and inspiring to me.

CEO 的"温水煮青蛙"优势

One hard problem is becoming a CEO and scaling as a CEO is in and of itself is a hard problem. What has surprised you about, you know, all of a sudden you're a CEO and you got to build this company? What is what what do people have wrong about the CEO journey?

It can sometimes be misleading to just take a snapshot of someone like deep into it and and just assume it's some linear path on on on how you actually get there. I was actually having this discussion with another CEO. you know, when you're a founder CEO, you sort of have this benefit of uh sort of, you know, the the boiling frog syndrome where, you know, right now things are really crazy at Cruso. There's just so much happening. Everything's happening very quickly. The scale at which it's happening is crazy.

Uh, you know, when people get dropped into Crusoe and they start working at Crusoe, it's like it's intense and there's there's just a lot going on across the company. And you know there's a question of like how do you actually hold that all in one person's head and you know when you're the founder CEO you have so much context of like the history of how you got here and it wasn't always this crazy right like when we first started it was just me and my co-founder it was just the two of us for for for you know quite a while and then we you know had our first hire and we had our first you know incremental hires and you know when we were 10 people it felt crazy but it's nothing compared to what it is today.

And the journey of a CEO is journey of a founder CEO is like you have to continually be upping your game. You have to be continually investing in yourself to be able to scale if if you want to have a scaled business. And you know this is partially reflected like you know at Cruso we have a core company value that's like live on the infinite growth loop — like nobody is nobody's a finished product right no nothing we've done here is a finished product uh everything is a work in progress every person is a work in progress and every single day we try to improve on who we were yesterday and if you look at those compounding returns of those continuous focus on improvements and how how you actually get better when you zoom back out over you know the course of a month, a year, five years. Uh the results can be astounding.

"我的业务复杂得让我头晕"

Okay. My I had an actually I had quite an interesting day today. I run something called the kids table and the adults table for SEOA. And it's basically getting a bunch of CEOs together, all founder CEOs to kind of talk about their problems and try to help each other with the journey. And we've got a bunch of them between 20 and 2,000 employees. All of them are ripping, like really ripping. And I got a quote from one of the CEOs today. My business is becoming dizzyingly complex beneath me. How the hell do I keep up? Did you do you have that feeling today or did you have that feel?
