And if you can play on that emotion, play on the heritage — and to use the Globetrotter example, have a travelling band of cricketers playing the trade here, there and everywhere. Playing good cricket is obviously most important. But the entertainment value — there's so many good teams that aren't entertaining. And when West Indies are good, they're also entertaining. So imagine taking that now to different markets — whether it be new, whether it be old — and just saying: ensure that we don't lose money, and that we can make money whilst putting out a good entertainment product.

Content Strategy and Storytelling

Host: We talked before we came on about the media opportunity. The biggest danger now for anyone — well, not the biggest danger, but I think what people get bored of now is just another sports documentary series without any real purpose, story, reason, narrative. Everyone wants to be a Drive to Survive type thing, as we were saying. But that doesn't mean that there aren't amazing stories to be told, and if you get them right, they are the most powerful tools that sporting organizations can use to build some of that interest.

Like, to me, West Indies fits in that. There is an amazing story to tell here. If you've ever watched Welcome to Wrexham type thing, one of the reasons that's been successful in my eyes at least, and one of the reasons I loved it, is because it was only partly about football. So immediately it kind of stood out as something different. And from the West Indies story perspective — whether you play, you could play partly on the history and the heritage. You can go around and look at what it means to each of the islands and how it varies in those places, where the money flows go at the moment and where the challenges lie.

You can do a job of almost using a piece of content like this as a bit of a pitch deck. If I got an opportunity to look inside West Indies cricket with a major distributor — whether it's a Netflix or a Disney Plus or an Amazon or whatever — I would, as a fan, be absolutely fascinated. Because I think there's a story in there. I think it has everything. I think it has the people. I think it has the broader value, like a cultural angle. And I think it has the sport.

Fire in Babylon and Beyond

Carlos: And to add on to that, I think it was in my year in High Performance Centre when Fire in Babylon came out. And that was well before Drive to Survive. But it just gave you context. It just showed you why these teams were all conquering. It showed you the magnitude of what they played for before they even went on the field. They had interviews in there either from fans or from players talking about how people from the Caribbean diaspora living in the UK would walk into work with the chest up because West Indies have won. So it meant more than just winning a game.

And even though I talk about it, it got goosebumps. I remember watching that documentary and just feeling immense pride to be a West Indian, to watch the forefathers lay the ground that I walk on.

And I think past Fire in Babylon, you've had the era with Brian Lara, Carl Hooper, Courtney Walsh, Curtly Ambrose — those stories haven't really been told. And then you can lead into the 2012, the 2016 World Cup wins. There was Courtney Browne and Ian Bradshaw 2004 here in the UK Champions Trophy. Those sorts of things, if we can produce them often enough, consistently enough, it then raises the pores of a younger player who's at academy level or primary school level, and it just continues the pride.

So we've got a situation where we're begging for people to appreciate the history of West Indies cricket, but we're not telling them the stories of why we are proud of West Indies cricket.

Host: And if you're going to build a heritage brand value around this, telling the stories of why it matters in the first place is everything, right? Combining a modern-day content strategy with a look at the establishment of the value — well, it seems like it would be really cool.

Carlos: Yeah. We had Clive Lloyd on the podcast, and I think Nikhil and I, we sat back and we just like — did we ask enough questions? Like it was two of us here and there — Clive Lloyd was there, and we were just like, you know —

Host: I had those moments. Petr Čech sat there, and I just — I said, I just grinned at him for like an hour and 45 minutes.

Carlos: You know, you got granddad sitting by the fireplace, and everybody just there sat just listening to these stories. But then yeah, like we are privileged to be able to sit — have him sit across from us and tell it. If you watch the episode, you're privileged enough to hear it. But you don't get to go into the mind any further.

Because yeah, they did what they did on the field — that's one. The second thing is, what was the reason for it — two. But then, how did you every single day wake up and push toward this passion with this purpose and why? So if you can encapsulate all of that into a series — be powerful.

Host: Yeah. Okay — that's our challenge. Any producers out there? I know there are. I know there are a few. Come on. And there's more than enough drama, I can imagine.

From Critic to Participant

But you know, I think, as you said, if you're looking at — rather than always just being the people that sit here and go "oh isn't this bad" — eventually to change fortunes, you have to be the one that, you have to try and be a part of a solution.

Carlos: Yeah. And I think for me, that is why I did put my name in to try to be a director of the board. Because it's so easy — like I've stepped into commentary, I absolutely enjoy it, but we do have a privilege where we just sit, we watch the game. And I don't want to devalue the preparation we do before — but we sit, we watch the game, we call it as we see it. And then there are certain things that we are made aware of, and we can just say "this is wrong, this is wrong, this is wrong," or "this is good, this is good, this is good." But we don't always offer solutions.

I just felt, looking from the outside, it's quite easy to say "this should happen, that should happen." But isn't it more powerful to put your face, put your identity, put your — sometimes respect — on the line to try to get something done? And I think you mentioned earlier about players coming on board. That is one of the reasons that players, I think, can be good administrators — because we've heard no so often in our careers. "No, you're not going to bowl." "No, you're not going to bat right now, we're going to send somebody before you." "No, you're not being selected." "No, you're not going on the tour." "No, you're not getting a contract." That we are okay working hard and then being told no — but it's working hard to win hopefully a decision, or a group of decisions, that potentially save something that's given us all that we've ever dreamed of, and sometimes more.

So maybe it is for a few past players to come in and put their neck on the line, and say "I'm going to try this and try that," and everything won't work. I think you're naive to think that in a small market, multiple different islands, that there's just a silver bullet that says West Indies cricket. But at least you can try things, and you can hold yourself to a certain standard that you did whilst you were playing as a professional — all the whilst appreciating that there are a lot more no's than yes, because you're accustomed to it as a player anyway.

Closing

Host: I mean, that's a brilliant way to round it out. Because I would never want it to seem or sound like it's easy. Whenever we sit here and chat about these discussions, you do always have to find a balance between "why is something like this or why something like that?" But recognizing that there isn't one quick fix for it, but also recognizing that you can pull it apart piece by piece and try and solve those things individually, rather than trying to fix one collective thing that seems impossible to do — then that's a good way to do it. And I think you summed that up brilliantly there.

But honestly, from the cricket chats we have, it's amazing to hear about it. Because it is a heritage, it's a massive part of this sport. And as a cricket fan growing up and all of that, West Indies is a major part of my love for cricket. So hearing about it is brilliant. And I hope it turns around. But I'm so grateful for you coming in and talking us through it — because it's pretty cool to hear it. And I'm delighted that there was a nice story behind your cricket bat to cheer me up, anyway, and all other England fans out there still harboring a grudge. Where are you?

But no, seriously — I love it. It was really cool to have you in, and I'm so pleased you enjoyed the show. So thank you for coming and actually sitting in the chair with me. I appreciate it. And hopefully — hopefully there are some investors out there, there are some producers that they will —

Carlos: Yeah, exactly, yeah. No, hopefully guys get in touch, right? Come on. Let's go and raise a bit of money, and let's go and produce some really cool content.

Host: That's a call out to do it, if you're not. But yeah, anyway — appreciate it, man.

Carlos: Pleasure. Loved it.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、这不是板球问题，是**价值捕获**问题
Carlos反复描述西印度球员如何在IPL、BPL、CPL被买走、被变现，但变现的收益"not for the benefit of West Indies cricket"。这其实是体育版的**上游供应商困境**——西印度群岛生产"原材料"（球员），下游平台（BCCI、特许联赛、广播商）完成加工并捕获溢价。Shea Hope、Russell、Pollard在这个结构里像可可豆、咖啡豆、油棕——未经加工的作物运往孟买、迪拜、伦敦，加工后以数倍价格卖回。整个发展中世界的贸易困境，被西印度板球以最纯粹的形式演绎了一遍。
更隐秘的时间线是：Chris Dering提到的 **1997年巡回赛经济结构变化**（客队自费、主队全得），其实是体育界版的"注意力经济协议"——比YouTube出现早10年，比Spotify早11年，西印度板球就已经在体验今天OnlyFans作者、Substack写手、TikTok创作者的集体命运：**你是内容本体，但不是价值归属**。
## 二、那根球棒就是整部纪录片的全息投影
注意Errol的球棒故事的叙事结

item.title: [a16z] The AI School Kids Love More Than Vacation | Alpha School's Joe Liemandt
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

从「教不会」到「不想教」：教育系统的根本性误诊

Alpha School 最震撼的发现不是「2小时学会6小时的内容」，而是一个被所有教育改革者系统性忽视的事实：传统学校的瓶颈从来不是认知带宽，而是动机架构。

过去一百年，我们把教育问题诊断为"信息传递效率不足"——于是不断加课时、加作业、加教师、加评估。但 Joe 揭示的真相是：信息传递只占学习问题的 10%，剩下 90% 是动机问题。而工业化教育系统恰恰是一个反动机设计——它让孩子在"永远失败 1/3 以上"的区间里挣扎（时间制课程的必然副产品），然后用考试告诉他们失败是他们自己的问题。

这里有个让人意外的推论：AI 替代教师的真正威胁不是便宜，而是情绪稳定。LLM 可以无止境地提供 80-85% 正确率的个性化挑战——这是任何面对 30 个学生的人类教师在生理上都做不到的。教师不是输在知识上，是输在"心流工程"上。

跨领域连接：游戏设计师比教育学家更懂学习

Joe 顺口提到的"视频游戏开发者都知道失败率超过 2/3 用户就脱离"——这句话值得整个教育学界停下来思考 50 年。

游戏行业用 40 年时间，在没有任何学术委员会监督的情况下，解决了学习科学界 100 年没解决的参与度问题。暴雪、任天堂、Supercell 的难度曲线设计师，掌握着比任何教育部长都更精确的"认知心流算法"。为什么？因为游戏行业面对的是无强制力的注意力市场——用户随时可以离开。而学校有强制出勤权，所以从不需要真正解决吸引力问题。

更深层的洞察：Alpha 本质上是把"义务教育"重构为"订阅制产品"。当 Joe 说"magnet marketing（吸引对的人，排斥错的人）"时，他不是在说营销策略，他是在说整个教育哲学的根本转变——从"我们必须教所有人"（公共事业心态）变成"我们必须让想学的人上瘾"（产品心态）。这就是为什么 edtech 过去都失败了：它们把产品塞进一个反产品的分发系统里。

真正颠覆性的洞察：焦虑的替代品不是乐观，是「做难事的权利」

最反直觉的一点：Alpha 的孩子不是因为"轻松"而爱上学，是因为他们被允许做真正困难的事情。50% 的孩子选择上学而非度假——度假意味着无所事事，上学意味着解谜、挑战、团队协作完成四年级 MBA 测试。

这里藏着一个关于当代儿童心理健康危机的根本性诊断：我们这一代父母以为孩子不开心是因为压力太大，所以给他们更多舒适；而真相可能相反——孩子抑郁是因为被剥夺了"做有意义困难事情"的机会。所有被动化的童年（刷手机、看视频、被精心安排的"活动"）本质上都在传递同一个信息：你的能动性无关紧要。

跨领域连接到心理学：Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi 的"心流"理论说得很清楚——幸福来自技能略低于挑战的区间。现代教育系统把孩子要么放在挑战过高（跟不上进度就是永久失败），要么挑战过低（学得快的被迫等）的区间。两种情况都是心流杀手，而两种情况都制造心理问题。

一个预测性的大胆判断：五年内，"学校是否按学习曲线个性化"会成为儿童心理健康干预的一级指标，比屏幕时间、睡眠质量更能预测青少年抑郁率。因为心流剥夺是比我们想象中更严重的发育伤害——而这个伤害在工业化教育里是系统性的、每天 6 小时的、持续 12 年的。

一个被低估的时间炸弹：Alpha 毕业生进入大学市场

Joe 一句话轻描淡写："我需要地方让 Alpha 的孩子去读大学"。这句话里埋着一个将在 2030-2035 年引爆的高等教育危机。

想象一个场景：第一批真正在 Alpha 式环境长大的孩子，18 岁时已经做过真实的创业、拿过 MBA 级别的团队考核、建过 LLM、在非洲做过一年服务——他们走进常春藤大学的 100 人大课堂，看到的是什么？是他们在 10 岁就已经超越的学习方式。

这不是渐进竞争，这是消费者革命。就像当年习惯了 iPhone 的用户不可能再接受 Nokia 的功能机——这些孩子不会"适应"传统大学，他们会公开嘲笑它（Alpha 第一届大学生已经在校报写专栏骂了）。常春藤的真正护城河从来不是教学质量，是身份信号和校友网络——而 AI 原生一代可能是第一代不需要这两样东西来证明自己的学生。

📝 转录文本

开场：重新设计孩子爱上的校园

提问： Are you willing to redesign your school day so kids love it more than vacation? With cognitive science and learning science, plus the advent of LLMs, you can build a learning engine that teaches kids 10 times faster. The shift that I think you've been able to make is the believability of it. Pretty soon, people are going to ask, why would we ever do it any other way?

Joe： I want this next generation to be the ones who are optimistically capable with AI and saying, we're going to build an awesome future. That's what our job as educators are, is to go build that world.

提问： What would you say to the parent who's saying, "I'm sending my kid to Ivy League school. I know it's not perfect, but this is a new institution. Why should I take a risk?"

So, Joe, welcome to the podcast.

Joe： Thank you very much.

Alpha 的核心创新：重新发明学校日

So, we've had the luxury of spending some time together this year and touring the schools and what you've built with Alpha is just incredible and it's inspired us at HA. We're grateful to have your involvement. And for people who are unfamiliar, why don't you just briefly describe what you think of as the central innovations or what you've really brought to the space with Alpha.

Joe： Sure. So, we're reinventing how K12 school is — you know, the school day. How kids spend their six or seven hours that they're in class or in a school building. What is that like?

And the first part that you have to understand and buy into is that instructional design and delivery hasn't changed for a hundred years. You throw a teacher in front of the classroom — and what's the right way to do this? Now if you look over the last couple decades with cognitive science and learning science plus the advent of LLMs, you can build a learning engine that teaches kids 10 times faster.

And so as soon as you have that ability — where kids can learn 10 times faster than they could the last hundred years with a teacher in front of a classroom model — the question is, what do you do with it? And so that's what we're doing at Alpha, which is how do you reinvent the school day?

三大承诺

In our model, we make three commitments to the kids:

1. They love school. I just got the surveys back last week. 90-some% of our kids say "I love school." 50% of the kids at the school said "I would rather go to school than go on vacation." I actually have one campus where it's at 65% of the kids like "I'd rather go to school than vacation." Build a school where kids love it if you're going to be there for 12 years.

2. Twice the learning in a third of the time. With this engine, the kids learn twice as much in 2 hours a day as sitting in class for six and doing homework. If you're compounding and learning twice as much as you would at your other school, you're going to get to top 1%, no matter where you start given time. And so the kids crush it — the best on standardized tests, the best academic performing school.

3. What do you do the rest of the day? And I think that's a whole thing of what we're talking about now.

I believe now every school — and it doesn't matter K12, university — has to say: if the traditional way and the traditional curriculum is now 10 times faster, what do you do with the rest of the day? And as a principal, I can definitely tell you the one thing parents would hate is if I sent the kids home after 2 hours. You got them all day, six-seven hours a day, right? And the kids want to be there and they love it.

五大生活技能

What we do is: what are all the life skills that we consider critical to thriving in the world that's coming? The world's changing. We have five categories of life skills:

  • Leadership and teamwork
  • Entrepreneurship and financial literacy
  • Socialization and relationship building
  • Storytelling and public speaking
  • Grit and hard work

And so then you're doing projects in a group with all your friends with an adult who's writing them. And that's how you spend your afternoons.

So Alpha — we started, we were just in Austin, then we added 12 campuses last year. We're up to 50. Demand's insane. People want this new thing. We're sort of first, but everybody's going to have to look at this. Today no one believes "oh, does 2 hours work" — we have to get scale and more proof points. But once you realize, wow, kids could learn everything they need to in 2 hours, every family, every head of school, every education minister around the world is going to say: how do we rebuild the school day for the next hundred years, because we don't need to do it like we did the last hundred?

可信度与产品化

I remember visiting Alpha 6 years ago — this is before you were full-time on it. And I immediately got it because I've been in learning science and sort of education for 15 to 20 years. But I will say that the shift that I think you've been able to make is the believability of it. And I think you've done a great job of figuring out how to show that not only does this work, but pretty soon people are going to ask, "Why would we ever do it any other way?" And that's really the brilliance of, from a business standpoint, what you've accomplished over the last 5 years.

Joe： Yeah. I became principal four years ago and my background is product and entrepreneurship. This just needed sort of product packaging — which is how do you productize this into something that is understandable and scalable. That's the other part — it's really hard to scale schools. How do you scale them to quality?

That's for my first three years — how to do that. And that's actually one of the big benefits of bringing AI: it helps you scale at high quality. Our phrase is "we get better as we get bigger." If you look at anything over the last four years — our test scores, customer sat, student happiness, the quality of the workshops — all of those get better every year because the system gets better as it gets bigger.

为什么孩子爱上学：动机的核心作用

We have a number of teammates, colleagues, friends who send their kids off. Do you see the kids love it? What is it? I remember hating my K-12 experience. Is it this two-hour arrangement? What is it that you find is most contributing to kids loving it that other schools should be adopting? And similarly, we were also talking off camera about how motivation is underrated — or maybe one of the biggest elements in terms of what is separating outcomes for kids. How are you tackling that as well?

Joe： I think the biggest thing is edtech historically hasn't done well in schools, hasn't had the impact that people wanted. And if you look at this learning engine and say, "Oh, this is like edtech and I'm just going to put it into a normal school day," it'll fail. It'll be just like everything else.

When I talk to somebody who hears about Alpha and they hear all this learning engine, I have one question — and this is the core of everything — which is: are you willing to redesign your school day so kids love it more than vacation? If you have a head of school who says that, then you're all set. But that leap — and motivation falls under that obviously — which is if you are waking up and saying "how am I going to make kids love this," that is the core of what allows us to do everything else.

高标准即幸福

People are worried when they hear that: "oh, it's Disneyland and they're just running around and they're not learning," or "it's not rigorous — video games or TV." It's literally just the opposite. One of the things we talk about is: the key to your child's happiness is high standards. Kids want to go do hard things. They love to do hard things, and they love to do hard things with their friends. If it was just playing video games all day, they can go do that at home. But to sit there and say "I want to do this instead of vacation" — it's because they're doing challenging things with their friends that they love.

一个例子：团队合作

An easy example — teamwork and uplifting your classmates as a team. In traditional school they don't teach this. After school sports, absolutely, in America — teamwork, leadership. But in schools they don't. Most team projects in school — group projects — are terrible. One person does it, everybody else just sits around. You always remember those. They were terrible. So you learn the opposite of teamwork. You learn the anti-pattern.

A good indication of that: Wharton has an MBA challenge where they have a simulation — go up Mount Everest. 50% of MBAs fail the teamwork because they were never taught teamwork their whole way through school.

We take every third grader, mike them up, and throw them into an escape room. They're all getting through the escape room, and at the end of it we have AI analyze the transcript: what percent of your language were you team-oriented, were you helping, or were you — and I can give you the answer — less than 20% of the language is uplifting. 80% is "my idea, my idea, my idea," fighting and pushing. So we have an 8-week workshop. They keep going back to the teamwork, and to graduate, to pass the class, they have to get up to 85% team behavior. And we also show them that they finish the escape room three times faster when you're doing team environment.

That's a great fun way. Kids love it. It's a life skill that every parent's like "oh, that's the stuff I want my kids to learn." And because they don't have to sit in class all day, they can do that. By fourth and fifth grade, our life skills curriculum is as rigorous as our core — passing a physics test or a math test. You have to pass the escape room test. In fourth and fifth grade, we actually make them pass the Wharton MBA challenge that 50% of the MBAs can't. And you take a fourth and fifth grader and they pass it. That ties back to being proud and excited and wanting to do it. You can engage them and teach these skills much younger.

I believe as we look at the world, we haven't had the capability to teach kids all this at a much younger age because you're sitting in class all day. But now that we can, of course, we must.

学术引擎与「80–85% 正确率区间」

So the reason they're enjoying it is because they can feel themselves learning faster, growing faster, building deeper relationships — that's something you can't get on vacation.

Joe： Well, it's like that escape room — it's a high bar for your parents. The second is: let's talk academics versus life skills — there's two different sides.

为什么学生讨厌学业

On the academic side, kids don't like to do things they fail at. That's true on academics. That's true on anything. That's why in America we hold kids back on sports — you want to give them, they're bigger, all of a sudden they're playing better and they win, they get the accolades, and you get them on that path.

In academics in America, because we're a time-based system, once you fall behind, now it's torture the rest of the time. Wherever you fall behind.

In our system, because our learning engine will give you a personalized lesson — it doesn't matter what your age grade is. You can be in eighth grade, and if you need a fifth grade lesson because whatever before you came to Alpha you missed it, it's going to give you the fifth grade lesson. And you're going to be able to do it, you're going to be able to get it, you're going to be able to pass it and then move forward.

工程化的「赢」

We engineer wins for the kids in the academics. The core value of what the engine does is: you basically want kids in this 80 to 85% correct zone. What percent of the time, if you're engaging with something, is it too easy or too hard?

  • If it's 100% correct, it's too easy. You're not even learning anything — you're just regurgitating what you know.
  • Any video game developer will tell you: if you drop below 2/3 and you're failing more than 2/3 of the time, you're going to disengage.

So one of the things a learning engine can do that a teacher in front of a classroom with 30 people can't: make sure the kid gets an unending stream of lessons and questions that's 80–85% accurate. If it gets too hard, we can give them scaffolding lessons to catch up. Too easy — we progress them faster through the material. If you keep kids engaged because you're giving them work they can do, then they like that. And when kids actually do well and you hold them to high standards, they get very excited — they see themselves crushing their academics instead of struggling with it.

从 K12 到大学：HAA 的灵感

Katherine Boyle(?)： Gagen, I'm curious how you think about this conversation and what Alpha is doing in K-12 and how that informs what we're doing with HAA.

Gagen： Incredibly inspired. I've been inspired by Alpha School since I first visited, and it proves the thesis that we have at the Horowitz Academy — that if you redesign the system for the modern era with modern tools, you can have everything that you want in terms of outcomes:

  • You can have more network. A lot of people say you go to school for network — we're going to take your network and make it 10x better.
  • Everyone says you go to school to become a better person — Horowitz Andreessen Academy absolutely wants you to become a better person. We're going to engineer the system so that you're more likely to become a positive something.
  • You want to have high agency and you want to do hard things — Alpha has given me a lot of inspiration on how to ensure that students get that.

The one difference is that at every age range you have to do something very different. If you actually listen to Joe talk — K-8, high school, very different. When you go from high school to college era, very different. You can't just copy everything over.

Ultimately, if you have a student-centric mindset — if you just told the leaders of any major university in the country that their number one job and no other job was to make sure that the students were succeeding — I'm sure there would be many great schools in the United States. Unfortunately, there aren't many, because most university leaders are required to spend 90% of their time focused on all the adults around them and not enough on the students. And one of the things you see with Joe is he's always talking about the kids.

Joe 看大学的重新发明

提问： Joe, I'm curious — you've very generously gotten involved with HAA as an investor and adviser. What excited you about what we're up to, and how have you thought about the differences between college and high school?

Joe： I'm super excited because I absolutely believe that university needs to be reinvented just like we have in K-12. I'm focused on K-12, but I'm very excited that you guys jumped in and said "let's do this." Anything I could do to help, I want it. One, I need places for Alpha kids to go. There's going to be a whole set of kids who are like "I want to go there."

To your point, it's completely different. Our high school is very different than our K-8. And I believe university needs to be different. And I don't believe the whole concept of "is university — is everybody just going to come out of high school and not go to university anymore?" I actually don't think that's true. I believe there's a huge opportunity to reinvent university and make it awesome. No one wants to go to a bad school where it's terrible and it's not getting the kids ready.

实习生的恐惧

As an example, we had over 70 MIT and Stanford kids and UT come to Alpha this summer as interns, and part of what we were saying is: tell us about university, how's it going, what do you think? I was like, "How many of you guys expect that this university — whatever one you're going to — is getting you ready for the world when you graduate?" And one kid raised his hand. I was like "seriously? none of you?" And they're like, "We're terrified. We worked our 12 years really hard to get into these great universities, and now we're terrified that when it comes time to graduate, there's not going to be those jobs that you used to get coming out of it. Those first one and two-year jobs aren't there, AI is going to be doing it. What do we do?"

They spent a lot of time this summer as interns coming up with what they thought would be reinvention of university and what they would want. And back to kids wanting to do hard things — they came up with: "We're going to build this educational LLM so we can make it free for everybody in the world, because every sovereign is going to need its own educational LLM — small language model that sits on a device."

Those kids worked 80 hours a week, figuring out, doing research, figuring out the concepts of learning. They're going to be published. At the end of it they're like, "This is what we would love the university to be — where we're all working together on this super hard thing that has meaningful impact to the world, that could really help change the world. I wish these could be classes at MIT and Stanford and UT, but they're not."

When I think about what you guys are doing — reinventing it and letting kids really build — it's not just about the classes. It's about getting ready for the real world and all those skills you need. I believe those are different at university, but I'm very excited about what you're building around that.

大学体验：动机与格式

提问： It's really important to understand that an average student who's going to university who's really ambitious — they need to get their hands dirty. They are entering the real world in 3 to 4 years and it's super critical for them to be going and building things and understanding what it's like and making mistakes and dealing with the challenges.

I really love that you said that they were studying as part of the 80-hour — they're in Austin for an 80-hour week internship, and you mentioned studying. I'm guessing you didn't assign any textbooks.

Joe： No, they had to go do all the research to build an LLM. So they literally are researching learning science, researching — we have this data structure called the brain lift — and they were working hard on what would be considered classical stuff you need to do at a university, but it wasn't just the studying part. It was: how do you apply it and be a builder?

提问： Your point of getting ready is both. Well, you talk about learning as being 90% motivation. And when you're 18 years old, you're motivated by building things that people will use. You're motivated by revenue and getting a job and that kind of thing. So why not make the entire learning experience driven by that motivation and using that motivation to actually go and learn things?

My concern with college is — I mean, I know Erik and I had this experience, we've talked about it — I didn't learn very much because I did not like the format. And to be honest, now I go to Stanford's campus or someone else's campus, no one seems to like the format. 20 years ago I was a little bit in the minority — maybe 20% of students agreed with me. Our classes were about half full, I would say, in attendance. I hear they're now way under 10% full. Students are not finding the format to work. You need to reinvent the format in order to create motivation so they actually learn things. That's one of the main focuses of the Academy.

Alpha 高中毕业生在大学的反馈

Joe： Another example — our first graduating class from Alpha High was three years ago. So at Christmas after they'd all been at university, I got them together. I was like, "How's it going? How do you do in real?" That's right — how do you do in university after you come out?

They're like "we love it." They all had 4.0s, they were crushing it. But they were like, "These 100-series lecture classes are a complete waste of time." Five of them had written editorials to their school paper about how it's just a charade — how the kids come in and are like scrolling TikTok or on their computers not paying attention, or not showing up, and the teachers aren't teaching. Those don't need to exist anymore.

I was like, "Well, what do you like?" They're like, "Oh, there's all these great small group seminars we were working on, clubs and all the activities around it." A university is a bundle of products — and they liked the bundle. But the actual academic part of these big lecture classes — they're like "that needs to go away."

提问： And what's crazy is that that academic part that you're talking about is the only thing the university formally provides. So the rest of the bundle is student-driven.

Joe： Well, I dropped out of Stanford. And I was this kid — it didn't take up 50% of my time because I — but if you go to the classes, it takes what you said. Back to my experience there — for the couple years I was there, it was great because of all the other things, the people I met. You know, Steve Jobs came down, was giving a talk, and one of my friends went and was working at NeXT. Bill Joy and Scott McNealy would come and talk, and you'd go spend time with them afterward or have lunch. All of those experiences of who you met and seeing the real world, plus building stuff with my friends that eventually became our company — that was what was great about the product to me. And sitting in these lecture classes were the opposite of that.

和家长的对话：从哈佛到替代路径

提问： One thing we've talked about is how to make the students love it. But of course, even more important constituent in terms of where kids go to school is their parents. So talk about how the conversations you're having with parents are evolving — whether it relates to early education or higher education — and some of the advice that you give them.

Joe： So I talked to tens of thousands of parents now in the K-12 range, and I've been shocked actually at the switch — which is: there's still some families who are like "I'm a kindergarten parent and I want to see the direct path right into the Ivy League." But an equal number — maybe even more — of parents who went to Stanford or Harvard who are like, "No, I know I don't want my kid on that path. How are you going to get them ready for a world that's not that?"

They absolutely want to see this alternative path. Especially even in kindergarten, they're looking forward 12 years from now and they're like, "What am I going to do? How are you preparing my kid for the world?" Their vision of the world is "yes, I went to the Ivy League, but that's not going to be for my kid. I don't think that's going to get him ready. And if you're telling me that, I don't want your K-12 school."

That's happening a lot now. They're looking for — I think there's recognition now versus maybe the last 30 or 40 years that the world is really changing. If you're an 11th grader or a 12th grader, the parents are sort of done — they're like "just get my kid into college," they're at the five-yard line, not throwing all the cards up in the air. But when you look younger, those parents are like "there's just no way that the current path is going to be the right one."

1910 年的历史先例

When I think of this — I would expect, and I don't know, when you get your demand, you're going to have massive demand from all the kids who are going to be like "okay, I have to go do this, it's so obvious, this is awesome." And then you will have to have a separate sales job with the parents to show them: "Look, while it wasn't the way you did it, this is the way."

There's a historical precedent for this that might be useful. In 1910, 90% of America had an eighth grade education. There was no high schools, basically. And over 30% of America were farmers. Everybody's on the farm. Eighth grade was enough — you're working in the fields.

Then in 1910, the Case tractor rolled up on the American farm. Literally you can go look at the ads — it literally looks like an Anthropic ad. "Does the work of 50 programmers." "Does the work of 50 farm hands." Literally everybody in America realized: 30% of the jobs are going away. "My kids and grandkids, we've been doing this for generations — it's gone. That path is gone. And we have to get our kids ready for this new future."

It was that same recognition I think that parents have today. The traditional path — those jobs — it's the kids coming in the summer where they're like "I'm going to get out of Stanford, MIT, I'm not going to have a job."

But what America did back then is: 130,000 towns voted to actually raise their taxes — and this is the key part — fund an education that they'd never experienced. They'd never seen a high school curriculum. They'd never been to high school. They had an eighth grade education, but they knew they had to do something different than their background to get their kids ready — to get them the good jobs. Back then, that school system became the industrial system we've had the last hundred years. It served us really well for a hundred years. But now it's time for the next change.

You're going to have to convince the families to be like those 1910 rural farmers who realized: "While I haven't experienced it and it's different than what I did, this is what my kid needs to thrive in the future."

常春藤 vs. 新机构：风险与采纳曲线

提问： And what would you say to the parent who's saying, "Hey, I'm sending my kid to an Ivy League school. I know it's not perfect, but this is a new institution. Why should I take a risk? Why would you consider taking a risk on the Academy?"

Joe： I've been living this actually at the K-12 level now for four years. The lucky part is you don't need everybody. There's going to be that set — when I talk to families, it's an adoption curve just like any other, and there's a set of families who absolutely realize the current system's just not there, or the people who sit there and say "I feel it but I just need to be moved over."

Both my daughters were told they're not going to get into college when they were in eighth grade — if they went to Alpha and they had to go to a traditional school, there was just no chance that would occur. So there is that dichotomy. But for parents, if you look sort of across the families who went to Alpha four years ago versus the ones who didn't — went to Alpha High versus not — there's a lot more families who are like, "I totally should have sent my kid to Alpha. I went the traditional path, I thought it was the safe path, and it totally wasn't. Look at how those Alpha kids are thriving. I thought those guys were crazy and risky, but now looking at the reality of what happened with my kid who didn't go to Alpha versus those — they regret it."

I believe that you have to get through the first year because you don't have any data. But one year in, people are going to see that the students are thriving. Once you see that, then that's the comparison.

Joe 自己的两年犹豫

I'll even go back to my own experience on this — I sort of am talking very positive and optimistic, but I didn't start Alpha 12 years ago. MacKenzie Price and Brian did. I had — I went to Catholic school, my kids were in Catholic school. I didn't like it, but parents want their kids educated the way they are. That's the legacy. That's the problem — that's what we have, you have to overcome.

So my kids are in Catholic school. And MacKenzie's like "well, come to my new school." And I — I dropped out of college. I started a startup in a garage. And I'm like, "Schools shouldn't be in a garage. This is so weird. You have a janky weird school, MacKenzie." And I was totally right. It took two years for me. I was the slow — it took me two years to move over. That was 10 years ago. Obviously turned out great for our family. But my kids still yell at me for being slow those two years — "You should have started earlier, Dad."

招生现实：先锋者先到

That concept of finding those families — we travel all around the country, we've opened 50 campuses. You get a thousand people in the info session and you're like, "Who wants to be the first 10? Who wants to be the first 25 or 50?" A year ago when we were opening the 12 campuses — literally thousand-plus people in info sessions, and we couldn't get 25. We would get 10. We opened New York City with 10 or 12. Now the campus is full — the 150 total people. They had to go see the first ones that it works, and then it's there.

Your first class is always those people who are like "I know it's bad, I want to jump in." What you will see immediately — and sort of what we're seeing on the demand — is people just need someone to go first. Once you get that first and it works, the demand just skyrockets.

磁铁式营销与社群

提问： The benefits of being first are high. What I see in colleagues and friends who are sending their kids to Alpha, or even friends who've done something like Thiel Fellowship (which is also small application numbers in the beginning) — those people who are applying early have the courage of their conviction. It's positive self-selection. So you're around some of the most brilliant people, some of the most courageous people — both on the kid level and the parent level — and it's really just a phenomenal experience.

Joe： Back to advice on that — you absolutely want the families who are all-in on both sides, because there will be hiccups. There's hiccups that happen when you're starting. Someone who's super skeptical and on the late adopter side — they're just going to not, it's going to destroy them. They won't be able to handle it. The people who are over here who really want the product —

We talk about magnet marketing — you want to attract the right people and repel the wrong. People who want to be laggards — "I don't like AI or screen time" — that's a set of people in the info session. I'm like, "You shouldn't. If you can't balance what this offering is —"

Being clear on your product definition is a thing that I don't think most schools do. But if you're clear on your product definition — this is what we are, this is what we're not — it helps you find that right group. When the right groups together, part of it's community — you're building the community. All the kids who are there and the parent community does matter when you're doing a startup. Our founding families are one of our biggest assets now at our school. I believe it'll be the same for what you're doing.

提问： That makes me think of two things. One is I think we're going to be pretty strict about who gets in and less about class size. You've told me this. I think that's a very important lesson. The second lesson is that this is the type of thing where you don't want most people to want it — you want the people who really want it to do it.

Actually I'll add one more thing: we did make it one year and it's no tuition the first year. So it is also a little bit less risky than, you know, you're missing eighth grade. You don't want to miss eighth grade, but if you take one year detour from college, you can always go back. It's really no different. So I do think that's one of the things we have the benefit. It's interesting to see the nuances of a college experience versus a high school experience, because the stakes are different in different directions.

Joe： I believe that is going to be one of your assets with the parents on the one year — there's no downside to trying it. You can always defer at some other college or reapply. So you're not shutting down other options.

To the parents stuff, what you'll see is — when your kid loves it, back to schools being 90% motivation — if I was talking to the parents here and their kid really wants to go, I'd just give you advice: just let them go do it. Let's even just say it doesn't work out for them — it'll be the best learning experience of their life, and they'll be ready to do the other. Fighting that the other way — it just isn't as risky in this.

提问： No, it's much riskier. And we can go to a lot of stories I have of those at our high school level.

代理感与叛逆：围绕学生设计

提问： I think if you think about the three of us — there are actually many people we all know who are like us who didn't love school at some point. And what is the thing that we dislike the most? For me, it was that I was being forced to do things that I was not bought into. My agency had started to grow — 13, 14, 15 years old — and I started to see the emperor had no clothes. I started to believe, "Wait a second, my teacher doesn't actually know how to teach math. This might not be the best way to teach math. Oh shoot — so I got to take this stupid test now, you know?"

One of the pedagogical philosophies of the Academy and of Alpha is that you design it around the student to increase the chance — or to decrease the chance — that you get that rebellion. Instead, if you have buy-in, they're much more likely to thrive and do things.

Joe 的个人故事

Joe： I'll tell the personal story on this. During my K-12, I was always in trouble. I was skipping school all the time. I did the minimum to get into Stanford, and then I dropped out. When I dropped out, my dad had a famous quote that was like on Forbes or whatever — "my son's a [whatever]" — and he was not happy.

But then the part that didn't get in the article was: a couple years later — so I dropped out, started my company, it was awesome, and all of a sudden I'm working 100 hours a week and we're sleeping under the desks and it's crazy. Two years later, he's like, "I got to change my mind. This was the greatest thing ever that you dropped out. I have to admit, I was really worried that you were going to be a lazy little [whatever] — because that was your academic career. As a dad, I was just terrified that I had done poorly. Now I see that now that you're doing what you love, you're fully engaged — I should have gotten this done earlier."

That's the same thing when you have a student. When we talk about building a school they love more than vacation — you're engaging them around stuff they love. When you do that, that's what causes all the parents who say "my kid changed in a month." It's because we have them doing hard things that they want to do. All of a sudden it does change, and it's that quick.

Having a school where your kid wants to go to it because they're going to be doing hard things is a great thing. That's one of the reasons why I think this is going to be a home run — because you're going to get all these kids who are like "I know it's hard, I want to go do this. I can coast through normal school and I'm not going to pick that path. Instead I'm going to pick this, and this is going to be harder than all the other schools." Kids love it.

World School 与非洲一年

We have in our high school — we have a World School where they're spending a year in Africa, a year of service. They have to sign a contract that's like "I realize this will be the hardest year of my life." And they all sign it, and they all love it, and they're super excited to go.

提问： By the way, one note — I've spent a fair amount of time in Africa. I would send some kids to India or Sri Lanka. It's going to be much harder.

Joe： Okay, that'll be on the list. It's called World School, so they're going to be going. But I love that. Africa — it's such an amazing thing that you're doing.

提问： One of our wishes that we've talked about — we have a stipend, we don't talk about this too much, but we've already allocated $5,000 per student for a travel budget. My personal goal — now they get to decide how they use the travel budget, I'm not going to force anything on anyone — but my personal goal is that a lot of them go solo to countries with less than $20,000 GDP per capita. It's a great idea. This perspective.

Joe： No, I totally — I think that is super valuable.

提问： You learn so much about yourself and about life, and I think that it also will provide perspective that will help in business.

懒惰的孩子与被结构化的 A+ 学生

提问： It's so funny going back to this idea of kids — the story you mentioned your parents reminds me — kids like us when we were younger and others who are quote-unquote "lazy" in school, that they don't get 4.0 because they're just not bought in. But when they find the thing, they're willing to put in 100-hour weeks. There's so many people like that.

And conversely, there are people on the other side who will get straight A's, but once you take away the structure, they haven't really cultivated this inner desire or this ability to find what they love. When they get to the working world, in which the skills are just remarkably different, they can't operate in the same way.

It just strikes me that we're going to just create the space — and you're creating the space from a much earlier age — where people really get to get in touch with what they care about, be much more self-driven. It's just really powerful.

Joe： The correct — those are what are all the life skills. That's when you talk about a holistic person. It's not just what their GPA was. You can max score on just your grades, but that is not something that means you do well in the real world. Parents actually realize that — you need to be more well-rounded, they just don't have a path of doing it.

I believe that one of the things back to reinventing university — you're going to show them: here's all these things that should be part of the university curriculum, not a club after that the kids optionally do. I think that's going to be a great thing. Employers obviously will realize the same thing.

提问： The employers seem very bought in, honestly.

Joe： Yeah, that part's — there's no problem on that pitch. The number of employers who are like "these kids coming out don't have the skills and capability to do it" — well, if you had just taken me before I actually started my company and looked at me and said "are you ready for a job?" — I wasn't. But then two years later, after I was doing this outside project — I'm probably a pretty good employee to hire.

提问： It's funny actually — the issue that most employers have is not one of a skills gap in the "do you know how to code or build products or design?" What we hear more than anything is: people skills, maturity, and systems thinking. Those are the actual skills. The only way to learn those things is to actually just interact with lots of people, have to build complex systems, forcing yourself to deal with the reality of rejection and the maturation process of not having things structured for you but having to structure them yourself.

Joe： Back to AI commoditizing intelligence — when you can ask it "what are the human traits you want?" — it is leadership, being able to work in a team, agency, ownership, receiving feedback. All of those skills — that you can get from doing projects, but you don't get from sitting in class.

AI 时代的学习：认知装载 + 建造者模式

提问： There's a lot of questions around what is AI doing to coding, what is AI doing to math, what's it going to do to physics. If you were 18 years old today with your interests — if you had the flexibility at something like HAA to design your own education — how would you think about what you would be motivated to learn based on where you see the world going and your own interests?

Joe： I have this framework — there's sort of cognitive onload. AI allows you to fill your head with knowledge 10 times faster. These kids can become domain experts in their field that they want to faster than ever. I have kids in my high school who are rebuilding the TimeBack software stack that I wrote. They were becoming experts in learning science, which wasn't able to be done before in high school.

The cognitive onload part — because it's 10 times faster, you do it and it doesn't take that long. I can get the equivalent of a master's while I'm in a year.

But then the second part is: AI gives you a chance to be a builder. It gives you superpowers to build like no one else. That's the kids who are at your university — they're going to realize, "I want to build something, and I'm going to learn faster than I ever have whatever prereqs" — just like the interns this summer were doing. They were doing research, learning all this stuff, but they were doing it to build.

不是末日论者，是建造者

If you talk to our high school kids at Alpha High, they're definitely not doomers about AI in the future. They're like, "You adults are cooked — like, we're coming for you and we have superpowers." These kids are building apps. I'm like, "Two years from now, I absolutely expect most learning software is going to be written by students. Most students are going to learn from learning software written by their peers" — because it'll embed all the learning science concepts, and they will make it more engaging.

Shout out to Austin who built our AP curriculum — he built this crazy great curriculum and all our kids who took it got a 5 on their APs. He built a world history one, but he did it because he built this GeoGuessr game where he took all these world history events and did an S-tier ranking with a snarky AI. All these things — I'm throwing those words out because I don't actually know what they really mean — but every kid was engaged and loved it and did it. And I'm like, "Okay, me and the old adult team are never going to be able to build that ever."

That's what these kids are going to be able to do — they're gonna go build the future. AI gives them the capability to build the future and start freshman year of college.

关于「选什么专业」的误问

提问： Just to take a stab at your question — I think the question of "what field should I study so that I can be sure that I'm resilient to the future?" is not the right question. The question is: what field am I interested in?

I have enough faith that if you're AI-native in any field, it does not matter. A lot of people are concerned about coding or math — look, there's going to be a whole new type of coding and math that happens with the AI-native mathematicians. It's just that the old school ones who are still doing chalkboard and pen and pencil and paper are cooked. But the new students who love math — they're going to do just fine. In fact, they're going to go and do things none of us ever thought possible. There's going to be a whole new era of mathematicians who are going to be successful.

That's actually something that we are trying to screen for a lot at HAA — we really don't want someone who's like, "I want to make sure I'm resilient to the future." It's a very defensive way of approaching the world, and we want you to be on offense. We want you to say: "What are you interested in? I'm going to go figure it out."

As an example, I work in education. Education has not been the most lucrative founder field of the last 15, 20 years. It just so happens that I built one of like four wins in education in the last 15 years. It is a terrible market. It's been historically a terrible market. We're going to change that. We absolutely are changing it.

But I'm still super happy and proud that this is what I work on. I still get to feel like I know how to operate at the level and quality of someone who's doing something in AI or doing something in SaaS or whatever. I've chosen a field, I love it. I have a very healthy and fulfilling life. I'm not a billionaire, but I'm doing well. Anyone who gets to that level in any field — if they're in the top 1% of their field, it's going to be fine.

Joe： I love what you said — what we have to do, back to raising kids and building high-character kids for the future. Your point of: they're not — this isn't passive. "What is going to happen to the world and it's going to be imposed on me" — no, we're going to go make the world. These kids are the ones who are creating it. You can have the passive view of what happens — "oops, it's going to be bad" — or you can be the other, which is: "No, I'm building it."

We need to create a generation of builders who look at this optimistically. All our kids read The Rational Optimist, and they sit there and say, "Yes, I'm in control of it. We need to build our future." We need to raise the next generation and have our kids coming out of university — I want this next generation coming out of university to be the ones who are optimistically capable with AI and saying, "We're going to build an awesome future." That's what our job as educators is: to go build that world and make sure that our universities do that.

Founder School：高中创业学校

提问： Joe, this was an amazing conversation. The last thing that I'm thinking about: you're actually building an entrepreneurial school for high school students called Founder School. Can you tell us a little bit about why you built it, how it works, and why you think it's a good model for us to be inspired by?

Joe： Sure. Back to skills — one of our life skills stacks is entrepreneurship and financial literacy. We have a very strong point of view: when we look at the jobs of the future, big Fortune 500 companies are going to be smaller because of AI. But I believe it's going to lead to an explosion of entrepreneurship. AI gives entrepreneurs this great opportunity, and it's something we just don't teach.

We teach it. We have a stack starting in kindergarten. We literally teach every kindergartener how to earn and save, spend, invest, donate — get them that foundational going. We have a currency called alphas to start teaching them this. Entrepreneurship is not a bolt of lightning that just happens. It's a set of skills that you can teach people.

百万美元保证

By the time you get to high school, we have a high school Founders — this is for kids who want to spend their high school building businesses. The part that's crazy that parents don't believe is: we guarantee that you'll start a business that will earn a million dollars of profit while you're in high school, or we give you all your tuition back.

We absolutely believe that these are skills that can be taught repeatably and reliably — where I actually can build a business on that. It opened in August. We have Alpha High kids — people who've been able to build businesses over the last four years. So we have data points, but this is now a specialized school for that.

It's scaffolded. They come in and they have to earn $100, and there's a set of skills they have to learn. Then $1,000, then $10,000, $100,000, and a million dollar. We're only a couple months in, and kids are speed-running it. We're like "okay, they're going to earn a million dollars in the first year." I'm out of curriculum and they're freshmen. The kids are like, "Okay, well, I'm going to then obviously just do a bigger one after that."

关系与导师网络

A lot of it is just — there's a set of skills around it. But there's also the relationships and networking. That's one of the things I believe that you guys are bringing at the university level that we're trying to bring even down in the high school level — networking, relationship building.

A lot of it for kids — I always thought a lot of the magic of Stanford was: you had all these luminaries come, and then you'd meet them and you'd be like, "Oh, this is like a normal human." I mean, they're obviously really impressive, but they're just like a normal human. And it makes it accessible to you to be able to say, "Well, I can do that too." Especially when you're young and dumb and super arrogant, you're like, "Oh, I could do that."

That is part of it. We're doing the same thing here at the high school level where they're able to build up relationships. Actually, one of the stories: one of our 14-year-olds cold-called Jensen — literally. He was having a cold call thing and he literally called him. Jensen returned the call, realized it's a kid, gave him 90 seconds for his pitch, and then at the end gave him really good feedback — which basically, if I had to summarize, was: "All these qualification questions you're asking me — you could have done research or asked other people in my organization about it. You just used your bullet with me, and you should have done your prep work. It would have been much better instead of wasting it by calling me. So kudos for aggressiveness, but you get an F on call prep."

Okay, that kid — he's tweeting about it. Everybody in the school — it's like the best learning lesson in that kid's life.

Successful adults are willing to invest in the next generation. I believe that kind of networking and relationship building that they're going to get at HAA is just going to be awesome — and more valuable than what normal universities, traditional universities, don't do.

收尾：抬高雄心

提问： It's something that Erik is a true expert at, if I may say so myself, and you and have helped us galvanize this really large network of amazing people from all disciplines to come and help the HAA students succeed. I think it's really cool what you're doing with Founder School as well, because I actually know a bunch of people who are speakers or coming in and investing time at Founder School — and it's just completely invaluable for a student who's in high school or college level to have the opportunity to get access to that.

Joe： For me that's always the most valuable thing, and you guys are putting it intentionally at the center of what you guys do. That's really important. Max Levchin was in this chair a few weeks ago and he was talking about how he was inspired to think so big and so ambitiously because he worked with Elon, he worked with Reid Hoffman, with David Sacks — and he saw that they just like him went through the ups and downs. Hopefully us having Jensen and Sam Altman and Satya and all these legends come and share war stories with the kids, share their ups and downs, will also elevate their ambitions as well.

Joe： It does. And that point he also made — your ambition is set when, for kids, somebody has to — I think it was Tyler Cowen who's like, "The number one thing a teacher can do is raise a student's ambition for themselves." We try to live that at Alpha. I believe that's very much when you sit here — it's intentionally in your guys' design: the people you're getting, the culture you're building, that you're going to be raising their ambition for what they can do in life. That's just so important.

提问： Well, lastly, I'll say from my end — we've been talking about some major differences between K-12 and college, but one similarity is that, you mentioned 1910, in the last 100 years there hasn't been a ton of disruption in the model. There hasn't been a ton of major new entrants, certainly on the college side. What you guys are doing in K-12 and college — and we're all doing — is elevating the ambition of what's possible in education. You guys are pioneers of the work that you've been doing the last few years and decade-plus. So I'm inspired to be part of your respective journeys.

Yeah, thank you.

Joe： Kids are awesome. They can do way more than all of us expect. I believe that coming out of yours, you're going to just raise that to the next level.

提问： Proud to do this with y'all.

Thank you, Tandon. Thank you.
